highlight each department. Perhaps 
most importantly, merchandise in the 
new prototype has been completely re- 
positioned and grouped into distinct

pharmacy and drug store area, which

customer interactions. The store 
averages 150 to 200 scripts on

NACDS changes show dates 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — Citing demand for exhibit space, 
NACDS has booked the Infomart center, across from Loew’s 
Anatole in Dallas, to hold an estimated 450 booths at next sum- 
mer’s Marketplace conference. All sessions will be at the Ana- 
tole. The show dates were also changed to June 10-13. 

NACDS also changed the dates of this winter’s Distribution 
Conference, to Feb. 25-27 at Innisbrook Resort in Tarpon 
Springs, Fla. 

In an unrelated matter, —- Ron Ziegler has agreed to 
serve on an, American Red Cross relief committee, which is com- 
mitted to raise $42 million in corporate donations to help people 
recover from the effects of Hurricane Hugo. 


High court to eye Lucky/Alpha Beta deal 


SALT LAKE CITY — The U. S. Supreme Court has agreed 
to review the antitrust lawsuit i against American 
Stores by the State of California, delaying once more the 
planned merger of its Lucky and Alpha Beta grocery chains. 

John Van de Kamp, the state’s attorney general, is looking to 
block the merger on antitrust grounds, contending that the 
combination of the two chains will lead to higher consumer 
prices. American Stores, however, has maintained the merger 
will allow for a consolidation of operations and therefore lead to 
lower prices. 

In August, a U.S. Ninth Circuit Court ruled the merger could 
commence, and returned the decision on the suit to a lower 
court. Van de Kamp, however, appealed this move to the Su- 
preme Court and Justice Sandra Day O’Connor agreed to con- 
tinue the merger block until the full court had a chance in Octo- 
ber to discuss possible review of the case. 

The Supreme Court’s decision on the merger is not 2, Shoat 
for several months. American Stores, which purchased Lucky 
fer $2.5 billion in June 1988, has said the merger delay is costing 
the company about $1.5 million a week. 


American Greetings buys hair care line 


| ©LEVELAND — American Greetings announced its pur-

card firm, in this diversification move, expects to transfer its 
marketing strengths at mass retail to Wilhold.

Floor plan of new Pay Less NW prototype. 


Pay Less prototype is paying off 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. — 
Pay Less NW is posting dou- 
ble-digit sales gains in stores it 
vernecehad this year to match 
the company’s prototype. 


The 282-store chain has so 
far converted four locations to 
the new format, and opened 20 
new stores in this same vision. 
The company first unveiled its 
upscale look at Cameron Park, 

alif., in January. 


Tim McAlear, chief opera- 
tions officer, said sales im- 
provements are attributable 
to the format’s emphasis on 
pharmacy, OTC, cosmetics, 
toiletries, greeting cards, sta- 
tionery and consumer elec- 
tronics. Indeed, McAlear said 
it is these areas at the remod- 
eled stores where volume is 
running well above the compa- 
ny average. “One of the objec- 
tives of the layout was to em- 
phasize those core 


departments.” 

‘ew changes have been 
made since the initial store 
was opened, McAlear said. 
Some differences exist in its 
three sizes of 23,000, 27,000 
and 31,000 square feet. Only 
the largest stores carry appar- 
el; smaller stores, primarily in 
Southern California, carry a 
reduced selection of automo- 
tive, hardware and sporting 

oods. With these reductions, 

cAlear said, the smaller 
stores can still maintain the 
same square footage in the 
core departments. 

Pay Less expects to open 13 
more stores under the new 
format by the close of its fiscal 
year at the end of January. All 
remodels for the year have 
been completed. In 1990, 
McAlear said the chain is look- 
ing to open 41 new stores and 
plans to complete eight re- 


models.

Dave comes full circle with Peoples 


The year: 1952. The place: Washington, D.C. Nation- 
al feelings about America’s involvement in another less- 
than-popular war, in Korea, were running high. The 
threat of communism and war with Russia had uncov- 
ered a deep well of fear and paranoia in the traditionally 

brash and carefree American spirit. Still, 


IN THE MARKET 


the country’s mood was largely buoyant. 
A decade of unparalleled growth and 
prosperity had just begun to unfold: the 
American decade. 

In June of that year, a friendly and am- 
bitious teenager by the name of Dave Ei- 
senberg was about to start anew summer 
job as a soda jerk at one of Peoples’ 200- 
plus drug stores. The Washington-based 
Peoples, which then resembled a collec- 
tion of small, urban independents rather 
than today’s modern, suburban-oriented 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


chain, was offering 65 cents an hour to 
young entry-level workers. 


Dave began his new job on June 13, 
1952, one day shy of his 16th birthday. Last week, 37 
years after he first began to dish out sundaes, malts and 
sandwiches to a hungry drug store clientele, Eisenberg 
was named president of Peoples Drug Stores. 

What a remarkable story — especially in this age of 
the disposable executive and management musical 
chairs. What a reward for talent, loyalty and, of course, 
extreme flexibility, in the face of the momentous chang- 
es that have taken place at Peoples over the past three 
decades. To Dave, in a congratulatory phone conversa- 
tion this week, I remarked on the uniqueness of his situ- 
ation. Had he ever considered leaving Peoples? 

“Every time I got itchy feet, something always hap- 
pened, a promotion or something else,” he told me in the 
friendly and ebullient fashion that has made him one of 
the industry’s most popular executives. Even when 


things got bad, he said, something always“kindled” his 
belief that the situation would turn around. 

The past five years are an example. Based on many 
factors, including — perhaps most importantly — a 
failure to keep pace with ever-more potent competition 
in widely spread markets, Peoples hit a low ebb. Under 
Eisenberg as chief operations officer, and with the 
strong support of Imasco and David Bloom, the chain 
began a vast restructuring that involved people, mar- 
kets and basic operations. The result: A slimmed-down 
Peoples has begun to turn in sparkling results and is 
looking confidently to the future. 

Eisenberg told me that the turnaround has ignited a 
resolve to begin growing, after a vigorous retrench- 
ment. Peoples will probably never expand again as it did 
in the chain’s “go-go” years of the sixties and seventies, 
Eisenberg said, but it will be there aggressively picking 
up independents and small chains in contiguous markets 
and thereby strengthening its position as one of the pre- 
mier operators in the business. The focus, he said, will 
be on discovering what customers want and fulfilling 
those expectations. 

Research and technology has become increasingly im- 
portant in Peoples’ long-term strategy. Eisenberg says 
Imasco is “betting the book” on technology, which in- 
cludes intensive consumer research and increasing in- 
vestment in new performance measurement. tools. 
Whatever it takes, he says, “Peoples will be there.” 

Yes, it’s a far cry from the days when a young Dave 
Eisenberg wrapped customer packages in brown pa- 
per and string while chatting about the weather or the 
latest doings of the Senators — the baseball team not 
the Congressional kind. Yet, in Peoples’ renewed fo- 
cus on its relationship with customers, the chain 
seems to have come full circle — back to an earlier, 
friendlier time when the world wasn’t in such a hurry. 
What a great way to regress. 


‘Anticompetition bill’ bad for businesses 


Imagine this: The wholesaler you’ve been dealing 
with for years suddenly cuts back on deliveries. You 
check your records and discover that the service 
you've been receiving from this firm has been slipping 
for the past several years. Worse yet, you find that 
competing distributors have been regu- 


larly beating your wholesaler’s prices! 
You talk things over with the whole- 
saler, but get no assurance that these 
problems will be corrected. What do you 
do? 
That’s easy — switch to a different 
wholesaler! Right? 


distributors have been pressing Congress for immuni- 
ty to demand the same exclusive territorial rights that 
soft drink bottlers now enjoy. That “beer bill” — the 
Malt Beverage Interbrand Competition Act — has 
now given way to DeConcini’s even broader proposal, 
which would affect everything from H&BAs to candy 
to pharmaceuticals. 

Let’s take the example that we started with — the 
independent druggist with an over-priced, unrespon- 
sive wholesaler. Dropping that firm may be difficult if 
it is the only wholesaler in one’s area authorized to sell 
the number one line of hair coloring products, or the

Store managers, operations 


manager? As this year’s 

Store News survey on 

the role of store managers 

shows, the answer depends on 
whom you ask. 

Compiled in late August, the 
second annual study points up 
clearly that score managers of- 
ten have a different perception 
of what their job limits are than 
do their ultimate bosses at 
headquarters, the operations 
executives who set policy. For 
the second year, the study re- 
veals a lot of gray area between 
the company policy set by head- 
quarters and the way that poli- 
cy is interpreted by store-leve! 
people on the front lines. 

The survey points up some 
startling divergence of opinion, 
often among store-level and 
headquarters people in the 
same company. For instance, 
nearly one-thz of the store 
managers in tne survey say 
they get “very involved” in de- 
Hie He overall planograms 
for the store, and 53.8 percent 
of them say they are very in- 
volved with checkstand mer- 
chandising. 

Compare their responses 
with those of the operations ex- 
ecutives at headquarters who 
answered the same questions 
about their store managers. 
Not one of them agreed that 
their store people get much in- 
volved with planograming, and 
only one in four said the store 
managers had input into mer- 
chandising checkstands. Some- 
one, it seems, is misinformed. 

A majority of store manag- 
ers — 59.3 percent of those 
polled — also feel they can 
change product facings and po- 
sitions at their own discretion, 
and only 25.9 percent of them 
say they must check with head- 
quarters first. This may come 
as news to some operations ex- 
ecs, half of whom said the man- 
agers must check with them 
first before shifting product 
around.

This exclusive Drug Store News study on 
the role of store managers was undertaken to 
explore their overall autonomy and decision 
making authority at many of the nation’s larg- 


the study. 


Telephone interviews were conducted in 
late summer. Thirty-seven interviews made 
up the study. These included 12 vps or direc- 
tors of operations, and, for each headquarters 
respondent, at least two different store man- 
agers of the same drug chain, adding 25 store 
manager interviews.

Bergen’s fiscal ’89 sees 
sales, earnings growth 


ORANGE, Calif. — Bergen 
Brunswig Drug Corp.’s results 
for fiscal year 1989, ended Aug. 
31, saw net earnings of $47.6 mil- 
lion, a 28-percent increase from 
last year, on $3.92 billion in reve- 
nues, a 13-percent increase. 
Fourth-quarter earnings were 
$10.7 million, a 13-percent in- 
crease from last year’s period, 
with $997.8 million in revenues 
posted, an 1l-percent increase 
over the wholesaler’s figure for 
last year. 


Cardinal’s 2nd-atr. net, 
sales post healthy gains 


DUBLIN, Ohio — Cardinal 
Distribution’s net earnings rose 
53 percent and net sales 28 per- 
cent in the second quarter ended 
Sept. 30. Net earnings were $2.8 
million on net sales of $210.2 mil- 
lion. For the year-earlier quarter, 
net earnings were $1.8 million on 
net sales of $164.4 million. Cardi- 
nal closed its smallest distribution 
center, in Albany, N.Y., in Sep- 
tember, and transferred its vol- 
ume to a new DC near Hartford, 
Conn. 


Durr-Fillauer sees gains 
in net, revenue for 3rd qtr. 


MONTGOMERY, Ala. — 
Durr-Fillauer Medical, Inc., the 
wholesaler based here, reported 
net income for the third quarter 
ended Sept. 30 of $3.8 million, up 
from $3.4 million reported last 
year. The gain came on revenues 
of $172.0 million, up from $148.3 
million reported last year.

Thrift experiments 
with self-serve food 
in high-traffic store 


MONROEVILLE, Pa.— Thrift Drug is experiment- 
ing with a self-service snack shop in one drug store here. 
The 600-square foot shop includes a self-serve frozen 
yogurt machine, a self-serve beverage bar with hot. 
dogs, coffee maker, and post-mix soft drinks, and a con- 
vection oven with a showcase for breakfast products, 


pizza and chicken. 


“It goes back to the fountain days,” said Rich John- 
son, Thrift vp-facilities, planning and construction, who 
noted that Thrift will likely introduce some of the shop’s 
features into at least one other store soon, following 
three months of observing this initial setup. 

Like many drug chains, Thrift has added convenience 
food sections in selected stores. The self-service angle 
is a new twist for Thrift. Johnson said the department 
has been successful, generating mostly incremental 
sales in the high-traffic store. Besides being a 24-hour 
store, it is well located along major commuter roads in 
this densely populated Pittsburgh suburb.

NEWo IN BIRIEF 


Arbor opening five units in November 


TROY, Mich. —- Arbor Drugs will boost store count to 92 
units with the opening of five new drug stores this month in 
Southeastern Michigan. The openings include the first of sever- 
al units Arbor plans to put into the Saginaw-Bay City-Midland 
Tri-City market north of Detroit. 

The other four stores are in Ann Arbor, Chelsea and Mt. 
Clemens. 

By the mid-1990s, the chain plans io have 150 stores in Michi- 
gan. 

“Our experience, as well as our research, confirms that the 
metropolitan Detroit market can support a substantially great- 
er number of Arbor drug stores,” noted Arbor chairman and 
chief executive Eugene Applebaum. “In the most densely popu- 
lated areas, we are able to operate multiple, high-volume stores 
which are located just five minutes apart. 

“Convenience-oriented shoppers,” he added, “today are more 
apt to measure the time it takes to drive to a store than they are 
the actual mileage to it.” 


Bergen’s Good Neighbor ads get raves 


ORANGE, Calif. — The launch of national cable television 
advertising spots to support its Good Neighbor Pharmacy pro- 
gram is generating positive feedback from stores and customers 
for wholesaler Bergen Brunswig. 

Tom Allison, vp-merchandising, said that about 150 new 
stores have joined the voluntary, since the campaign, which be- 
gan Sept. 1, was announced in July: “There has been a definite 
upsurge in the program during the last three months.” 

The commercials are running on a two-week-on and two- 
week-off schedule through the end of the year on such shows as 
“Health Week” and “Nutritional News.” Allison said Bergen 
will probably continue the campaign in 1990. 


Douglas names Robinson, Haronian vps 


PROVIDENCE, R.I. — Douglas Drug has named Michael D. 
Robinson its new vice president of finance, replacing Rudolph 
Charpentier, who had been with the 16-store chain since 1980. 

In addition, Kathleen Haronian has been promoted to vp-cor- 
porate development. The “eye wid of Douglas president John 
Haronian, she was formerly advertising coordinator. 

Robinson was previously senior vp-cfo of American Touris- 
ter, the luggage company based in Warren, R.I. 


Jacob Schein dead at 49 


POUND RIDGE, N.Y. — Jacob M. Schein, 
chairman and ceo of Henry Schein Inc., Schein 
Pharmaceutical and their subsidiaries, died at 
home of cancer Nov. 4 at age 49. 

The Schein Group of Companies, which he 
headed, is a privately held organization with 
two major components: Henry Schein Inc. and 
its subsidiary, Zahn Dental Co., and Schein 
Pharmaceutical and its subsidiaries, Danbury 
Pharmacal and Steris Laboratories. 

Schein was a founding member of the board of directors of the 
Orphan Drug Foundation and was active in the American Den- 
tal Trade Association, the Dental Manufacturers’ Association 
and the Generic Pharmaceutical Industry Association. He also 
was a trustee of Alfred University, of which he was a graduate.

LONGUEIL, Québec — The Jean Coutu 
Group (PJC) has reached the final stages of its 
takeover of much of the Cloutier drug store 
group from Metro Richelieu, with eight former 
Cloutier units already under the Coutu banner 
and four others closed. 

Coutu agreed late last summer to purchase 15 
of 22 Cloutier drug stores from Metro, including 


all the Cloutier units in the metro Montreal mar- > 


ket. The takeover eliminated another chain drug 
competitor from Montreal — Shoppers Drug 
Mart had pulled out earlier in the decade — and 
boosted Coutu’s dominance in the metro market, 
especially in Montreal’s northern suburbs. 

All 15 Cloutier stores were franchise opera- 
tions, and those that remain open have been

convert those two stores in the next month or 
so,” he said. “Eight of the 10 full-line drug

verted to the Jean Coutu logo.” 

A clinic pharmacy was also among the 15 
Cloutiers purchased from Metro.

Christmas to completely overhaul the former 
Cloutier stores. “Some of the product mix was 
quite different from ours, and we have to read- 
just,” said Coutu.

DRUG STORE NEWS, November 20, 1989 


OPINION | 


Lean & mean team drives Reliable 


At Reliable Drug’s dinner for vendors last month in 
Indianapolis, Roger Grass referred in a light moment to 
his crew of “100-hour executives.” He meant the amount 
of time his “lean and mean” management team puts in 
every week. At 8 o’clock the next morning at headquar- 

ters, it became obvious that Reliable’s 


new chief executive hadn’t been exagger- 
ating — at least not by much. Business 
had been going full blast for at least an 
hour. The impression: someone had been 
feeding these people rocket fuel. 

Since last March when Roger Grass 
learned that his former company, Rite 
Aid, had passed on the chance to buy Peo- 
ples’ Midwest operation, Grass’ quest to 
acquire and recast the 115-store India- 
napolis-based former Haag chain has 


IN THE MARKET _ been going on at, well, Indy 500 speed. 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


At the dinner Roger spoke almost 


nostalgically about the seemingly end- 
less car trips that he and Chuck 
Conaway, now executive vp, made from Harrisburg 
to New York to arrange financing for the deal. Roger, 
33, and Chuck, 29, ate a lot of late-night pizza and Haa- 
gen-Dazs to sustain their energy levels during the 
long months of uncertainty and stress. 

Eventually they succeeded in lining up the needed 
support: $15 million in equity financing from Acadia 
Partners (the same Robert Bass-led group that has 
now made an offer for Revco) and $50.7 million in loans 
from the Bank of America. 

Since the acquisition early this summer, the new 
venture has been moving at a blurring pace. Debt is 
rapidly disappearing. At the dinner, Grass announced 
that almost $18 million in bank debt had already been 
repaid. By February the debt will be whittled down to 
less than $15 million, he promised. 

While the stores still carry the Peoples logo and some 
of the same merchandise (the $60 million sale price in- 
cluded some $58 million in inventory), a lot of changes 
have been quietly taking place that will eventually re- 
sult ina complete makeover at the chain. Here are some: 

e A new everyday low-pricing policy has an added 
wrinkle: a “bonus buy” program that uses deal buying to 
create deep discount-like super specials. Prices on hun- 


Roger Grass (center) and Chuck Conaway greet vendor. 


dreds of prescription items have been reduced. 

@ Every department in the store is being replano- 
grammed. Thousands of items are being cut as Relli- 
able pares down its selection to 12,000 SKUs, heavily 
weighted to core drug categories. Inventory will be 
reduced to about half of the total under Peoples, as the 
chain aims to rev up its turns. 

e@ New automated systems are being introduced. In 
pharmacy, where a great deal of emphasis is being 
placed, Reliable introduced the Condor Rx computer 
system chainwide. Through PCS, on-line third-party 
adjudication has been added. Reliable is pursuing third- 
party aggressively, so management is seeking to handle 
that low-calorie profit business as efficiently as possible. 

@ Reliable’s stores are in good shape, the result of a 
heavy investment by Peoples. Leases average nine 
years (with options to 14). Many stores will be down- 
sized to conform to a smaller Reliable prototype. 

e A partly automated, 250,000-square-foot distribu- 
tion center is capable of servicing twice Reliable’s cur- 
rent store base without even adding a second shift. 

Reliable Drug will emerge fully remade sometime af- 
ter the new year breaks. It will be doing business in 
some of the most competitive markets in the country. 
The guess here is that the youthful energy that has car- 
ried Grass and his team this far is going to create some 
real sparks in the Midwest. 


Entrepreneurship, the heart of American retailing, is 
being pummeled today by the greater muscle of take- 
overs and leveraged buyouts, fed by high-risk debt. 

The most graphic example of their impact on the chain 
drug industry was tendered recently by Alex Grass, 
chairman of Rite Aid, when he declared 


there is less competition for acquisitions 
and store sites today than at any time in 
the company’s history. 

Restructurings and LBOs, often done 
as takeover defenses, continue to hinder 
retailers from expanding aggressively; 
managers concentrate instead on run- 
ning their businesses to pay down debt. 

This is truly a bonanza for Rite Aid, 
which has grown 57 percent since early 
1987 by stepping in where others can’t, 


THE HUMAN SIDE _ but indeed marks a disturbing trend of 


AL HELLER 


low growth for the industry. Had Rite 


Aid, for example, been pressed by com- 
petitors to build new stores in order to 


_ grow, that would mean plus-growth for the trade. 


So, entrepreneurship barely has a pulse because ac- 
countants, rather than people with gusto for building 
businesses, are in prominent positions today. The days 
are over when the Skaggs family could develop the 
Skaggs and Sav-on chains without fear of being swal- 
lowed, or on a smaller scale, when Nat Lipsyc and Ger- 
ald Zlotnik could gTOW Medic Discount in Cleveland, de- 
spite an abhorrent business climate there in the 1970s. 

The Hafts played a large role in setting this tone. 
The mayhem they created when pursuing Supermar- 
kets General, Kroger and Safeway has altered the em- 


Fiscal plays killing off entrepreneurship? 


phasis of management at possible target companies — 
those with strong balance sheets or valuable real es- 
tate. Their takeover attempts prompted massive 
breakups of companies, derailed careers and shat- 
tered the growth dreams of many who labored de- 
cades to build their businesses. 

One ranking Supermarkets General executive told 
Drug Store News not long ago that the food-drug re- 
tailer would be far stronger today had it not been 
forced to engage in the battle for ownership. 

Managing with one eye over your shoulder can’t be 
as effective as making legitimate and sensible moves 
to grow one’s chain. 

Many innocent people get hurt, not the least stock- 
holders, whose investments are affected by defensive 
management practices or by steps that are publicly 
taken to “enhance shareholder value.” These steps 
typically enhance value just enough to keep share- 
holders quiet. 

For example, the managers of company X YZ decide 
to undertake an LBO, and offer stockholders-a $15 
premium per share. Outsider ABC tops that offer by 
$20. XYZ managers ultimately beat ABC’s offer by 
another $10. 

What happened here? XYZ managers sought to 
“enhance shareholder value” by $15 when they recog- 
nized it deserved to be enhanced by $45; they would 
pocket the difference. Then they pay by floating high- 
risk bonds. It’s beautiful, if they can get away with it. 

Today’s lack of entrepreneurship is a clot in the cir- 
culatory system of the drug trade, leaving it vulnera- 
ble to encroachment by other trade classes on its core 
health care businesses.

Retailers set sights 
on modern mature 


By Christine Bizzarro and Elizabeth Richardson 

ver the next decade, the 50-plus age group will grow by 
18.5 percent, to 76 million people. Drug retailers, anxious 
to carve a piece of this market for themselves, have already 
begun staking a claim by launching marketing programs aimed di- 
rectly at the emerging “modern mature.” 

The modern mature, unsaddled by a sedentary image, lead ac- 
tive, productive lives. As a group they are becoming increasingly 
concerned about health issues and the prolonging of youth — atti- 
tudes held over from their 1950s “baby boomer” generation..They 
account for 40 percent of total U.S. consumer demand, and with 
their $800 billion combined annual income, control 51 percent of the 
country’s discretionary income. 

According to Duff and Phelps, Inc., a Chicago-based investmen 
research and financial consulting firm, this group is important to the 
future of the retail drug industry.

~My way of thinking. . . 


“My Way of Thinking” is intended to give responsible members of the health care community a profes- 
sional forum to air their views on crucial issues confronting pharmacy today. Presentations should be no 
longer than 500 words and may be edited for space requirements. Interested participants should mail their 
presentations to Harold Cohen, Editor, Inside Pharmacy, 425 Park Avenue, New York, N.Y., 10022. Arti- 
cles will be chosen and published at the editor's discretion. 


In your Cohen’s Capsules of May 1, 
you said that we should “settle on a 
workable and pure AWP so that every 
facet of retail pharmacy can play on the 
same playing field.” Pharmacy is play- 
ing on the same playing field as insur- 
ance companies or third-party admin- 
istrators, but they never give us a 
chance at bat! 

The only reason that pharmacies re- 
sort to using generic products with 
high AWPs and low actual costs is be- 
cause the dispensing fees are never in- 
creased. So, when we use a high-AWP 
generic, we are now getting a chance 
to bat. But then when the union real- 
izes this, and they drop the reimburse- 
ment level, they take away our bat. 

Other ways, besides the above, of in- 
creasing margins on prescriptions is 
joining a buying group to get contract 
prices from manufacturers and a big- 
ger discount from wholesalers. But 
then, PCS or the union will take 10 per- 
cent off or want actual acquisition cost! 
Why should we give any 
tra profit? Did they earn it? 

en your back is to the wall, you 
improvise to survive. Without that ex- 
tra discount to pharmacies you cannot 
survive. . . chain or independent. 
Don’t third-party administrators, 
unions and insurance companies real- 
ize this? 

The insurance companies, unions 
and the like are playing games with re- 


y this ex- 


tail pharmacies, so why can’t we play 
games with them? They prevent the 
reimbursement levels from increas- 
ing, so we bill them for AWP plus a fee. 


That’s the agreement. It doesn’t mat- 
ter if the AW P is $10.00 and the actual 
cost is $2.00. 
Larry Hort 
Sheffield Pharmac 
Schaumburg, Il.

Retail pharmacy buying 

ups — during their past

to are pharmaceuticals 
and OTC items at the same

hey encourage generic drug

They also negotiate “cost-

wholesaler, typically conver-

Benji Wyatt, by “bidding” ge- 
neric and branded manufac- 
turers, PACE can save mem- 
bers an average of 36 percent 
on generics in the first year.

rcent, while chains were pay- 
ing cost plus 2 to 3 percent. 
PACE members today pay cost 
plus 2 percent, says Wyatt.

macist buying $200,000 worth

the savings might translate 
into $10,000 a year.

SupeRx network serves as safety check 


PHOENIX — With many 
retirees moving here, SupeRx 
is taking the lead when it 
comes to marketing to the 
modern mature. 

“We’re very dedicated to 
the senior market,’ Bob 
Uecker, vp-pharmacy, said. 
“Arizona is one of the biggest 
areas for retirement commu- 
nities and we’re very dedicat- 
ed to making sure we serve 
their needs.” 

The chain offers many of the 
same services for elderly per- 
sons as other retailers. How- 
ever, SupeRx goes a step fur- 
| ther for its customers. 

Currently, plans are under- 
way to unveil a new link-up ser- 
e vice with its Synercom comput- 
er system. All prescription 
information will be linked by a 
SupeRx computer network to 
all pharmacy locations. Installa- 
tions on the system started last 
month and the chain hopes to be 
fully operational by the first 
quarter of 1990. 

“This gives our customers 
the advantage of a safety 
check,” Uecker said. “That 
way if a patient goes to a phar- 
macy close to their doctor’s of- 
fice once, then, at another 
time, goes to one nearer their 
home, all of the information is 
there, so we can catch any 
‘medications that might possi- 
bly interact with one anoth- 
er.” 

Supe Rx also houses a larger 
home health care unit than 
most chains. 

“We target the high-retire- 
ment areas, and provide home 
oxygen, durable medical 
equipment (DME), home 
health care products, as well 
as home IV therapy,” Uecker 
 -aecapen 

uch of SupeRx’s emphasis 
resides in Phoenix and the sur- 
rounding Maricopa County 
area. The chain is currently 
the sole pharmacy provider 
for all county-paid long-term 
medical facilities, which totals 
approximately 3,900 beds. 

‘I believe that the long- 
term care delivery system in 


Maricopa County is state of 
the art,” Uecker said. “There 
are no homes with county-paid 
beds that we don’t serve. Our 
goal is to put together services 
which enable the senior to stay 
at home as long as possble. 
But when they and their fam- 
ilies deem it necessary for 
them to move into these facili- 
ties, we’re there once again to 
service them.” 

Although other counties in 
the state contract on a home- 
by-home basis, SupeRx has 
many of these contracts as 


well and Uecker hopes that 
eventually, more plans like 
the one in Maricopa County 
will be developed. 

The pharmacists also man 
“Careline,” an information 
line available for persons to 
call the pharmacists and ask 
questions about their medica- 
tions. 

“The reasons behind this 
program are basically to serve 
the senior population,” 
Uecker explained. “This 
group uses the pharmacy 
more than any other segment. 


“With specialized medicine, 
these people see several doc- 
tors at one itme, and they get 
different prescriptions from 
each,” he added. “Most of the 
time, the doctors are aware of 
this, but sometimes they 
aren't. Plus, when people go to 
a doctor’s office, many times 
it’s a stressful situation and 
they forget very quickly what 
their doctor told them to do. 
This hotline serves as a rein- 
forcement service.” 

Uecker stresses that in each 
of the programs directed at 


the modern mature, the chain 
is dedicated to the best possi- 
ble service for the r custom- 
ers. 

“If we can’t do a quality job, 
we just won’t do it at all? he 
said. “It takes a lot of exper- 
tise to market these areas ef- 
fectively, and we’re not going 
to do the job halfway.”

NEWS IN Bieler 


Arbor adds three stores in Michigan 


TROY, Mich. - Arbor recently added three stores to its Michi- 

gan roster, in keeping with its plan of opening 12 to 15 stores 
uring fiscal year 1990, which began Aug. 1. 

The company unveiled a 10,220-square-foot store in the Vil- 
— Mall at 1125 Highway M-52 at Old U.S. 12 in Chelsea. An- 
other store, measuring 12,500 square feet, opened at 36800 Gar- 
field Rd. at Metropolitan Parkway in Mt. Clemens. 

In addition, Arbor acquired the assets of Mey Pharmacy in 
Saginaw, including its operations and prescription files, and 
opened its 91st store at 2525 State St. Larry Mey, former owner 
of Mey Pharmacy, joined the Saginaw store as an Arbor phar- 
macist. 


McKesson to build 5th D.C. in St. Louis 


ST. LOUIS — McKesson Corp. is preparing to build a larger 
distribution facility here to help Pre a its market coverage. 

Construction on the new 234,000-square-foot site is expected 
to begin early next year, with completion due by early 1991. It 
will replace an 86,000-square-foot site which McKesson has 
used since 1966. 

Company-wide, McKesson currently operates 47 distribution 
centers that add up to more than 4 million square feet of ware- 
house space. The new St. Louis facility follows McKesson’s 


building and opening of four new DCs this year. 


Wal-Mart, mall get yes vote 


IOWA CITY, Iowa— Wal-Mart recently came up against a 
resident’s revolt here in November when local merchants prc- 
tested to block the opening of the retail giant’s proposed 87,000- 
square-foot store in a 28-acre downtown shopping center. 

Actually, said Brenda Lockhart, Wal-Mart spokesperson, 
the residents were opposed to the building of the shopping cen- 
ter, of which Wal-Mart will be an anchor store. 

Residents feared the discount store would take away from the 
community’s small-town ambiance, and they took their city council 
to court to vote on a referendum banning the proposed site. 

Despite the opposition, the ballot passed witha “yes” vote. 


Ex-Reliable’s Dalton to head MedNet | 


HARRISBURG, Pa. — David Dalton, formerly senior vp- 
pharmacy ae a for Reliable Drugs, is the new president and 
ceo of the MedNet Group, an administrator of prescription drug 
programs and durable medical equipment with a national provider 
network for insurance carriers and self-insured companies. 

“My experience in the business side of pharmacy will help con- 
tinue to establish MedNet as a prescription drug administrator 
that can truly contain costs, but not on the back of the pharma- 
cist,” said Dalton, who was vp-professional relations at ite Aid 
before joining Reliable as one of the new chain’s original man- 


agement group. 


Drug Castle opens Ohio store 


SPRINGFIELD, Ohio — Drug Castle Franchises opened a 
new 27,000-square-foot store in Middletown, Ohio. 

The deep discount drug store, owned and operated by South- 
western Ohio Drug Distributors, offers brand name H&BAs, 
packaged foods and household chemicals in its product mix. Its 
computerized pharmacy departments boast savings of up to 50 
percent off prescription prices charged by other drug stores. 

Drug Castle franchise stores —— operate in Ohio in the 
towns of Dayton, Springfield, Akron, Lima and Warren; Tampa 
and St. Petersburg, Fla.; and Fort Wayne, Ind.

conducted their business

competition.

their products. Thus, the

DRUG STORE NEWS, December 11, 1989 


OPINION 


“One company can’t reform all of the problems of a 

troubled inner-city neighborhood — but we can help.” 
With this statement, summing up the driving force 
behind Walgreens’ new “One on One” tutoring program 
for Chicago inner-city grade school children, Charles R. 
Walgreen III, chairman and ceo, encap- 


sulated the spirit bringing more and more 

businesses into civic areas once dominat- 

ed by government programs. 
Walgreens’ new program combines a 


ball for an unbeatable work and play for- 
mula designed to pick up grades and teach 
teamwork, paving the way for success in 
high school and, eventually, college. 
That may sound like a big leap for kids 
on Chicago’s Near West Side who will be 


~IN THE MARKET __ the first to benefit from Walgreens’ new 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


program. But the Midtown Educational 


Foundation, recipient of Walgreens’ 
pledge of $190,000 to support the pro- 


_ gram for the next four years, has scored points since 


1965 with just such a program, aimed at seventh- and 
eighth-grade boys. In 1985 an affiliated program for 
girls was launched. More than 60 percent of kids in the 
program go on to college. 

Walgreens’ new program aims to pick up youngsters 
at an earlier, more impressionable age — the fourth- to 
sixth-grade levels. It starts this fall with 30 boys, and 
will later be expanded to girls. Eventually 100 children a 
year will be helped by volunteer tutors trained in Wal- 
greens’ program. 

As Walgreens’ chief executive describes it: “We chose 
our company’s hometown, Chicago, and a program that 
helps kids on a personal level... . Our program will 


few hours a week of tutoring with basket- — 


Civic duty: good ‘personal’ strategy 


reach students at an earlier age, build their confidence 
and open some options to them.” 

“Walgreen hits the nail on the head when he points out 
the need for business to get involved in such programs: 
“This isn’t just civic duty, it’s concern for future em- 
ployees. . . With a national high school dropout rate 
nearing 30 percent, our next generation is at risk.” 

‘Walgreens is not, of course, the only drug chain or in- 
dependent pharmacy giving its resources to worthwhile 
endeavors. The spirit of volunteerism that has burned 
bright in the ’80s has moved many companies to greater 
involvement in their communities. We'll be portraying 
some of these outstanding efforts in future issues. 

I wanted to focus on Walgreens in this column be- 
cause, first, it is the premier chain in the industry —one 
of the oldest and certainly the most successful. Second, I 
wanted to mention a project we’re undertaking. In 
March, we will publish an issue entirely devoted to Wal- 
greens and the factors that have made it such a success. 
It will be the first full-issue study on a chain that Drug 
Store News has published in more than a decade, we be- 
lieve it will be a notable publishing event. 

Walgreens’ contribution to. Chicago's children cap- 
tures as much as anything the kind of creative imagina- 
tion that has made the company the industry leader. It 
combines civic good with a strategic vision of how the 
welfare of young children in Chicago’s inner-city neigh- 
borhoods is linked to Walgreens’ future. The children 
are, after all the employees and customers of tomorrow.

Special thanks to Alert Marketing, Inc., the retail 
merchandising service company based in Waterbury, 
Conn., for interviewing store managers on brand pref- 
erences, part of our special section beginning on page 7. 


A refreshing view. of ‘Fetailing 


Refreshing. After spending a day with Tom Rosen- 
thal, the 33-year-old president of 66-store Standard 
Drug in Virginia, I feel confident that “down-home re- 
tailing” will be with us for quite some time. People re- 
spond to drug store retailers who practice with a feel for 

the human side. 


The chain’s attitude flows from the top, 
where chairman Gilbert Rosenthal and 
son, the third generation in the business, 
share a deliberately informal but increas- 
ingly disciplined approach to manage- 
ment. Gilbert looks the picture of comfort 
at his desk, attired in sport shirt and cable 
knit sweater; ask him a question, and he 
can spew out category statistics and dis- 
cuss trends in rapid-fire fashion. 

Tom, a Wharton School graduate, has 


THE HUMAN SIDE worked at Standard a dozen years al- 


AL HELLER 


ready, and, coming into his own as presi- 


dent the past year-and-a-half, is nearing a 
decision on which scanning system to 
bring into his chain. But increased disciplines won’t strip 
Standard of its human feel. 

Consider that the chain gives career pharmacist Rich- 
ard Martin three extra weeks of paid personal time an- 
nually so he can fulfill his duties as president of the State 
of Virginia Parent-Teachers Association. Says Tom: 
“We did the same for another employee who was on the 
state pharmacy association.” Not all chain presidents 
would equate the two positions and give such latitude. 

He addresses store staffers by their first names and 
listens when they speak. He gives them the confidence 
that action will be taken by making verbal notes into his 
microcassette recorder right in front of them. 

Tom served recently as president of the Jewish Fam- 
ily Services social work agency, and belonged to the 
United Jewish Appeal Young Leadership Cabinet, re- 
flecting his desire to serve less privileged people. 

What he enjoys less is part of his role as chairman of 
the Virginia Association of Chain Drug Stores. “It’s 
frustrating,” Tom said, with growing intensity. “I just 
spent a day driving through eastern Virginia with a lob- 
byist giving out checks. 

“I don’t like being beholden to a political system to de- 


Tom Rosenthal chats with store manager Kathy Aljabar. 


termine our economic future. It’s us versus the hospi- 
tals. This is not a nice way of doing business.” 

I like to consider Tom, who is helping to keep the $80 
million (annual sales) chain competitive in a tough mar- 
ket, as part of a “new guard”—including Jim Harrison 
III of Harco, Alan Levin of Happy Harry’s, Mark Griffin 
of Lewis Drugs and Steve, Mike and Jeff LaVerdiere of 
LaVerdiere’s. At these strong, family-owned regionals, 
the management mantel is increasingly being passed to 
young executives in their 30s, who’ve grown up in the 
businesses and know what their local markets demand. 

Tom, for one, sees industry consolidation and en- 
croachment by formidable combos, and expresses con- 
cern that the regionals will be a “swallowed guard. 
There won’t be many of us left in a few years.” 

He is right, of course, when he says efficient pharma- 
cy providers will be the survivors, and Wal-Mart makes 
it tough to compete on front-end business. 

But I like to think there is room for both. Local talent, 
flexibility and resourcefulness, and knowing one’s mar- 
kets best, can be effective weapons against rigid busi- 
ness sharpies who bring their specific retail formulas to 
town. Hometown non-trendy merchandising, and a sin- 
cere human concern, still counts for a lot across much of 
America. That gives me a warm feeling as I slosh my 
way across Manhattan to my Park Avenue office.

Key findings 


The survey reveals brand 
preferences in 21 H&BA cate- 
gories among 600 female con- 
sumers in six major markets 
across the country. [See meth- 
odology box.] It also probed 
consumers’ reasons for their 
selections. Among the main 
findings: . 

@ A high percentage of re- 
spondents — ranging from 71 
percent in sun care to 95 per- 
cent in film — said they have 
a brand preference in the cate- 

ories studied, including four 

TC, nine toiletry, five cos- 
metic/fragrance and three 
general merchandise catego- 
ries. 

@ Brand loyalty, gauged by 
percentage of consumers who 
said they would not switch if 
their brand was not in stock, 
was generally strong across 
all categories. The highest de- 
gree of brand loyalty — 90 
percent or better — was in 
the hair color, eye/lens care, 
laxatives, nail treatments and 
men’s fragrances categories. 
The lowest brand loyalty was 
found in toothpastes, deodor- 
ants, batteries, shampoos and 
cough/cold products.

Methodology of the study 


The Brand Preference Study was conducted by Fairfield 
Research, Inc., Lincoln, Neb., for Drug Store News. The 
study represents interviews with 600 female consumers 18 
years of age or older who shop at least once a month in a drug 
store. The study was conducted in six major metropolitan ar- 
eas: Boston, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, Washington, 
D.C. and Atlanta, Ga. The data was collected in May and 
urvey methodology.

products, toiletries, cosmetics/fragrances and general 
merchandise. The study focuses on the brand preferences, 
buying patterns and reasons for brand choice for each of 
the 21 categories within these four groups.

Dual-income households and other demo- 
grog trends are changing shoppers’ buying 
abits. One marketing researcher suggests 
that consumers’ time constraints will result in 
more impulse purchases and greater reliance 
on price and brand in product selection. 
onsumers may be busier, but F&M presi- 
dent Frank Newman thinks too much is made 
of people es with a stopwatch. “We 
don’t see people trotting through our stores. 
We see them reading labels ant studying in- 
gredients. Consumers are more intelligent 
now in deciding what they need and want.” In 
addition, “You have two people shopping 
now, rather than one. And the biggest im- 
pulse shoppers are men.” 
ig Tim McAlear, president of Pay 
Less , agrees that consumers are studying 


labels as much or more than ever, he sees time 
constraints as the most dramatic difference be- 
tween shoppers today and in the past. “People 
just don’t come in to browse anymore. Shop- 
ping is not as recreational as it used to be. 

“I think they shop a little more often, but 
they don’t buy as much, and they don’t come 
in with shopping lists as much,” he continued. 

But consumers do tend to lean more toward 
quality products now, he said. “They’re will- 
ing to pay more if the value is there, because 
it’s a more affluent society and because the 
want to get it right the first time. They don't 
want to have to take something back.’ 

But all in all, “The consumer hasn’t changed 
as much as retailers and manufacturers have 
begun to listen more, rather than try to lead 
them,” McAlear said.

BRANDS: Batteries 


Performance, price charge battery buying 


erformance, price and 

past experience are all 

considered by consum- 
ers when they buy batteries, 
Drug Stores News’ Consumer 
Brands Preference Study 
shows. 

Chain buyers often maintain 
batteries are commodity-type 
products. Thus, consumers re- 
spond mostly to price and im- 

ulse displays. Stores have 
eavily adopted off-shelf pro- 
motions to cater to this. 

Yet, merchandisers add, 
brand name is important to an 
extent: The brand has to be ei- 
ther Eveready, Energizer or 
Duracell. These brands have 
dominated the drug store chan- 
nel, in part through the clout 
they’ve built with consumers. 
Their aggression has equally 
endeared them to store manag- 
ers, who reap high margins and 
.— sell-through. 

e vendors are spending 
millions of dollars a year in 
tooth-and-nail efforts to project 
distinct brand characteristics 
for the products. Long life has 
been the main theme. 

Thirty-four percent of con- 
sumers named Duracell alka- 
line batteries as their favorites. 
Ralston-Purina’s zinc-carbon 
Eveready plus the Energizer 
alkaline line gained a total of 
41.2 percent, with 15 percent 
naming the Energizer. Store 
managers even more strongly 
favored the two leaders. 

Both vendors have benefited 
this year from their television 
adds employing toys to convey 
the assertion the batteries last 
longest. This is a key feature 
that consumers respond to, in- 
dustry execs say. 


Eveready’s “bunny” ad, 


launched in October 1988 on the 
heels of similar Duracell toy 
ads, sparked wide consumer re- 
sponse. That enthusiasm has 
continued with the October 
1989 launch of the innovative 
60-second “bunny” series in 
which the rabbit disrupts sev- 
eral simulated commercial 
spots. Eveready has since 
launched a promotion in which 
each store will receive a bunny 
to auction off to consumers. 

Duracell’s different tack has 
been to educate the consumer 
on battery shelf life through TV 
ads. Vendors now promote the 
“freshness dating” on packag- 
ing, also. 

While this emphasis on prod- 
uct attributes is seen as key, 
price is apparently no less im- 
portant. The leaders continue 
to offer a constant stream of 
coupons and rebates. Ever- 
eady took a new angle this 
spring by offering premium 
values of free batteries, or “in- 
stant gratification,” with two

Kodak can sell at a full price. 
The price point for a three- 
pack, for example, will typi- 
cally be $2 more thar Fuji, ac- 
cording to chain drug buyers. 

The consumer survey sup- 
ports this, as price was named 
by only 11 percent as a reason 
for making a purchase. Brand 
attributes such as “trust” and 

“good past experience” were 
much more important, as was 
simple “habit.” 

Drug chains have per- 
formed better than anyone in 
exploiting consumers’ quality 
concerns by building their im- 
age of expertise, and empha- 
sizing the processing side. A 
1988 consumer preference 
survey by the Photo Market- 
ing Association found that 43 
percent of consumers polled 
named drug stores as the pre- 
ferred source for photofinish- 
ing. In a survey that gave mul- 
tiple responses, discount 
stores came in a distance sec- 
ond with 27 percent. 

Kodak scored big in drug 
stores this year with its “Co- 
lorKins” promotion in which 
consumers who purchased Ko- 
dak items accrued points that 
they used to qualify for four 
stuffed animals. “I’ve never 
seen such [store] support in 
advertising and display,” not- 
ed an observer. 

Consumers were won over 


by the stuffed animals. The 
stores had the chance to bun- 
dle Kodak products such as a 
camera (worth ten points), 
and camera batteries (one 
point) and film (one point per 
roll). 

Multipacks are a continuing 
source of retailer enrichment, 
and a top Kodak seller this 
year was its discounted three- 
pack with 12 free exposures. 

Despite the excitement 
over 35mm photography, the 


Kodak brand, particularly in 
drug stores, also captures a 
high percentage of sales in dise 
and 110 format film. These for- 
mats still account for as much 


as 25 percent to 30 percent of 


drug stores’ film business, as 
consumers in some cases con- 
tinue to get mileage out of old- 
er cameras whose styles are 


no longer in production. 

The Photo Marketing Asso- 
ciation found in 1989 survey 
that while 58.6 percent of 
households used 35mm film 
35.7 percent used 110, and 
19.7 percent used disc. 

Chain buyers expect film to 
provide steady growth ahead. 
Almost two-thirds of film buy- 


ers are women, the major 
class of drug store shopper. 
Perhaps more importantly, 
Americans who own cameras 
continue to use them. The 
PMA reported last year that 
virtually all of the 92 percent 
of U.S. households that own a 
camera purchased film over 
the previous 12 months.

DRUG STORE NEWS, December 11, 1989 


BRANDS: Color Cosmetics 


31 


Shades, packaging 
influence purchases 
of color cosmetics 


a ip, eye and face make- 
ups are all considered 
“fashion” categories, 
categories that help women 
realize their most cherished 
fantasies, so you would expect 
that women would be much 
more experimental, switching 
their favorite cosmetic brands 
almost as often as they switch 
shades. 

However, our consumer 
brand survey found that was 
not the case. 

Just two out of 10 women 
will switch from her favorite 
brand. 

For brand shifters, the 
strongest incentives were 
price and, even more impor- 
tant, color and packaging. 


Packaging and colors 


Women can be lured by a 
bargain in the fashion catego- 
ries, but they’re even more 
susceptible to pretty colors 
and packaging. The compa- 
nies that make the brands 
with the strongest consumer 
loyalties in the survey, Rev- 
lon, Maybelline, and Cover 
Girl, are all very careful about 
their packaging. Each of these 
lines hel packaging that pops 
off the shelf, and their product 
managers do outstanding jobs 
with promotional packages 
and pre-packs. 

Yet while superior packag- 
ing or a good price/value rela- 
tionship will help induce a trial 
sale, consumers who use lip, 
eye and facial makeups are 
looking for a name they can 
commit to. 

They want to be brand-loyal 
shoppers because they want 
to feel sure that when they use

will be right for them. And to 
feel that sense of security, 
women have to trust the 
brands they buy. 

Product benefits are not 
really an issue with this con- 
sumer. Women don’t have to 
be sold on lip, eye or face 
makeups. They know these 
products have benefits for 
them. The question they 
have to settle is which brand 
to buy. 

The amount of advertising 
women are exposed to, as well 
as their familiarity with the 
line’s name and with the prod- 
uct’s accessibility, all have a 
lot to do with the choice they 
finally make, as one would ex- 
pect. 

Names like Maybelline, 
Revlon and Cover Girl have 
been around for years, and 


they have long ago become 
names that women felt they 
could trust. 

Among the three, Revlon is 
the least available on the mass 
market, being still primarily a 
prestige line whose distribu- 
tion is basically limited to drug 
and department stores. But 
the Revlon name and its cos- 
metic heritage is so well estab- 
lished and so carefully culti- 
vated by marketers that its 
position of dominance in the 
popular mind or the mass mar- 


ket is assured. 

Maybelline is particularly 
strong in the eye category, es- 
pecially among heavy users of 
mascara and eye shadow prod- 
ucts. Both Maybelline and 
Cover Girl still have a strong 
following with young women, 
especially teens and pre- 
teens. Revlon is the brand 
they often move to as they get 
older. 

Our findings suggest that 
while brand-loyal shoppers 
will probably stock up when a 


retailer promotes or adver- 
tises these lines, the ad may 
not be as successful in induc- 
ing new users to try the line. 
Only 2 percent of our sample 
said they’d buy a brand “= 
cause it was on sale. 
Retailers who want to get 
brand-loyal shoppers to devel- 
op a second preference, a sort 
of “wardrobe” of brand favor- 
ites, should work with manu- 
facturers to create promotions 
that would develop trust in the 
brands being advertised. 


tatives.

categories.

the line also has a reputation

Not getting ‘burned’ big reason behind sun care buys 


advantage in having high a year-round category and 


Suntan lotion and sun block 
users in Drug Store News’ 
Brand Preference Study most 
often cited good past experi- 
ence, trust and simply liking 
the item — sometimes for its 
smell or packaging — as rea- 
sons for picking the sun care 
product they last bought. 

These reasons seem ironic, 
given the heavy emphasis sun 
care-product marketers put 
on protection, SPFs, formulas 
for sensitive skin and the like. 
While only 1 to 2 percent of 
regular-brand buyers men- 
tioned such benefits, SPF's 
and protection did matter 
more in the buying decision of 
brand shifters and consumers 
with no regular brand, who 
also were more likely to pur- 
chase an item because it was 
new and they wanted to try it. 

Only respondents with no 
regular brand were especially 
swayed by price: About four in 
10 of them said low price or a 
sale influenced what sun care 
product they bought. 

However, the study also 
found a high degree_of brand 
loyalty among sun care cus- 
tomers. Whereas 71 percent 
of the total sample said they 
had a regular brand (a rather 
low percentage with a favored 
brand, compared with the oth- 
er 20 categories surveye‘), 
only 17 percent of that group 
said they would switch brands 
if their favorite wasn’t in 
stock. That’s a comparatively 
low percentage of switchers. 

Consumers in our study 
may be reflecting a certain im- 
perviousness to marketing 
messages when faced with the 


proliferation of products and 
forms in this category, which 
retailers say is confusing to 
them, as well as to their cus- 
tomers. Consider: Forms of 
sun care products include oils, 
gelees, creams, sticks, 
sprays, lotions, zincs, towe- 
lettes and sponges; and func- 
tions include high SPF's, chil- 
dren’s items, sensitive-skin 
products, broad-spectrum 
items, photo-aging protec- 
tion, pre-sun and after-sun. 
As one buyer put it, “I look at

- Growing concern 


But there undoubtedly has 
been a growing concern in the 
past few years over tanning 
too much or too fast: Consum- 
ers increasingly want prod- 
ucts that block the ultraviolet 
rays that are most likely to 
cause sunburn or lead to skin 
cancer, and they’re more 
aware of the sun’s drying and 
aging effects on the skin. The 
concern over protection helps 
explain why the category’s 


strongest growth is in the 
higher-SPF segment, with 
SPF 15 the best-selling SKU. 

While the biggest growth 
has been in high-SPF' prod- 
ucts, tanning products are still 
the larger segment of the sun 
care category, accounting for 
more than half of skin care 
sales. According to Drug 
Store News’ latest estimates, 
the suntan segment’s total 
sales in drug chains reached 
$100.3 million, and sun protec- 
tion sales were about $91.7 
million for 1988. Tanning 
products still appeal especial- 
ly to high school and college 
students, but merchandisers 
predict the sun protection seg- 
ment will equal suntan-seg- 
ment sales next year. 

This year, consumers ap- 
pear to be cutting through the 
clutter, because buyers are 
beginning to discern best-sell- 
ing lines, enabling them to 
start thinning out their selec- 
tion to a few top items. Some 
buyers are looking to pare the 
very low SPF's (0-4), which 
they’re sensing consumers are 
moving away from. In our 
study, consumers’ top choices 
were Coppertone, Bain de So- 
leil and Hawaiian Tropic, in 
that order of preference, and 
store managers’ rankings, ina 
separate poll, agreed. Cop- 
pertone perhaps has an added 


name recognition gained 
through longevity.

ments. Proof of performance (e.g., tear sheets) and proof of delivery (whole-

Space allocations 


In 1989, Nielsen also discovered that both 
drug and food stores are expanding their 
space allocations for select H&BA categories 
Miia large-volume independents are cutting 

ack. 

In 1989, for example, drug chains expand- 
ed shelf space for 18 of the 27 select H&BA 
categories monitored by Nielsen. Food 
chains gave more space to 19 of the tracked 
categories. 

Large independents, on the other hand, 
expanded space for only two categories and 
even these increases were very marginal, 
averaging just about one linear foot of shelv- 


ing. 

‘See the larger high-volume indepen- 
dents, however, can’t compete with chains 
and food stores on product presentations and 
assortment because they simply don’t have 
the space in most cases. 

But the typical chain drug store, which is 
usually at least 8,000 square feet and can be 


three times larger, is striving 
very hard to stay ahead of their 
food competitors on assortment. 

Chains added another three 
feet to dentifrice products in 
1989, for example, to give them a 
total of 60 linear feet, compared 
to the 10 feet food chains aver- 
aged in early 1989. 

Only in bulk — like dis- 
posable diapers do drug chains 
cede growth to their food competi- 
tors. In 1989, food chains added 
another 4 feet to disposable diapers 
to give them a total of 65 linear 
feet. Drug chains, on the other 
hand, only expanded their dispos-

Annual inventory turns have increased 7.6

@ The number of chain drug stores with 
cosmeticians on duty is growing. In 1987, 34

@ Today’s drug chain is also much more 
committed to institutional or image advertis- 
ing. In 1984, just 13 percent of total ad 
space was allocated to an institutional mes-

e@ In terms of disposable income, the econ- 
omy has been reasonably strong. For the

percent increase in real disposable income. 


H&BA Sales Trends 


Chart 9: Real drug store H&BA sales 
growth, as measured in unit sales, was vir- 
tually flat for the first half of 1989—up only 
1 percent. The same was true for HBA 
unit sales in food stores. | 

However, mass merchandisers generated 
tremendous growth in unit sales, with vol- 
ume up 16 percent. The growth reflected 
their increasing commitment to building this 
category in their stores. 

Mass merchandisers have traditionally 
been the strongest with the remedial H&BA 
categories, such as cough/cold and flu prod- 
ucts, and with basic necessities like oral hy- 
giene. Now they are competing more ag- 
gressively for the hair, skin and overal 
toiletries customer. Their drive is paying off 
in stronger sales. 

Mass merchandisers have also done .-..2 
best job in holding down prices on H&BA 
products. Prices increased only 3 percent for 
the first half, compared to a 4-percent in- 
crease in prices for both drug and food 
stores. 


Chart 10: For the first half of 1989, the 
growth rate of H&BA sales in mass mer- 
chandisers more than quadrupled the growth 
rate in drug stores — 18 percent vs. 4 percent. 

Drug stores also lost ground in their share of 
H&BA sales. Their share for the first half of 1989 
is down nine-tenths of a point from the same peri- 
od last year. 

Share of H&BA sales for mass merchandisers, 
on the other hand, increased 1.8 points. This is 
partly because many mass merchandisers have 
expanded space for H&BA and cosmetic products. 
At the same time, they are advertising and pric- 
ing them more aggressively. 

As a category, H&BA increased 7 percent for 
the first half and should end the year with sales 
at or over $32 billion. In 1988, the category was 
also up 7 percent, to $29.9 billion. 

Food stores are showing only modest growth 
with the category. Their sales for the first half 
were up 5 percent, but their share of sales, like 
that of drug stores, was down 0.9 of a point.

sales — drug stores are not having an exciting

creases of 15 percent or better in the first_ 
half of 1988 to sales increases averaging 10 
to 15 percent. They were diaper ras 
creams, sleeping tablets and face creams and 
lotions.

declined, dropping from 11 categories with 
dollar sales growth between 10 and 15 per-

growth that strong this year.

ened towelettes — maintained its growth 
rate from 1988.

chart shows that drug stores are not cur-

in the toiletries and fashion segments of

ing less growth this year than last, and the basic 
toiletry categories, like deodorants, shampoos, 
sun care, face make-up and nail color, are flat or 
only showing marginal growth.

Chain Drug Stores Store Merchandising Char- 
acteristics 

Chart 18: The most popular “extra” that drug 
stores can provide convenience-minded shoppers 
is still film developing, now offered by 98 percent 


of all U.S. chain drug stores. 

Making sure there is a computer in pharmacy to 
track consumer needs is the next most popular op- 
tion, and in 1989 94 percent of all chains provided 
that service, compared to just 71 percent in 1987. 

Today’s chain drug store is also working harder 
to satisfy the consumer’s growing need for service 
at the mass level. In February 1988, just 30 per- 
cent of all the drug chains surveyed had a cosme- 
tician on duty. In February 1989, that number 
had increased to 40 percent. 

Lottery tickets did not decline in popularity as 
a service option, but neither did they grow dra- 


riety of styling aids. 


Retailers’ space allocation strategy tries to maximize SKU facings while mak- 
ing a strong presentation. This Arbor store in Southfield, Mich. promotes a va- 


ear foot per month, well in excess of the $19 
chain drug stores were generating in this 
category. Nasal sprays and drops were up 
$4 to $59, again much better than the $39 
chain drug stores were generating.

harmacists are fighting a new kind of turf war that could 
change the way they practice pharmacy. Only this time, the 
turf they are trying to protect isn’t on city streets, it’s in 
their own prescription departments. 

As though it weren’t enough for today’s pharmacist to fend off en- 
croaching competition from supermarkets, combo stores, mail or- 
der and physicians who dispense, many are faced with a more per- 
sonal problem closer to home: how to define the role of pharmacy 
technicians working behind their counters. : 

The controversy surrounding the role of supportive personnel is 
nothing new to pharmacy. Ever since pharmacists’ workload start- 
ed prohibiting them from leaving the prescription counter to counsel 
patients, the definition of what a pharmacy technician’s duties 
should be has been the topic of discussion among state associations 
and boards of pharmacy. Unfortunately, the industry as a whole has 
yet to come to a consensus on the issue. As heavy workloads contin- 
ue to plague pharmacists, many state boards and associations have 
begun to seriously address the issue head-on by formulating regula- 
tions for technicians and their duties amid much controversy.

The multi-tier curse 


Another problem I see looming large in the year ahead is 
multi-tier and discriminatory pricing. It doesn’t take a ge- 
nius to figure out that the pharmacy getting the best 
pee from manufacturers is in a better position to deal in 
ow third-party reimbursement contracts. Is it fair that 
one segment of our market eee treated to substantially 
lower prices than another? Absolutely not. Pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturers who continue to practice multi-tier pric- 
ing are simply choking the profession. It should be 
spe, and stopped now. 

- Toalesser extent, I think physician dispensing will con- 
tinue to plague retail pharmacy in some geographical ar- 
eas. Although I don’t see it wreaking the same kind of hav- 
oc nationwide as I envision third-party doing, it will 


sional marketing pharmacists. A use| 
of tachalcians ik alow giapiaamaee sa nsult with pa- 
tients and become more visible to the public. Along those 
lines, some states are already conside

sultation laws. While the process is certain to be evolution- 
ary, I think eventually, as more sophisticated flood 
the market, the pharmacist will be able to charge for his or 
her services. 

I think we will see less fe bay dispensing as 
states put into action laws that will force physicians to fol- 
low the same regulations as pharmacists. At that point, I 
think most physicians will become disgusted and give up 
their practice of dispensing prescriptions. 

Once retail pharmacy begins to show that it has some 
clout again, pharmaceutical manufacturers will come 
around and discontinue multi-tier pricing.

My Way of Thinking. . . 


“My Way of Thinking” is intended to give responsible members of the health care community a profes- 
sional forum to air their views on crucial issues confronting pharmacy today. Presentations should be no 
longer than 500 words and may be edited for space requirements. Interested participants should mail their 
presentations to Harold Cohen, Editor, Inside Pharmacy, 425 Park Avenue, New York, N.Y., 10022. Arti- 
cles will be chosen and published at the editor's discretion. 


One would be hard-pressed to find a 
harmacist who would support or con- 
one physician dispensing. While the 

work being done on state and federal 
levels by a number of organizations is 
admirable, there is no solution or relief 
for the short-term problems facing 
pharmacy. 

The most recent frontal attack is be- 
ing made through home medical equip- 
ment (HME) dealers. At least one 
drug repackager is pie to broaden 
its penetration into the physician dis- 
i Yay market by bringing the HME 

ealer in as an ally. 

During a recent home health care 
conference, a drug packager told HME 
dealers they could make a $2,000 profit 
per physician by cg physicians in 
their area to dispense. They suggested 
that the HME dealer could make as 
much as six figures without an invest- 
ment. 

Perhaps it is time for the pharmacist 
to stop waving the S.0.S. flag while 
the ship is sinking, and start bailing 
and allow those retailers with the abill- 
ty to plug up the holes the time to do 
their job. 


Who is : a better oe to one 
proper packaging an ing of pre- 
abe a ieeeat Who is more a 
than the neighborhood pharmacist? 
Who is in a better position to help as- 
sure that the proper auxiliary labels 
and printed patient instructions are 
made available to the patient? Who is 
in a better position to benefit from a 
good pharmacist-physician relation- 
ship and fill those prescriptions that 
the dispensing physician does not 
stock or for the third-party who will 
not pay the physician or the physician 
who elects not to do the paperwork? 

Some might consider such a proposal 
heresy or an unprofessional attitude, 
others claim that a pharmacist can’t sit 
on both sides of the fence. 

How can pharmacy be so naive as to 
think that it is going to stop physician 
dispensing in its tracks without sus- 
taining any casualties? Most of today’s 
pharmacists have computers which 
could easily be modified to produce 
multiple labels which would provide 
adequate inventory and other con- 
trols. 

If a particular physician or group of 


hysicians are going to dispense, is it 
tter for them to obtain their inven- 
tory from across the country or state 
or through a local source such as a local 
pharmacy? 

In today’s marketplace, diversifica- 
tion is a necessity, not a luxury. My 
strategy for survival is simple: oe gl 
tect your base by going after mail or- 
der contracts or by supplying physi- 
cians who wish to Panes: (2 
diversify in home medical equipment 
or other such areas; and (3) find niches 
where services are wanted and people 
are willing to pay for them. 

By protecting your base, you will 
help ensure your long-term survival. 
You will aiso have the ability to wait 
for the powers-to-be to prohibit physi- 
cian dispensing or until third-party 
payers “weed out” rye physi- 
ogg by eliminating the “cash” mar- 

et. 

Your future is in your hands—are 
you a flag waver or a bailer? 

Steven R. Ariens, P.D.

“They’re afraid we’re going to

“The controversy over

(pharmacists) act like they

a correspondence course espe- 
cially for techs. 

Some state associations, 
such as Michigan and New 
Hampshire, have set up their 
own certification programs, 
aimed at improving the know]- 
edge base and credibility of 
technicians. 

In 1981, the Michigan Phar- 
macists Association, realizing 
the need for technicians to 
have some kind of formal edu- 
cation, set up its Pharmacy 
Certified Technician (PCT) 
program. The association also 
set up an MPA affiliated chap- 
ter in 1984, the Michigan Soci- 
ety of Pharmacy Technicians 
(MSPT) to serve the techni- 
cian sector in the state. 

Larry D. Wagenknecht, ex- 
ecutive director MPA, ex- 
plained that the association 
conducts a full-day exam twice 
a year which includes ques- 
tions on basic science, math 
and pharmacology areas. Indi- 
viduals must also be familiar 
with common drugs — their 
brand and generic names — 
as well as basic allegations 
and dilutions, he added. 

“The philosophy in Michi- 
gan is a little different,” Wa- 
genknecht said. “It’s so com- 
petitive price-wise and 
pharmacists realize they can- 
not afford to do all of the 
counting and pouring and they 
must use these techs in order 
to survive. It’s the only thing 
we could do to deal with the 
competition.” 


Difference of opinion 


Other states, such as Texas 
and California, are taking steps 
to define the role of the pharma- 
cy technician. On average, 
most states advocate a 1:1 ra- 
tio, but oppose certification or 
licensure of technicians. 

In Texas, the issue of techni- 
cians’ duties ended in a court 
battle. Texas Pharmaceutical 
Association recently settled a 
lawsuit with the state board 
which resulted in a regulation 


stating the pharmacist has the 
ultimate authority for supervi- 
sion of supportive personnel 
and is responsible for their 
training. 

In California, a similar regu- 
lation is under review to allow 
non-licensed personnel to assist 
pharmacists in the community 
setting, according to igo 
Harris, assistant executive offi- 
cer of the California State 
Board of Pharmacy. The regu- 
lation was sent to the Office of 
Administrative Law, and a de- 
cision is due this month. 


Baby steps 


Harris states that certifica- 
tion in California will be a 
while in coming if the regula- 
tion passes. 

“We've got to take the baby 
step first and get recognized in 
the community setting first,” 
she said. “Let’s get some his- 
tory there. Then I think we 
might evolve to where we’ll 
have voluntary certification 
through different associations 
and companies.” 

State boards and associa- 
tions aren’t the only ones in- 
terested in technician certifi- 
cation. Bob Duffy, vp- 

rofessional services at 

appy Harry’s, states that his 
chain plans to roll out a certifi- 
cation process by the begin- 
ning of the year. 

“It’s going to be a series of 
testing, with three different 
stages of testing and three dif- 
ferent levels of certification, 
defining and recognizing the 
role and knowledge of the 
tech,” he explained. 

“There’s no question about 
it in my mind that if properly 
monitored, I think the role of 
technicians is extremely valu- 
able,” he continued. “If we 
provide a higher level of train- 


ing, then we’re even better 
off.” 


National attention 


The issue of defining a phar- 
macy technician’s duties has 


drawn national attention and a 
heightened awareness in the 

harmaceutical community. 

ast year, for example, the 
University of Maryland Cen- 
ter on Drugs and Public Policy 
conducted an Invitational 
Conference on Technical Per- 
sonnel in Pharmacy. More 
than 70 pharmacists and phar- 
macy technicians discussed 
certification and training re- 
quirements, the pharmacist- 
technician relationship, and 
the legal constraints imposed 
on the use of technicians. This 
was one of the first efforts of 
its kind to bring together 
pharmacists and techni- 
cians — in a harmonious fash- 
ion. 

Many technicians are also 
joining associations such as 
the Association of Pharmacy 
Technicians to let their voice 
be heard. 

“Until a few years ago, 
many pharmacy technicians 
didn’t even know that’s what 
they were,” APT’s Smith said. 
“A lot of techs are pharmacy 
students waiting to get their 
degrees. Others are people 
who just draw a Scale. ut 
the majority are really career- 
minded people. Most are very 
involved in their jobs and are 
very motivated and dedicated 
to health care.” 

The association currently 
has over 600 members, rang- 


ing from 16 to 18 different 
fields in pharmacy, according 
to Smith. The majority are 
from hospitals, but the num- 
bers are increasing from home 
health care, nursing homes! 
and related areas, she added. 


Salaries vary 


Salaries for technicians 
vary greatly. In an APT 1985) 
survey, the salary range for 
technicians was betwee 
$8,000 and $25,000. Smith ex- 

ects technicians’ salaries to 
increase in the future as more 
seek specialized positions 
within pharmacy. 

Michigan’s Wacnekneil 
agrees. “Pharmacists have tv 
realize that some tasks could 
be performed by technicians,” 
he said. “You don’t use 5 to 6 
years of education just to go 
out and count and pour. Un- 
less we can get ourselves away 
from that, I think our profes 
sion is in serious trouble. We 
need to move toward provid 
ing patient information and 
patient care management. 

“This is where we’re going 
to look toward our national or 
granizations so that betwee 
all of us, we can really put oui 
arms around a direction tha 
will lead pharmacy into the fu 
ture, instead of building a wal 
around ourselves and letting 
technology go beyond us.”

According to the 1989 Drug 
Store News Consumer Brands 
Preference Study (a telephone 
survey that investigated buy- 
ing habits of 600 female shop- 
pers 18 years of age or older in 
six major markets), 83 percent 
of the shoppers polled reported 
that brand is a very important 
factor in their decision to pur- 
chase one OTC pharmaceutical 
product over another. The sur- 
vey investigated some of the 
hottest OTC categories in the 
marketplace, including cough/ 
cold, analgesics, eye care/lens 
care, laxatives and dental. 

Although dental products 
such as toothpaste, mouth- 
washes and rinses were once 
_ perceived as toiletries in the 
minds of many consumers, ad- 
vanced formulas to fight plaque 
and tartar have prompted 
many drug store owners to 
planogram them closer to more 
familiar OTC pharmaceutical 
categories. 


No doctor visit 


Over-the-counter pharma- 
ceutical products enjoy their 
healthy sales picture, in part, 
because of a desire by many 
consumers to treat uncompli- 
cated medical problems them- 
selves, avoiding a costly visit to 
their family doctor. 

As Jack Walden, senior vp 
and director of public affairs for 
the sips hice ws Drug 
Manufacturers Association, 
points out: “The average OTC 
[remedy | still costs about $2.50, 
and you can still cure a head- 
ache for less than a dime.”

switches and self-care are im- 
portant to increased OTC sales, 
nothing promotes brand pref- 
erence like advertising and 
public relations campaigns.

ous method of increasing brand 
awareness, companies occa- 
sionally are treated to “free” 
advertising, thanks to impor- 
tant medical studies that can

Analgesics 


Despite some temporary

ing 


habits 
best-seller among adults and

due to its link with Reyes

ing it the prevention of heart

most preferred by consumers 
in the study was Bayer.
