BRIEF SUMMARY OF PRESCRIBING INFORMATION 

CONTRAINDICATIONS: Patients hypersensitive to ibuprofen or patients with all or part of the syn- 
drome of nasal polyps, angioedema, and bronchospastic reactivity to aspirin or other nonsteroidal 
anti-inflammatory ts. Anaphylactoid reactions to ibuprofen have occurred in such patients. 
WARNINGS: Risk of Gi Uicerations, Bleeding, and Perforation with NSAID : Physicians 
should remain alert for ulceration and bi ng in patients treated chronically with NSAIDS even in 
the absence of previous GI tract symptoms. in patients observed in clinical trials of several months’ 
to two years’ duration, symptomatic upper Gl ulcers, gross bleeding or perforation appear to occur 
in approximately 1% of patients treated for 3-6 months, and in about 2-4% of patients treated for 
one year. 


Except for a prior history of serious GI events and other risk factors known to be associated with pep- 


tic ulcer disease, no risk factors have been associated with increased risk. Elderly or debilitated 
patients seem to tolerate ulceration or bleeding less well than other individuals and most sponta- 
neous reports of fatal GI events are in this populction. 
PRECAUTIONS: i: Because serious GI tract ulceration and bleeding can occur without 
warning symptoms, physicians should follow chronically treated patients for the signs and symp- 
toms of ulceration and bleeding. 

Blurred and/or diminished vision, scotomata, and/or changes in color vision have been reported. If 
a patient develops such complaints the drug should be discontinued and the patient should have 
an ophthalmologic examination. 

Fluid retention and edema have been reported with ibuprofen; therefore, the drug should be used 
with caution in patients with a history of cardiac decompensation or hypertension. 

Ibuprofen can inhibit platelet aggregation and prolong bieeding time. CHILDREN’S ADVIL * 
SUSPENSION should be used with caution in persons with intrinsic coagulation defects and those 
on anticoagulant therapy. 

The antipyretic and anti-inflammatory activity of ibuprofen may reduce fever and inflammation, 
thus diminishing their utility as diagnostic signs in detecting complications of presumed noninfec- 
tious, noninflammatory painful conditions. 

Small decreases (usually not exceeding one gram) in hemoglobin and hematocrit with an appar- 
ent dose response relationship have been observed following chronic administration. If there are 
no signs of bleeding it is probably not clinically important. 

To avoid exacerbation of disease or adrenal insufficiency, patients on prolonged corticosteroid 
therapy should have their therapy tapered slowly when CHILDREN’S ADVIL * SUSPENSION is added to 
the treatment program. 

Aseptic meningitis: Aseptic meningitis with fever and coma has been observed on rare occasions 
in adult patients on ibuprofen therapy. Although it is more likely to occur in patients with systemic 
lupus erythematosus and related connective tissue diseases, it has been reported in adult patients 
who do not have underlying chronic disease. If signs or symptoms of meningitis develop ina 
patient on CHILDREN’S ADVIL® SUSPENSION, the possibility of its being related to ibuprofen should be 
considered. 

Renal Effects: As with other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, long-terrn administration of 
ibuprofen to animals has resulted in renal papillary necrosis and other abnormal renai pcithology 
in humans, there have been reports of acute interstitial nephritis with hematuria, proteinuria, and 
occasionally nephrotic syndrome. 

Asecond form of renal toxicity has been seen in patients with prerenal conditions leading to reduc- 
tion in renal blood flow or blood volume. In these patients, administration of a nonsteroidal anti- 
inflammatory drug may cause a dose dependent reduction in prostaglandin formation and pre- 
cipitate overt renal decompensation. Patients at greatest risk of this reaction are those with 
impaired renal function, heart failure, liver dysfunction, and those taking diuretics and the elderly. 
Those patients at high risk who chronically take CHILDREN'S ADVIL * SUSPENSION should have renal 
function monitored if they have signs or symptoms of azotemia. Discontinuation of nonsteroidal 
anti-inflammatory drug therapy is typically followed by recovery to the pretreatment state. 

Since ibuprofen is eliminated primarily by the kidneys, patients with significantly impaired renal 
function should be closely monitored and a reduction in dosage should be anticipated to avoid 
drug accumulation. 

information for Patients: Physicians may wish to discuss with their patients the potential risks and 
likely benefits of treatment with CHILDREN’S ADVIL" SUSPENSION. 

Laboratory Tests: Meaningful (3 times the upper limit of normal) elevations of SGPT or SGOT (AST) 
occurred in controlled clinical trials in less than 1% of patients. A patient with symptoms and/or signs 
suggesting liver dysfunction, or in whom an abnormal liver test has occurred, should be evaluated 
for evidence of the development of more severe hepatic reactions while on therapy with ibupro- 
fen. If abnormal liver tests persist or worsen, if clinical signs and symptoms consistent with liver 
disease develop, or if systemic manifestations occur, CHILDREN’S ADVIL" SUSPENSION should be 
discontinued. 

Diabetes: Each 5 mi of CHILDREN’S ADVIL® SUSPENSION contains 2.5 g of sucrose which should be 
taken into consideration when treating patients with impaired glucose tolerance. It also contains 
350 mg of sorbitol per 5 mL. Although in clinical trials CHILDREN'S ADVIL™ SUSPENSION was not asso- 
ciated with more diarrhea than contro! treatments, should a patient develop diarrhea, the physi- 
clan may wish to review the patient's dietary intake of sorbitol from other sources. 

Drug Interactions: Coumarin-type Anticoagulants: Bleeding has been reported when ibuprofen 
and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents have been administered to patients on cou- 
marin-type antic lants; the physician should be cautious when administering CHILDREN'S 
ADVIL® SUSPENSION fo pctients on anticoagulants. “ 
Aspirin: Concurrent use of aspirin is not recommended. 

Methotrexate: In vitro studies indicate that ibuprofen could enhance the toxicity of methotrexate 
Caution should be used if CHILDREN’S ADVIL® SUSPENSION is administered concomitantly with 
methotrexate. 

H> Antagonists: In studies with human volunteers, coadministration of cimetidine or ranitidine with 
ibuprofen had no substantive effect on ibuprofen serum concentrations. ; 

Furosemide: louprofen can reduce the natriuretic effect of furosemide and thiazides in some 
patients. During concomitant therapy with CHILDREN’S ADVIL ® SUSPENSION, the patient should be 


observed closely for signs of renal failure as well as to assure diuretic efficacy. 

Lithium: \lbuprofen produced an elevation of plasma lithium levels (15%) and a reduction in renal 
lithium clearance (19%) in a study of 11 normal volunteers during the period of concomitant drug 
administration. Patients should be observed carefully for signs of lithium toxicity. Read package 
insert for lithium before its use. 

Pregnancy: Administration of ibuprofen is not recommended during pregnancy or for use by 
nursing mothers. 

infants: Safety and efficacy of CHILDREN’S ADVIL® SUSPENSION in children below the age of 

12 months have not been established. 

ADVERSE REACTIONS: The most frequent type of adverse reaction occurring with CHILDREN’S 
ADVIL® SUSPENSION is gastrointestinal. In clinical trials among adults involving chronic administration

OVERDOSAGE: Patients with a history of ingestion of greater than 100 mg/kg should have induced 
emesis or gastric lavage. Multiple dose oral administration of activated charcoal may be useful 
Supportive therapy may include oxygen, respiratory support, and parenteral fluids. Because the 
drug is acidic and excreted in the urine, administration of sodium bicarbonate and induction of 
diuresis may be beneficial. 

DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION: Juvenile arthritis: 30-40 mg/kg day in 3 or 4 divided doses 

Fever: 5 mg/kg if baseline temperature is 102.5°F or below or 10 mg/kg if baseline temperature is

and OA: 1200-3200 mg per day in 3 or 4 divided doses

Eckerd expansion 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — Flush with a healthy cash flow and a 
revitalized store network, Eckerd Drug is expanding more ag- 
gressively and adding improvements to enhance its core business. 

“Our plan is to add about 50 new stores a year; that’s sort of 
our schedule,” said Harry Lambert, Eckerd’s president, in an 
interview at the company’s headquarters here. “We’ve got plen- 
ty of site opportunities in our markets, and for now, there are no 
plans to expand outside the states we’re already in.” : 

Lambert added that the company’s financial performance in 
the wake of its post-LBO turnaround has been such that “we’ve 
had no problem with our capital needs” in adding stores and im- 
proving Eckerd’s retail systems. The chain made a series of ac- 

uisitions last year, including the seven-unit Hilley’s chain in 
ees and 10 SupeRx stores in North Carolina, and now num- 
bers 1,605 drug stores in 14 states. 

Meanwhile, Eckerd has made plenty of improvements in the 
stores. One major change is a redesigned onion with easier 
patient access to pharmacists and an easier working area for 
practitioners. The new layout, which Eckerd began retrofitting 
into existing remodeled stores in 1989, eliminates the clerk’s

NEWo IN BIRIEF 


Smitty’s chain again for sale 


PHOENIX, Ariz. — Smitty’s Super Valu, this city’s chief 
food and combo store power, is again on the selling block. 

The chain is being offered for sale by new parent company So- 
canav, a Montreal-based conglomerate which purchased Smit- 
ty’s parent firm Steinberg last summer. Socanav is said to be in 
need of cash to pay down $300 million in debt following its acqui- 
sition of Steinberg for more than $1 billion. 

Smitty’s operates 24 stores, all in the greater Phoenix mar- 
ket, including 17 units with pharmacies. 


McKesson tabs Johnson as PCS ceo 


SAN FRANCISCO — McKesson Corp. named Robert C. 
Johnson, ceo of the California Pharmacists Association, ceo of PCS 
upon completion of a proposed buyout of all outstanding shares of 
PCS’s common stock for $15 cash per share. McKesson currently 
owns yes tely 86 percent of PCS’s stock. McKesson came 
under fire recently when pharmacists who use the drug wholesal- 
er put pressure on the company to stop PCS, the nation’s largest 
provider of third-party prescription claim services, from seeking 
contracts that discount third-party reimbursments. 


Ex-Reliable exec heads MedNet Group 


HARRISBURG, Pa. — David Dalton, formerly senior vp- 
pharmacy operations for Reliable Drugs, is the new president 
and ceo of the MedNet Group, an administrator of prescription 
drug programs and durable medical equipment with a national 
provider network for insurance carriers and self-insured com- 
panies. 

MedNet has offices in Ft. Lauderdale, Fla.; Washington, 
D.C. and Harrisburg, where Dalton will be located. 


Woolworth Express beefs up expansion 


NEW YORK — Woolworth Express, the specialty chain that 
emphasizes a tight assortment of H&BA, OTC, stationery, 
greeting cards and candy in a 6,000-square-foot format, will 
open 20 to 25 stores in 1990, according to Hank Von Speegle, di- 
rector of operations. The chain, which has been on a fast-track 
expansion schedule, added seven stores to its roster in the past 
three months and ended the year with 36 outlets. The seven new 
stores are in California (4), Detroit (2) and Chicago. Von Spee- 
gle also said that a Woolworth Express is slated to open a unit in 

ew York City on Jan. 26. 


NWDA\'s McHugh to be J.E. Goold prez 


PORTLAND, Me. — Robert E. McHugh, 7 of industry af- 
fairs for the National Wholesale Druggists’ Association, has 
been named president and chief operations officer of J.E. Goold 
& Co., a drug wholesaler based here. William G. Waldron, who 
had been president of the company, becomes chairman and ceo. 


Drug Fair chair Jane Matteucci dead 


GREAT FALLS, Mont. — Jane A. Matteucci, who was 
chairman of the board of Drug Fair Northwest based here, died 
last month at her home in Palm Desert, Calif. She was 83. 
Through her marriage to Paul A. Matteucci, who died in 1982, 
she became involved in Drug Fair Northwest, the family busi- 
ness of her husband. 

Mrs. Matteucci is survived by her sons Ed (the new president 
of Affiliated/Associated Drug Stores), Bill and Bob; as well as a 
sister, Bernice Allen, and five grandchildren.

4 DRUG STORE NEWS, January 8, 1990 


1 TSR RRR ES ES 
The decade’s top 10 retail stories 


It occured to me that my years at Drug Store News 
span the entire decade of the eighties — no more, no 
less. And, since the end of the decade is traditionally a 
time for looking back, I thought I’d outline my own 
personal list of the decade’s 10 most important retail 
drug stories. You’re welcome to write or 
call with your own suggestions. 


IN THE MARKET 


Rise of deep discounters. Low-mar- 
gin H&BA stores were not a new phe- 
nomenon at the start of the decade. But 
the concept of chains of super-sized 
H&BA discount stores began to gather 
steam in Ohio with Drug Emporium and 
in Detroit with F&M. Today there are 
several dozen companies that have 
latched onto the concept. But only three 
have leaped aggressively into new mar- 
kets all over the country: Drug Empori- 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


um, F&M and Phar-Mor. 


The pharmacy turf wars. The eight- 
ies was also the decade of the combina- 
tion store. The idea of combining a full-scale drug 
store and supermarket in a one-stop shopping envi- 
ronment got its start with Skaggs and Albertson’s in 
the previous decade, but really took off in the eighties. 
By the end of the decade there were more than 4,000 
supermarkets with pharmacies. Discounters like 
K mart and Wal-Mart weighed in with their own high- 
ly competitive pharmacies. 

Consolidation. The concentration of drug store 
sales among the top companies became particularly 
pronounced in the eighties, as big chains used their fi- 
nancial clout to become even bigger. By mid-decade, 
however, chains tempered their “growth for growth’s 


sake” philosophy, and began to concentrate on 
strengthening existing markets. 

Increasing importance of pharmacy. Drug chains 
pulled back from trying to be all things to all custom- 
ers, and began to concentrate on their strengths in 
health care. The trend is fueled by the increasingly 
large percentage of people found among the heaviest 
users of prescriptions—the elderly. 

Back to basics. Drug chains also turned back to their 
traditional strengths in H&BA, cosmetics, film and pho- 
to-finishing, and greeting cards and to newer core cate- 
gories like home/office and convenience foods. 

Investment in store renewal. As chains scaled 
back growth plans, they also began to pour more mon- 
ey into store renewal. That investment, along with 
convenient locations, is perhaps the most important 
strength for drug stores as they enter the retail wars 
of the nineties. 

Revolution in technology. The decade started with 
the beginnings of the pharmacy computer rollout. It 
ends with an explosion of new technological tools that 
are automating every phase of drug store operations. 

Personnel shortages. A pressing problem for the 
nineties began to manifest itself in the eighties as the 
baby boom generation came of age and shortages, es- 
pecially of pharmacists and entry-level clerks, became 
painfully apparent. 

Return to service orientation. Drug stores, in their 
attempt to differentiate themselves from the competi- 
tion, began to put more emphasis on customer service. 

Overstoring. Market after market is already saturat- 
ed. But chain drug stores, with their ability to fit into the 
smallest of niches and their concentration on crucial 
product lines, seem well-armored for the future. 


Is R&D to blame for 


Are prescription drug prices too high? Lots of peo- 
ple on Capitol Hill think so. Sen. David Pryor (D- 
Ark.), for one, is convinced that pharmaceutical man- 
ufacturers are charging too much for their products. 

Indeed, during recent hearings of his Senate Spe- 
cial Committee on Aging, Pryor blamed 


the collapse of the Medicare “Cata- 
strophic” drug benefit on rising Rx drug 
prices. 

Additionally, Pryor has charged that 
the pharmaceutical industry is price 
gouging state Medicaid programs, 
which have been “chopping and chisel- 


high Rx prices? 


According to PMA’s study, 80 
percent of of U.S. pharma- 
ceutical research spending is 
earmarked for NMEs. 


A report issued last summer by the Senate Aging 
Committee contends that much of the pharmaceutical 
industry’s R&D emphasis is on developing so-called

Industry officials justify their pricing practices as 
necessary to finance the research and development of 
new pharmaceuticals. And, indeed, no one can ques- 
tion the fact that American drug manufacturers invest 
huge amounts into R&D. 

Last year U.S. pharmaceutical firms invested over 
16 percent of their total sales revenue into R&D—the 
strongest commitment to research of any industry. 
Moreover, that commitment is increasing. Industry 
R&D spending has doubled every five years since 
1970, and today it costs an average of $125 million to 
bring each new drug to the market. 

According to Pryor and other industry critics, howev- 
er, the issue is not how much Rx drug manufacturers are 
spending on R&D, but whether these funds are really 
being used to bring important new drugs to the market. 


have been successful.” 

But is that really the case? A new analysis released 
by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association 
suggests that the industry is not focusing R&D on me- 
too products at the expense of breakthrough drugs. 

According to that study, some 80 percent of all U.S. 
pharmaceutical industry research spending is ear- 
marked for NMEs—New Molecular Entities which 
have never before been marketed. 

The report reveals that PMA member firms spent 
more than $26 billion on the development of NMEs be- 
tween 1981 and 1988, vs. $6.5 billion on improvements 
to existing products. 

Based on that, it’s difficult to criticize pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturers for not trying to develop important 
new drugs.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 8, 1990 


Ten Hot Categories: Foods/soft drinks; household cleaners 


Convenience drives chains’ grocery sales 


here’s a simple reason why gro- 

cery products, especially candy, 

snacks, beverages and conve- 
nience items, are one of the fastest 
growing categories in today’s drug 
stores. 

They need frequent replenishment. 
Today's time-harassed customers ap- 
preciate the convenience of picking up 
consumables in their neighborhood 
drug stores. 

They can shop a drug store in less 
than 10 minutes. It takes half an hour, 
on average, to get in and out of a food 
store. 

This year, buyers say candy and 
snacks are still their fastest growing 
grocery categories, up over 20 percent 
on a same-store basis in many cases. 

Soft drink and juice sales are also up 
dramatically, thanks to an expansion 
of cold soft drink programs as well as to 
tremendous feature activity in these 
categories. 

Convenience food sales are up, yen- 
erally between 10 percent and 15 per- 
cent on a same store basis in the stores 
that stock them. 

Walgreens has been the most ag- 
gressive chain with this category, put- 
ting c-food departments into almost 
two-thirds of all new stores and adding 
it selectively to existing stores in the 
right markets. Its current total: about 
590 c-food departments. 

However, SupeRx, Eckerd, Perry, 
Arbor, Osco, Longs, Thrift, Thrifty, 
Snyder Drug and many smaller chains 
like Best Buy Drug in Florida and 
Bill’s in California, all have c-food de- 
partments. Most are expanding them 
whenever they find the right locations. 

“Convenience foods are a viable cat- 
egory for us and we do very well with 
it,” says David Coleman who super- 
vises that program for Cincinnati- 
based SupeRx. “We constantly experi-

Red-hot meal replacement sales 


hat happens when a 

new product tastes 

good, works as it’s 
supposed to and receives na- 
tionally broadcast kudos from 
well-know TV personalities? 

If its Thompson Medical’s 
Ultra Slim Fast meal replace- 
ment diet product, it kicks the 
retailing equivalent of a game- 
winning 50-yard field goal. 

Drug chain merchandisers 
say their diet aid category 
sales soared — doubling or 
even tripling — after Thomp- 
son in mid-year launched UI- 
tra Slim Fast, an upgraded, 
better-tasting version of its 
seven-year-old Slim Fast. 

As a result of Slim Fast’s 
sales growth, the meal re- 
placement segment eclipsed 
appetite suppressants, which 
continued to weather bad 
press on phenylpropanola- 
mine, said to cause nervous- 
ness and palpitations in some 
individuals. Yet, suppres- 
sants, some buyers said, sus- 
tained growth, led by Thomp- 
son Medical’s Dexatrim, 
which has gained prominent 
shelf space at many stores.

Verschleiser, Thompson’s

600 percent in 1989, from 60

ries II shake, a dense formula-

ough and cold prod- 

ucts, a perennial leader 

in drug store OTC 
sales, are expected to contin- 
ue their upward sales trend as 
manufacturers and retailers 
prepare for the 90s. 

In 1990 alone, marketers 
anticipate cough and cold sales 
gains of 20 percent to approxi- 
mately $2.2 billion. 

With many OTC cough and 
cold products slated to be 
switched to Rx status in the 
next decade, retailers will 
have to find shelf space to ac- 
commodate the new products. 

“The switches are what 
really drove the category in 
the decade,” Paige Ilderton, 
buyer for Kerr Drug Stores, 
said. 

Another factor that will fuel 
the growth of the category is 
the grouping of allergy prod- 
ucts with cough and cold prod- 
ucts in consumers’ minds. 
Many cold sufferers will con- 
tinue to take an allergy prod- 
uct for their colds, and vice 
versa. This interchanging of 


product has helped boost 
cough and cold sales in the 
summer months. 

Increasing medical costs 
and a continuation of the trend 
toward self-care will also have 
a positive impact on the 
growth of cough/cold product 
sales. “The price of going to 
see a doctor and getting a pre- 
scription is increasing,” said 
Jan Stoffers, OTC buyer for 
Lewis Drug Stores. “Most 
customers will now try an 
OTC [remedy] before they 
spend the additional money to 
go to the doctor.” 

Picking up on the self-care 
movement, manufacturers 
are spending more advertis- 
ing dollars which, in turn, in- 
creases consumer awareness 
of product availabilty. “People 
are more aware of their health 
than ever,”’ said Norman 
Klein, buyer for Rockbottom 
Stores, a deep discounter 
based in New York. “They 
have the same symptoms that 
they did 50 years ago, but 
through advertising and pro- 


motion, they are becoming 
more knowledgeable.” 

Many retailers refer to this 
category as the “‘Plus’ Mar- 
ket,” due to the expansion of 
existing product lines. There 
seems to be a “quick fix” for al- 
most any ailment. 

“You have a kind of product 
for anything you need: regu- 
lar, maximum, maximum 
plus, maximum one, maxi- 
mum two,” Lewis’ Stoffers 
says. “A lot of these compa- 
nies are just duplicating them- 
selves. There are new intro- 
ductions right and left. I think 
that eventually the retailers 
will end up dropping the earli- 
er versions, because they’re 
going to start losing on them.” 

Rockbottom’s Klein thinks 
that manufacturers are really 
creating the market. By de- 
veloping line extensions, man- 
ufacturers believe they can 
— greater shelf space.

ticular line of 
persuades them

product an

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 8, 1990 - 


Ten Hot Categories: Film 


Film category boasts 
double-digit gains 
plus high-turn rates 


ilm continues to develop 
as a proven performer at 


the front end of the chain 
drug store, with high turn 
rates making up for relatively 
slim margins in an increasing- 
ly competitive market. 

For the second year in a 
row, chain drug buyers and 
merchandise managers rated 
film as one of the 10 hottest 
categories. Their faith in the 
film category is well-ground- 
ed, given the double-digit 
sales gains film has made in re- 
cent years. 

“We look for good sales 

owth this year from all our 
film] vendors, and I’d be hap- 
py but not surprised at a five 
to 10 percent gain,” noted a 
spokesman for Perry Drug 

tores. “Film’s really a ‘turn’ 
category for us; where the 
margins are narrow, but the 
turns are very high.” 

“Film margins are not 
great; the margins are in de- 
veloping,” added a spokesper- 
son for Smith’s Food & Drug 
Centers in Salt Lake City.” 


Three key forces 


The healthy sales gains 
most retailers expect to con- 
tinue in the 1990s are still com- 


ing from three key forces: the 
continuing boom in 35mm am- 
ateur photography, new prod- 
uct development from the big 
film manufacturers, and con- 
tinuing strong promotional 
support from both the manu- 
facturers and the retailers. 

At Kinney Drugs in upstate 
New York, for example, film 
sales benefit from heavy chain 
support, eee ag buyer 
Jerry Houghton. The catego- 
ry is featured in “every major 
circular, every two or three 
weeks,” Houghton said, and 
was given a second location 
last spring when Kinney add- 
ed a spinner rack from Kodak 
near the front registers. 

“Since we added the spin- 
ner, film sales are up, no ques- 
tion,” Houghton told Drug 
Store News. “I’d say Kodak’s 
sales are up nine to 10 percent 
since we put it in.” 

Kinney carries just two 
brands, Kodak and Fuji, and 
reaps “average” margins of 
about 30 percent, according to 
the buyer. 

Perry has also added a Ko- 
dak spinner rack on an “almost 
permanent” basis, according 
to a company source. The 
chain’s biggest gains, howev- 


the 


er, came after it made film a 
self-service category, with 
four to 12 linear feet of in-line 
positioning in “a high-traffic 
aisle,” the spokesman said. 

“Film is a demand item, with 
a lot of impulse buying, and the 
more you feature it, the more it 
moves,” he said. “It goes hand- 
in-hand with photofinishing; 
the more film we sell, the more 
we get back for photofinishing, 
and vice-versa.” 

The buyer credits the 35mm 
boom for much of the category’s 
growth. “Point-and-shoot cam- 
eras, that’s what pulling people 
in,” he said. “The 35mm format 
isn’t as sophisticated as it was a 
few years ago.” 

At Arbor Drugs, Perry’s 
hometown rival for the great- 
er Detroit market, film and 
photofinishing sales were up 
21.3 percent in fiscal 1989, to

New promotions 


Film manufacturers them- 
selves are keeping the sales 
pot boiling with massive ad 
support and new product de- 
velopments. In the last year, 
two of the biggest suppliers 
overhauled their product 
lines—Kodak with its new Ko- 
dacolor Gold series and Fuji 
with its Super HR film. 

Meanwhile, Polaroid is bank- 
rolling last year’s launch of its 
OneF lm all-purpose color film 
with another multimillion-dol- 
lar ad campaign in 1990. And 
Konica is attempting to build on 


its estimated 1.5 percent mar- 
ket share with its first-ever se- 
ries of television ads to boost 
brand name awareness. 

Despite intense competitive 

ressures from Kodak and 
uji, OneFilm is making in- 
roads in some markets, ac- 
cording to chain drug buyers. 

“OneFilm is doing surpris- 
ingly well here,” said a combo 
chain buyer in the Southwest. 
“The initial ads helped, but it’s 
too early to tell how it will do 
long-term.” 

One new product develop- 
ment that may spark additional 
business late this year will be 
the introduction of Kodak’s 
Stretch 35 camera. The cam- 
era, loaded with a 12-exposure 
roll of Kodacolor Gold 200 film, 
is designed as the first pan- 
oramic one-time-use camera for 
capturing broad, scenic views.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 8, 1990 


or the second straight 

year, chain drug buyers 

put batteries into the top 
10 list of Drug Store News’ Hot 
Categories Study. 

The reason is simple: bat- 
teries are ultra-competitive, 
but they fly off the shelves. 
This year, well over 3 billion of 
them will move past the regis- 
ters for the nation’s retailers, 
and drug chains will again be 
in the thick of the promotional 
slugfest for market share. 

“Batteries have always 
been a traditional volume cat- 
egory and they’ve become a 
dynamic end of the business,” 
noted a spokesman for Perry 
Drug Stores, which frequent- 
ly promotes batteries in sec- 
ondary store locations. 
“They’re a disposable, high- 
impulse, consumable item 
with fairly low margins but 
tons of dollar volume.” 

“I get an increase in battery 
sales every year,” added Mike 
Gentry, assistant vp for Crown 
Drugs in Advance, N.C. 

“Batteries move very well, 
and price doesn’t matter that 
much,” added Bob Tansle, a 
store manager for Sid’s Get It 
For Less in Canton, Ohio. 
“People are going to buy them 
whether we get them on deal or 
not, because they need them.” 

Indeed, a host of consumer 
electronics products have 
found their way into consum- 
ers’ lives in the past decade — 


Ten Hot Categories: Batteries 


products that weren’t around a 
few years ago, but which have 

iven rise to enormous market- 
ing opportunities. The revolu- 
tion in consumer electronics — 
including camcorders, porta- 
ble tape decks, boom boxes, 
electronic games, point-and- 
shoot 35mm cameras and other 
items — has fueled the rapid 
escalation in demand for bat- 
teries and made the category 
one of the most competitive in 
chain drug retailing. 

According to Eveready 
Battery Co., more than 230 
million portable audio units 
are in use now in the U.S., and 
they alone account for more 
than 40 percent of batteries 
sold each year. Toys and 
games account for another 21 

recent of battery sales; flash- 
ights and lanterns generate 
17 percent; and photo ac- 
counts for 12 percent of the to- 
tal market. 

Another manufacturer esti- 
mates that the average U.S. 
household now carries nine or 
10 battery-operated devices, 
and makes 22 to 25 battery 
purchases a year. 

Equally significant, says 
Eveready, the high-end, long- 
lasting alkaline segment of the 
market is up more than 60 per- 
cent in the past six years, to 
well over $2 billion in annual 
revenues.

able segment of the market

cut package size to one-third

Rayovac has a way to go be-

Climbs in net, revenues 
in Rite Aid’s 2nd atr. 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — 
Rite Aid corporate revenues 
gained 14 percent to $791.7 mil- 
lion, and net income increased 
35.8 percent to $22.5 million, or 54 
cents a share, for the third quar- 
ter ended Dec. 2. 

Included in the net income is an 
$18.4 million after-tax gain from 
the sale of the company’s 46.8- 
percent interest in Super Rite 
Foods Inc. 

Excluding a $22 million write- 
off to provide for the chain’s video 
department closings, income 
from continuing operations was 
$17.5 million, up 10.7-percent 
over last year’s period. After the 
pre-tax charge, income from con- 
tinuing operations was $4.1 mil- 
lion, or 10 cents a share, down 
from $15.8 million, or 38 cents a 
share, in the prior-year period. 
This charge reduced income from 
continuing operations by an after- 
tax amount of $13.4 million, or 32 
cents a share. 

Revenues from the drug store 
segment, which operated 2,340 
stores on Dec. 2, advanced 13.7 
percent to $749.0 million for the 
third quarter. Net income before 
the video provision was up 12.1 
percent, to $16.5 million. 

Year-to-date, corporate sales

compared with $1.9 billion for the

cluding the video provision, gained 
4.9 percent, to $56.9 million. 


Revco’s 2nd qtr. sees 
sales, op. income hikes 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — With 
46 fewer stores in operation com- 
pared to this time last year, 
Revco D.S., Inc. reported an 8.6- 
percent increase in sales, for the 
second quarter ended Nov. 12, to 
$620.9 million. Net loss for the 
quarter decreased to $8.7 million, 
from last year’s $17.9 million, and 
operating income rose to $7.2 mil- 
lion, from last year’s $9.7 million 
loss. 

For the first six months of the 
year, Revco’s sales improved 5.5 
percent, to $1.22 billion, and op- 
erating income rose to $2.1 mil- 
lion, from last year’s $20.9 million 
loss. 

As Revco entered the holiday 
selling season, improved inven- 
tories contributed to the 9.1-per- 
cent increase in comparable store 
sales posted for the six-month pe- 
riod.

Dart Drug puts seven leases on market 


LANDOVER, Md. — Dart Drug, Inc., which operates Fan- 
tle’s Drug Stores and Total Plus deep discount stores, an- 
nounced plans to sell seven store leases—five in Virginia, one in 
Mar aad, and one in Washington, D.C. . 

All seven stores are presently closed, and in three of the 
stores subtentants are paying rent. Dart, which filed Chapter 
11 in August last year, retained the services of Keen Realty 
Consultants, a Great Neck, N. Y.-based company, to dispose of 
the store leases. Keen previously disposed of several hundred 
retail outlets for Revco D.S. when it filed Chapter 11 nearly a 
year and a half ago. 


Red Cross, NACDS aid disaster victims 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — The Red Cross Relief Fund, aided 
by NACDS efforts, raised $92 million to assist victims of Hurri- 
cane Hugo and the San Francisco earthquake. 

In a separate matter, NACDS has promoted Stephen Per- 
lowski, former director of trade programs, to the newly created 

sition of executive assistant to the president. He reports to 

n Ziegler. The trade group is also taking steps to develop a 
“strong” state affairs department, Perlowski said. 


Super Gen’ taps public affairs head 


WOODBRIDGE, N.J. — Betty Greitzer has been named di- 
rector of public affairs at Supermarkets General Corp. Greitzer, 
an attorney, was promoted from manager of public affairs. 


Ryan named CVS’ exec vp-operations 


WOONSOCKET, R.I. — Thomas Ryan, senior vp-phai macy 
the past 10 months at CVS, has been promoted to executive vp- 
operations. He is responsible for store operations and pharmacy 
activities. Ryan, who joined CVS in 1974, replaces J. Kevin 
Hughes, who has retired. 


May’s opens 5th Okla. deep discounter 


TULSA, Okla. — May’s Drug Stores recently opened its fifth 
Drug Warehouse deep discount store in this market. 
The remodeled 19,000-square-foot store, which offers more 
than 20,000 beauty, cosmetic, drug and household items, re- 
laces an older, 8,900-square-foot May’s Drug store vacated in 
ovember. The store features a one-hour photo lab and the ar- 
ea’s largest discount greeting card department. 


Hallmark to purchase Dakin 


KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Hallmark said it has agreed to buy 
Dakin, Inc., the maker of plush toys, in a move the card compa- 
ny said will allow marketing synergies. Dakin had $150 million 
in revenues last year. 


Rite Aid appoints Hansen vp, treasurer 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — Rite Aid has appointed Doug 
Hansen vp and treasurer, replacing Robert Brown, who retired. 

Hansen comes to Rite Aid from Tambrands, based in Lake 
Success, N.Y., where he was treasurer the — five years. Pre- 
viously, he was vp and treasurer of Geo International Corp., 
formerly Peabody International, of Stamford, Conn.

Fire destroys an Amherst tradition 


AMHERST, Mass. — 
Many Amherst College stu- 
dents paused to read the 
sign on the door. It began, 
“To all our loyal friends and 
customers: It is with great 
difficulty that we aave 
reached a decision not to re- 
open College Drug Store.” 

The sign went on to note 
that the drug store had 
served Amherst since 1910; 
that it was “truly an old- 
fashioned neighborhood 
drug store,” with a soda 
fountain that later gave way 
to cosmetics; and that it was 
among the first pharmacies 
in the state to computerize. 
The message was signed, 
“John and Kate Hersey.” 

Kate Hersey’s grandfa- 
ther, William McGrath, 
bought the business 79 

ears ago. Her father, Wil- 
iam McGrath Jr., took over 
in the 1930s, and in 1954, 
~oved the business to its 
current corner location. 

“T don’t even like to come 
in here anymore,” said 
aapeioerre ohn Hersey as 

e picked his way past the 
debris and empty shelves— 
about all that’s left in the 
store after a fire spread 
from the shoe shop next 
door on Nov. 4. 

“The computer was run- 
ning, and it just sucked in 
the heat and smoke,” Her- 
sey recalls. 

Hersey had a full cellar of 
inventory, and the insur- 
ance company sent the sal- 
vagers in within three or 
four days. “Everything 
went,” he said. 

Then the state came in: 
“We sealed all the boxes, 
and $60,000 worth of drugs

But the coup de grace for 
the Herseys was a state law 
requiring that they install 
an elevator to accommo- 
date the handicap as 
part of renovations. The el- 
evator would have to be in- 
stalled at the rear of the

That spelled the end for

where to buy,” he said. 

But that’s history. Now 
Hersey, 41, plans to be- 
come a hospital pharmacist.

operated by a licensed op- 
tometrist, who leases the 
space. A pair of glasses, in- 
cluding frames and lenses,

Bindley Western tabs prez, COO 


INDIANAPOLIS — Keith 
W. Burks, 31, has been named 
president and chief operating 
officer of Bindley Western 
Drug Co., the main operating 
division of Bindley Western 
Industries, William E. Bind- 
ley, chairman and ceo, an- 
nounced. 

Burks, who was also elected 
a senior vp of the parent com- 

any, replaces C. Richard 
Zartman, who retired Jan. 1. 

Burks, a certified public ac- 
countant, joined the company 
in 1977 as a management 


trainee in the warehouse and 
progressed to controller in 
1985 and vp and !adianapolis 
division manager in 1987. The 
following year, he was elected 
a group vp. 

artman, 65, came to Bind- 
ley Western in 1976 and in 
1985 as vp and general manager 
of the Southeastern division in 
Orlando, Fla. In 1985 Zartman 
was promoted to executive vp. 
Two years later he was elected 
president. Zartman will contin- 
ue to serve as a director of the 
parent company.

new to anyone reading this column. But there’s a hell 
of a difference between talking squeeze theory in the 
office and actually living it on the street..The parties 
and monies involved here aren’t important, but the at- 
titude is. And it lends a fresh positive perspective on 
today’s buzzword, partnering, which is the antithesis 
of what happened to me this day. 


The problems begin 


I was irked by my mid-afternoon delivery to this 
popular multi-million-dollar Manhattan eatery—not 
just because the client wanted more for less, but be- 
cause of the implicit threat, the lack of fairness and the 
lack of recognition of how these high-quality hors 
d’oeuvres contributed to his image. 

As I entered, customers were lined up waiting for 
tables. People parted so I could maneuver toward a 
rear counter with the order. One of the proprietors 
met me to examine the merchandise and invoice. Then 
the fun began. 


patrons. 

This, of course, is a small-time example of the client- 
vendor relationship that has existed since time imme- 
morial: favors, special services and buying the busi- 
ness have always been around. 

I’m an editor, not a supplier. But I felt like one for 
the day, and can now lend more sympathy to people 
caught in these squeeze plays regularly. 

On the bright side for the chain drug industry, 
heavyweight marketers from top retail chains are 
talking beyond platitudes about developing true part- 
nerships with suppliers—and moving deliberately in 
that direction. Without large and small suppliers, af- 
ter all, merchants would miss a lot: new product ex- 
citement to draw customers, incentives to promote 
lots of lines, and the knowledge with which to plano- 
gram effectively and derive maximum benefit from 
what’s on their shelves. 

After the way I felt that day, I hope these partner- 
ing efforts work.

Execs predict acceleration of mergers & acquisitions: survey 


NEW YORK — Merger 
and acquisition activity will 
stay at the current level or 
pick up over the next five 
years, rather than decrease, 
predicted 53 percent of the 150 
top executives at Fortune 
1000 companies who respond- 
ed to a survey by Braxton As- 
sociates, the strategic consult- 
ing arm of Touche Ross. 

oreover, 77 percent of re- 
spondents expect merger ac- 
tivity in their own industry to 
maintain current levels or in- 
crease next year. 

The survey was done to pro- 
vide insight into the increas- 


ingly important corporate 
strategy of growth by merger. 
Braxton noted that 1988’s deal 
value of about $250 billion, as 
reported by W. T. Grimm, 
represents 40 percent of the 
annual capital expenditures of 
U.S. corporations. 

Mergers and acquisitions 
represent significant invest- 
ments and are typically a com- 
pany’s largest and most time- 
consuming investment 
decision in the year the deal is 
done, Braxton said in the sur- 
vey report, yet, “In spite of 
the stakes involved, the ac- 
quiring companies’ odds of 


success are lower than for re- 
investment into the base busi- 
ness.” One reason, according 
to Braxton, is the 40-percent 
premium above market value 
that acquirers typically pay. 

Ninety percent of survey 
respondents said their own 
companies are likely or possi- 
bly will do additional mergers 
within the next two years. 
Those who report past success 
with mergers are more likely 
to plan future ia

place in the 1980s is not a cycli-

Sales top $1B in 
Bergen’s first qtr. 


ORANGE, Calif.—Bergen 
Brunswig’s net sales and other 
revenues broke the $1-billion bar- 
rier for the first quarter ended 
Nov. 30, increasing 13 percent to 
$1.09 billion, from $968 million in 
the year-ago period. 

Net earnings were a record 
$14.9 million. The quarter in- 
cludes the impact of the 3.3 mil- 
lion additional shares resulting 
from last February’s recapitaliza- 
tion. For the prior-year quarter, 
earnings were $12 million. 


Sales up, net down for 
Genovese’s 3rd qtr. 


MELVILLE, N. Y. — Geno- 
vese Drug Stores reported sales 
for the third quarter ended Nov. 
10 of $90.2 million, a 12.5-percent 
increase from last year, with net 
income of $599,000, down from 
last year’s $657,000. Year-to-date 
sales were $294.7 million, up 13.9 
percent over last year, with in- 
come of $2.1 million, down from 
last year’s $2.9 million.

McK plans big, new Sf. Louis DC 


SAN FRANCISCO — McKesson Drug Co. plans to break 
und on a new 234,000-square-foot distribution center near 
St. Louis, Mo., early this year. 

The facility, which will replace a smaller DC in operation since 
1966, will be constructed on a 15-acre site in O’Fallon, about 25 
miles west of St. Louis. 

McKesson has opened four new distribution centers in the 
past 15 months, in Cincinnati; Tampa, Fla.; Oklahoma City; 
and Salt Lake City, bringing the company’s total warehouse 
space to 4.4 million square feet. With the planned DC in St. 
Louis, McKesson’s warehouse count will be 47, all linked by 
satellite communications to a computer center near Sacra- 
mento, Calif.

charges of attempted bribery of an Ohio State Board of Pharma- 
cy member, which they vigorously deny.

SAN FRANCISCO — Judie Doherty, vp-merchandising for 


McKesson Drug Co., was named may le of the National 
Wholesale Distributor’s Association ( A) consumer prod- 
ucts marketing committee. 

She will serve as chairperson for one year, and has served on

her current position at McKesson in 1985, and is responsible for 
developing merchandising policies, plans, selection of new 
items and categories, and selections with suppliers.

DRUG STORE NEWS, February 5, 1990 


OPINION 


Corner drug store’s style still vital 


— * 
ica vr eal 


4 


ne 


A film presentation at Walgreens’ recent annual 
meeting had a brief and funny historical vignette por- 
traying the founder of the chain, Charles R. Wal- 
green, speaking on the telephone with a customer. 
The customer, a pleasant, matronly woman, was or- 

dering “powders” for her husband. As 


IN THE MARKET 


the woman gave her order, Mr. Wal- 
green repeated it loudly to a pharma- 
cist, who filled it and dispatched a deliv- 
ery boy. And before the conversation 
with the drug store owner had ended, 
the delivery boy was knocking on the 
customer’s door. It was perhaps the ear- 
liest use of telecommunication as a pow- 
erful retailing tool. And it helped Wal- 
green cement a reputation for friendly 
and efficient service that hasn’t dimin- 
ished over the years. 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


The attributes of the “corner drug 


store” that marked Walgreens in the 
early part of the century are as competi- 
tively potent today as ever. And it is these attributes 
that have the potential of setting drug stores—both 
chains and independents—apart as they do battle with 
the giants of food retailing and mass merchandisers in 
the nineties. 

Convenience, in terms of both location and store 
size, is the main competitive attribute that drug 
stores have going for them. Female customers, who 
comprise about three-quarters of the typical drug 
store shopper base, also make up an increasingly 
large portion of the national work force. As such, 
they are pressed for time. Often they will choose a 


nearby drug store to pick up those two to three items 
that make up a typical transaction, rather than driv- 
ing to a more remote supermarket, parking a long 
distance from the door, walking hundreds of feet to 
pick up those items and then standing in a slow-mov- 
ing line to check out. 

The focus on health and beauty care is the second 
potent attribute that drug stores inherit from the old- 
time corner drug store. It has become almost a cliché 
to talk about getting back to basics, but as competitive 
pressures intensify it’s worth constant repetition. 

Service is another attribute that needs to be pre- 
served. That doesn’t mean making deliveries before 
the customer hangs up the phone. But it does mean 
knowledgable and friendly pharmacists and clerks, 
speedy and accurate check-out and even more modern 
services like credit card acceptance, as the article in 
this issue suggests. The idea of service can also ex- 
tended to fostering ease of shopping (Is there any re- 
tailer who hasn’t heard the complaints of customers 
after a store layout is changed?), and to store ambi- 
ance: good lighting, lack of clutter and cleanliness. 

There’s much more, of course, and all of it is woven 
together like a complex spider web. But it it is these 
main attributes of the corner drug store that will help 
ensure drug stores’ survival over the long haul. 

The Wal-Marts, the huge combo stores and the su- 
per-sized deep discounters may seem as big and bad to 
drug store retailers as Tyrannosaurus Rex seemed to 
early mammals in the Age of Dinosaurs. But the mam- 
mals exploited their niche and won out. That’s not to 
say that drug stores will win this battle, but they 
won’t be luncheon morsels either. 


Rx ad decision shows high court asleep 


In one of the most important rulings of the 1970s, the 
U.S. Supreme Court struck down Virginia’s law prohib- 
iting price advertising of prescription drugs on grounds 
that this violated the First Amendment. 

Certainly that was a landmark decision for retail 
pharmacy. It quickly lead to the elimina- 


WASHINGTON 
PERSPECTIVE 


tion of similar pharmacy price disclosure 
bans in a number of other states. But the 
importance of that ruling transcended the 
drug store industry. 

In overturning the state’s Rx ad ban, 
the high court held for the first time that 
“commercial speech” (e.g. advertising) 
is entitled to many of the same First 
Amendment protections as speech by 
private individuals. 

Suddenly, it became acceptable to ad- 
vertise a wide range of goods and servic- 
es that previously had been taboo. Doc- 


KEN RANKIN 


tors, lawyers and other professionals 


began to advertise their services, and in 
the process the marketplace became a little more com- 
petitive. 

Soon private, non-governmental restraints on 
pharmacy price disclosure came under fire. Under 
pressure from Federal antitrusters, APhA and a num- 
ber of state pharmacy organizations were forced to re- 
cind long-standing “ethical” codes prohibiting phar- 
macists from advertising prescription prices. A little 
more competition crept into the system. 

Needless to say there was considerable resistance 
to the notion that pharmacists should be free to adver- 
tise Rx prices. Indeed, many independent pharma- 
cists and pharmacy leaders favored pharmacy board 
rules outlawing even the disclosure of prescription 
prices in response to telephone requests. The way this 
group saw it, if consumers wanted to compare prices 
for Rx drugs, they could darn well walk from pharma- 
cy to pharmacy to do it. 

Organized pharmacy groups in a number of states 


did their best to circumvent both the spirit and the 
substance of the Supreme Court’s Rx ad ruling. One 
common ploy was to allow ads for prescription medi- 
cines, but to require disclosure of so much irrelevant 
information that advertising became impractical. 

Over the years many of these thinly-veiled state re- 
strictions on Rx price disclosure have been identified 
and shot down for what they are. 

Suddenly last month, the tables turned. In one ofits 
first actions of the 1990s, the Supreme Court decided 
not to review a lower court’s ruling which upheld an 
anti-competitive New Jersey law that flagrantly re- 
stricts prescription price advertising by pharmacists. 

Indeed, not only does that statute bar price ads, it 
also prohibits the offering of discounts, “premiums or 
rebates of any kind whatever in connection with the 
sale of drugs” by New Jersey pharmacists. 

How in the world can pharmacists in the Garden State 
justify such a blatant ban on prescription price competi- 


tion? According to state officials, “razzle dazzle” price 


For another viewpoint, see Cohen’s Capsules, p. 43 


promotions for prescription products will encourage pa- 
tients to switch to pharmacies offering lower prices. 

Of course, that’s exactly how the free enterprise 
marketplace is supposed to operate. But supporters of 
the New Jersey law contend that such pharmacy hop- 
ping by consumers would undermine the state’s goal 
of enrolling all Jerseyites in a pharmacy-based patient 
medication profile system. 

That’s baloney. Nobody really believes that New Jer- 
sey’s ban on Rx price cutting has nothing to do with the 
ongoing effort of independent pharmacists to insulate 
themselves from price competition. 

I suppose we can’t really blame independent drug- 
gists from trying to avoid competing with more effi- 
cient chains on the basis of price. But we certainly can 
blame the U.S. Supreme Court for falling asleep at the 
switch when this case came up for review.

DRUG STORE NEWS, February 5, 1990 


Baby Care | TREN IDs 


Convenience to 
drive baby care 


market sales 


he U.S. birth rate is ex- 
pected to drop through 
the mid-1990s, and more 
women, as many as 60 per- 
cent, will be entering the labor 
force at this time, predicts re- 
search firm Frost & Sullivan. 

But that doesn’t mean a dry- 
ing-up of the baby care mar- 
ket—far from it. Busy moms 
will be eying store shelves 
with greater intensity for con- 
venient, time-saving prod- 
ucts. 

The market will grow, de- 
spite the drop in the birth 
rate, to $7.5 billion by 1993, up 
from $5.9 billion in 1988, esti- 
mates Frost & Sullivan. Dis- 
posable diapers are the larg- 
est segment, with 1988 sales of 
$3.1 billion expected to reach 
$3.9 billion by 1993. 

Drug chains will see thin- 
ner, more absorbent prod- 
ucts, as well as alternatives to 
the disposable diaper crisis 
that environmentalists say 
adds to the solid waste prob- 
lem. 

Jean Allen, corporate com- 
munications director at Kim- 
berly-Clark, said that as far as 
biodegradability is concerned, 
“time will tell whether it will 
be a major factor in the diaper 
industry.” Diapers represent 
less than 2 percent of material 
found in landfills. 

But, opponents argue that 
there is little evidence that de- 
ge plastics actually can 

reak down in landfills. 

Yet, some chains are seeing 
the merit of offering alterna- 
tives to disposable _— 

Hannaford Bros., New En- 
gland combo operator, 

— Gerber Childrenswear’s 
reusable cloth diapers in all of 
its stores in December. 

Pay Less NW plans to de- 
vote space in its Feb. 25 circu- 
lar promoting cloth diapers and 
other diaper accessories—such 
as diaper pails, diaper pail lin- 
ers and rash ointments. Jim 
Culpepper, merchandiser, not- 
ed t e’ve always sold cloth 
diapers in our sections, but be- 
cause of environmental con- 
cerns, we decided to advertise 
them—to increase awareness 
and bring them to the fore- 


front.” 

chains are still 
taking a wait-and-see attitude 
on the sale of cloth diapers. As 
one Midwestern buyer put it: 
“It will be hard for a majority of 
consumers to break the conve- 
nience factor of disposables, 
but it’s a good idea to stock 
cloth diapers for those consum- 
ers who are aware of the envi- 
ronmental problem and want to 
do something about it.”

Ketchum & Co. posts $7.3M loss: 
margins, debt hamper turnaround 


By Paul W. Cockerham 

CLARK, N. J. — Ketchum 
& Co., the regional dru 
wholesaler based here, aakad 
a $7.3-million loss, on $238.9 
million in sales, for the fiscal 
year ended Sept. 30, 1989, its 
fifth straight year of red ink, 
according to financial docu- 
ments obtained by Drug Store 
News. 

This compares to a $2. 1-mil- 
lion loss, on $97.8 million in 
sales, for the five-month period 
ended Sept. 30, 1988 (when a 
reorganization of the compa- 
ny’s financial calendar took ef- 
fect), and a $7.2-million loss, on 
$231.3 million in sales, for the 
fiscal year ended April 30, 1988. 
The current figures reflect a 
$14.4-million decline in sales in- 
curred by Ketchum’s Michigan 
operations when the Farmer 
Jack chain, a — account, 
was bought by A&P and suppli- 
ers were subsequently 
switched. 

Hoping to reverse Ket- 
chum’s fortunes is Steven 
Young, the company’s chief op- 
erations and and chief financial 
officer, who added the title of 
president on Dec. 19. Efforts to 
reach Young for comment were 
unsuccessful at press time. 

The latest results indicate 
that Ketchum’s parent compa- 
ny, Paris-based Office Com- 
mercial Pharmaceutique, has 
yet to overcome persistent op- 
erational and market position- 
ing issues that had aired 
Ketchum for a couple of years 

rior to OCP’s gaining control- 
ing interest in the company in 
late 1987. 

Company officials at the time 
hoped that economies of scale 
would be realized through ac- 
quisitions, and once losses in 
were controlled, profitability 
would increase. But this strate- 
gy has been delayed, as the 
competitive metropolitan New 
York market (where Ketchum 
maintains a 15-percent share) 
has not yielded the margins the 
aggressively-priced company 
has sought. eidiie capital 
_— largely come from loans 
rom the parent company: more 
than $12.6 million in such loans

Sales soar, net slips for 


Drug Emporium 3rd atr. 

COLUMBUS, OHIO — Ag- 
gressive pricing caused 3rd-qtr. 
net earnings for Drug Emporium 
to slip, despite record sales, com- 
pany officials said. 

Net income for the quarter, 
which ended Nov. 30, was $1.4 
million, versus $1.7 million for 
last year’s period. Net sales 
reached $120.6 million, up 20 per- 
cent from last year. 

For the nine months, net in- 
come was $5.5 million, up from 
last year’s $4.9 million, on sales of 
$354.2 million, up from last year’s 
$294.0 million. 

During the quarter, the compa- 
ny completed the acquisition of 
the Milwaukee franchise opera- 
tions. Negotiations for the pur- 
chase of the Minneapolis fran- 
chise were suspended, according 
to acompany spokesperson, when 
agreement could not be reached 
on terms. 


Cardinal scores gains 
in 3rd-qtr. net, sales 


DUBLIN, Ohio — New mar- 
kets and increased hospital busi- 
ness helped boost Cardinal Distri- 
bution’s earnings and net for the 
third quarter ended Dec. 31. Earn- 
ings climbed 53 percent, to $3.3 
million, and sales increased 21 per- 
cent to a record $220.7 million.

As we enter a new decade, the staff at Drug Store 
News/Inside Pharmacy is pleased to present the 
1990 edition of our valuable Pharmacist’s Refer- 
ence to Patient Counseling. 

Pharmacy has changed dramatically over the past 
several decades. The professon being practiced to- 
day is very different from that of yesteryear. With few 
exceptions, pharmacists are no longer required to 
_.«e| | Compound prescriptions. Most of the labor-intensive 
compounded prescriptions have given way to so- 
phisticated and more potent prescription products al- 
ready prepared by drug manufacturers. While these new products bring vast im- 
provements in health care and the style of living for millions afflicted with disease, 
they also require a closer evaluation of a patient’s medical and drug profile by the 
pharmacist. 

The name we chose for this publication was not by accident. It is a reference 
book expressively prepared for pharmacists to aid them in counseling their pa- 
tients. Therefore, it is our hope that you, the pharmacist, wiil use this book fre- 
quently, so that your patients may continue to receive the quality health care they 
have come to expect from their pharmacist.

rweex | REVCO to refocus with selloff 


TURES 


By James Frederick 

TWINSBURG, Ohio — The planned sale of 712 
drug stores by Revco D.S. is likely to trigger a piece- 
teal buying spree by rival drug chains in 17 states, 
while leaving Revco free to focus on its strongest mar- 
kets. 

Revco announced that it was planning to concentrate 
its limited resources by selling off more than a third of its 
1,873-store network. The sales would leave Revco with 


Revco looks to trim down 


Revco currently operates 1,873 stores in 27 states and has annual 
sales in excess of $2.7 billion. Map shows current numbers of stores in 
each state. 


Ongoing operations: z Locations targeted for divestiture: LJ 


Revco’s proposed downsizing strategy draws a largely \ 
favorable response from analysts, investors and trade 
creditors. See page 85 for an analysis. 


1,161 stores generating nearly $2 billion in sales in 10 | 12 
contiguous Eastern and Southern states, and leave in- - 
tact its strong presence in the Carolinas, Georgia, Ohio, 
Virginia and other states. 31 

Revco will take a one-time, $230 million charge 
against third-quarter earnings to cover costs associated ;

DRUG STORE NEWS, February 19, 1990 


OPINION 


Revco’s decision to pare down its store base and re- 
focus on stronger markets east of the Mississippi 
makes a lot of sense. It is also highly reminiscent of ac- 
tions taken by other troubled retailing giants who 
have gone on to kindle smaller but hotter competitive 

fires in the ashes of their former em- 


IN THE MARKET 


pires. 

Safeway is one recent example that 
comes to mind. Like Revco, the Oak- 
land, Calif.-based food/drug operator 
was saddled by an onerous debt load fol- 
lowing its $4.2 billion leveraged buyout 
in late 1986. Once the supermarket in- 
dustry’s highest-volume performer, 
Safeway today is a far smaller yet more 
dynamic retailer. Its return to profit- 
ability was largely the result of a radical 
retrenchment back to a core of 1,100- 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


plus stores in the chain’s best markets. 
Revco’s retreat gives the chain its 


best shot to follow Safeway’s lead. In 
the go-go years of the ’70s and early ’80s, Revco gob- 
bled up stores with reckless abandon. No market 
seemed too distant or forbidding to discourage its in- 
satiable appetite. Though not the only drug chain pur- 
suing a “damn the torpedoes” growth strategy, Revco 
was the industry’s top honcho in store count. Its down- 
fall was as much a result of the oppressive weight of 
this far-flung empire as of some poorly conceived ac- 


Inflation no longer papers over 
poor performance, and the competi- 
tion has developed Jaws-like teeth. 
The best operators focus their re- 
sources on the most viable markets 
and forget the rest. 


quisition and financial decisions, most notably the Odd 
Lot purchase and an overly ambitious LBO plan. 
The prevailing industry strategy today is much 
more conservative. 
Now Revco has joined the group. It will use its 


Revco’s selloff key to revitalization 


limited resources to improve strong markets as well 
as to enhance crucial support systems. Though suc- 
cess is by no means assured, Revco has vastly im- 
proved its chances. 


* * * 


Now a quick report on my recent column suggesting 
a change in the traditional term health & beauty aids 
(H&BA) to health & beauty care (HBC) 

The response was small but decidedly opposed to any 
change. 

From T. Pat McLaughin, president of HABA 
West, Santa Ana, Calif., came this reply: 

“Being a basic traditionalist, my vote is to keep the 
category as it has been—H&BA. My two main rea- 
sons for this opinion are as follows: 

“1. H&BA started in the drug industry. Why let a 
food publication change the description. Let them 
stick to frozen food! 

“2. I'd really be in trouble. (I would have to get) a 
new company name, new stationery and new license 
plates [See photo above]. No way!” 

And from pharmacist Gerald Eger, Lebanon, Ohio, 
this tongue-in-cheek response: “An earth-shaking is- 
sue such as this surely makes third-party reimburse- 
ment, the generic drug controversy, the budget defi- 
cit and the plight of the homeless seem so trivial!” 

Ouch! 


Are retailers more skeptical than journalists? Are 
they too ‘knowing’ to consider a program for their chains 
that could pay huge return: -m a fairly modest invest- 
ment and convince line and stati people they are valued? 

I’m speaking of a corporate culture change, a major 

undertaking that needs total support 


from the chairman to store clerks in or- 


THE HUMAN SIDE 


der to work, yet has been proven to pro- 
duce tangible performance and profits 
improvements in companies committed 
to change. Hundreds of major packaged 
goods companies and others have such 
programs underway. 

Among them: Lebhar-Friedman, Inc., 
this newspaper’s parent company— 
which explains why this is on my mind. 
When thinking about how this program, 
Performance Management, is being en- 


AL HELLER 


acted where I work, I saw its tremendous 
retail applications. 


Retail, after all, is where customers in- 
teract mostly with part-time store staffers, who are in a 
position to foster shopper loyalties or cause them to be 
severed. Store staff is turning over at greater than 20- 
percent rates in many markets, and with the available 
pool diminishing, it makes sense to involve staff more 
deeply in the company’s mission and pay greater atten- 
tion to their achievements. Don’t underestimate them; 
assume they want to contribute to a chain’s success. 


Involvement key to motivation, productivity 


This proactive program may help many workers stay 
longer, work better and satisfy more customers. 

Nowhere but in retail are the fortunes of even the 
most disciplined, far-flung operators so vulnerable to 
the performance of fairly transient part-timers. In- 
deed, store staffers play a large role in a chain’s public 
image—and consequently, store-level productivity. 

Performance Management has so impressed J. Roger 
Friedman, this company’s president, that he is commit- 
ted to making Lebhar-Friedman one of the nation’s 50 
best companies to work for. The program emphasizes 
and rewards positive reinforcement, personal and team 
initiatives, and encourages each worker to assume an 
active role in defining his or her duties and goals. 

Some examples of how Performance Management 
has been working across the country: 

@ A Kodak division cited 60 percent more customer sat- 
isfaction and 70 percent more order-filling accuracy. 

@ First National Bank of Kansas City reduced cus- 
tomer complaints 97 percent and employee absentee- 
ism 51 percent over a one-year period. 

@ Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama boosted ad- 
judicated claims per employee by almost 300 percent 
over three years, and slashed unprocessed 30-day-old 
claims by more than two-thirds over 18 months. 

Are old cultural habits and negative politicking dif- 
ficult to kill? You bet. Bank on five years or more of 
patience and diligence, then count the emotional and 
fiscal rewards.

For the year ended Dec. 1, 
1989, SAMI was tracking drug 
store movement in 162 product 
categories. Their annual retail 
volume grew 5.8 percent over 
the preceding year to $12.2 bil- 
lion. Among these categories, 
55 were food, 50 were dry gro- 
cery/non-foods, and the re- 
maining 57 were health and 
beauty aids, which accounted 
for 68.5 percent of the total 
drug store universe measured 
by Arbitron/SAMI in drug 
stores. 

Shelf-stable foods showed 
the highest annual growth 
rate, 14.8 percent; combined 
non-food sales rose 6.2 per- 
cent, and health and beauty 
aids advanced 4.1 percent dur- 
ing the 52-week span.

produced annual drug store 
sales greater than $100 mil- 
lion, topped by internal anal-

($103.3 million). The most im-

“product advertisers” to disclose the country or countries in

Ads for a hair dryer assembled in the U.S. from components 
made in Japan, for e le, would have to include a statement

er survey found that the number of Americans who “conscious-

percent in 1985 to 37 percent last year.

dered, ever, consumers “are confused and misin- 
formed about where many products are made.” Wise said. This 
is at least partly due to the growing proliferation of goods which 
are assembled in the U.S. from imported parts, he told Con- 


gress. 

“As more and more finished products are made from foreign 
components, it becomes more difficult to discern the country of 
origin,” he said.

Chains weigh pros and cons of in-store photo mini-labs 


Photofinishing minilabs 
hold the promise of adding 
new dimension to a drug store. 
So far, chains experimenting 
with them are seeking ways to 
parallel the success of Eckerd. 

Longs, Genovese, Stan- 
dard, Pay Less NW, and 
SupeRx of Phoenix are among 
chains that have tested or are 
testing minilabs, following 
Eckerd, which has demon- 
strated how the labs can be 
winners.

Yet no drug chain besides 
Eckerd has launched a major 
commitment to the technol- 
ogy, although an in-store lab 
has the potential to enhance a 
chain’s image in the photo 
business. Maintaining trained 
staff and complex equipment, 
and investing to build the busi- 
ness, are all necessary, chain 
merchants told Store 
News. One chain, for example, 
found that store managers 
trained in the technology were 
forced to spend too much time 
running the equipment when 
assigned staff was absent. 


Expanding minilabs 


None of this has slowed 
down Eckerd. The chain now 
operates 130 minilabs 
throughout Texas and Flori- 
da, and has used minilabs stra- 
tegically to carefully cultivate 
its image as a film processor. 
The chain advertises its labs 
extensively as being “exten- 
sions of” its captive out-lab 
service. The labs occupy domi- 
nant front-of-store positions 
and feature high-profile, dis- 
tinctive fixturing as part of a 
total film/photo presentation. 

This view, of course, is not 
universally held by chain drug 
retailers. “Photofinishing [us- 
ing a wholesaler] is a very, 
very profitable business.

No matter who’s at NI’s helm, 
FoxMeyer runs steadily: analysts 


PITTSBURGH — A move 
by miffed stockholders to re- 
make the board of directors of 
National Intergroup is unlike- 
ly to hasten the FoxMeyer di- 
vision’s steady effort to attain 
industry performance stan- 
dards, in the view of some re- 
tail analysts. 

Assuming that Centaur 
Partners Group succeeds with 
a proxy vote to restack the 
board, it should have no more 
success than current manage- 
ment in a assets and 
improving FoxMeyer opera- 
tions, analysts felt. 

In response to Centaur’s fil- 
ing of a 13-D form, NI said 
that Centaur can add nothing 
to its ongoing business refo- 
cusing. Indeed, NI spokes- 
man Ed Klein says that NI has 
slashed long-term debt by half 
the past year, cut headquar- 
ters staff by 50 percent, and 
looks for a strong profit in- 
crease from its FoxMeyer di- 
vision in fiscal 1990. 

The drug wholesaler, de- 
spite modest gains in the third 
quarter, continued to post 
weak results and, with an op- 
erating margin of just over 1 
percent, compared poorly 
with the industry’s 2.5 per- 
cent average. To report signif- 
icant profit improvements, NI 
relied on special charges. 

“I’m not sure that a new 
management would do dis- 
cernibly better. This is not an 
opportune time to sell any of 
the key divisions of National 
Intergroup,” said John Tuma- 
zos, an analyst with Donald- 
son, Lufkin and Jenrette, re- 
ferring to NI’s effort to sell its 
steel and aluminum business- 
es. 

Centaur declared it owns 
16.53 percent of shares and 
will seek shareholder endorse- 
ment to increase the number 
of directors from 12 to 15 to 

ain a majority of the board. 

e group’s 13-D said it be- 
lieves that a higher value can 
be most quickly realized by 
selling some or all of the as- 
sets. 

Aldo Mazzaferro, analyst at 
C.J. Lawrence, pegged NI’s 
breakup value at $26 a share. 
NI closed at $16 Feb. 2 on the 
New York Stock Exchange, 
and has climbed only up to 
$20.25 in the last 52 weeks. 
The drug company, Mazza- 
ferro estimates, could fetch 
$490 million, without buying 
debt. At 20 percent of its reve- 


nue base, that’s “a pretty rea- 
sonable value,” he said.

and nine month lage that

Hikes in 1st-qtr. net, 
sales at Med Shoppe 


ST. LOUIS — Net earnings in- 
creased 20 percent, to $2.0 million, 
for Medicine Shoppe’s Ist quarter 
ended Dec. 31. Sales reported by 
franchised pharmacies increased 
18 percent, to $122.7 million, and 
franchise fees increased 19 percent 
for the quarter. 


Higher 2nd-qtr. results 
are posted by Staples 


NEWTON, Mass. — Central- 
ized distribution and high in-stock 
levels helped Staples, Inc. post 
higher sales and earnings during 
its second quarter, and contributed 
to double-digit comparable store 
sales gains, the company said. 

For the quarter, Staples earned 
$1.5 million on sales of $49.4 mil- 
lion. The earnings include a 
$500,000 credit for a net operating 
loss carry-forward, and compare to 
a $1.5 million loss for the same peri- 
od last year. The sales figures are 
75.5 percent higher than last year’s 
$28.2 million. 

Thomas G. Stemberg, chairman 
and ceo, noted that the chain’s cen- 
tralized distribution has helped 
control shrink, labor, freight and 
administrative expenses and re- 
duced goods’ cost. A “closed-loop 
direct marketing system” has af- 
fected marketing efficiencies and 
helped the chain gain share in com- 
petitive markets, he added.

Nichols dives into deep discounting 


NEW YORK — Taking a new tack, 
S.E. Nichols, Inc. said it will remake 
its discount stores into deep discount 
drug stores. 

It will be the first deep discount 
drug chain created through a conver- 
sion from another retail format. Called 
“Pharmhouse,” it will be among the six 
or seven largest deep discount drug 
chains. 

With stores in rural markets in New 
York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Mary- 
land and Delaware, Pharmhouse's 
toughest hurdle might be educating 
the consumer on the new health care 
and pharmacy slant, and putting over a 
consistent image. About half the Nich- 
ols stores have had pharmacies which 
will now be rolled out. chainwide. 

“We have a very good pharmacy op- 
eration. It’s been a growing part of the 
business,” said James Herlihy, sr. vp.- 
finance.

build a significant chain,” referring to 
store roll-out plans after the new for-

Downsizing results 


The downsizing took 
Safeway out of most of its ma- 
jor markets east of California, 
and reduced its store count by 
almost half, from more than 
2,200 units to 1,117 stores lo- 
cated primarily in the western 
U.S., the Mid-Atlantic region 
and western Canada. Among 
major Safeway assets to go 
were its southern California 
stores, to Vons; its Houston 
and Kansas City store divi- 
sions, to local ement 
LBOs; and its 60 Salt Lake 
City units, to Borman’s. 
Safeway also shed its store di- 
visions in E]] Paso, Dallas, Lit- 
tle Rock, Ark., and other mar- 
kets. 

In the process, however, 
Safeway raised enough money 
from the sales to cut its debt to 
$3.1 billion from $5.6 billion in 
1986, and shed many stores 
where profits were low and la- 
bor union headaches high. The 
asset sales also enabled the 
company to concentrate its re- 
sources on a few core markets, 
where it has been able to clean 
up and remodel stores, raise 
prices to boost margins and 
cash flow, and boost capital 
spending to improve its mar- 
ket share. 

Thus, Safeway now makes 
more in profits on a $14 billion 
sales base than it did ona pre- 
LBO base of $20 billion, when 
its store count was nearly 
twice as large. In addition, 
return on assets has gone 
from 13.5 percent to more 


than 20 percent; all divisions 
are “highly profitable,” ac- 
cording to Magowan, and the 
chain now ranks first or sec- 
ond in all its remaining mar- 
kets. 

“The LBO process itself 
caused us to transform the 
company into a truly excel- 
lent one,” Magowan said last 
year. “The discipline of pay- 
ing down the enormous ia t 
we owed forced us to set high 
hurdle rates for performance 
and new capital spending.” 

In addition, the chairman 
said, “The transformation of 
our operators from being man- 
agers to being co-owners of 
the business may have been 
fade powerful stimulus of

ras | worked,” said Jonathan

profitability quite nicely,”

rug stores can ex-

Stephanie Hayter, cosmetic

Space key to skin care merchandising 


that lines like Almay and Clar- 
ion are probably best left with 
their family. 


Family sets make statement 


“Almay first evolved as a 
skin care line and has been 
very successful in that area,” 
said the director of cosmetics 
for one major Southeastern 
chain. 

“If you separate skin from 
color, you’ll probably lose 
some color sales, and the same 
for Clarion. Clarion is strong- 
er as a color line, but its skin 
has been doing very well too. 
Now if we separate skin from 
color, we'll probably lose some 
Clarion skin sales. But with 
space so tight, it’s really hard 
to know what’s right to do.” 

This chain hopes to begin 
testing four or five different 
ways of merchandising skin 
care within the next two 
months. They feel that hair 
color should not be located too 
far away from the cosmetics 
area because their own con- 
sumer research indicates that 
customers have plenty of 
questions about this category. 

Because the chain has 
stores ranging in size from 
6,000 to 10,000 square feet, 
the final skin care planograms 
will have to be modified by 
store type. Management 
thinks a 20-foot set will be im- 
plemented, although 28 feet

Space constraints 


At SupeRx in Cincinnati, 
where management is also 
working on a new skin care 

lanogram, space is also tight. 

he chain is trying to develop 
a minimum 20-foot set that 
would link mass skin with 
some everyday sun care and 
deplilatories, as well as an 
“ideal” 36-foot set that would 
expand the 20-foot set with 4 
more feet for franchised 
brands as well as space for 
bath and shower products. 

Mike Russell, cosmetic 
merchandiser at the chain, 
said placing franchised brands 
with mass would give mass 
customers a chance to “trade 
up” to the more expensive 
franchised lines. So far, 
ogg for franchised lines 

as been relatively slow in 
most SupeRx stores, but the 
mass category has been able to 


generate double-digit growth 
in the low teens. 

By merchandising all skin 
care products together and 
giving the planogram a more 
organized presentation, Rus- 
sell thinks it may be possible 
to generate growth between 
15-20 percent a year or better. 

But because space in Su- 
peRx stores is tight, Russell 
will probably not continue to 
carry his franchised lines on 
the cosmetic wall with their 
families. 

He’s been working with Al- 
may on fixtures that would or- 
ganize his generic set by man- 
ufacturer for the franchised 
companies and by lines for the 
mass brands. He’s also hopin 
more mass manufacturers wil 
develops shelf organizers like 
the ones used by Neutrogena 
and L’Oréal for Plenitude. 

Russell was hoping to get 
the planogram seliina out to 
the stores by March and to fin- 
ish by mid-year.
