Drug store units pace Imasco 


to hikes in sales, earnings for ’89 
MONTREAL — Strong performance in its drug store units 


helped Imasco, Ltd. 


st a 16-percent gain in net earnings for 


the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, to $366.1 million (Canadian), com- 


pany officials reported. 


orporate sales increased 6 percent, to $14.7 billion. Sales 
and revenues for 1989 do not represent figures for the Grisanti’s 
restaurants and Peoples stores sold, or for the Howie’s discount 
drug stores that were converted into associate-owned Shoppers 


Drug Mart stores, officials said. 
rted a 24-percent increase in earn- 


Shoppers Drug Mart re 


ings, to $70.6 million, which Imasco attributed to —- growth 


and efficiencies realized from the Howie’s and Super 


conver- 


sions. Revenues decreased from $194.9 million to $136.2 million, 
excluding the Howie’s stores’ performance for the current year. 
Officials noted that if the Howie’s stores performance were ex- 
cluded from 1988 figures as well, 1989 revenues would show a 


19-percent increase. 


Meanwhile, Peoples returned to profitability last year, post- 
ing $8.0 million in earnings, compared with the previous year’s 
$8.3-million loss. Peoples saw 325 of its units, “where Peoples’ 
potential was limited,” sold last year, Imasco said, and as a re- 
sult revenues fell from $1.841 billion to $1.207 billion. 

Corporate performance for the fourth quarter saw Imasco’s 


net earnin 
sales were 


climb 14 percent, to $118.2 million. System-wide 
.9 billion, up 6 percent; revenues were $1.5 billion, 


down 2 percent (again, largely due to the sale of the Peoples 
units and the Howie’s stores’ conversion); and operating earn- 
ings increased 7 percent, to $205.0 million. 


S&P raises ratings 
of McKesson’s debt 


NEW YORK — Standard & 
Poor’s Corp. announced that it 
had raised its ratings on the se- 
nior debt and preferred stock of 
McKesson Corp., the San Fran- 
cisco-based drug wholesaler, to 
single-A plus from single-A. Rat- 
ings on the company’s subordinat- 
ed debt were raised to single-A 
from single-A minus. 

About $345 million of debt is af- 
fected by the upgrade. S&P said 
in a New York Times report 
that the upgrade reflects its 
“greater confidence” that McKes- 
son will “maintain its fine record 
of financial health.” 


O&M hits sales record; 
net income plunges 


RICHMOND, Va. — Weak 
gross margins caused Owens & 
Minor’s earnings to plunge, de- 
spite record sales, over the past 
fiscal year and fourth quarter, the 
wholesaler announced. 

Sales for the year ended Dec. 31 
were $952.9 million, a 30-percent 
increase, while earnings fell 70 
percent to $2.5 million. The 12- 
month results allow for a $2.5-mil- 


lion pretax loss from the devalua- _ 


tion of foreign glove inventory. 
For the quarter, sales increased 
nearly 46 percent, to $277.1 mil- 
lion, while earnings fell from $2.1 
million to $300,000. 


G. Gilmer Minor, III, president 
and ceo, attributed the company’s 
peformance an overall decline in 
gross margins, a doubling of in- 
terest expense due to acquisi- 
tions, and higher tax rates sus- 
tained from non-deductible losses 
incurred by the Harbor Medical 
subsidiary. Minor was encour- 
aged by declining S, G & A ex- 
penses and the improved working 
capital resulting from increased 
inventory turns, saying “al- 
though disappointed with the re- 
sults, we are not deterred from 
reaching our profit objectives in 
1990.” 


Hikes in net income, 
sales for CVS’s parent 


WOONSOCKET, R.I. — In- 
creases in both sales and net in- 
come were realized by Melville 
Corp., parent of CVS, for the 
year and fourth quarter ended 
Dec. 31. 

Year-end net income increased 
to $398.0 million, from last year’s 
$354.5 million, on sales of $7.553 
billion, up from $6.780 billion last 
year—all reflecting the acquisition 
of Bermans Specialty Stores, Inc. 
in November 1988. Per-share 
earnings increased $.30, to $3.56. 

For the quarter, net income in- 
creased from $205.3 million to 
$238.1 million, on sales of $2.519 
billion, up from last year’s $2.291 
billion. Earnings per share in- 
creased $.44, to $2.23.

@ WILLOWDALE, Ont. — The new-

Revco set for Charlotte H&BA expo 


CHARLOTTE, N. C. — This city will host its first Revco 
Health and Beauty Expo March 30-31 at the downtown Conven- 
tion Center. 

The free show, the first Revco has held outside its home mar- 
ket of Cleveland, will feature some 100 exhibitors of health, 
beauty and fitness products re demonstrations, product 
samples, celebrity ap ces and beauty makeovers. The 
event will also include health screenings and entertainment. 

Co-sponsors are American Greetings, American Vitamin/ 
Fields of Nature, Clairol and Pepsi-Cola. 

Celebrities will include gold-medal diver Greg Louganis, 
NFL great Gale Sayers and actor Jeff Conaway. 

This is our first expo to be held outside Cleveland,” said vp- 
marketing services Bob Newmark. “We chose Charlotte be- 
cause it’s a poe city and an iy sa market for Revco. It’s 
the heart of our business in the South.” 

Last year’s Cleveland Expo, to be held again this May, drew 
100,000 visitors, he said.

now on,” in light of the current 
highly leveraged environment. 

Bindley Western took a 
$2.98 million charge for Revco 
account receivables in the 
fourth quarter, but Burks 
said, “We look on the bright 
side in a case like this [and 
ask]: What have we learned?”

amount of our time” and not- 
ed, “We work on incredibly 
small margins, and whenever 
you have even a small wri- 
teoff, there’s a substantial ef- 
fect on earnings.” But he said 
he expects “things will fall into 
place sometime this of 
with Revco’s planned selloff of 
712 stores. 

Burks noted that, with 1989 
revenues of $1.6 billion, Bind-

“tremendous amount of

Agreement reached on McK buy of PCS common stock 


SAN FRANCISCO — 
McKesson Corp. and PCS 
have reached a definitive 
merger agreement whereby 
McKesson will make a tender 
offer to acquire all the public- 
ly held shares of PCS com- 
mon stock at $20 per share in 
cash. McKesson, which cur- 
rently owns about 86 percent 
of PCS’s outstanding stock, 
had originally proposed, on 
Dec. 22, to acquire the out- 
standing shares for $15 a 
share. 

Under the agreement’s 
terms, McKesson will acquire 
any PCS shares not purchased 
in the tender offer in a subse- 

uent merger transaction at 
the same $20 per share cash 
price. 

Approval of the merger 
agreement and offer was 


based on several factors, in- 
cluding the recommendation 
of a special committee of the 
PCS board and the opinion of 
First Boston Corp., the PCS 
committee’s financial adviser, 
which was that the proposal is 
fair from a financial point of 
view. 

McKesson said that in con- 
sideration of its agreement to 
proceed with the acquisition, 
its lawyers and lawyers for 
the plaintiff in a outstanding- 
stockholder lawsuit have 
reached an agreement in 
principle to settle the suit, 
which related to McKesson’s 
ownership of PCS and its pro- 

osal to acquire PCS’s public- 

y held shares. The settle- 
ment is subject to judicial 
approval, which is being 
sought. 


McKesson said the tender 
offer will begin soon. Morgan 
Stanley & Co. is acting as 
McKesson’s financial adviser 
on the transaction and will act 
as dealer manager for the 
tender offer. 


McKesson Corp. also re- 
cently announced completion 
of a previously reported trans- 
action in which Provigo Inc. of 
Montréal sold its subsidiary, 
Medis Health and Pharmaceu- 
tical Services Inc., to a new 


corporation jointly owned by 
Provigo and McKesson. Me- 
dis, based in Kirkland, Qué- 
bec, is the largest pharmaceu- 
tical distributor in Canada and 
the only one with nationwide 
distribution. 


AKRON, Ohio — U. S. 
Bankruptcy Court here 
has granted Revco D.S. a 
further extension of the 
period within which the 
chain has the exclusive 
right to file and gain ap- 
proval of a plan of financial 
reorganization. 

The court in late Febru- 
ary gave Revco until Jul 
31, 1990 to file a reorgani- 


Revco D.S. gains more time for reorganization 


zation plan, and until Oct. 
31, 1990 to obtain approval 
of the plan from its credi- 
tors. 

The exclusivity arrange- 
ment, common in Chapter 
11 bankruptcy proceed- 
ings, leaves Revco free to 
negotiate with its creditors 
without having to entertain 
takeover or reorganization 
proposals from outside bid- 


ders. 

In January, the compa- 
ny completed and shared 
with its creditors a revised 
five-year business plan 
which calls for the sale of 
more than 700 stores in 
Western markets, and the 
focusing of Revco re- 
sources on more than 1,100 
stores in 10 contiguous 
Eastern states.

Assortments, in-stocks 


drive tobacco profits 


Ithough unit sales of 
cigarettes are declin- 
ing at some drug 
chains, mirroring the tobac- 
co industry overall, many 
operators have been able to 
maintain and even boost cat- 
egory profits. 

Some chains buck the slid- 
ing sales trend by commit- 
ting to broad assortments 
and in-stock positions 
so smokers always know 


where they can find their 
favorite brands. Another 
important trv.id is that 
higher-margin generics, 
sub-generics, and single 
packs are assuming larger 
shares of category volume, 


buyers told Drug Store 
News. 

Sub-generics—lower- 
priced generics which can 
sell for half the price of 
branded goods—are bursting 
onto the scene at a time 
when vendors’ costs hikes 
and federal and state excise 
taxes have pushed the price 
of a carton of branded ciga- 
rettes to over $15 in many 
states. 

Some buyers feel that 
kind of price advantage 
gives sub-generics the po- 
tential to follow in the foot- 
steps of generics, the sy 
ment that in eight years has 
captured 15 percent of the 


market. 

“T think they'll catch on 
just because of the price 
point. And there will be a 
variety of choices,” said Rick 
Burns, Snyder Drug’s tobac- 
co buyer in Minneapolis. 

At Snyder’s, a carton of 
sub-generics such as Philip 
Morris’s Bristol and Liggett 
Group’s Pyramid retails for 
$9.99, compared with $12.99 
for a branded generic and 
$15.69 for a brand.

has posted annual same- 
store sales gains by empha- 
sizing in-stock positions and 
variety. The stores capture

DRUG STORE NEWS, March 26, 1990 


Bill proposes new agency to regulate 
tobacco advertising and ingredients 


WASHINGTON, D.C. — 
Tobacco interests are battling 
a U.S. Senate bill that would 
create a new agency to regu- 
late tobacco-product ingredi- 
ents and advertising, and 
spearhead stepped-up educa- 
tion and counter-advertising 
on the negative effects of to- 
bacco. 

Sponsored by Sen. Ted 
Kennedy (D-Mass.) and Sen. 
Orin Hatch (R-Utah), the bill 
would also restore to states 
and localities the power to 
write their own tobacco pred- 
uct labeling and advertising 
laws. Now the federal govern- 
ment has “preemptive power” 
over the states in that area. 

The agency would be called 
the Center for Tobacco Prod- 
ucts, and be under the Center 
for Disease Control, which is 
Sox of the Department of 

ealth and Human Services 
(HHS). 

“It’s unnecessary, it’s un- 
fair and the thinking behind 
the bill is based on false prem- 
ises,” said Michael Kerrigan, 
president of the Smokeless 


‘This is the most signifi- 
cant piece of anti-tobac- 
co legislation that I've 
seen in the last 12 years.’ 
—Michael Kerrigan 
Smokeless Tobacco 
Council 


Tobacco Co:ncil. “This is the 
most significant piece of anti- 
tobacco legislation that I’ve 
seen in the last 12 years,” he 
added. 

Tobacco interests argue 
that restoring state and local 
control over advertising will 
create a confusing universe of 
laws, and that the agency 
would be redundant. Louis 
Sullivan, HHS cag: tag tes- 
tified last month that the ex- 
isting Office of Smoking and 
Health covers many of the is- 
sues proposed for the new 
agency. 

Smokeless tobacco inter- 
ests further say the bill would 
require them to give up trade 
secrets by revealing products’ 


ingredients. 

“We have about eight co- 
sponsors now and support for 
the bill seems to be gaining 
momentum,” said a spokes- 
man in Sen. Kennedy’s office. 


A significant rewrite? 


However, a second source 
involved with the legislation 
maintained the bill is likely to 


be “significantly” rewritten in 
order to address opponents’ 
concerns that it infringes on 
freedom of advertising. 

The aspects most likely to 
be retained would be those 
stele resources for 
counter-advertising and more 
education, including $185 mil- 
lion in local/state grants, the 
source predicted.

LIVERPOOL, N. Y. — Fay’s, Inc. saw net earnings drop in 
its fourth quarter ended Jan. 27, but still showed record results 
for year-end revenues, net earnings and earnings per share for 
the year, the company annouced. 


For the year, net earnings were $10.4 million, or 68 cents per- 


share, up from $10.0 million, or 66 cents per share, the previous 
year. Revenues climbed 9 percent to $574.1 million. _ 

For the fourth quarter, net earnings were $3.5 million, or 23 
cents per share, down from last year’s $4.8 million, or 32 cents 

r share, for the period. Revenues did increase 8 percent to 

161.7 million for the quarter. 

Henry A. Panasci, Jr., Fay’s chairman, noted that “soft sales 
of seasonal merchandise. . . resulting in larger-than-expected 
markdowns” hurt earnings performance for the quarter, as did 
expansion-related administrative costs and POS system imple- 
mentation expenses. 

Measures were being implemented to contain expansion costs, 
Panasci added. During the fiscal year, Fay’s opened 11 super drug 
stores, eight Wheels

Rubber gloves snap at 
Moore’s profits 


NEW BRITAIN, Conn. — The 
Great Rubber Glove Massacre of 
1988 has claimed another victim. 
Moore Medical Corp. announced it 
would tak: a $4.2-million charge 
for costs and reserves associated 
with latex examining gloves ($2.5 
million after taxes), which it ex- 
pected would lead to losses being 
posted for the fourth quarter and 
year ended Dec. 30, 1989. Those 
figures had yet to be released as 
Drug Store News went to press. 

Moore becomes the second ma- 
jor wholesaler io absorb losses tak- 
en from devalued glove inven- 
tories. Owens & Minor last month 
announced it had taken a $2.5-mil- 
lion pretax loss for similar reasons 
(DrSN, March 5, 1990, p. 46). 

AIDS-related health concerns 
had depleted glove supplies during 
1988, forcing many wholesalers to 
seek gloves from alternative sup- 
pliers. Huge inventories were 
bought, but demand soon fell and 
with it, prices. Moore had ex- 
pensed $11.4 million on gloves for 
1988; after the current charge, its 
glove inventory is now valued at 
$1.3 million, the company said.

Despite woes,

has brand-name com-

Big B names vp-professional relations 


BIRMINGHAM, Ala. — Big B named Dr. Timothy Burelle 
to become of vp-professional relations, effective with the retire- 
ment this June of John F. Hight Jr., who has served in the posi- 
tion since 1979. 

Burelle, who has been dean of the Samford University School 
of Pharmacy since 1985, will be responsible for the operation of 
Big B’s 300 pharmacies. The chain opened its 300th store in Feb- 
ruary. 

Burelle joined the Samford faculty in 1973. He holds a phar- 
macy degree from Samford, a Doctor of Pharmacy from the Uni- 
versity of Tennessee and a Master’s degree in public health from 
the University of Alabama in Birmingham. He is a member of 
the American Pharmaceutical Association and the American 
Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, as well as several other na- 
tional and regional pharmacy professional organizations.

Krelitz to buy Eagle, drug wholesaler 


MINNEAPOLIS — Krelitz Industries, Inc. has signed a let- 
ter of intent to buy Eagle wee Inc., furthering its plan to em- 
phasize drug distribution. A definitive agreement for Krelitz’s 
purchase of all outstanding shares for an unnamed amount is ex- 
pected soon, Krelitz announced. 

Kagle, based in Eden Prairie, Minn., is a pharmaceutical, 
H&BA and general merchandise wholesaler, which, according 
to a source, posted about $35 million in sales for its latest year. 

In its plans to divest non-drug businesses, Krelitz will close 
“momentarily” on a pact to sell its James Phillips Co., a medical 
and surgical supply distributor. It is still “actively ursuing” the 
sale of Ulmer Pharmacal, a maker of skin care products, accord- 
ing to Barry Krelitz, president and ceo.

cades of using technology to 
drive down operating costs 
and gross margins while 
boosting sales, the wholesale

ways to stabilize gross mar-

share, according to Charles

the National Wholesale Drug- 
gists’ Association. 

In a talk at the NWDA’s 
1990 Marketing Conference 
here last month, Trefrey 
called for a new approach to 
boosting sales and profits for 
the nation’s drug wholesalers. 
“We’ve been playing the same 
game for about 30 years, start- 
ing when we brought technol- 
ORY into the business,” he told 

WDA members March 22. 
“We’ve enjoyed tremendous 
market share growth and tre- 
mendous sales growth, while 
driving down operating costs.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 9, 1990 


«ac ESR ese eR RR 


Drug store industry’s vital signs strong 


The pulse rate is good, the heart is healthy. There’s 
far less of those lethal fatty deposits gunking up the 
arterial system. 

What am I talking about? The drug store industry— 
particularly the chain drug portion of the industry. In 

our Annual Report published in this is- 


sue, we make note that in 1989 drug 
store sales were up by a strong nine per- 
cent, to $63 billion, while chain drug 
store sales alone rose 11 percent to $40 
billion. 

Why such a good year when other retail 
segments experienced the long overdue 
softening of consumer spending? There’s 
more than one reason, of course, but the 
main one is the growth of the retail phar- 


macy business. It’s become almost a cli- 


IN THE MARKET che to talk about the far-reaching effect 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


that a longer-lived population will have on 


the nation’s drug stores. Explosion may 
be too strong a word, but it’s not too far 
from reality. I mean, just mention the word gray and ev- 
eryone starts seeing green. 

Small wonder then that everyone is trying to get in 
on the act, from food stores to mass merchandisers to 
convenience stores to doctors to hospitals. It’s like a 
poker game. The pots get big enough and everyone’s 
adrenalin begins to pump. What the latest sales fig- 
ures show is that the drug stores are so far holding 
their own against the high-stakes crowd. For pre- 
scriptions, consumers by and large still prefer the 
drug store’s neighborhood convenience and small 
scale to the endless acres of the super food stores and 


giant discount chains. In consumers’ minds, drug 
stores are still more convenient for having their latest 
roll of film developed, for picking up greeting cards or 
looseleaf paper, or for buying lipstick or eye shadow. 

That’s not to say the competition hasn’t had an im- 
pact. Price pressures are forcing drug retailers into 
finding other ways of sustaining their bottom lines. 
Efficient distribution and inventory management 
have become crucial weapons in the battle to control 
costs. Just as important: retailers’ endless efforts to 
fine-tune their mix for maximum turns. Investment in 
technology to drive these efforts grew every year in 
the eighties, and will continue to increase in the com- 
ing decade. 

Meanwhile, greater investment is also being made 
in stores to create a pleasant shopping atmosphere 
and keep customers coming back. Look at what 
Eckerd, Perry, Pay Less, Walgreens, Arbor, Fantle’s 
and Revco (to name just a handful) have done in revi- 
talizing and maintaining their store base. It’s clear 
there’s more than one way to grow the business. 

While the industry’s prospects are good, there are 
some ominous trends ahead. Demographics feeding 
the business on one end will starve it on the other. 
Fewer younger people will be available to-work in the 
stores, and the competition for future stock clerks, 
cosmeticians and managers will drive up salary scales. 
It’s already happening in many places. The growth of 
third-party prescriptions will put more pressure on 
margins. And if that weren’t enough, more and more 
stores will crowd the retail ijandscape. 

It’s enough to turn a drug store retailer gray. But 
this week, why not think green, right? 


The granddaddy of third-party Rx plans—the 
Medicaid drug program—appears headed for major 
changes. 

At first blush, that may sound like good news to the 
drug store industry which has been complaining about 


WASHINGTON 
PERSPECTIVE 


Medicaid Rx reimbursement for @e- 
cades. But considering that Medicaid 
represents an increasingly critical 
source of revenue for many of the na- 
tion’s retail pharmacies, industry lead- 
ers are carefully sifting through the im- 
plications of various Medicaid “reform.” 

What’s in store for Medicaid? Here’s a 
sample: 

eThe Health Care Financing Admin- 
istration is pressuring state Medicaid 
officials to tighten the screws on partici- 
pating pharmacies by curbing “Average 
Wholesale Price” drug reimbursement; 


KEN RANKIN 


eThe bi-partisan “Pepper Commis- 


sion” on comprehensive health care 
wants to federalize the program as part of a controver- 
sial, $66-billion scheme to provide health insurance for 
all Americans; 

@Chrysler’s Lee Iacoceca and a number of other ma- 
jor corporate chieftans have joined with organized la- 
bor to press for a new national health insurance plan 
which would absorb Medicaid. 

The most recent (and in some respects, the most 
radical) of these proposals to overhaul Medicaid was 
advanced late last month by the chairman of the Sen- 
ate Aging Committee, David Pryor (D-Ark). 

Pryor, you may recall, was urged by the National 
Association of Retail Druggists to investigate soaring 
manufacturer drug prices in general, and discrimina- 
tory pricing practices against drug stores in particu- 
lar. 

Officials at NARD and other drug store industry 
groups had hoped that Sen. Pryor would challenge the 
pharmaceutical industry’s practice of offerng drugs to 
hospitals and other institutions at low-ball prices not 


Leaders carefully eye Medicaid reforms 


available to retail pharmacies. 

Instead, the new Medicaid “reform” proposal out- 
lined by Pryor is designed to force manufacturers to 
negotiate prices with state Medicaid program offi- 
cials—a practice that the drug industry has religiously 
avoided so far. 

Under the plan, federal Medicaid officials would set 
up an outside “non-governmental” National Pharma- 
cy and Therapeutics Committee responsible for com- 
piling a list of “therapeutic equivalents” which could 
be used interchangeably to treat certain conditions. 

Multi-state buying groups would then negotiate 
with pharmaceutical manufacturers of the listed ther- 
apeutic equivalents. The products of the lowest bid- 
ders would be designated “preferred drugs” and phar- 
macists would be expected to dispense them unless 
the prescriber specifically demands that the product 
or brand prescribed be dispensed. 

For their part, pharmacists would not only be au- 
thorized to engage in therapeutic substitution, but 
would be required to do so. A separate provision of 
Pryor’s plan would offer pharmacists immunity from 
liability resulting from the substitution of a “pre- 
ferred” drug for the one prescribed. 

As with the ill-fated Medicare “Catastrophic” Rx 
drug program, Pryor’s proposal for revamping Med- 
icaid would establish a natienwide electronic in- 
store claims transmission and processing system, as 
well as pharmacy-based drug utilization review pro- 
grams. 

Details of pharmacy reimbursement under the new 
plan are skimpy, but Pryor would allow pharmacists 
to recoup product costs at the lower of the “actual 
charge” for the drug, or the 90th percentile of all actu- 
al charges in the state. 

Is this plan the solution to pharmacy’s problems 
with Medicaid? Hardly. At best, it’s a well-inten- 
tioned scheme designed to cut government spending 
on drugs. At worst, its a proposal that could reduce 
the level of care available to the nation’s needy and 
sidestep the concerns of Medicaid pharmacists.

drug, combo and discount 
store chains around the nation 
continue to tinker with their 
store formats. Their efforts 
range from slight adjustments 
in merchandise presentation 
and mix, to complete store 
overhauls and the develop- 
ment—from scratch—of com- 
pletely new floor plans, decor 
packages, fixturing and de- 
partments. 

Whatever efforts most 
chains are making to keep 
their shopping formats and 
mixes fresh, their reasons are 
the same: all are trying to 
adapt to consumer demands 
with stores that are conve- 
nient, well-merchandised and 
even fun to =. 

“We’re providing a shopping 
experience, rather than a trip 
to the drug store,” noted Tony 
Civello, executive vp-stores for 


pletely new formats being 
rolled out by drug chains and 
their competitors. Others ef- 
forts include Revco D.S., 
K mart, Wal-Mart and Pay 
Less NW. 

Reveco’s new format, first un- 
veiled in Bedford Heights, Ohio 
last spring, is now serving as 
the model for new stores and 
retrofits, with some elements 
of the design being used in 
many locations. It features an- 
gled aisles, a more prominent 
pharmacy, graphic departmen- 
tal presentations and lower 
gondolas for greater visibility 
and shopping ease. 

Pay Less is reportedly post- 
ing double-digit gains in its pro- 
totype stores, which first ap- 


Meanwhile, both Walgreens 
and SupeRx of Arizona have 
successfully tested versions of a 
age oF gab eed format for use 
in tight urban locations. The 
tiny stores feature full pharma- 
ey counters and popular OTC 
products in settings as small as 
1,500 square feet. 

Both K mart and Wal-Mart 
are also rolling out new retail 
formats as they battle for dis- 
count store leadership in many 
markets. K mart’s new “Store 
for the 90s,” now in the begin- 
ning stages of an accelerated 
rollout, gives greater emphasis 
to pharmacy and H&BAs. Wal- 
Mart, meanwhile, has opened 
the first examples of its new 
“vendor store” concept.

Financially, the 675-store division of

percent to $72.2 million, same-store

total sales in the drug stores were up 
14.4 percent.

positioning and promotional program 
at American Drug’s Sav-on division in

energizing of the division’s workforce.

boost.

eo retailers, had been dropping off

During the year, the chain made 
strides in integrating major acquisi- 
tions of previous years, including 533 
Gray Drug and SupeRx stores in 1987 
and the Begley Co. (39 stores) in 1988. 

At a meeting with analysts in Octo- 
ber, chairman Alex Grass said 470 of 
the acquired stores had been remod- 
eled to date. Comparable-store sales at 
acquired stores were “strengthening 
each month,” president Martin Grass 
told the group. 

In the second quarter ended Sept. 2, 
comparable-store sales at acquired 
stores increased 3.5 percent (8.1 per- 
cent for core stores), and Grass pro- 
jected they would reach 6 percent (pre- 
tax, pre-interest operating margin) by 
the fourth quarter. He added that the 
Peoples and Begley stores would prob- 
ably take longer to hit that level. 

Because of similarities of store size 
and merchandise mix, the integration 
of the Lane acquisition from Peoples 
and the smaller acquisition of stores in 
New Jersey are expected to go more 
smoothly than the large earlier acqui- 
sitions. The stores acquired in south- 
central New Jersey, in particular, are 
comparable in size to the chain’s proto- 
type and complement the 137 other 
stores Rite Aid has in the state. 


Technological advances 


Rite Aid also pressed forward on the 
technological front, an area it considers 
a vital investment in its future. During 
the year, it completed upgrading com- 
puter systems in all its pharmacy de- 
partments and finished rolling out its 
front-end Data Collection System 
(DCS). 

This electronic linkage system 
sharply reduces the time required to 
communicate between store managers 
and headquarters and makes possible 
instant tracking of most operating and 
accounting tasks, enabling the chain to 
monitor individual store performance 
faster and more accurately. Most im- 
portant, it eliminates hand-generated 
reports and related expenses, such as 
mailing and telephone costs. The num- 
ber of stores equipped with scanning 
remained static for the second year, 
with 599 stores currently equipped. 

In pharmacy, Rite Aid continued to 
roll out an on-line eligibility verifica- 
tion and adjudication system, which al- 
lows immediate verification of eligibil- 
ity and significantly reduces the 
waiting period between filling a pre- 
scription and receiving payment from 
third-party insurance carriers. 


Third-party battle 


The company also kept up its battle 
for what Alex Grass has called “a fairer 
level of compensation from third-party 
providers.” A company-sponsored 
study released last June found that 64 
percent of the chain’s third-party cus- 
tomers purchasing prescriptions made 
no purchases from the front end of the 
store.

Bribery charges 


During the year, Rite Aid became 
embroiled in litigation involving al- 
leged bribery charges brought by the 
state of Ohio against its president, 
Martin Grass, and the company. Grass 
and the company were indicted on 
charges alleging that Grass had 
“bribed” former Lane Drug pharma- 
cist Melvin Wilczynski to resign from 
the Ohio State Pharmacy Board. 

The defendants pleaded not guilty 
Aug. 18, arguing that the payment was 
a legal buyout of a consulting contract 
and that the charge stems from a long- 
standing “vendetta” the pharmacy 
board has against the chain. 

This January, a Circuit Court judge 
denied a Rite Aid motion to dismiss the 
case and set Jan. 15 for a trial. The trial 
date was subsequently rescheduled for 
April 16. 

The chain operated 2,353 drug and 
H&BA stores on March 3 of this year, 
compared with 2,184 last year, and 
completed 237 major remodels during 
the year, versus 204 major renovations 
the previous year. It targets opening 
110 stores this year and plans to equip 
100 with pharmacy computers. 

The chain closed the distribution 
center acquired from Peoples (Lane) 
and currently operates five ware- 
houses, comprising a total of 1,389,000 
square feet. 


In its latest posted results, for third- 
quarter 1990 ended Dec. 2, Rite Aid 
corporate revenues gained 14 percent, 
to $791.7 million, and net income in- 
creased 35.8 percent, to $22.5 million.

That decision, announced early this 
year, is being praised by most of Rev-

smart-—if painful—move to insure the 
company’s future. It involves the 
planned sale of 712 drug stores in 17 
states as Revco concentrates all its ef- 
forts and resources on its denser core 
markets. Strategically, it will mean 
that store renovations, technological 
enhancements and other improve- 
ments to operations and merchandis- 
ing systems will be done that much 
faster in the 1,161 Revco stores that 
remain part of the company. 

“Since total capital expenditures for 
the chain will not be reduced, ongoing 
areas of operation will see remodelings 
and technological enhancements much 
earlier than previously planned,” not- 
ed Revco chairman and ceo Boake Sells 
after the restructuring plan was re- 
vealed. “We will still be a very large 
chain, with sales close to $2 billion.’

Reveo received another boost in 
January when the U.S. Bankruptcy 
Court approved a 16-month extension 
of the maturity date of a $145 million 
credit line Revco’s lending banks made 
available. The chain used some of that 
money to beef up inventories last 
Christmas, but has left the bulk of it 
untouched and relied on current oper- 
ating cash flow to fund most ongoing 
operations and improvements. 

Meanwhile, the chain continues to 
work its way back to fiscal health and 
viability as a chain drug retailer. Ex- 
haustive efforts over the past two 
years to revamp Revco’s stores and 
merchandise mix have yielded steady 
improvements in sales and operating 
income, despite a massive one-time 
charge against earnings taken to cover 
the costs associated with the upcoming 
store divestiture program. 

One sure sign of improvement was a 
10 percent upturn in same-store sales 
in the first three quarters of the new 
fiscal year. Operating profit for the 
first nine months, excluding one-time 
charges, depreciation and amortiza-

Three key factors

” st year, and comparable prescription

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 9, 1990 


Annuai Report Part |: Pay Less Drug Stores NW 


Pay Less charges into 1990s on a fast growth track 


WILSON- 
VILLE, Ore. — The 
Northwest’s biggest 
drug chain is on a 
tear. Backed by the 
financial muscle of 
its parent company, 
meee KK mart Corp., bol- 
stered by a young, aggressive manage- 
ment team and increasing sales and 
earnings momentum, Pay Less Drug 
Stores NW is. pushing ahead with new 
stores and new strategies. 

In mid-March, the chain opened its 
300th drug store in Clackamas, Ore., a 
suburb of Portland. That milestone 
comes in the midst of a planned 40- 
store expansion this year, on top of 32 
new stores in 1989. 

Meanwhile, Pay Less has upped its 
store renovation schedule based on a 
new store prototype first unveiled ear- 
ly last year outside Sacramento, Calif. 
The chain plans 12 major remodels this 
year, and will do less extensive reno- 
vations to another 10 units. 

For the most part, new stores are 
serving to strengthen Pay Less’ pene- 
tration of existing markets and extend 
the chain into smaller communities in 
the nine-state western region it 
serves. The chain is 2 ageg to reap 
big rewards by snapping up locations 
in rapidly growing communities to the 
east and south of Los Angeles, where 


store sales are reportedly rising 10 to 
15 percent and pharmacy sales are 
growing a whopping 35 percent. 

Pay Less is also generating big gains 
in new and remodeled stores thanks to 
its successful introduction of the new 
store format. The prototype empha- 
sizes pharmacy, cosmetics and other 
core departments. 

The company’s expansion and reno- 
vation efforts are pushing it rapidly to- 
ward the $2 billion sales mark. Sales 
were up a healthy 23 percent last year, 
to $1.6 billion. 

Meanwhile, Pay Less is pushing 
ahead with the rapid installation of 
front-end scanners, already in place in 
more than 200 stores. Installation 
should be 90 percent finished by the end 
of the year and chainwide by the first 
quarter of 1991, according to McAlear. 

Pay Less marked another milestone 
last year with the retirement of long- 
time chairman and chief executive Ed 
Hart after more than 40 years with the 
chain. 

Pay Less is now run by a cadre of 
young and enthusiastic executives and 
managers, headed by president and 
ceo Ron Schiff, McAlear, vp-merchan- 
dising Jerry Kuske and others. Those 
top leaders have demonstrated a 
marked receptiveness to new ideas-- 
many of which have percolated up from 
the stores and support people.

Big B consolidates 85 Reeds.

BESSEMER, Ala. — This 

= past year was crucial in posi- 

tioning Big B for the ’90s. It 

completed its consolidation 

of 85 Reed Drug stores ac- 

f quired last year from Peo- 

f ples, and moved into a major 
new market—Atlanta. 

By expanding into Atlanta, Big B has made 
Georgia its second-largest market. Today, 
with the Reed stores almost 
completely converted into Big 
Bs, the chain now operates 
about 130 stores in Georgia, 
almost as many as in its home 
state of Alabama. 

For the rest of 1990, Big B 
plans to concentrate on satu- 
rating Georgia with more 
store openings. Most of a pro- 
jected 15 new stores slated to 
open this year will be in great- 
er Atlanta, executive vp Ar- 
thur “Mac” Jones said. 

“We'll still open some stores 
in Alabama,” he said, “but 
with 140 stores here, we’re 
close to saturation.” Big B also 
plans to fill in more stores in 
Tennessee, Florida, and Mis- 

Sissippi. 

Since acquiring Reed, Big 
B’s total volume increased 54 
percent to $417 million. Same- 
store sales rose about 8.5 per- 
cent, Jones said. 

Pharmacy accounts for 
roughly 40 percent of chain- 
wide sales, and H&BA 25 per- 
cent. Food and photo are the 
next strongest categories, 
with food showing above-av- 
erage double-digit growth, ac- 
cording to Jones. 

Some Big B stores have con- 
venience food departments in 
neighborhoods with no food- 
store competitor nearby, but 
most display expanded dry 
groceries, including candy, 
snacks, microwavable meals 
and other convenience foods, 
as well as bottled waters, soft 
drinks and juices. All stores 
also have coolers for single- 
serve beverages. 


Growing deep discount side 


Big B also opened five more 
Drugs For Less deep discount 
stores in 1989, including three 
in Atlanta, and plans to open 
five more in 1990. 

Jones said Big B opened its 
first Drugs For Less about 
five years ago as an “experi- 
ment,” but added that it has 
been able to grow without can- 
nibalizing sales of Big Bs. 

“We think the Drugs For 
Less shopper is coming from 
food stores, Wal-Marts and K 
marts. The drug stores are 
still attracting the conve- 
nience shoppers,” he said.

_ Since tripling its 
store count the past 
five years through new store develop- 
ment and acquisitions, the industry has 
looked to the chain as a sterling example 
of a regional operator with its tentacles 
on a market. Observers note manage- 
ment’s trained focus on drug store ba- 
sics, tight expense controls and chain- 
wide disciplines as marks of a well-run 
operation. Indeed, Arbor was voted 
Drug Store News’ REX Small Chain of 
the Year in industrywide ballotting. 
Specifically, Arbor operates 93 drug 
stores in the state, each averaging more 
than $3.5 million annually on $350 sales 
r square foot. In the fiscal year ended 
uly 31, 87 stores generaied sales of 
$300.2 million, a 21.8 percent hike from 
$246.5 million. Net income rose 37.7 
percent to $9.2 million. In the period, 
comparable-store sales climbed 14.6 
percent as new and acquired drug stores 
continued to build business. 
Pharmacy volume itself was up 30 
rcent for the year, and now accounts 
or 36.8 percent of chainwide sales. 
The uptrend is continuing through 
the first half of fiscal 1990. Net income 
for the six months ended Jan. 31, 1990 
has risen 28.1 percent to $6.1 million, on 
a 14.3 percent sales gain to $169.7 mil- 
lion. Comparable-store sales rose 10 
percent in the half. 


rs firm grasp on home 


During the latest quarter, Arbor 
opened five new stores, part of plans to 
open 12 to 15 and remodel eight to 10 this 
year. 

The chain has also introduced Arbor- 
tech Plus, an enhancement to the chain- 
wide pharmacy computer system, and 
has completed a pilot point-of-sale scan- 
ning test. Technological advances will 
bring even greater efficiencies to the 
distinctly well-merchandised stores. — 

Stores average 10,800 square feet, in- 
cluding 9,300 square feet of selling 
space. All are staffed by service cosme- 
ticians and have full convenience food 
departments. 


Very disciplined 


“The stores are set up to do a lot of vol- 
ume, and we spend the money to keep 
them up-to-date and consistent,” Max 
Ernst, executive vp and chief operating 
officer once told Drug Store News. 
“We’re very disciplined. . . all the 
stores have the same layout.” 

“We pay attention to detail, and we 
know our customers like what we’re 
doing,” said chairman Eugene Apple- 
baum. 

Their operating guidelines: constant 
review of the merchandise mix; a cen- 
trally-controlled buying and pricing 
policy that encourages store managers 
to focus on customer service and run- 
ning the store; careful cultivation of a 
company image stressing health care, 
nae and everyday low prices 
through aggressive advertising; and 
neat, uncluttered stores cut from the 
same mold. 


A trimmer Perry returning 
to basics amid turnaround 


PONTIAC, 
MICH. — Perry 
Drug Stores, leader 
of the Michigan mar- 
ket, is recognizing 
that there’s no place 
like home. 

The 215-store 
chain is busy culling unprodu ive sites 
from its roster as it refocuses . Michi- 
gan and Illinois markets. It is spending 
this spring leaving Wisconsin and Indi- 
ana, and “redeploying assets where 
they can be most effective,” said chair- 
man and ceo Jack Robinson. 

When the divestiture is completed, 
Perry will be operating 166 conven- 
tional drug stores and 16 A.L. Price 
deep discounters in Michigan, and 24 
conventional stores in the Chicago 
area. After two years of gradual 
downsizing, Perry plans to add 10 
new stores this year, including one 
A.L. Price and another 20 in fiscal 


1991. Most of the growth will be in 
Michigan. 

The subject of growth is a positive 
one at Perry, which is turning itself 
around after two prior years of big 
losses. In the latest fiscal year, ended 
Oct. 31, Perry posted net earnings of 
$7.1 million on sales of $669.6 million, 
after applying tax-loss carryforwards. 


Causes of turnaround 


The Perry turnaround can be attrib- 
uted to: top managers drawn from a 
broad se Pom a shift to basic drug 
store merchandise, with an accompa- 
nying refocus on health care; aggres- 
sive efforts to spruce up Perry’s home- 
market image; and a major store 
renovation and remodeling program, 
based on development of a new store 
prototype. 

Those efforts will continue without 
Gary Allen, senior vp-store opera- 
tions, who was recruited two years ago

thrives on the best of both 
worlds. “As a chain, we re- 
ceive programs and systems 
needed to compete, yet all our 
stores are independently 
owned,” said Jeft Atkinson, 
vp, strategic planning. 


is 


Specialization is key 


The company’s uniqueness 
lies in its specialization. The 
average store generates more 
than 90 percent of volume 
from prescriptions, in a for- 
mat of approximately 1,200 
square feet. That is 15 percent 
the size of the typical chain 
and one-:hird that of most in- 
dependents. Yet, MSI stores 
average $529 sales per square 
foot, nearly double the rate of 
some chains and indepen- 
dents. The company also tar- 
gets the 45-plus age group, 
which represents over 60 per- 
cent of its business. 

MSI spent 1989 stepping up 
the pace of independent con- 
versions into its system. 
Twenty converted stores 
opened in 1989, more than 
double any prior year. This 
growth is expected to contin- 
ue, as traditional indepen- 
dents seek greater clout. 


Focus on prescriptions 


MSI’s focus is on prescrip- 
tions, but it has lately been 
aying greater attention to its 
ront-end. “We’re intent on 
creating ‘care departments,’ 
with specialized departments 
for patients with diseases like 
arthritis and diabetes,” Atkin- 
son said. This also helps build 
the consultation function for 
the store’s pharmacist. 

Promotions and sales share 
of high-margin private label 
are also on the rise at MSI. 

Since much of the company’s 
business is in third-party, MSI 
recently created its owned sub- 
sidiary, Medicine Shoppe In- 
terNet, a managed care net- 
work. “This network allows our 
stores to speak as one voice 
when negotiating contracts 
with third-party payers—un- 
like independents, who often 
get locked out of these con- 
tracts,” said Gary Levine, vp- 
managed health care. 

President Jerome F. Shel- 
don believes the network is also 
an advantage for third-party 
payers. “We are able to quickly 
review and evaluate potential 
third-party contracts to assure 


a reasonable level of profitabili- 
ty,” he said in a prepared state- 
ment. “Furthermore, we are 
developing additional special- 
ized mom Roc programs that 


market them internationally. 


are likely to substantially en- 
hance the added value we can 
provide to third-party sponsors 
who truly seek cost contain- 
ment.”

sales compared to a 9-percent rise for 
all drug stores.

to higher average wholesale costs of 
prescription drug products, which

rise in the average retail prescription

My Way of Thinking 


To the Editor: 

Let me take Mr. Stuart Tobin’s letter in the Jan. 22 
issue of Inside Pharmacy one step further. 

In New York, when a physician marks the prescrip- 
tion DAW, the pharmacist must dispense the brand in- 
dicated or else he is in violation. 

However, when a Medicaid prescription is received, 
the physician must also write “Brand Medically Neces- 
sary” in his own hand. If not, Medicaid will pay only for 
the generic even though the physician does not want it. 
If we dispense the generic in this case, we are in viola- 
tion of the state law. 

So what do we do in this case? We must send the pa- 
tient back to the physician to amend the prescription, 
losing time in filling the prescription. 

What is the message here? It says do not violate state 
law and we will reward you with a lower cost price, or 
violate the law and get the proper price and also look 
forward to a fine by the board of pharmacy. 

Does this make sense? It certainly makes none to me, 
nor to the patient who is turned away because the phy- 
sician did not add the three magic words. This is the 
state of pharmacy in the state of New York! 

Warren Askenas, Brooks Drugs, Lawrence, N. Y. 


“My Way of Thinking” is intended to give responsible. 
members of the health care community a professional 
forum to air their views on crucial issues confronting 
pharmacy today. Presentations should be no longer 
than 500 words and may be edited for space require- 
ments. Interested participants should mail their pre- 
sentations to Harold Cohen, Editor, Inside Pharmacy, 
425 Park Ave., New York, N.Y., 10022. Articles will be 
chosen and published at the editor’s discretion.

Chain drug store prescription sales ended the year with a nearly 14-percent rise in sales. 


Despite third-party woes, Rx strong 


Continued from page IP1 

Many chains saw a quick re- 
turn on investment when they 
made capital improvements to 
their pharmacy computer sys- 
tems. 

Some installed faster ma- 
chines with work stations to 
handle the additional informa- 
tion needed to fill third-party 
prescriptions. Others in- 
stalled “black boxes” and com- 
puter software, enabling the 
store to transmit third-party 
claims electronically for on- 
line adjudication, thereby 
eliminating costly resubmis- 
sions. The problem of nega- 
tive cash flow usually associat- 
ed with third-party 

rescription programs was all 

ut eliminated in these stores. 
The savings dropped to their 
bottom line. 

But many facets of doing 
business in the third-party 
arena still plague some retail- 
ers. Exclusive third-party 
contracts that favor larger 
and financially stronger drug 


stores continue to enrage 
smaller chains and indepen- 
dents who cannot cut deals 
that return very low reim- 
bursement levels. 

The widespread anger that 
exclusive contracting creates 
touched off cries for “freedom 
of choice” legislation nation- 
wide. Such legislation is struc- 
tured so that no drug retailer 
desiring to participate in a 
third-party contract would be 
locked out. Illinois has already 
passed such a law and other 
states have similar bills up for 
review. 


More fuel for fire 


Adding more fuel to an al- 
ready freely burning third- 
party fire is the intense com- 
petition for the third-party 
customer. In highly industri- 
alized states like Michigan and 
Illinois, where third-party ac- 
counts for 70 percent or great- 
er of the prescription business 
in some markets, it is not un- 
usual to see customers’ co- 


payments discounted or 
waived, while the supply and 
demand of the drugs stores 
that are ready to fill these pre- 
scriptions have cut reimburse- 
ments drastically. 

Another pressing issue for 
pharmacists is that of dis- 
criminatory pricing. Several 
months ago, Senator David 
Pryor (D-Ark.), chairman of 
the Senate Special Committee 
on Aging, held a hearing on 
discriminatory pricing by the 
pharmaceutical industry. 

In his presentation, Pryor 
singled out 10 brand name 
drugs for which hospitals pay 
from 4 percent to 99 percent 
less than the prices charged to 
retail drug stores. 


IP17 


Generics scandal 
rocks the industry 


As though third-party and 
discriminatory pricing prob- 
lems weren’t enough for retail 
pharmacists to deal with last 
year, the industry was 
stunned by a scandal of im- 
mense proportions when it 
was discovered that some 
FDA officials had been accept- 
ing gratuities from several ge- 
neric pharmaceutical compa- 
nies in return for quick drug 
approvals.(See the generic 
drug investigation review on 
page [P19.) 

Hardest hit during the kick- 
back scandal were Bolar Phar- 
maceuticals, Par Pharmaceu- 
ticals, American 
Therapeutics, and Vitarine 
Pharmaceuticals. While the 
scandal began to unfold pub- 
licly last summer, the back- 
ground investigation actually 
started some two years be- 
fore, when Mylan Laborato- 
ries hired a private detective 
to help explain why smaller 
companies were consistently 
beating Mylan to market with 
aga generic drug approv- 
als. 

It wasn’t until two years lat- 
er that the scandal broke wide 
open when Vitarine admitted 
that it submitted SKF’s Dya- 
zide for approval instead of its 
generic equivalent. Last July, 
an FDA official pleaded guilty 
to illegal payoffs from Ameri- 
can Therapeutics. Other accu- 
sations followed, forcing sev- 
eral generic companies, even 
those remotely implicated, to 


remove product from retail- 
ers’ shelves. 

The scandal left an already 
stressed industry shell 
shocked. FDA approvals 
came toa grinding halt and re- 
tail pharmacists were forced 
into a position of defending 
their use of generics. Al- 
though it’s been nearly a year 
since the scandal surfaced, 
FDA approvals still only 
trickle out of the much-criti- 
cized government agency, 
causing anxieties among many 
“honest” generic and PMA 
companies that have a pletho- 
ra of drug approvals waiting to 
be acted upon. 

The generic industry has 
taken matters somewhat into 
its own hands. According to 
the Generic Pharmaceutical 
Industry Association (GPIA), 
a special Blue Ribbon Com- 
mittee on Generic Medicines 
will examine the generic drug 
industry and the drug approv- 
al process at the FDA. This 
committee consists of an inde- 
pendent group of individuals 
with scientific, pharmaceuti- 
cal, regulatory, and legal ex- 
pertise. 

The committee will develop 
and make public its recom- 
mendations for whatever 
changes may be necessary to 
reassure the American people 
that generic drugs are proper- 
ly tested and evaluated and 
are safe and effective. 

In reality, the burden of

Direct-to-consumer 
ads are on upswing 


While retail pharmacists continue to struggle with 
problems affecting their businesses, some pharmaceutical 
manufacturers are trying to increase sales by stepping up 


One such campaign includes manufacturers advertising 
prescription products directly to the consumer. The idea is 
to get consumers more involved in the selection process of 
the prescription drugs they are taking, hoping this will 
translate to more sales for these products at drug store 


Although the pharmaceutical industry as a whole has 
approached the idea of advertising prescription products 
directly to the consumer cautiously, several companies 
have. been aggressive with this kind of advertising, and 


One of the first companies to venture into the direct-to- 
consumer (DTC) advertising of prescription drugs was 
Marion Merrell Dow Consumer Products (formerly Lake- 
side Pharmaceutical). While its non-sedating antihista- 
mine; Seldane, was never mentioned by name in the ads, 
the commercials suggested consumers ask their physician 
for the non-sedating antihistamine manufactured by the 
company. The company later featured Nicorette, a prod- 
uct to help people stop smoking, consumer ads targeted di- 


Over the past year there have been other pharmaceuti- 
cal companies advertising their products as well. These in- 
e Upjohn, advertising Rogaine, and Lexis Pharma- 
ceuticals, advertising its brand of oral contraceptive,

OTCs mainstay of traditional core mix 


Key players in mix benefit from more promotions, repositioning 


or generations, the 

American drug store 

built its reputation pri- 
marily on two areas of the 
store, the prescription de- 
partment and the over-the- 
counter (OTC), or propri- 
“rn drug department. 

Although the sale of OTC 
products in recent years has 
spread to non-traditional drug 
stores such as supermarkets, 
discount and convenience 
stores, OTCs still remain a 
core he peggy for tradition- 
al retail drug stores, one they 
hope will help maintain their 
identity as key players in the 
health care network. 

iy the new competi- 
tion, drug retailers and man- 
ufacturers of OTC “sig 
remain optimistic about the 
traditional drug store’s role 
in selling OTC products. 
Both are hoping to cash in 
on the $18 billion to $23 bil- 
lion in sales the category is 
expected to generate by the 
end of the next five years. 

To help accomplish that 
goal, retailers and manufac- 
turers are teaming up to pro- 
mote more OTC products by 
boosting ad budgets and mak- 
ing available more co-op ad- 
vertising monies. The chains 
are positioning the more pow- 
erful OTC medications closer 
to the pharmacy so that the 
store’s pharmacist can act as 
an consultant. The 
stores are also paying closer 
attention to those prod- 
uct categories that contribute 
most to the overall growth of 
the OTC department. 

The retail marketplace has 
seen very little in the ty of 
Rx-to-OTC-switched prod- 
ucts over the past year. Still 
on everyone’s number one 
“hit list” to make the switch 
is Marion Merrell Dow’s Sel- 
dane, the best-selling pre- 
scription antihistamine on 
the market today. Many be- 
lieve that the recent generic 
scandal has the FDA over- 
cautious about new drug ap- 
provals, including Rx-to- 
OTC-switched products. 

While OTCs as a whole did 
very well last year, certain 
categories continue to shine 
with better than 10-percent 
increases in sales. These in- 
clude cough/cold, analgesics, 
dental care, eye and lens 
care, and family planning. 


Cough and cold 


— One OTC category that 
continues to do well, despite 
the introduction of few truly 
innovative products, is that 
of cough and cold. Last year 


the average drug store real- 
ized a 13-percent increase in 
sales of cough and cold prod- 
ucts. While this category is 
called “cough and cold,” it 
encompasses allergy medica- 
tions as well. Some of its 
success is attributed to cus- 
tomers buying antihistamine 
allergy preparations to treat 
their colds, and allergy suf- 
ferers buying non-antihista- 
mine cough and cold prod- 
ucts to treat their allergies. 
(See further coverage on

NEWS IN BIIEF 


Revco’s Charlotte Expo draws crowds 


CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Reveco’s first Health and Beauty 
Expo held outside its home market drew 67,000 visitors to Char- 
lotte’s Convention Center March 30 and 31, and led to “a clear 
increase in sales” in this key Revco market, according to Bob 
Newmark, director of advertising and marketing services. 


_ Revco drew some 100,000 Cleveland-area consumers to a sim- 
ilar event last May, and is gearing up for another home-market 
expo next month. 


It clearly has an effect on sales, both near- and long-term,” 
said Newmark. “Another clear benefit is the excitement it 
raises for both customers and Revco employees.” 

The free event in Charlotte featured health screenings, fit- 
ness workouts, product demonstrations and giveaways, and 
visits by sports and media celebrities. 

Revco pharmacists also staffed an advice-only “pharmacy” at 
the expo for patient consultations. 

The two-day event was given a major sendoff with a 48-page 
insert in The Charlotte Observer betore opening day. The ta 
loid included co-op advertising from pores exhibiting at the 
expo, as well as feature stories about Revco and the event. 


NACDS plans fall session for MIS issues 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — The National Association of Chain 
Drug Stores (NACDS) will sponsor three separate conferences 
this fall where members will discuss operations issues: MIS; hu- 
man resources and loss prevention; and administration and op- 
erations. 

The human resources and loss prevention meeting will be 
held Oct. 14-17 at a place to be announced. Officials plan to an- 
nounce the other two meetings’ times and places at the NACDS 
Marketplace in June, according to Jim Huber, NACDS’ vp-fi- 
nance and administration. 

In the past, NACDS covered these topics in one meeting, but 
members felt that pulls too many ke people away from their 
companies at one time. Also, the MIS execs have felt they can 
achieve more with their own meeting, said Huber. 

Last year, yy the session on human resources and loss pre- 
vention was held; there were no workshops in 1988, after mem- 
bers had voted in 1987 to hold the meetings every other year.

LIVONIA, Mich. — B&E Merchandising Corp., a distribu- 

tor of advertising and retail promotional merchandise, has 
ed to acquire certain assets of Shawnee-Evans, Alco 

ealth Services’ promotional merchandising division. 

B&E will take over development and sales of Shawnee-Ev-

[companies] by combining buying power and consolidating dis- 
tribution networks.”

Bill’s Drugs, dies in Calif. at 57 


BENICIA, Calif. — Calvin 
Hendricks, 57, president and 
chief administrative officer of 
Bill’s Drugs and formerly a 
ig ony executive with Pay 
’n Save Corp., died April 6 in 
Mount Diablo Medical Center, 
Concord, Calif., after suffer- 
ing a stroke April 2. 

“Cal brought many talents 
to Bill’s Drugs, particularly in 
the finanelal budgetary, ad- 
ministrative, and real estate 
areas,” said Bill Eames, chair- 
man and ceo. “He brought a 
number of experienced people 
into our organization who will 
be able to bridge the gap while 
we search for his successor. 
Yet his counsel and experi- 
ence will be sorely missed.” 

Eames, who had worked 
with Hendricks since 1977, 
added, “He was a very bal- 
anced individual—able to bal- 
ance family, church, and busi- 
ness. And he was able to sit 


Calvin Hendricks 


down and help people sort out 
problems and find solutions. 
He was always very caring.” 

Hendricks joined Bill’s 
Drugs’ board of directors in 
1977, when Bill’s bought sev- 
eral stores from Pay ’n Save. 
At the time Hendricks was an 
executive with Pay ’n Save, 
and in 1982 became vice chair- 
man and cfo there. 

In 1986, Hendricks pur- 
chased the approximately 
one-third stake in Bill’s Drugs 
that had been held by Seattle 
Standard, a corporate off- 
shoot which resulted from the 
purchase of Pay ’n Save by the 
Trump Group. He joined Bill’s 
in December of that year as 
president and chief adminis- 
trative officer. 

At the time, Eames said 
Hendricks “wanted to have 
the fun and excitement of 
helping another company 
grow and at the same time 
participate in the equity por- 
tion.” 

Hendricks was born in Cen- 
terville, Utah, in 1933 and 

w up in Utah and Payette, 
daho. He declined a basket- 
ball scholarship at Brigham 
Young University to serve in 
the Air Force during the Ko- 
rean War. He then attended 
BYU, and after duation, 
joined the accounting firm of 
Price Waterhouse in Seattle. 

In 1962 he was hired as con- 
troller by the Pay ’n Save 
Corp., beginning a long asso- 
ciation with that company, 
which during his tenure in- 


cluded Pay ’n Save Drugs, La- 
monts, Bi-Mart, Price Savers, 
and other retail businesses. 

“He was one of the guidin 
lights of Pay ’n Save,” sai 

alter R. Guidinger, former 
vp-real estate at Pay ’n Save, 
who worked closely with Hen- 
dricks for 18 years. “He was a 
very busy, energetic, inter- 
ested person.” 

A Mormon, Hendricks was 
for 23 years one of three ruling 
members of the Seattle Stake 
of the Church of Jesus Christ 
of Latter-day Saints. 

He is survived by his wife, 
Lona; his mother; two sisters; 
six children; and nine grand- 
children.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 30, 1990 


Annual Report Part ll: Performance 


69 


Drug chains eye the 1990s 


focused sharply on core mix 


he chain drug identity crisis 
seems to be over. 

Drug chains spent a good 
part of the 1980s trying to position 
themselves in a rapidly shifting re- 
tail landscape against a raging sea of 
new and resurgent competitors. 

In the process, the chains were 
forced to look long and hard at just 
what kind of business they conduct- 
ed. They had to make fundamental, 
top-to-bottom decisions about mer- 
chandising and marketing—what 
kinds of merchandise they were go- 
ing to carry, and how they were go- 
ing to distinguish themselves from 
their competitors. What followed 
was an era of experimentation, as 
many drug chains sought the perfect 
balance between a merchandise mix 


ting into the same business, eroding 
the old distinctions between trade 
classes and challenging drug stores 
for every part of their business. 
Even the most professional aspects 
of retail pharmacy were no longer 
off-limits for mass merchandisers ea- 
ger to share in the profits offered by 
prescription drugs, H&BA, greeting 
cards, and other traditional drug 
store items. 

Supermarket chains en masse de- 
cided in recent years that the drug 
and H&BA sides of the business 
were just too important to leave to 
drug stores. 

Drawn by high margins, the aging 
of the population, and the growing 
appeal of one-stop shopping to today’s 
time-pressed consumers, food retail- 


sively to combo store formats. They 
hired pharmacy experts to help per- 
fect the drug side of the format, lis- 
tened to what their customers want- 
ed, developed giant new store designs 
with ample space for drug store cate- 
gories, and advertised their one-stop 


appeal long and loud. 


Discount powerhouses like Wal- 
Mart and K mart have also swal- 


lowed big chunks of the nation’s 


drug store business. Deep discount- 
ers have sprung up like mushrooms 
after a rainshower, further roiling 
the competitive picture. Consumers 
themselves have proven a remark- 
ably fickle group in recent years, of- 
ten putting price and convenience 


above old retail loyalties. 


Little wonder, then, that the 
chain drug industry has passed 
through a decade of turmoil and 
soul-searching. After years of diver- 
sification into distracting, non-core 
businesses and general merchandise 
categories that deterred from their 
image as health- and beauty-care 
providers, many chains were caught 
at a disadvantage by the slew of 
new competitors in the 1980s. All 
were challenged to re-establish 
themselves by redefining their core 
business and image. 

For the most part, that process is 
largely over. Most changes in the chain 
drug merchandise mix at this point are 
evolutionary rather than revolution-

Chains starting 1990s focused sharply on core mix 


Continued from page 69 

ary—a matter more of fine-tuning 
than of wholesale additions or dele- 
tions of departments. The drug 
chains and independents that weath- 
ered the competitive onslaughts and 
social transformations of the ’80s face 
the same challenges in the ’90s, but 
they are far more streamlined and fo- 
cused than they were a decade ago. 
Most of them have rekindled the core 
aspects of their business—pharmacy, 
H&BAs, stationery, convenience 
foods, to name a few—and have repo- 
sitioned themselves in those areas by 
building on and marketing the funda- 
mentals that continue to drive the 
drug store business: convenience, 
service, value, selection and a strong 
emphasis on professionalism and 


health care. 

Many chains also have a valuable 
new tool in their efforts to finetune the 
merchandise mix, with the addition of 
point-of-sale systems that capture de- 
tailed item movement information. 
The industry has also reaped big gains 
in the oy gl department with sys- 
tems that cut down on third-party-bill- 
ing headaches, build detailed patient 
profiles, and free up pharmacists for 
patient counseling. 


Efforts pay off 


Efforts by drug chains to distinguish 
themselves from their competitors and 
refocus on their core merchandise eat- 
egories continue to bear fruit. Overall 
chain drug sales were up a healthy 11 
percent last year, with prescription 


sales leading the way with a powerful 
13.7 percent gain. Thanks to the aging 
of the population, continued manufac- 
turer price hikes and a greater reliance 
on pharmaceuticals in the health care 
spectrum, pharmacy continues to ac- 
count for a growing share of total sales 
at many chains, including Walgreens, 
Arbor, Perry and Pay Less NW. In- 
dustrywide, the Rx counter now pro- 
duces nearly a third of total store reve- 
nues. 

Drug chains also racked up big 
gains in OTC/proprietaries, statio- 
nery, toiletries, cosmetics, general 
merchandise and photo in 1989. Mar- 
gins for some categories have been 
squeezed by competition, but chains 
are holding their own in sales of film, 
blank videotapes, candy and other 


categories against strong competi- 
tion. 

Despite an overall trend back to ba- 
sic core categories in recent years, 
many chains are finding new opportu- 
nities in convenience foods, which 
drove ahead nearly 9 percent last 
year. Walgreens, for instance, is put- 
ting c-food departments in hundreds 
of stores where direct competition 
from supermarkets is minima]. Man 
chains now stock cooler cases, inelud- 
nge ery, SupeRx, Snyder and Osco. 

he industry is also beginning to re- 
spond to growing concerns about the 
environment. Biodegradable products 
and packaging made from recycled ma- 
terials are beginning to show up in a 


few chain drug stores, including those 
of Pay Less NW.

Cosmetics sales up 8.9% to nearly $2 billion 


Deep discounters, mass merchants, and comb 


Bae at kt 


Chains that cultivate a department-st ore image and offer service and a broad assortment of franchised items attract more traffic. 


1989 cosmetics 


ooking beyond modest advances 
made by cosmetics and fra- 
grances in chain drug stores the 
past year, buyers are spotting strong 
owth segments: men’s fragrances, 
oundations, mascaras, eye and lip lin- 
ers, nail treatments, bath preps, and 
eye/face creams. 

Overall, cosmetics grew 8.9 percent 
to nearly $2 billion in chain drug stores 
in 1989. Deep discounters, who are 
making increasingly stronger presen- 
tations, report their category sales are 
up in the double digits. Many manufac- 
turers indicate their sales gains at 
deep discounters, mass merchants, 
and combos are far more dramatic than 
at conventional chain drug stores. 

One example from a major supplier: 
more than 30-percent gains at deep 
discounters and other trade classes, 
compared with estimated 10-percent 
gains at conventional drug chains. His 
sales analysis indicates that K mart, 
Wal-Mart and other mass merchants 
have built their combined cosme- 
tics/H&BA sales to about a 10 percent 
share of all commodity volume, up 
from virtually zero five years ago. 


Combos up dramatically 


He also estimated that combos now 
generate 15 to 20 percent of all his cos- 
metics/H&BA commodity volume, 
twice the rate of five years ago. 

Many buyers rh om that their 
stores are feeling the effects of this 
shift. That’s why so many chains are 
trying to upgrade their cosmetics de- 
partments, add more upscale and di- 
verted department store lines when- 
ever possible, improve lighting, 
provide more and better service, and 
price more competitively.

With trade-ups’ help, toiletries increase 9.6% 


ncreased competition has made 
selling toiletries harder for many 
traditional drug chains. They find 
themselves banging heads with food 
and mass merchandise chains and deep 
discounters, which regularly promote 
or display the best-selling and most- 
sought-after brands at extremely low, 
competitive prices. 

However, the overall category did 
continue to grow in the chain drug in- 
dustry in 1989, up 9.6 percent from a 
year ago to $4.13 billion, according to 
Drug Store News’ latest survey. 

Some segments within the category 
did exceptionally well in ’89. Sales of 
professional and premium-priced hair 
care brands increased as drug stores 
tried to trade customers up to the high- 
er-priced products. Many chains re- 
vamped their planograms to group the 
products by families to further at- 
tempt to generate trade-ups. 


Skin care items popular

lotions were popular, both with the 
mature woman who has long been the 
category’s mainstay, and with a grow- 
ing number of teenagers concerned 
about how they will appear later in life. 
Skin cleansers and sun tanning/sun 
protection products were also popular, 
as people tried to care for their skin 
now and protect it against the ravages 
of time for the future. 

Sales of children’s grooming prod- 
ucts also increased. These were funded 
for the most part by aging, affluent 
baby boomers who will purchase entire 
lines, ape | that nothing is too good 
for their offspring. These same over- 
stressed parents helped the bath preps 
segment, as they bought bubble and 
mineral baths to soak away their own 
cares and help them relax. 

Another important trend concerns 
the use of natural ingredients and com- 
panies that have environmental integ- 
rity. Buyers said that manufacturers

Home office pads bottom line 


ome office supplies, picked as 
i: one of the 10 hottest segments 
for 1990 in a Drug Store News 
survey released in January, spearhead 
owth in drug chains’ stationery/ 
ed office departments. 

Many chains have responded to the 
increasing number of consumers work- 
ing out of their homes—a projected 
36.8 million home workers by 1992, or 
almost 29 percent of the workforce— 
by expanding their home office sec- 
tions. Some tacos reaped double-digit 
sales increases as a result. 

Chains with stringent space con- 
straints sometimes opt to broaden 
their selection rather than slgpain | 
increase space for home office prod- 
ucts, and many are grouping all home 
office merchandise together into a sec- 
tion distinct from the rest of the statio- 
nery department. This is being done so 
customers “don’t have to search among 
the Snoopy folders for home office 
items,” reasoned one buyer. 


Fashion is important 


Drug chains often look to fashion in 
home office and school supplies to dif- 
ferentiate them from the competition. 
A growing number also use warehouse 
pricing and small bulk packs of legal 
pads, index cards and other heavily- 
used items to attract the home office 
consumer. As one merchandiser point- 
ed out recently, customers prefer to 
buy six legal pads rather than just one, 
but “not a whole pallet.” 

While such items as file folders, 
business envelopes and note pads are 
the bread and butter of the home office 
segment, many chains, especially 
those operating in suburbs, find cus- 
tomers are willing to pay for better 
quality and fashion upgrades. 

Some have added or are considering 
adding computer supplies and fax pa- 
per to their mix, but others remain un- 
convinced. Several buyers report they 
stock computer paper in order to have 
a well-rounded selection or because 
they expect the business to grow even- 
tually, rather t: 1 because sales justi- 
fy it currently. 


Advertising schedules 


Many chains include some statio- 
nery items in almost every ad, with tax 
time a particularly good opportunity to 
promote home office supplies and let 
consumers know they’re in this busi- 
ness. Some buyers maintain that tax- 
time advertising should start as early 
as January and continue right up to 
taxpayers’ day of reckoning. 

hile a few chains report feeling the 
impact of specialty office supply me- 
gastores, others say their target cus- 
tomers differ: specialty stores such as 
Staples aim for the small- and medium- 
sized office customer, while drug 
chains target the home office worker. 

The school/home office category is a 
year-round, profitable area for drug 
chains, many of whom report gros; 
margins of 40 percent to 50 percent and 
average turns ranging from four to 
double digits. 

At drug chains, school/home office 
had the largest increase in sales—16.2 
percent—of any segment in the statio- 
nery department for 1989 over 1988, 
and represented 30.9 percent of total 
category sales in 1989, second only to 
greeting cards’ 35.2 percent.

the Back-To-School seminar in Febru-

Chain operators are contending with 
white-hot competition in the photofin- 
ishing market, much of it coming from 
the roughly 16,000 one-hour photo labs 
that have sprung up in the U.S. over the 

ast decade. According to the Photo 

arketing Association, drug stores held 
a slight edge as the nation’s top outlet 
for photoprocessing in number of rolls 
developed in 1988, the last full year for 
which figures are available: a 23.8-per- 
cent share, with stand-alone aind tbe 
close behind, at 21.1 percent. 

Meanwhile, supermarkets and dis- 
count stores reap steady gains in pho- 
toprocessing market share as they pro- 
mote the service more aggressively 
and add in-store labs. 

“While all outlet types experienced 
actual roll-count increases [in photo- 
finishing], only discount stores and su- 
permarkets experienced growth 
above the market average,” the PMA 
noted in its last industry report. 

One example: Smith’s Food and 
Drug Centers, based in Salt Lake 


City, finished 1989 with 15 in-store 
mini-labs, and will probably double 
that number this year, according to a 
company spokesman. “The good mar- 
gins are in developing, but it’s a very 
competitive business,” he told Drug 
Store News recently. 

Most drug chains, meanwhile, re- 
main cautious about the feasibility of 
in-store mini-labs. Despite big im- 
provements in mini-lab technology 
over the past few years that have elim- 
inated the need for special plumbing 
and cut down required space signifi- 
cantly, most chains have yet to try the 
concept, or are testing in-store labs 
only on a small scale. 

One major exception: Eckerd Drug, 
which has put Express Photo one-hour 
labs into 130 of its stores in Florida and 
Texas and reached enough of a “critical 
mass” with that approach to make it 
profitable. “We weigh a lot of criteria 
when putting them in, like demograph- 
ics and location,” Eckerd president 
Harry Lambert said. 

Other chains which have waded 
slowly into the in-store processing 
business include Longs, Rocuaar 
Pay Less NW, SupeRx of Arizona, 
Walgreens and Standard Drug. Revco

Price hikes by the major film manu- 
facturers late Ben year forced some 
new decisions on chain merchandisers, 
who had to choose between passing the 
higher prices onto their customers or 
swallowing them to maintain or build 
business. Bither way, they face steadi- 
ly increasing competition for the film 
business from supermarkets, dis- 
counters and other trade classes. 

Drug chains are fighting hard to hold 
their share of the business for obvious 
reasons. Film continues to generate 
some of the most rapid turns in the dru 
store, with a minimum of required re 
estate. And the 35mm boom has pushed

Prices, mix give chains an edge in mature tape market 


ideocassette recorders have 
V found their way into nearly 

three out of four American 
homes, fueling a market for blank vi- 
deocassettes that has boomed to more 
than $2 billion annually. Drug stores 
have captured roughly 13 percent of 
that market, according to a market es- 
timate by 3M/Scotch, by jumping in 
aggressively with broad product selec- 
tion and continual discounts and pro- 
motions. 

Now, with household VCR penetra- 
tion at near-saturation levels, the vid- 
eotape market has matured into sin- 

le-digit sales gains every year and a 
attle for market share among a hand- 
ful of major manufacturers. The mar- 
ket has also become segmented by 
varying grades of tape quality and new 
labeling and packaging systems to give 


customers more choices and more con- 
venience. 


High-quality lines 


In general, videotape and audiotape 
manufacturers have moved to over- 
come the rampant price-cutting on 
standard-grade blank tapes by offer- 
ing more expensive, higher-quality 
lines and new tape grading systems. 
Increasingly, they are also responding 
to consumer demand for multipacks of 
three or more tapes. 

Even on promotion, blank tapes 
yield gross margins of 20 percent or 
more, most retailers say. And they re- 
main fast turners and traffic-builders, 
despite the maturity of the market. 

Increasingly, however, the chain 
drug industry has become disenchant-
