Chains’ consumables sales increase 8.8% 


Category benefits from promos & tests with new items and c-food 


Having sold groceries for some 
time now, buyers are more com- 
fortable and receptive to promot- 

ing new items. 


ales of grocery products in 
S chain drug stores rose 8.8 per- 

cent in 1989, thanks largely to 
increased promotional activity with 
groceries, and to more experimenta- 
tion with new items and convenience 
foods. 

Most chains promote at least some 
grocery items, even if it’s just soft 
drinks, snacks or candies, in every cir- 
cular. Some chains also use direct mail- 
ers for stores with convenience food 
departments. 

aving sold groceries for some time 
now, buyers are more comfortable and 
receptive to promoting new items— 
especially when buyers feel confident 
that food stores won’t be too aggres- 
sive with these items. 

“We are still selective about the new 


ey 


Chains have discovered that an ideal mix of dry groceries includes juice, cereals and canned soups. 


items we'll promote, but we are more 
willing to try them. We were one of the 
first to promote Chef-Boy-Ardee’s 
new microwavable Lunch Buckets, 
and we did very well with them,” said 
Dennis Wozniak, vp-purchasing for 
Arbor Drug. 


Avoiding head-on competition 


Drug chains are also discovering 
new ways to avoid head-on competi- 
tion with food stores over the items 
they promote. Wozniak said Arbor de- 
cided to advertise Campbell’s soup last 
year, but it didn’t want to feature the 
flavors that food chains tend to pro- 
mote, like chicken or tomato soup. So 
the chain decided to advertise flavors 
that were less price-sensitive, such as 
celery soup. 


1989 grocery-snacks-soft drinks-beer 


-liquor-wine 


Rite Aid has a different strategy for 
groceries. It does a high percentage of 
its business in og a agers so traffic 
is available. What Rite Aid’s manage- 
ment wants from groceries is incre- 
mental sales. 

So, Rite Aid buys top brands on deal 
or closeouts and then stacks them out 
in their stores. The business is all in- 
and-out, but Rite Aid is able to take a 
Ne margin, pick up incremental sales 

rom customers already in the store, 
and pass along a good “value” to its 
shoppers. 

- In one recent incidence, Rite Aid 
made an “opportunistic buy” of Vlasic 
pickles at a special closeout price. Be- 
cause it acquired the pickles at an espe- 
cially low price, it was able to seil them 
for about 40 cents less than grocery 
stores were charging. But even at that 
price, a source said Rite Aid took close 
to a 20 percent margin. 

For small chains like the 10-unit 
Florida-based Best Buy chain, grocer- 
ies have proven they can draw traffic 
and build sales, but the challenge now 


is to fine tune the program to make it 
even more profitable. 

Best Buy’s grocery buyer, Marv 
Fletcher, says warehousing more con- 
sumables will increase his profit mar- 
gin. “When we warehouse some pro- 
motional items like potato chips, we 
get an extra 5 percent to 10 percent for 
drop shipping them to the warehouse,” 
he pointed out. 


Seasonal promotions 


Last year more drug chains did sea- 
sonal cross promotions using grocery 
items. Particularly popular was holi- 
day season pairings of pumpkin pie 
mixes or canned pumpkin, either with 
evaporated milk, jars of marshmallow 
cream, or packages of ready-to-bake 
pie crusts. 

Besides advertising groceries as 
traffic builders, many drug chains also 
stock selected groceries aggckao | as a 
convenience to customers, as well as a 
way to create incremental sales and 
become a destination store for fill-in

-Single-packs pace chains’ tobacco profits 


iven well-merchandised, se- 
G cure tobacco displays, drug 
store operators derive good 
profits from the category, even in this 
period of diminished unit consump- 
tion. Single packs are accounting for a 
greater share of sales, chain buyers re- 
port, for two reasons: customers who 
are trying to lessen the amount they 
smoke buy fewer cigarettes per visit, 
and carton prices are reaching new 
high levels. 

That is good news for drug chains, 
since single-pack margins are in the 
mid-20 percent range compared with 
10 percent on cartons. 

Overall, tobacco sales rose 4.7 per- 
cent to nearly $2.5 billion at drug 
chains in 1989. 

Profits are enhanced, of course, by 
vendor allowances. New programs 
which pay for behind-the-counter shelf 
space are encouraging drug chains to

Drug stores’ ho 


mid the glamour and gadgetry 
A of the latest International 
Housewares Exposition, drug 
chain buyers generally homed in on ba- 
sic merchandise, promotable items, 
and fashion colors and styles rather 
than high-tech or high-end items for 
their housewares departments. 
That’s because most drug chains see 
housewares as a steady, no-frills busi- 
ness. The industry is dominated by dis- 
count stores, which in 1988 accounted 
for 27.5 percent of the $35 billion (man- 
ufacturer sales value) housewares 
market, versus drug stores’ 4.4 per- 
cent share, according to the National 
Housewares Manufacturers Associa- 
tion (NHMA). The trade group’s 1989 
figures aren’t out yet. 


$2.4B in sales 


For 1989, the housewares category, 
in which Drug Store News included 16 
segments, garnered $2.4 billion in 
sales at drug chains. 

Although chains may differ on what 
they classify as part of the housewares 
category, certain segments stand out 
as areas of opportunity, however 
they’re classified. 

Health-oriented personal care prod- 
ucts, for instance, are a hot segment 
for drug chains. This is because items 
such as whirlpools, massage devices, 
dental care appliances, and air and wa- 
ter filter systems dovetail nicely with 
their health care image and provide 
higher price points. 

Sales for the personal care segment 
as a whole, including hair dryers and 
other grooming products as well as 
such health-oriented items, increased 
7.4 percent over last year and repre- 
sented 11.4 percent of total house- 
wares category sales, according to 
Drug Store News research. Vaporizers 
and humidifiers, broken out separate- 
ly, gained 9.2 percent in sales for 1989

Sales leaders 


“Rubbermaid is a leader in innova- 
tion and long-term fashion,” said mer- 
chandise manager Andy Striefel of Pay 
Less NW, whose large (up to 31,000 
square feet) stores house extensive 
housewares departments. “But for ex- 
citement, small companies such as 
Frem, with its new fashion colors, cre- 
ate incremental sales.” 

Striefel added that in housewares 
generally, “The trend is definitely to 
upscale products. Consumers are 
more demanding; they want better 
quality and unique products—for ex- 
ample, gadgets such as slicers and 
whips. sag has become a call word 
everywhere. The consumer is willin 
= pay more for something that will 
ast.” 

One impetus, he suggested, is that 
specialty stores which have sprung up 
in the past few years have raised con- 
sumers’ expectations for upscale and 
unique products, and they now expect 
drug chains such as Pay Less to have 
similar items. “We see it as an opportu- 
nity,” Striefel said. 


Cleariing products strong 


In household supplies, which as a 
segment grew 8.6 percent in 1989 over 
1988, household cleaning products are 
top draws. Chains surveyed by Drug 
Store News at the end of 1989 looked to 
cleaning supplies as one of the 10 hot- 
test segments for 1990. Chains report- 
ed taking advantage of pre-pricing, ad- 
vertising, and new products (160 
introductions in 1989, according to the 
Marketing Intelligence Service) to fuel 
sales. 

While many chains promote house- 
wares regularly, some of their most 
aggressive promotions and merchan- 
dising tactics are concentrated on 
lighting and paper products, and these 
efforts have paid off in increased pro- 
ductivity. Lighting product sales for 
1989 grew 7.9 percent over tine previ- 
ous year, and paper products ‘senerat- 
ed a 9.8 percent increase in sa'*s, 1989 
versus 1988.

or all the talk about drug chains 
reemphasizing health care, that 
shouldn’t be interpreted as an 
abandonment of general merchandise. 
Far from it. Indeed, batteries, sun- 
glasses and hosiery ranked among the 
strongest growing categories at drug 
chains in 1989. 

The three segments, which together 
account for 40 percent of the general 
merchandise department, leaped 
ahead in the double digits. In large 
part, they are frequently replenished 
items that sell well in drug stores, 
which are perceived as outlets of con- 
venience. 

Their success is also driven by mer- 
chandising advances, such as cross- 
promotions, space-efficient pene 
and displayers, that are well accepte 
by retailers and consumers. 

Overall, general merchandise grew 
9.8 percent at drug chains in 1989 to 
$1.96 billion, equal to 4.9 percent of to- 
tal chain volume. Retailers generally 
take 35 to 45 percent margins on goods 
from this department.

performer in Drug Store News’s mid- 
1989 General Merchandise Survey.

at drug chains to $230.5 million, as the

Watches 


Drug chains benefitted from wom-

shifting to more, lower-cost models as 
fashion accessories. Sales of under-$50 
items drove 7 percent segment growth 
the past year. 

Brand staples at drug chains: Ti- 
mex, Casio, Armitron, Lorus and 
Sharp International, according to buy- 
ers, who seek a broad range of afford- 
able styles and healthy margins. 

Moreover, new styles and licenses 
help keep watches interesting. Strong 
lately: Little Mermaid, Ninja Turtles 
and Dick Tracy. Large face watches, a 
Russian-styled watch, and sports 
models endorsed by professional ath- 
letes were prominent, as chains as- 
sured sales with regular promotions. 


Sunglasses 


Sunglasses advanced 14.4 percent to 
$263 million at drug chains in 1989. 
More a chains are playing them up 
as an easily obtained fashion accessory 
by displaying spinners near cosmetics, 
or else grouped by the front end, to in- 
crease impulse purchases. 

The Food and Drug Administration 
has endorsed a voluntary program put 
forth by the Sunglass Association of 
America, a manufacturer trade group, 


to label sunglasses according to the de- 
gree of ultraviolet protection provid- 
ed.-As protection becomes a more sig- 
nificant issue, drug chains stand to 

in share because of their health care 
image and the ability of pharmacists to 
answer questions.

Arbor adding five Michigan units 


TROY, Mich. — Arbor will open five new stores in Michi- 
within the next month, including the store being designated as 
tore No. 100. That milestone unit will open May 19 in the subur- 


ban Ketones St. Clair Shores, northeast of Detroit. 
Three of the new units will open in upstate Michigan, includ- 
ing an opening in Midland May 21 and two stores set for a May 14 


opening in nearby Saginaw. Arbor will also add its third store in 
Ann Arbor June 9. 

Several more units are in final stages of completion, a spokes- 
man said. Arbor will “easily” have 150 units on line by the mid- 
1990s, he added. 


Bergen opens 71,000-square-foot DC 


ORANGE, Calif. — Bergen Brunswig Drug Co. recently 
opened a 71,000-square-foot full-service distribution center in 

ansas City, Mo. 

The wholesaler’s Kansas division, which opened April 2, is a 
full-line supplier of OTC and H&BA products as well as pharma- 
ceutical items. The DC will serve customers in Kansas, Missou- 
ri, Iowa and Nebraska.

riously, when the canopy ‘shay Se the sidewalk at a CVS store

NACDS speakers tap industry future 


In all of the vast number of words spoken at the 

NACDS annual meeting, two themes stood out. 
First, pressures on pharmacy are going to intensi- 
fy, and chains had better gird themselves for a long 
siege by government and industry cost-cutters as well 
as a whole range of tough competitors. 


Second, the war being waged for the 
drug store’s other core categories is 
bound to get even hotter. Only those op- 
erators who are able to stay fresh, trim 
costs and find and train good people will 
thrive. 

Of course, there’s nothing new in this. 
But what was valuable was the classy 
way that the NACDS meeting speakers 
addressed those issues. Speeches and 
commentaries were jam-packed with 


IN THE MARKET 


facts and delivered in doWn-to-earth 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


language. Who could ask for more? 
In a limited space it’s difficult to cap- 


ture even a small portion of the meet- 
ing’s flavor, but let me play back a brief sampling of 
notes scribbled in the dark of the vast meeting room: 

C. Everett Koop, former U.S. Surgeon General: 
“The medical care system in this country is laissez- 
faire, but it is not competitive. .. I know you [mem- 
bers of NACDS] take pride in the competitive nature 
of community pharmacy even if pharmacy drug costs 
have risen.” 

Jim Harrison Jr. of Harco Drug: “The surviva! of 
our industry rests on pharmacy, which makes up 30 to 
40 percent of drug store sales and a larger percentage 
of profits. [It’s important for drug stores] to dance 
with who brought them.” 

Mike Wright of Super Valu: “I suggest you seek 


ways to better appeal to the practical or smart shop- 
pers who are pressured for time and largely oriented 
to making their life more comfortable — but who are 
also price sensitive.” 

Fred Canning of Walgreens: “Deep discounters 
such as Phar-Mor and Drug Emporium are obvious 
price threats, but I think the jury is still out on this 
concept. Some will execute well and be successful, but 
there will be fallout.” 

Peter D. Hart of Hart Research Associates: 
“Don’t ever lose that trust [that customers have in 


‘The survival of our industry rests on phar- 
macy, which makes up 30 to 40 percent of 
drug store sales. . . [It's important for drug 
stores] to dance with who brought them.’ 
— Jim Harrison Jr. of Harco Drug 


their pharmacists]. People who know their pharma- 
cist by name shop in drug stores more.” 

Jerry Heller of May’s: “If I succeeded in raising the 
profile of small chains with their peers and with suppli- 
ers during the past year [as chairman of NACDS], 
that may be my most important accomplishment.” 

Dick Eils of Thrifty: “We have a great case. We 
know that markets work. We know that free market 
pricing is the best guarantee of safe, affordable 
products for consumers. And we know that’s what 
we can deliver. We have the trust of the American 
people. We must now aggressively take our case to 
the [third-party] payers and to State Houses across 
the country.” 


A Tribute to Dick Groberg 


Dick Groberg served Lebhar-Friedman 
for 32 years in many capacities. He re- 
tired in December, and died last month of 
complications from multiple sclerosis. 
The following is a tribute to Mr. Groberg 
written by J. Roger Friedman, president 
of Lebhar-Friedman, Inc. 


Yesterday I attended a funeral service. 
The casket was draped with an American 
flag. This flag symbolized Dick Groberg’s 
life. Dick believed in the values of our 
country. Like our people, he was honest, 
outspoken and wielded great influence. 

Dick joined Lebhar-Friedman 32 years 
ago as an associate editor. Over the years 
he was promoted to editor, publication di- 
rector, group publications director and, 
during the last few years, vice president 
of human resources. 

For several years Dick knew he had 
multiple sclerosis. He initially had to 
give up tennis. His comment was, “This 


is a young man’s game, let them play it.” 
Eventually Dick reached the point 
where he could no longer take the train 
to work and was forced to drive. As his 
condition worsened, he had to use a 
cane. Never once did he complain or fee] 
that life had treated him unfairly. 

He was a great believer in corporate 
training, and up to his retirement he 
continued to develop instructional pro- 
grams for our new associates. He was 
honest. During our executive commit- 
tee meetings, Dick could be counted on 
to give his opinion without emotionalism 
or prejudice. His famous line, “My tum- 
my tells me... ” meant that over and 
above the reports and the figures, there 
was another factor. This intuitive evalu- 
ation was based on his belief that indi- 
viduals had a basic responsibility to help 
themselves, to be honest to their asso- 
ciates and to uphold the standards and 
values of the organization that they rep- 


His famous line, ‘My tummy tells me...’ 
meant that over and above the reports and the 
figures, there was another factor. This intuitive 
evaluation was based on his belief that individ- 

uals had a basic responsibility to help them- 
Selves, to be honest to their associates and to 
uphold the standards and values of the organi- 
Zation that they represented. 


Groberg 


resented. 

Several years ago, Dick discussed 
with me the possibility of his retiring 
and I told him that the company still 
needed him. We needed his calm, level 
voice, and we needed his even-handed 
approach to business problems. He 
agreed to stay on. 


Retirement tribute 


His retirement dinner this past De- 
cember was a tribute to the affection 
and esteem his business friends held for 
him. The restaurant was filled to capaci- 
ty. Many of his associates flew in at their 
own expense. 

At our December luncheon, Dick was 
surprised when he was the recipient of 
the Arnold D. Friedman Citizenship 
Award. This award is given annually to 
the individual in the company who most 
personifies my father’s spirit of “treat- 
ing his associates as family.” Part of this 
award is a two-week trip for the recipi- 
ent and his spouse to any place they so 
desire. As recently as three weeks ago, 
Dick was talking about his trip. 

He never will take this well-deserved 
vacation, but every time we have a busi- 
ness problem at Lebhar-Friedman, ev- 
ery time the atmosphere begins to heat 
up and every time tempers begin to 
flare, I will think of Dick and try to 
imagine what his tummy would have 
told him. 

I know the Executive Committee on 
High is saying, “Dick what do you feel?” 

— J. Roger Friedman

bulbs, merchants

General Electric continues

outlets for commercial users 
and has no immediate plans to 
expand them into other retail 
channels such as drug stores. 
However, GE in December 
launched a 14-sku non-screw- 
in halogen line of specialty and 
decorative bulbs aimed at all 
trade classes. 

Besides emitting a better 
quality light, halogen bulbs 
will last more than twice as 
long as standard incandescent 
bulbs, vendors claim. Some 
see them as an opportunity for 
drug chains to compete 
against discount stores by up- 
grading the assortment with 
value-added items, where 
they can recover profits lost 
from promoting standard 
bulbs as loss leaders. 

Chains usually take 30- to 
50-percent margins on light 
bulbs, even when frequently 
discounting the ‘A-line’ 
SKUs. They recover margin 
from the specialty bulbs, the 
fastest-growing bulb segment 
because of trends such as: 
“nesting,” or staying at home; 
and the perception that deco- 
rative lights are an inexpen- 
sive way to improve the home.

Batteries 


atteries are leading the 

charge as traffic draws 

and generators of im- 
pulse sales—especially with 
many chains advertising mul- 
tipacks to draw heavy battery 
users, who account for more 
than 70 percent of all house- 
hold battery volume. 

Chains feel it is important to 
create an image as a source for 
batteries, as the category con- 
tinues to post about 5 percent 
annual unit growth, which is 
projected to continue. 

Besides adding multipacks, 
chains increasingly are follow- 
ing discount stores’ lead and 
merchandising batteries 
throughout the store, wherev- 
er impulse purchases can be 
captured. Batteries are the 
most profitable item at the 
checkout, topping candy, gum 
and cigarettes, according to the 
latest Drug Store News’ Check- 
stand Merchandising Study. 

Underscoring the impor- 
tance of space-efficiency, im- 

ulse and cross merchandising, 

veready this year launched 
its ietlk-wra ped multipacks 
with bold graphics, which oecu- 
py one-third the space of blister 
packs, fit neatly at the checkout 
and attract customers. They’l! 
be launched in mid-June. 


Yet chain’s strategies differ 
significantly. 

Leroy Pharmacies, the 11- 
store Manhattan chain, for ex- 
ample, has found that C and D 
batteries are strong sellers, al- 
though the AA size is the top 
SKU, as it is industrywide. Le- 
roy stores in Greenwich Village 
and on the Upper East Side 
typically advertise 2- and 4- 
pack C and D sizes “at least 
once a month” at “close to loss- 
leader prices,” said Jerry 
Gmuer, merchandiser. Leroy 
offers a 2-pack at $1.79 with a 
$1 rebate and a 4-pack at $2.99 
with a $1 rebate, Gmuer said. 

Gmuer stopped Eveready 
and Duracell floorstands with- 
in sight of the front registers 
because of shrink problems. 


Genovese Drug Stores 
takes a more typical promo- 
tional approach by running 
regular group promotions of 
its Eveready and Duracell bat- 
teries that include all sizes, 
with emphasis on 8-pack AA 
and 4-pack Cs and Ds. The cat- 
egory, paced by multipack 
sales, continues to produce 10 


ercent annual growth, said 
ier Lenny Genovese. 
Regarding Eveready’s 


shrink wrapping, Genovese 
said, “I don’t have the space on 
the counters. They may make 
a great fourth-quarter item.” 

uracell is breaking new 
ground in responding to con- 
sumers’ concerns about bat- 
tery life. This year it’s launch- 
ing liquid-crystal-display 
battery testers that will be in- 
cluded as free premiums in the 
blister card with the battery 
on top-selling SKUs. 

Buyers said the jury is out. 
One buyer speculated the tes- 
ter could “keep consumers out 
of the market” by allowing 
them to keep batteries longer. 

Eveready, meanwhile, will 
be the first vendor to tap into 
consumers’ concerns about 
the environment. Its top-mov- 
ing sku’s will bear an on-pack 
notice: “New: First Low Mer- 
cury Battery in U.S.”

at Eveready concedes, is “more 
of a perception of being a prob- 
tem than it is a problem.”

and checkout merchandising 
system, and claims about sev- 
en percent of the drug market.

SmartPack for the checkout.

9% some ground. Duane

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 14, 1990 


Batteries 


Rechargeables predicted Heavy battery users drive category 


echargeable batteries 
are awaiting their day 
in the sun. 

“[Rechargeables] are batter- 
ies of the future. Consumers 
are just getting their feet wet,” 
said Dan Halaburd?, market- 
ing manager, Panasonic. 

Price and consumer under- 
standing of the product have 
been barriers. Yet growing 
battery use promises to make 
rechargeable systems — and 
the nickel-cadmium batteries 
they employ — the method of 
choice for certain types of bat- 
tery users, some contend. 

Heavy battery users, who 
can dispose of 96 batteries a 
year compared with the aver- 
age users’ 35, have been most 
prone to use rechargeables, ac- 
cording to Rayovac estimates. 

Rechargeable sales have 
been growing more than 20 
percent a year as vendors “fill 
in the pipeline” and secure 
sales with new accounts. 

But since the rechargeable 
battery loses its life very 
quickly — it loses about 1 per- 
cent of its charge a day —it’s 
suitable for only certain types 
of heavy-use functions, such 
as in radios, toys or office dic- 
taphones. 

The advantage, of course, is 


having the chance to buy one | 


battery rather than dozens, a 


potentially economical prac- | 


tice, which also holds appeal 
for consumers concerned 
about battery waste disposal. 

Thrift, Peoples and Rite Aid 
are among chains that have 
picked Panasonic recharge- 
ables. 


Faster recharging 


The latest twist was the 
launch in 1988 by General Elec- 
tric and Eveready of chargers 
that work in one hour, com- 
pared with the typical seven to 
sixteen hours required. 

GE’s Fast Charger retails 
for about $30, for use only with 
AA batteries, charged two at a 
time. 

Eveready has launched two 
models of its Generator, a 
$39.99 version for four AA 
batteries and a $49.99 version 
fo. four AAs, Cs or Ds. 

“We have the capability to 
take the charging time to as 
low as 15 minutes,” said Hala- 
burda of Panasonic, whose 
system requires six hours. 

Why not do it? Panasonic 
found in a survey that consum- 
ers would rather pay less and 
wait longer. Panasonic’s un- 
der-$15 price point was ac- 
ceptable; over $20 was not, 
said Halaburda.

Safeway’s parent company, 
Kohlberg ‘oan Roberts & 
Co., reportedly thought it 
could fetch for the stock last 
year. 

Safeway went private in a 
$4.3 billion leveraged buyout 
in 1986 financed by junk bonds 
and other borrowings and ar- 
ranged by KKR, which also 
put up most of the $175 million 
that accounted for the equity 

ortion of the buyout. The 
avect— ora was the larg- 
est LBO in history up to that 
time—turned Safeway into a 
highly leveraged company 
with a massive, $5.6 billion 
debt load and interest ay- 
ments of $576 million the first 
year after the buyout. 

To ease those debt pres- 
sures, Safeway quickly began 
selling off store divisions 
around the U.S., Canada and 
in Europe. It left key markets 
such as Dallas, Kansas City, 
Salt Lake City and Southern 
California and raised enough 
in store sales to trim its debt 
by $2.5 billion. In the process, 
interest payments declined to 
$401.2 million in 1988 and 
$382.8 million last year, and 
Safeway’s operating network 


declined to 1,117 higher-vol- 
ume stores in the U.S. and 
Canada. 

Nevertheless, Safeway is 
still saddled with $3.1 billion in 
debt. 

The supermarket giant 

lans to spend roughly $3.2 
billion for new and remodeled 
stores, lease obligations and 
other ‘capital improvements 
pts the next five years. KKR 
~~. to generate $104.4 
million by offering 10 percent 
of the company. 

Safeway plans to use those 
funds to open approximately 
70 new stores and complete 
major remodeling projects in 
another 240 units over the 
next two years. 

Pharmacy growth 

Pharmacies are now found 
in 31 percent of Safeway’s 
stores, compared with 13 per- 
cent five years ago. In 
Safeway’s newer superstores, 
the percentage of Rx counters 
is even higher, at 56 percent. 

Thanks in large part to store 
im rovement programs, 
Safeway’s operating profits 
rose to 462 million in fiscal 
1989 from $326 million the pre- 
vious year. Same-store sales 
were up a healthy 5.5 percent.

Bartell to open second-biggest unit 


SEATTLE — At press time, Bartell Drugs was set to open its 
33rd store May 21 in Lake Meridian. At about 14,000 square 
feet, the newly constructed store, situated in a strip center with 
a supermarket, is the chain’s second largest. Both the Lake Me- 
ridian unit and a new store opened in March in Canyon Park 
Place shopping center have pre-recorded tapes, a section Bar- 
tell is introducing in a few stores. 

At least one more store opening is planned this year; it’s slat- 
ed for September in Bellevue, according to Gordon O'Reilly, vp- 
merchandise for the chain. 


Dot picks pharmacy and POS systems 


KANSAS CITY — Dot Drugs, the 14-store deep discounter, 
has announced that it will use National Data Corp.’s DataStat 
Pharmacy application, and NDC’s point-of-sale system. Dot 
was purchased from Wal-Mart by a four-person management 
team Feb. 1. 

Both applications run off an IBM PS/2 computer, with a level 
of integration. For example, pharmacy files are automatically 
updated when drug purchases are made at the front-end POS. 
sal application features also include on-line pharmacy in- 
ventory records, price calculation, and medical records. 

The point-of-sale application employs TEC M-2300 electronic 
cash registers and supports scanning with automatic inventory 
tracking and price ee-ae. 

While there is a second IBM PS/2 in each store, it’s not used 
for the pharmacy/POS applications, but as a work station.

SAN FRANCISCO 
McKesson Drug has promoted 
two regional vps, Robert 
McGuire and Hank Wilde, to 
the newly created positions of 
senior vp-operations. 

In addition, McKesson has 
realigned its 46 distribution 
centers into seven rather than 
eight regions. 

The organizational changes are aimed at achieving closer co- 
ordination between staff and operating units. 

McC.uire, 49, will be responsible for four regions with 21 dis- 
tribution centers in the eastern United States. Zee Medical 
Products, the company’s distributor of first aid supplies and 
emergency medical products, will also report to McGuire. 

Wilde, 56, will have responsibility for three regions with 25 
DCs in the western and central U.S.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 28, 1990 


American mulls over sale 
of Buttrey Food and Drug 


SALT LAKE CITY — Stung by legal chal- 
lenges that continue to tie up its planned merg- 
er of its Lucky Stores and Alpha Beta divi- 
sions, American Stores is considering the sale 
of its Buttrey Food and Drug subsidiary. 

Headquartered in Great Falls, Mont., But- 
trey operates 44 supermarkets and combo 
stores in Montana, Idaho, Washington, Wyo- 
ming, and North Dakota. The company an- 
nounced in mid-May that it will “wait to review 
the bids for Buttrey before making a final deci- 
sion to sell the chain.” 

Bids are being solicited by Shearson Lehman 
Hutton Inc., and American reported that a 
“number of parties interested in the purchase” 
have surfaced, including an employee group led 
by Buttrey’s managers. 

American appeared eager to link the possible 
sale with its unsuccessful efforts to merge 
Lucky and Alpha Beta. Besides the fact that 


Biggest draw is low prices: 


the division “is not yet performing at the levels 
desired” despite recent improvements in sales 
and earnings, American noted that its legal 
headaches stemming from the planned merger 
are a factor. 

“The continuing litigation with the Califor- 
nia Attorney General, which has prohibited 
American from merging Lucky and Alpha 
Beta, has forced the company to review all its 
marginal performing assets for possible sale,” 
the company announced. 

The U.S. Supreme Court handed American 
its latest legal obstacle in early May by ruling 
against the company’s appeal and granting the 
State of California the power to exercise feder- 
al antitrust laws to block the merger while the 
matter is reviewed in court. That decision “will 
cause American Stores to return to federal 
court for an antitrust trial,” the company an- 
nounced.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 28, 1990 


Good service generates customer loyalty 


I went shopping for garage door grease last week- 
end in my local hardware store, not a particularly mo- 
mentous event, except that I was impressed by what 
the proprietor did for a customer who came in looking 
for a painter’s hat. 

The proprietor strolled into the stock- 


>» 
IN THE MARKET 


room. When he came back with the hat 
he wordlessly pushed it across the 
counter. 

“How much do I owe you?” the cus- 
tomer asked. 

“No charge.” 

The customer hesitated. He was obvi- 
ously uncomfortable because he hadn’t 
purchased any paint at the store. “Come 
on,” he insisted, thrusting his hand in 
his pocket. “How about a buck or some- 
thing?” 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


“Nope,” the owner replied. “The hat’s 


on us. But if you need any paint in the fu- 
ture, think about us.” 

A simple, inexpensive gesture. A small bit of in- 
vestment in customer relations and future business. 
It’s the kind of free service that’s been done by Main 
Street shopkeepers for generations, yet has been dif- 
ficult for most large retailers to replicate with any con- 
sistency. And, of course, consistency of service and 
presentation is where the retail wars of the 90s are go- 
ing to be won or lost. 

We know one executive of one of the nation’s most 
successful drug chains whose principal criterion for 
hiring a new store employee is: Does the candidate 
smile? 

Too simplistic? Not to my mind. A bright smile on a 
gloomy day can be a better promotion than a free hat. 


Speaking of free services, Drug Store News plans to 
launch a new electronic publication next month aimed 
at providing confidential job-wanted listings for exec- 
utives who may be temporarily out of work because of 
consolidation, cost-cutting moves, or other disloca- 
tions so prevalent in the industry nowadays. 

The publication is called JOBFAX. 

As the name implies, the new publication will be 
sent by facsimile machine to a list of hundreds of key 
executives at drug chains and manufacturing compa- 
nies nationwide. We plan to issue JOBFAX twice a 
month starting in June. Our intention is to provide this 
service on a completely confidential basis—no fees or 
later favors expected. 

So, what do you doif you’re a live wire in marketing, 
operations, pharmacy, MIS, or any other retailing dis- 
cipline and you suddenly find yourself out in the cold, 
looking for another headquarters job? Just send a 
blind want ad describing your strengths and needs in 
75 words or less to Drug Store News, Confidential Box 
100, 425 Park Ave., New York, N.Y. 10022. Don’t for- 
get to include your name, address, and daytime tele- 
phone number. We won’t publish it, but we’ll need it 
for verification purposes. 

We'll publish your blind listing in the first avail- 
able JOBFAX, along with a free box number, to 
which interested companies can write. No charge to 
you or the companies. When letters arrive ad- 
dressed to your box number, they’!l be mailed to you 
unopened. The rest will be up to you and the inter- 
ested companies. 

What’s in it for us? Well, for our part, a free listing in 
JOBFAX is a little like that painter’s hat: a small invest- 
ment in reader loyalty, which we’re pushing to maintain 
in the publishing/information wars of the ’90s. 


service is the challenge of the decade 


Can a person become ill from reading incessantly 
about the importance of service? If you think so, pop 
two aspirin, dust off your resume and think about 
where you want to work next—because you may not 
be welcome at your drug chain for long. 

Fred Canning, Walgreens board 


member and former president, declared 


THE HUMAN SIDE 


at the recent NACDS Annual Meeting: 
“One-third of all Americans between 18 
and 65 always feel rushed today. Retail- 
ers who survive in the ’90s will either re- 
spond to this time crunch—or lose a lot 
of customers.” 

Time poverty may well be the con- 
sumer cry of this decade. That will be 
manifested in value-bent, practical pur- 
chase decisions, and destination shop- 
ping, where people visit a store for a 


AL HELLER 


specific item and browse less. They'll be 


tougher to entice, even through the 
most clever marketing gambits—unless 
retailing basics are in place. 

For the one in three Americans who visit their drug 
store at least once a week, and the 29 percent who 
shop there two to three times a month, service is the 
biggest improvement they would make in the drug 
stores they use. In a national survey of 1,000 consum- 
ers conducted for NACDS by Peter D. Hart Research 
Associates this spring, service came up by a 2:1 mar- 
gin over prices as the most frequent unaided, volun- 
teered suggestion on how to make stores better. 

“Forty-five percent say their pet peeve is waiting in 
long lines while other cash registers are closed. . . to 
those whose time is at a premium. . . this is unforgi- 
veable. . . People seem most riled by poor checkout 
service and poorly informed sales people,” the study 
said. “Nothing could do more to improve the drug 
store’s image than to upgrade the service.” 

Which services will be especially important to con- 


sumers between now and the year 2000? Which would 
they be willing to pay for? The survey probed respon- 
dents, and came up with some opportunities. 

Among all adults surveyed, 45 percent said “they 
will pay higher prices or submit to the inconvenience 
of returnable containers for products that are environ- 
mentally safe.” The same percentage said they want 
direct third-party billing. 

FAX and postage services seem especially sought 
by working women and people who visit drug stores 
regularly; 39 percent of all adults polled found this idea 
“extremely or very appealing.” Another 38 percent in- 
dicated they “will purchase products that help protect 
their skin from environmental damage.” 

Other notable followings: 35 percent favor interac- 
tive computer systems that give recommendations on 
health products; 34 percent would like shopping cred- 
its; 33 percent want to buy diagnostic aids at drug 
stores; and 32 percent would appreciate the offer of 
simple lab tests for strep throat cultures. 

The NACDS-Hart survey unveiled a pattern of 
niche buying among consumers that is apparent in the 
way they use drug stores. Nearly seven in 10 buy med- 
ications in drug stores, but just four in 10 make front- 
of-store purchases. “There is a considerable decline 
between loyalty to the pharmacy and loyalty to the 
rest of the store,” the report read. 

“Americans have divided loyalties,” it continued, not- 
ing that 53 percent of respondents “mainly use a drug 
store for some element of their purchasing. . . In every 
group of the population, a majority or plurality use a 
drug store for some purchases—but that means they 
also uses discount and supermarket stores.” 

Any drug store retailer who thinks service will not 
swing the consumer vote in his favor in the ’90s ought 
to pop those aspirin and go. Otherwise, replace the 
bottlecap and start developing meaningful services. 
That is truly the challenge of the decade, and the one 
that holds promise of the greatest payback—loyalty.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 28, 1990 


Boldest chains 
beat ethnic’s 
overall growth 


verall sales of ethnic products in chain 
drug stores appear to be up moderate- 
ly this year, with performance flatter 
in some weak economic regions of the country. 

Plenty of bright spots are enhancing ethnic 
productivity: relaxers, hair color, skin care, 
styling aids, shaving and hair conditioning 
products are strong, buyers and distributors 
report, with growth as high as 15 percent to 
30 percent over a year ago. 

Many of these surges are evident, however, 
in categories with a relatively small dollar vol- 
ume base such as skin, shaving, color and styl- 
ing aids. Their growth is offset by the decline in 
curl kit and cur! maintenance product sales, say 
buyers. 

In the Northeast, the Midwest, and some

hancing ethnic productivity: 
relaxers, hair color, skin care,

over a year ago. 


portions of the the West Coast, buyers and dis-

creases in overall ethnic category sales, partic- 
ularly for stores in dense _ ethnic 
neighborhoods. 


Tough times 


However, in some parts of the South and the 
Southwest (such as Oklahoma, Texas and Loui- 
Siana), where the economy is still relatively 
soft, some drug chains and ethnic distributors 
say sales are still soft on average, or at best, 
flat. One source said that in his stores in these 
markets, “times were tough” for ethnic hair 
care as well as other core H&BA categories. 

There are also certain chains that are doin 
an above-average job with the category, an 
sources say Sales in these companies are much 
better than the industry average. 

Chains like Eckerd, Big B, Perry, Peoples 
and Harco, for example, are currently very ag- 
gressive with the category, giving it more 
Space, pricing very sharply versus their com- 
petition, advertising the category more and 
working very hard with manufacturers and/or 
distributors to stay on top of sales and styling 
trends. 

Many chains such Arbor Drug, K&B, Wal- 
greens, Longs, Thrifty and Pay Less are do- 
ing reasonably well with the category, with 
sales in high volume stores still showing 
growth, in some cases up as much as 8 percent 
to 12 percent. 

But they are also taking time to review their 
pone looking for new strategies that may 

= them enhance growth for 1990 and be- 
yond. 

One buyer told Drug Store News that while 
his management is satisfied with ethnic’s per- 
formance to date, they feel they have to stock 


Chains are satisfied with ethnic’s performance but feel they have to 
adopt new strategies to beat out the competition and enhance their 
popularity with shoppers. Photo cour

some new strategies with the category, both to 
prevent competition from eroding their share 
of sales and to enhance their own popularity 
with ethnic shoppers. 

“We’re aware that ethnic shoppers tend to 
spend more on toiletry and beauty care items 
than white shoppers do, and we want to do 
more to court their total business,” this source 
said. 

“Overall, we’re doing okay with the catego- 
ry,” said Charles Monk, Harco’s H&BA/candy 
buyer, “but that’s primarily because we’re ex- 
panding it and we're advertising more to at- 
tract the business. 

“We’re also trying to make more of a state- 
ment with ethnic, to improve our pricing, our 
assortment and our selection so we can say to 
our customers, ‘We’re giving you a choice on 
the items you need,’ Monk added. “Selection 
and assortment are very important to ethnic 
shoppers, and we want to have that so we can 
make a better showing.” 

In fact, sources say that when they do 
“court” African-American shoppers, they get 
much stronger growth in overall store sales, 
with sales increases in the double-digit range, 
compared to an average 5-percent increase for 
the industry as a whole. 

Some of the growth is due to chains featuring 


In fact, sources say that when 
they do “court” African-Ameri- 
can shoppers, they get much 
stronger growth in overall 
store sales, with sales in- 
creases in the double-digit 
range, compared to an aver- 
age 5-percent increase for the 
industry as a whole. 


an enhanced product mix focused on growth 
segments and growth brands, more creative 
advertising using a variety of media ranging 
from direct mail to radio, and increased use of 
in-store circulars featuring a vast assortment 
of cents-off coupons and other bonus values. 


Preduct assortment 


The chains with the strongest performance 
are also paying much more attention to their 
product assortment. Either the chain’s own 
ethnic product buyers or their approved dis- 
tributors are weeding out slow movers or flat 
categories and replacing them with new and 
trendier products in the growth segments. 

For chains with strong ethnic programs, 
three of the hottest segments right now are re- 
laxers, up on average between 10 percent and 
30 peréent in sales, depending on the chain and 
region; styling aids, up 10 percent to 25 percent 
on average; and hair color, up between 10 per- 
cent and 30 percent. 

Shaving products are also showing growth, 
up 15 percent to 20 percent; skin care is up be- 
tween 15 percent and 35 percent on average 
and hair accessories are up, 30 percent to 35 
percent, sources say. 

Sales for curl kits and curl maintenance 
items, on the other hand, are still down be- 
tween 10 percent and 15 percent on average, 
especially in the South and Southwest where 
curl styles have shown the strongest endur- 
ance. 

Many buyers for the chains that are showing 
growth report they have cut back on the declin- 
ing categories like curl kits to give more space 
to the growth segments like relaxers, color and 
styling aids. 

As a result these chains are getting better 
turns as well as better dollar growth.

and they began weeding out 
slow turning, unproductive 
SKUs, thereby increasing 
turns and overall profitability

Some Drug Emporium

or line to their mix. The line is 
called Theon and it’s been in

One source said Drug mmpori-

of customer requests. He de-

Many chain buyers use dis-

their ethnic Deceetmonts. 
Sources like Charles Monk 
and Scott Gorley told Drug 
Store News that distributors, 
as specialists, know the cate-

than the average drug store

style and fashion changes or 
regiona! preferences. 

“We expect them to react to

Monk also pointed out that 
distributors who rack job 
stores can save drug stores 
lost sales by making sure they 
are always in stock on the hot- 
test selling items. 

“We have a lot of part-time 
people and it’s hard for them 
to stay on top of what’s selling. 
Also sometimes an item will do 
well in Tuscaloosa, but not in 
Birmingham, so we just feel 
we're better off with a paid 
service.” 

Monk said that years ago 
Harco did warehouse ethnic 


products, but gave it up be 
cause they were constantly 
out of stock on the items that 
were selling well, plus they 
were missing hot new prod- 
ucts as they came along. 


Distributor autonomy 


Some chains give their dis- 
tributors the autonomy to add 
potentially hot new items to 
the mix or to delete stale items 
as they think best. Others re- 
serve the right to make such 
changes from headquarters, 
but their reaction times can 
vary from 6 to 8 weeks to 6 
months or more, depending on 
how flexible they are in updat 
ing planograms. 

If chains take too long to re 
act, of course, they miss their 
chance to capture sales from 
new item at a time when they 
are at their strongest, the ear- 
ly stages of their launch when 
they are heavily supported by 
manufacturers with print or 
radio ads. 

To avoid this, some chains 
such as Perry, Eckerd and 
Peoples will let their distribu- 
tors put in new items whenev- 
er they feel such additions 
make sense. 

A decentralized chain like 
Longs will also give store 
managers the right to add or 
delete as they think best, and 
this approach, one source told 
us, lets individual stores mer- 
chandise to the customers. 
When enough customers ask 
for something or when a dis- 
tributor recommends some- 
thing, “we try to stock it,” he 
said. 

Other chains, such as Sav- 
on, leave some flex space in 
their planogram so buyers can 
take a chance on a new item, 
stocking it on a trial basis to 
see how well it will sell.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 28, 1990

& segments’ 
outlook bright 


his year, ethnic hair color is doing exceptional- 
ly well, up about 10 percent, according to many 
buyers and ethnic distributors. 

Several buyers said Dark & Lovely was “growing 
and growing” as it achieves broader distribution. 
Dark & Lovely’s Reviving Colors line was also sin- 
gled out for above-average growth. In some chains 
sales of Revlon’s Creme of Nature hair color were 
said to be good, but in some regions buyers reported 
it was just doing OK. 

Luster is still doing very well with its Pink Oil 
Moisturizer. One source said the movement was “un- 
believable.” Its S Curl line is also said to be showing 
very strong growth. 

PCJ, which is a press-and-comb preparation in a 
jar, is doing well. One buyer said he thinks its growth 
comes from positioning. He said as far as he knows it 
is the only value-priced mild relaxer targeted at 
mothers who can use it on their daughters’ hair. It 
sells for about $3 less than the premium-priced mild 
relaxers. 

Another value-priced line, Supreme’s Raveen, re- 
cently went up about 25 percent in price, but most 
sources said it hasn’t hurt Raveen’s sales. The line is 
continuing to sell well in its category. So is Raveen’s 
Duke relaxer for men. 

There are also some relaxer kits now out that are 
formulated to add volume or body to the hair as they 
relax it, and several sources said these either look 
promising or are starting off strong. Pro Line’s Soft 
& Beautiful Volume Plus and Carson’s Excelle and 
Excelle Plus were singled out as looking good. 

Right now no-lye relaxers without sodium are sell- 
ing better than sodium relaxers, most sources said. 
But sodium relaxers still have a core of loyal users 
because the formulation is stronger and can be more 
effective with medium or course hair. Now Revlon is

Men are wearing their hair short. This trend has helped 
sales of styling products, including a come-back for po-

Jim Normandin, who buys ethnic products for 
Beauty Enterprises, estimated his ethnic shampoo 
sales were up about 10 percent, almost entirely due 
to the Optimum shampoo. “At $4.25 for 16 ounces, 
it’s the first real value in ethnic shampoos,” he said. 

Dark & Lovely is extending its maintenance line 
with a new oil moisturizer, hair spray, and holding 
spray that is expected to sell well. 

Many sources also said that oil moisturizers in gen- 
eral are doing especially well this year. The growth is 
probably due to the fact that oil moisturizers are a 
very versatile styling aid. Buyers said they can be 
used with all kinds of hair styles, from relaxed 
through curled hair. 

Summit Labs’ Pre Con styling gel is doing very 
well. Summit’s Liv conditioners and Mend hair re- 
parative were also performing well, and a new item, 
Penetrator 37, looks promising. 

Most sources said hair foods, meaning products 
that nourish the hair, is a good, solid niche category 
with steady, consistent sales, mostly to older con- 
sumers. However, Chuck Lewman at Paul’s Sun- 
dries thinks the upcoming launch of some new “liq- 
uid” hair foods might open the category up to 
younger consumers, who may have been reluctant to 
try the solid hair foods their parents were using. 

Scientific Research’s Le Kair line has a new liquid 
food that Lewman thinks could do well, and Key- 
stone may also be soon bringing out a similar 
“bridge” food under its Long Aid brand. 

Across the country, the Always Natural line of 
conditioning products, made from all-natural ingre- 
dients, are continuing to do very well. Super Gro and 
9-11 were frequently mentioned as being exception- 
ally strong sellers. A number of buyers also singled 
out J&M’s Isoplus as also selling exceptionally well. 

Many blacks have problems with dry hair or with 
hair that breaks easily because of ironing, blow dry- 
ing, or chemical processing. That has we ody sales of 
moisturizing/conditioning products, and several 
sources reported that Lustrasilk’s MoistureMax 
line, in particular, has been doing very well.

Bodi.

Standard Drug’s Pata said that in skin care, prod- 
ucts with cocoa butter are still very popular, includ- 
ing Palmer’s Cocoa Butter and Woltra’s Stick Cocoa 
Buter. The Dr. Fred Palmer skin bleachers and 
whiteners are also doing well at Standard. So is 
Chatham Labs’ Nadinola skin cream. 


Some cosmetics lines show growth 


Cosmetics is holding its own. It’s not growing dra- 
matically, but some segments are showing growth. 

Posner continues to be the strongest ethnic line. It 
dropped its nail care line, which was its weakest line, 
and repackaged its best sellers in face, lip and eye. 

One source said the new packaging looks great and 
is also more compact and space efficient. He estimat- 
ed that stores should be able to get one facing of the 
entire assortment in two or two-and-a-half feet. 

At Drug Emporium headquartered in Atlanta, 
the Zuri line also does well in some stores. Buyer 
Kathy Covault said the popularity of her ethnic cos- 
metics lines varies by neighborhood. In some stores, 
Zuri is the best-selling line. In others, it’s Posner. 

Sales in the men’s market have been given a nice, 
strong jolt by the increasing popularity of the 
stacked or high-top look. Most buyers reported that 
this look is now popular with boys and young men na- 
tionwide, and to maintain it, consumers need at least

In many high-traffic ethnic neighborhood stores, mass market products are mixed in with ethnic brands in one 
planogram: all color together, for example, to make shopping easier for consumers. 


two or three maintenance products, usually a relaxer 
for the top and pomades for the sides. 

Soft Sheen’s new launch of Sporting Wave High 
Five Moist Gel and Sheen Spray is packaged to ap- 
peal to users of this and other currently popular 
styles, and buyers are betting it’s going to do well. 

In the pomade category, where some buyers are 


seeing a resurgence of growth, Murray’s is still num- 
ber one, Standard Drug reports. Other men’s lines 
doing well: Dax Wave and Grow, Soft Sheen’s Sport- 
ing Wave, and Posner’s Easy Wave. 

In shaving products, buyers said Magic Shave 
Gold, Royal Crown cream shave, Magic’s cream 
shave, and Palmer’s No Blade are doing well. 


The competition intensifies for the ethnic dollar 


Most buyers said 1989 and the first 
half of 1990 have been marked by in- 
creasing competition from mass mar- 
ket discount chains, food chains, and 
beauty and barber (B&B) supply 
stores for the ethnic consumer’s toilet- 
ry business. 

Buyer said the competition from 
chains like Wal-Mart, K mart, Drug 
Emporium, and F&M was intensify- 
ing, and noted that B&B shops contin- 
ue to proliferate, especially in urban 
areas. 

In Oklahoma, Kent Humphreys, 
president of Jack’s Service Co., a dis- 
tributor, said he is seeing a continuing 
shift of ethnic sales away from drug 
stores and into mass merchandise and 
B&B stores—because they are “less 
structured than drug and food chains, 
and therefore more responsive to 
shifts in consumer purchase prefer- 
ences.” 


B&Bs especially dangerous 


The independently-owned B&B 
shops are especially dangerous as com- 
etitors. At the American Health and 
eauty Aids Institute, executive di- 
rector Geri Duncan Jones estimated 
that company’s year-to-date sales of 
ethnic products are up between 30 per- 
cent and 40 percent versus last year. 
Because of B&B’s relatively low 
overhead as family-owned business- 
es, they can price much lower than 
most drug chains. B&B’s offers ser- 
vice, and is way out on the cutting 
edge when it comes to stocking the 
latest items and offering the fullest 
assortments. 
Until now, B&B stores have been 
the most visible in urban markets like 


Detroit, Chicago, New- 
ark, and New York, but 
now they are moving into 

w markets such as Los 
Angeles and Oakland. 

The West Coast is also 
just starting to feel the 
impact of deep discount- 
ers such as Drug Empori- 
um. 

Soon, too, Wal-Mart 
will begin opening stores 
in the California region.

ter off with a paid ser-

For the drug chains 
that are responding to 
customer needs for as- 
sortment, selection, com-

in spite of the difficulties. 
“The B&B stores are 


anticipating intensified 
competition across a variety of H&BA 
and cosmetics categories, including 
ethnic. 

As Humphreys said, it is really 
harder for highly structured organiza- 
tions such as drug and food chains to 
compete with the larger mass mer- 
chandise chains as well as the more 
flexible deep discounters and B&B re- 
tailers. 

Unless a drug store has a cosmeti- 
cian trained in ethnic products, it’s 
hard for it to provide service, and if an 
ethnic department is strictly plano- 
gramed, it is also hard for drug chains 
to react quickly to hot new products. 

Many use distributors, said a source 
who manages toiletries for a major 
drug chain, because they “know the 
professional side of the business better 
than we do and they can spot potential- 
ly hot new items faster and move fast- 
er to get them into the stores.” 

Charles Monk, ethnic buyer for 
Harco Drug, pointed out that distribu- 
tors base orders on what sells by re- 
gion, and they maintain the category 


really growing,” says AH- 
BAI’s Jones, “and unless chains look 
out, the B&Bs are going to be getting 
more and more sales. If the product se- 
lection isn’t there, consumers won’t 
shop that store. Price alone can’t do 
it.” 

Many food chains and their whole- 
salers are also trying to capture more 
ethnic sales. 

Kroger, Safeway, Alpha Beta, 
Vons, and Ralphs are among chains 
expanding their ethnic product assort- 
ments, as are grocery wholesalers and 
cooperatives like Certified Grocers. 

Some drug wholesalers are also do- 
ing the same. 


Keeping in stock 


This year, several distributors have 
worked out programs with both food 
and drug wholesalers designed to keep 
them, and their chain and independent 
customers, in stock on the fastest- 
moving ethnic items. 

The programs are similar to those 
that ethnic suppliers participated in 
with drug chains, except they don’t 


usually involve rack jobbing. 

The distributors recommend the 
brands and lines for wholesalers to car- 
ry, just as they do for many drug 
chains. They then ship the products 
into the wholesaler’s warehouse, help- 
ing to round out that wholesaler’s 
product mix with the items that sell 
the fastest in ethnic toiletries. 

Partly as a result of such collabora- 
tions, many food chains now devote 
more space to ethnic products, ex- 
panding their product mixes, updating 
and strengthening their product selec- 
tions, and advertising select products 
more frequently at competitive prices.

NACDS names key Officials 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — After naming Richard Eils, presi- 
dent of Thrifty Corp., to be NACDS chairman for this year, the 
board of directors elected two other prominent industry execu- 
tives to top-level posts. 

Philip Beekman, chairman and ceo of Hook-SupeRx, Inc., is 
vice chairman, succeeding Eils. Harvey Rosenthal, president of 
CVS, is treasurer, succeeding Beekman. 

Eils, an NACDS board member since 1986, succeeds Gerald 
Heller, president of May’s Drug Stores, in the trade group post. 
Beekman has been on the NACDS board since 1987, and Rosen- 
thal has served on the board since 1986. 

In addition, NACDS has elected David Eisenberg, president 
of Peoples Drug Stores to its board. Jack Futterman, chairman 
of Supermarkets General, and Henry A. Panasci, Jr., chairman 
of Fay’s, joined the executive committee. 

NACDS president Ronald Ziegler also announced the ap- 
pointment of Christopher Gallagher to the post of senior vp-ad- 
ministration and communications. Gallagher has served as di- 
rector of meetings administration since 1986. 


Revco expo helps draw 200,000 


CLEVELAND — The Revco Health and Beauty Expo, at 
the Cleveland Convention Center, was part of a mammoth 
three-day event in May sponsored by the drug chain, which has 
bs up mounds of goodwill through such fitness-oriented af- 
airs. 

The Expo ran the same weekend as the Revco-Cleveland 
Marathon and 10K races, and Criterium Bike Races, which have 
developed a following since the late-1980s. In all, over 200,000 
consumers attended. 

More than 150 Revco vendors exhibited at the Expo, where 
free health screenings were offered by Cleveland MetroHealth 
Medical Center. Celebrities included Corbin Bensen, Mary Lou 
Retton, Jim Palmer, Suzanne Somers and Bob Griese. 


K mart revving up pharmacy 


TROY, Mich.— At its recent stockholders meeting, K mart 
chairman and chief executive Joseph Antonini detailed the compa- 
ny’s accelerated, $2.3 billion expansion and modernization pro- 
gram, which has been set with the goal in mind to “develop a brand 
new chain of 2,500 full-size K mart stores by 1995 in the U.S.” 

K mart, he said, will enlarge, refixture and remerchandise 
620 existing stores, build 280 new units to gap older, smaller 
units, and totally refurbish the remain 1,260 stores “to make 
them the equal of our newest prototype store.” Antonini also 
noted that consumer acceptance of the chain’s new prototype 
has been “very rewardin iB 

K mart’s new format features a prominent pharmacy at the 
front end, with expanded selection of health na beauty aids and 
related ha store merchandise in a modern setting. Those fea- 
tures will play a big role in new and enlarged K mart stores, the 
company has indicated. 


O&M names Dozier cfo 


RICHMOND, Va. — Owens & Minor, Inc. has named Glenn 
J. Dozier its new vice president-chief financial officer, the com- 
pany announced. 

Dozier comes to O&M from AMF Bowling, Inc., where he had 
been cfo and vp of administration and control. He received a 
B.S. from Mes 5 Tech in 1972 and an M.B.A. from the Colgate 
Darden School of Business at the University of Virginia in 1975.

By Susan Ball 

NEW ORLEANS — Like a 
dormant plant after a long dry 
spell, K&B Drugs is putting 
out new shoots; a survivor in a 
depressed oil economy where 
less hardy businesses have 
withered. 

Since the mid-eighties, 
K&B has opened only one or 
two stores a year, but has al- 
ready opened four stores this 
fiscal year and plans to un- 
wrap at least four more before 
the end of 1990. The thrust 
will be in the Montgomery, 
Ala., market, where K&B ex- 
pects to have six stores by 
year’s end. 

Moreover, the 85-year-old 
company will start rolling out 
anew POS credit card system 
from Stratus this month to its 
155 stores. 

And it’s looking to start 
automating its merchandising 
and distribution systems later 
this year. 


New ad emphasis 


In addition, K&B has shift- 
ed from a heavy ROP newspa- 
per advertising emphasis to a 
circular program, significant- 
ly increased TV exposure and 
fewer print ads. 

The chain will also extend 
planogramming efforts to 
more core departments, in ad- 
dition to current planogram- 
ming of cosmetics and H&BA, 
and is relocating and expand- 
ing some departments, as well 
as modifying adjacencies. 
Lance Clark, who joined K&B 
this eal as vp-marketing, 
said that some realignment of 
buying departments and more 
specialization of buying func- 
tions are also planned. In addi- 
tion, endeaps and wings are 
getting more systemized at- 
tention, in-store signage has 
been streamlined and aisles 
have been cleared of things 
like floor displays, for a clean- 
er look, he added.

an unsuccessful, two-year ef-

pha Beta with Lucky Stores, 
which American purchased in 
June 1988.

mid-May that it will sell 152 of 
its 175 Alpha Beta stores and 
nine Lucky stores in southern 
California over the next five 
years to settle an antitrust ac- 
tion brought by state attorney 

eneral John Van de Kamp.

Me: Is this your new prototype? 

Retailer: Prototype? Well, um, not exactly... 

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard retailers 
resist the term prototype in talking about a newly de- 
signed store. The reason: there is something too solid 

about the word. A prototype is con- 


SS | 
IN THE MARKET 


ceived, designed, molded and baked 
hard before its offspring are “rolled 
out,” somewhat like a truckful of bagels. 
An exaggeration? Sure. But proto- 
types do seem, in the mind at least, to 
resist a lot of change. And retailers by 
~- nature are tinkerers. They like to see 
af how a design works for a while. Then 
| they like to play with it. It’s all part ofan 
evolutionary process that never reaches 
the ideal because there is no ideal. Be- 
sides, the size and configuration of avail- 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


able space varies all over the lot. One 
size bagel does not fit all. 


96 


I was thinking about retailers’ “proto- 
typical” reactions to prototypes on my way up to Ver- 
mont this past Memorial Day weekend after making a 
long side trip to Fair Haven, Mass., to view the latest 
example of Brooks Drug’s creative design efforts. 

Brooks is one of a number of drug chains that are reap- 
ing the rewards of a consistent marketing approach fo- 
cusing on basic drug store strengths. Though Hook-Su- 
peRx Inc., Brooks’ parent company, doesn’t disclose the 
financial results of its drug store divisions, it’s generally 
known that Brooks’ same-store sales—a very sensitive 
barometer of marketing and operational success—are 
among the strongest in the industry. 

Before my opening day trip to the store, John Jen- 
nings, Brooks’ executive vp of marketing, had been 
hesitant to use the word prototype to describe the new 


A new, er, prototype passes an acid test 


store. That had started me thinking about how many 
times I had heard similar comments. Jennings talked 
about making changes and then “stepping back” to 
look at the results. Were they an enhancement and 
could they be transported economically to other 
stores? As part of an LBO company, Brooks has to 
keep “portability” of design foremost in mind. 

Individually, the changes in the Fair Haven store 
were not overwhelming, but the sum of the parts was 
impressive. Creative lighting headed the list. Two 
rows of ceiling track lights, one focused on the statio- 
nery wall on one side of the store and the other on cos- 
metics on the opposite side, made those departments 
pop. Neon signs affixed to subtly colored walls above 
those departments also drew the eye—without being 
overwhelming. The angled fragrance wall was topped 
by a similarly tasteful neon sign. Eventually, parabol- 
ic lens coverings, which direct ceiling lights onto prod- 
uct shelves and minimize overhead glare, will be in- 
stalled. 

There were other eye-catching design touches. The 
newly-configured pharmacy department offered more 
privacy for pharmacist-patient talks. A vaulted ceil- 
ing above the center promotional aisles was a nice, 
low-key solution to the perennial problem of how to 
shout sale without making a lot of noise. A slotted, 
mirrored wall behind fragrances gave an opportunity 
to build display accents by varying the height and 
width of the fragrance shelves. 

In snort, it worked. The key departments—phar- 
macy, H&BA, cosmetics—made suitably strong 
statements. The high-grossing stationery section 
seemed practically to grab customers by the lapels. I 
put the store to the acid test. I asked my wife Joan 
about it. 

“Very nice,” she said. Sounds like a winner to me. 


Employment rules face dramatic changes 


Make no mistake—if Congress has its way, the fed- 
eral groundrules governing hiring and employment 
practices will shift dramatically within the next couple 
of years. 

In most cases, the requirements facing drug stores 


WASHINGTON 
PERSPECTIVE 


will be made more stringent, the penal- 
ties for violations will be stiffer, and the 
cost of complying with the new stan- 
dards will be higher. 

What’s more, employers won’t be 
able to count on the White House to 
run interference for them. Indeed, 
much of the impetus for the stricter 
hiring and employment rules is coming 
from within the Bush Administration 
itself. 

Take the new “Americans with Dis- 
abilities Act” (ADA) just passed by Con- 
gress with the support of the President. 


KEN RANKIN 


Under this legislation, drug stores and 


other businesses will be prohibited from 
discriminating against the handicapped in the work- 
place. Moreover, employers will be expected to re- 
move all unreasonable barriers to the employment of 
the disabled. 

In some cases that could mean just a minor adjust- 
ment in work procedures. In others, however, it could 
involve costly structural changes to fixtures, stores 
and other buildings. 

The new ADA law is just one in a series of actions in 
the pipeline now that would affect drug store industry 
employment practices. Here’s what else is on tap in 
Washington: 

Tough new federal restrictions on age discrimina- 
tion in the workforce. The Labor Committees in both 
the House and the Senate have already approved leg- 
islation requiring employers to offer equal benefits to 
workers, regardless of their age. Those bills would ef- 


*sctively reverse a recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling 
“hat held that employers could extend “fringe” bene- 
fits to younger workers without offering similar bene- 
ts to older employees. 

_ @Acrackdown by the U.S. Justice Department on 
illegal discrimination based on national origin. A re- 
cent General Accounting Office investigation re- 
ported “widespread discrimination” against job ap- 
plicants who “look or sound foreign” in the wake of 
federal immigration reform legislation requiring 
employers to be responsible for weeding out illegal 
aliens. 

Although Congress may repeal the four year-old 
penalties on employers of undocumented immi- 
grants, it’s more likely that lawmakers will instead 
press for more vigorous enforcement of the rules 
against national origin discrimination. 

@More vigorous enforcement against workplace 
“sexual harassment” by the U.S. Equal Employ- 
ment Opportunities Commission (EEOC). New 
guidelines issued by the EEOC earlier this spring 
hold corporate officials legally responsible for sexu- 
al harrassment violations by supervisory personnel. 
Additionally, the enforcement rules oblige employ- 
ers to protect all workers from a “hostile” work envi- 
ronment. 

eStiffer penalties for violations of federal child labor 
laws. Legislation now under consideration on Capitol 
Hill increase fines for child labor violations ten-fold 
from $1,000 to $10,000 each. In addition, the bill would 
deny firms that engage in these practices the right to 
bid on government contracts or obtaining federally 
guaranteed loans. 

eTight new rules on job safety. Congress is debat- 
ing a proposal to establish criminal penalties for seri- 
ous workplace safety violations, while the Bush Ad- 
ministration has uncorked a separate plan to triple the 
dollar fines facing businesses.

SPECIAL SAMI REPORT 


To assess trends and the 
magnitude of proprietary 
drug sales, Arbitron/SAMI 
has created a special universe 
of 20 product categories and 
classes. It tracks sales move- 
ment of all brands and items in 
both drug and food stores in 54 
major markets every 28 days. 

For the year ended Feb. 23, 
1990, retail drug store sales of 
these non-prescription goods 
increased 1 percent to reach 
the $4.4 billion mark. 

Medicated-dandruff sham- 
poo scored the highest growth 
rate nationally, at 12 percent. 
The second-highest gain was 
posted by the first aid prod- 
ucts category, which includes 
bandages, first aid kits, first 
aid tape, and cotton swabs. 

Two categories showed ma- 
jor losses: appetite suppres- 
sants fell 29.9 percent in drug 
stores, and proprietary tran- 
quilizers dropped 18.2 per- 
cent. 


Reasons examined 


The weakness among appe- 
tite suppressants is surely re- 
lated to the enormous growth 
of measured diet meals, paced 
by both the Slim Fast and UI- 
tra Slim Fast diet programs. 

Among the 20 categories 
and classes included in this 
special sales analysis, 14 post- 
ed gains in drug store dollar 
volume, while six showed 
losses.

these proprietary drug items

Blade razors popular win 


By and large, American 
men still to seem prefer a 
blade razor to an electric 
shaver. 

In Drug Store News’ Gal- 
lup survey of male consum- 
ers, 67 percent used a blade 
razor and only 30 percent 
used an electric shaver. 

Double-edge blades and 
disposable blades were the 
most popular with blade ra- 
zor users; they were chosen 
by 31 percent and 28 percent, 
respectively. 

Gillette was far and away 
the favorite brand of razor 
blade. A total of 53 percent of 
the respondents ‘ic used a 
blade razor said a Gillette 
blade was their favorite, 
while 18 percent picked Bic, 
and 13 percent of the resopn- 
dents picked Schick. 

More than half—57 per- 
cent—of the electric shaver 
users preferred the Norelco 
brand. Another 27 percent of 
electric shave users named 
Remington. 

When men take a razor to 


their face, they usually like to 
soften the procedure with a 
soothing aerosol cream. Of 
the respondents who used 
blade razors, 60 percent said 
they used a cream when they 
shaved; 13 percent said they 
simply feel. soap; 5 percent 
used a gel; and 3 percent a 
pre-shaving lotion. 

Gillette was also the 
popular brand of shaving 
cream, named by 27 percent 
of shaving cream users as 
their favorite brand, with 18 
percent specifically saying 
they preferred Gillette 
Foamy. 

Barbasol, Colgate Instant 
Shave, and Edge were the 
next most popular brands, 
named by 15 percent, 13 per- 
cent, and 12 percent of on 
ing cream users, respective- 
ly.

buyers think women usually 
buy men’s grooming prod- 
ucts and shaving aids, the 
Gallup survey found this is 
not necessarily the case.

this market research survey for Drug Store News to iden- 
tify the buying habits of men who shop for skin care, hair 

ooming, and fragrance products, and women who shop 

or bath, skin, and hair care products.

Convenience key to shaving buys 


When men shop they go for 
convenience, especially for 
commodity products like shav- 
ing cream. 

Men tend to be in drug stores 
or food stores more than they 
are in discount stores or depart- 
ment stores, so that’s where 
most men buy their shaving 
creams and lotions. 

Drug stores scored well with 
convenience-minded males, 
but some buyers think they 


could be doing even better. Ac- 
cording to Gallup, 41 percent of 
all men who use shaving creams 
buy them in drug stores. 
ut, since six out of 10 men 
don’t shop drug stores for shav- 
ing products, chains need to get 
the convenience message 
across to male consumers. 
Some buyers feel the shav- 
ing department needs to be 
more visible, and have its own 
identity. From chain to chain, 


it is paired with hair care or 
deodorants, or is displayed as 
an extension of fragrances. 
Buyers felt the shaving de- 
partment should have a more 
consistent home in dru 
stores, and have a more defi- 
nite, accessible, and conve- 
nient location. One suggested 
that an adjacency with skin 
care and bath care products 
would be the most logical way 
to merchandise shaving aids.

Aftershave/cologne use nears 19% mark 


Manufacturers of after- 
shave lotions and colognes 
have been more successful 
than manufacturers of hair 
styling and hair coloring 
products in convincing men 
to use their products. 

Almost three-fourths—72 
percent—of the male respon- 
dents in the Gallup survey 
said they used either an af- 
tershave lotion or a cologne. 

The frequency of use for 
these products is also up 
slightly, as 19 percent of lo- 
tion/cologne users said they 
are using these products 
more now than several years 
ago, and just 9 percent said 
they were using them less. 


Numerous benefits 


Several buyers think usage 
is higher in this category be- 
cause it is easy for men to 
perceive the social benefits of 
a cologne or aftershave as 


well as to feel the physical 
benefit. 

Many colognes and after- 
shaves are positioned to en- 
hance a man’s sex appeal. 
Many are also formulated to 
leave the skin feeling re- 
freshed and soft after a

Sensor puts drug chains on shaving’s cutting edge 


The Gillette Sensor shaving sys- 
tem is a classic example of a success- 
ful product somewhat tangled in its 
own success. 

Drug chain buyers feel that Sensor 
can be a category buster, if only they 
could get enough of it. Demand for 
the innovative twin-blade razor, 
driven by a massive consumer ad 
campaign, has reportedly doubled 
initial projections and caused product 
outages at some chains. 

Sensor didn’t show up in the Gallup 
consumer survey because it was 
launched in January and was initially 
distributed as the polling was con- 
ducted. 

Before the debut, Gillette predict- 
ed that by year’s end Sensor would 
have a 4 percent share of the wet 
shave market, made up of dispos- 
ables and systems. It is now project- 
ing Sensor revenues of $175 million, 
or 6 percent, said Michael Casner, 
vp-business manager, Gillette. 

Casner said Gillette expects to be 
meeting demand by the third quar- 
ter. By 5 the company was still al- 
locating product, fa experiencing ‘ ‘a 
couple of weeks’ delay” filling back 
orders, he said. 

He confirmed that in mid-Febru- 
ary the unexpected demand had

Cutting edge shaving entry 


Chain buyers interviewed by Drug 
Store News el agreed that Sensor 
is the sharpest new shaving entry in 
years, with performance and features 
that should continue to win over users. 
Its twin blades are mounted individ- 
ually on springs which sense and ad- 
just to the smallest curves of a man’s 
face, Gillette said. 

Yet some merchants reported out- 
of-stocks and were on back-order 
through May, especially on the five- 
and 10-count cartridge blade packs, 
they said. “It’s a terrific product. 
They’ve wiped out the competition. 
Now all they have to do is supply it, 
said Steve Demas, a buyer at Peo les 
Drug Stores. “This razor could be 
dominating the field for quite some 


time.” 

For its part, Peoples was loaded 
with product and ready by the time of 
the Sensor’s Super Bowl Sunday ad- 
vertising kickoff Jan 28. But it has 
been a scramble ever since to main- 
tain everyday stock, while promoting 
the razor about every fifth week. “I 
don’t think I’ve received one [full] or- 
der yet,” Demas said. 

At Duane Reade in New York 
City, “the razor itself is still back or- 
dered. We’re out of stock right now,” 
said Eli Cohen, president and chief 
operations officer. He said the chain 
received 20 percent of a March 1 or- 
der for 1,800 dozen of the razor five- 
pack. By April 17, 1,500 dozen were 
still bac k ordered. The full order ar- 
rived in May. The vendor “is not tak- 
ing orders” on the 10-count packs, 
Cohen said. 

Gillette’s Casner said that Big A 
ple consumers are “more hi hy 
aware” of the product through am 
tising. 

Rite Aid, Kerr, and Thrift also said 
they couldn’t meet market demand 
for the hot Sensor. 

Thrift fared well, except for three 
weeks in March when it was out-of- 


jer 


stock on blades. The chain received 
most of the product ordered and in 
time to meet stores’ demands be- 
cause it submitted orders early, said 
Marty Sheets, senior buyer of cos- 
metics and fragrances. 

“Gillette is on a first-come, first- 
served basis,” said Sheets. Thrift’s 
first order was delivered Oct. 10, and 
the chain placed its second order be- 
fore receiving the first, Sheets said. 
“We could see they were committed 
to a phenomenal advertising bud- 
get,” Sheets said. 


Systems gaining ground 


Buyers said Sensor will likely fuel 
the consumer trend away from dis- 
posables to systems. As a category, 
shaving systems “_ ground in su- 
permarkets in the first quarter of 
1990, according to Towne-Oller & As- 
sociates, New York. 

In the quarter, systems accounted 
for 60.1 percent of wet shave dollar 
volume in supermarkets, compared 
with 56.7 percent in the first quarter 
of 1989. Disposables, in comparison, 
had 39.9 percent of share, compared 
with 43.3 percent in last year’s quar- 
ter, Towne-Oller said.

Frequent use of skin care items grows among men 


The number of men who use 
skin care products isn’t high 
yet, but frequency of use is 
definitely growing. 

Gallup found that although 
the number of men who use 
skin care products is still rela- 
tively low (19 percent), more 
than half of the users (51 per- 
cent) said they use skin care 
items more frequently now 
than several years ago. At the 
same time, just 6 percent of all 
users said they use skin care 
products less frequently. 

Most male skin care users 
also like to buy their own skin 
care products; 73 percent of 


skin care users said they 
bought their own brands, 
while just 25 percent let some- 
one else shop for them. 
Notably, more than three- 
fourths (79 percent) of male 
skin care users said they 
bought skin care products in 
drug, food, or mass merchan- 
dise stores most of the time— 
not department stores, where 
most colognes are bought.
