anufacturers and re- 

tailers of blank video- 

tape are scrambling 

for ways to squeeze higher 

sales and profits from a ma- 

ture but still-lucrative mar- 

ket. Their efforts have begun 

to slow the price erosion in 

videotapes as consumers 

gradually get the message 
about quality and value. 

Nevertheless, videotapes 

make for tough competition. 


For manufacturers, the chal-. 


lenge has been to distinguish 
their brands and gain precious 
shelf space in a category 
crowded with nearly a dozen 
major players and a slew of 
smaller, low-priced imports. 
The result has been a growing 
emphasis by suppliers on 
higher-grade tapes, additional 
formats like 8mm, longer- 
playing tapes, and other niche 
opportunities. 

For retailers, the category 
has also been a competitive 
slugfest. The competition has 
reached fever pitch as two 
forces have converged: the 
maturity of the market and 
the nearly universal distribu- 
tion of blank videotapes into 
every trade class and nearly 
every mass market outlet. 

Blank videotape was one of 
the true boom categories of 
the 1980s, leaping from a few 
million units sold at the begin-

aud spin to 


ning of the decade to more 
than 300 million in annual unit 
sales, generating between 
$1.5 billion and $2 billion at re- 
tail. Since 1986, however, the 
market has flattened out as 
household VCR penetration 
reached near-saturation lev- 
els of more than 60 percent of 
U.S. homes.

Arbor 3rd qtr. sees 
income, sales gains 


TROY, Mich. — Arbor 
Drugs reported a 15.5 percent 
increase in net income and a 
12.3 hag fom gain in net sales 
for the third quarter ended 
April 30. 

Third-quarter net income 
was $2.3 million, compared 
with $1.97 million in the year- 
earlier period, on net sales of 
$82.8 million, which rose from 
$73.8 million. Comparable- 
store sales were up 7.8 per- 
cent for the quarter. 

For the nine months, net in- 
come was $8.3 million, a 24.4 
percent increase over the pre- 
vious year’s $6.7 million. Sales 
for the nine months were up 

8.6 percent to $252.5 million 


from $222.2 million for the pe- 
riod last year. Comparable- 
store sales rose 9.3 percent. 

Commenting on the results, 
Eugene Applebaum, chair- 
man, president and ceo of the 
96-store company, said, “Our 
third quarter reflects the suc- 
cess of our continuing empha- 
sis on pharmacy as the core of 
our operation and the overall 
convenience of our traditional 
drug store format.” 

Arbor, which was recently 
named 1989-1990 Michigan 
Company of the Year by the 
Detroit Free Press, opened one 
store during the third quarter 
and has opened four more thus 
far in the fourth quarter. 


Cardinal sales, earnings 
break records in 4th gtr. 


DUBLIN, Ohio — Cardinal 
Distribution tallied record 
sales and earnings for the 
fourth quarter and fiscal year 
ended March 31. 

Fourth-quarter net earn- 
ings were up 42 percent, to 
$4.3 million, from $3 million in 
the comparable prior period, 
on sales of $239.6 million, a 21 
percent gain over the $198.2 
million reported in the period 
last year. 

For the year, net earnings 
from continuing operations in- 
creased 50 percent, to $12.8 
million from $8.51 million, 
with total net earnings at 
$12.8 million, compared with 
$13.3 million in 1989, which in- 
cluded net earnings from dis- 
continued operations of 
$336,000 and a $4.4 million af- 
ter-tax gain on the April 1988 


sale of Cardinal’s food whole- 
saling operations. 

Robert D. Walter, chair- 
man and ceo, said the record 
fourth-quarter and year-end 
results were achieved solel 
through internal growth, wit 
no acquisition impact occur- 
ring during the fiscal year. 

In March, Cardinal an- 
nounced an agreement in prin- 
ye to buy all of the stock of 
Ohio Valley-Clarksburg Inc., 
for $27.1 million. The deal is 
expected to close this month. 

hio Valley, a Wheeling, 
W. Va.-based wholesale drug 
distributor with annual reve- 
nues of about $190 million, 
serves primarily drug store 
customers in West Virginia, 
Pennsylvania, Ohio, Mary- 
land, Virginia and parts of ad- 
joining states. 


SGC’s 4th qtr. hits new highs 


EDISON, N.J. — Supermar- 
kets General Corp. has started to 
dig out from under its mountain of 
LBO debt, as seen in its record re- 
sults for the fourth quarter and 
fiscal year ended Feb. 3. 


Operating earnings for the year, 
not including a $36.2 million re- 
structuring charge related to the 
Rickel division, were a record 
$213.3 million, a 12-percent in- 
crease over the previous year. Af- 
ter interest expenses, taxes and 


LBO charges, the company 
showed a net loss of $56.3 million, 
excluding the restructuring 
charge, compared with last year’s 
net loss of $58.9 million. Sales, 
though also a record for the 53- 
week period, were essentially flat, 
rising 6 percent over last year’s 52- 
week period to $6.3 billion. 


In the fourth quarter, operat- 
ing earnings, not including the re- 
structuring charge, climbed 41 
percent to $76.8 million.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 18, 1990 


OPINION 


The pages of consumer and trade papers have been 
filled lately with news about the developing “green 
movement” among retailers and the manufacturers 
who supply them. The movement represents a kind of 
redawning of ecological consciousness that’s been 

triggered by the worldwide fear that — 


not to be too apocalyptical about it — we 
may all soon be facing the equivalent of 
environmental Chapter 11, if we aren’t 
there already. 

For example, this year Pay Less 
launched a campaign to manage and re- 
cycle solid waste — an area of crucial im- 
portance to environmentalists, and cer- 
tainly to Pay Less’ environmentally 
savvy customers. The chain kicked off 
the campaign with a one-day recycling 


IN THE MARKET fair, said to be the first of its kind in Ore- 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 8 28°. 


The aim of the fair: to educate employ- 
ees, vendors and the public about the 
value of recycling and waste reduction. By all ac- 
counts the event was a huge success, and in the ensu- 
ing months the chain has continued to provide strong 
leadership in the area of waste management and recy- 
cling. 

Pay Less is just one of dozens of companies that are 
reacting with urgency to the new environmental con- 
sciousness that’s sweeping the country. In recognition 
of the important role that retailers and vendors are 
playing in this area, Drug Store News will begin a new 
column next issue that will throw light on the 


“Green” column gets green light 


environmental concerns and activities of these retail- 
ers and vendors, many of whom are, of course, our 
readers. 

We’re calling the column Greenscape. 

Once a month you can look forward to news about 
the efforts of retailers to come to grips with waste re- 
duction and of their manufacturer partners to develop 
new compact products and packaging that not only cut 
waste but also reduce the amount of space required on 
retailer shelves —a solid two-bagger if there ever was 
one. 

We'll also be highlighting national and state legisla- 
tive and regulatory efforts in the environmental area 
that have a direct impact on retailers and their suppli- 
ers. And we’ll look at environmental causes in various 
markets and how retailers are reacting to them. 

These are just a few of the issues and trends we'll be 
addressing in the months to come. The column is being 
written by executive editor Al Heller, whose environ- 
mental consciousness was awakened long before the 
latest outburst of world concern. In 1979 Heller co- 
authored a how-to book on the use of solar energy to 
create low-cost, high-yield gardens year-round in vir- 
tually any climate. It was called “The Passive Solar 
Dome Greenhouse Book,” and it went through two 
printings. Solar energy may not be at the top of every- 
one’s environmental priority list today, but who 
knows what will happen down the road. 

In the meantime, Heller will be focusing his atten- 
tion on the new environmental issues and how they re- 
late to retail business concerns. We think the timing is 
right. 


Show respect! She could be your mother 


When people date, the saying goes, a woman tries to 
predict how the man may treat her in the future by 
watching how he treats his mother. If he shows proper 
respect and care, then the relationship could have a fu- 
ture. 

Treating your mom well is not only 


the right thing to do; it has payoffs — 
both in real life and in retailing. Chances 
are the way you treat your mom is the 
way you run your business — or at least 
the way you treat elderly customers in 
your stores. 

Much has been written about the 
graying of America, and how the 50-plus 
age group will swell 18.5 percent 
through the 1990s to 76 million people. 
This group, which is increasingly con- 


THE HUMAN SIDE cerned about health issues and the pro- 


AL HELLER 


ates — percent of U.S. consumer demand. 


longing of youth, already accounts for 40 


Their $800 billion combined annual in- 
come represents more than half of the nation’s discre- 
tionary income. 

As stated in Age Wave’s The Shifting American 
Marketplace, people 50 and over spend more in drug 
stores than any other age group, and purchase 37 per- 
cent of all OTCs. 

Now, a national survey of the mature market, “Older 
Consumer Orientations Toward Marketing Practices 
and Responses to New Products,” offers valuable in- 
sights into the thinking and motivations of these veteran 
shoppers. The study, sponsored by the American Asso- 
ciation of Retired Person’s Andrus Foundation, was 
conducted by George P. Moschis, director of the Center 
for Mature Consumer Studies at Georgia State Univer- 
sity. The study is based on a mail survey of 1,515, includ- 
ing responses from 951 adults aged 55 and over. 

Some highlights: 

@ Older adults are more loyal to stores they patronize 
than younger shoppers, with 72 percent saying they 
prefer to do most shopping in a particular store. Older 


consumers also expect more services from retailers. 
They value the presence of a personal advisor (notable 
for cosmetics and pharmacy) and efficient handling of 
returned merchandise. The report noted further that 
43 percent of mature shoppers “don’t mind paying 
higher prices if a store is conveniently located.” 

@ Promotions may not be as effective at encouraging 
brand trial or switching with older adults as they are 
with younger consumers. The older group is more 
likely to use such incentives to save on the products 
they usually buy. When asked about free samples, 46 


Treating your mom well is not 
only the right thing to do; it has 
payoffs — both in real life and in 
retailing. 


percent said, “I would hesitate buying a new health 
care product if I haven’t used a free sample of it.” 
@ Slightly more than half of older adults feel entitled 
to more discounts than younger people, the report 
noted. And while 27 percent said they “like advertise- 
ments that show products especially for older people,” 
they don’t respond nearly as well to advertisements 
they perceive as pandering. Close to one in three said 
they have avoided buying products when they felt ads 
improperly stereotyped an age group. Simply, they 
think of themselves as younger. 
@ Older consumers want to make intelligent product 
choices. To avoid costly mistakes, many stick with 
well-known brands rather than try new or lesser- 
known brands. 

The portrait I get of these people is that they are 
cautious, loyal, vigorous and value-seeking. 

When visiting your stores, keep these impressions 
in mind. And if you see some older ladies, think of your 
mom and treat them accordingly.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 18, 1990 


Gallup: Skin care. 


Aging 


t is easy to understand 

why facial moisturizers 

are one of the fastest 
growing categories in cos- 
metics and toiletries. 

America’s baby boomers 
have matured to the point 
where they worry about dry 
and sun-damaged skin. And 
they want to project a 
healthy body and a youthful 
appearance. 

Women are also better in- 
formed about grooming, and 
no longer try to conceal dry 
or flawed skin under makeup. 

Manufacturers are also 
stimulating the category by 
launching new moisturizing 
products and advertising 
them aggressively. 

Manufacturers are also 
helping women move away 
from simplistic products that 
promise to do everything for 
the skin to sophisticated regi- 
mens or combinations of spe- 
cialty products that can be 
used to cleanse, tone, and 
moisturize not only the whole 
face, but also specific problem 
areas like the eyes or neck. 

Packaging for mass mar- 
ket lines like Plenitude, 
Neutrogena, Almay, Clarion 
and Olay, to name a few, 
has become much more so- 
phisticated. Many mass lines 
are now as attractively pack- 
aged as the more expensive 
department store lines. 

Shelf displays like those 
used by Neutrogena and 
Plenitude also help organize 
the category for women, 
making it much simpler to 
find and identify the cleans- 
ing and moisturizing prod- 
ucts best for the individual 
shopper. 

Television and print ads 
also help explain the catego- 
ry as well as individual prod- 
ucts, and Clarion shoppers 
can use in-store computers 
to help identify their specific 
skin care needs. 


64-percent usage 


With this as background, 
it’s no w nder that Gallup 
discover: | that 64 percent of 
all American women use 
some type of facial moistur- 
izer today. Breaking it down 
further, 30 percent use such

Most of the fashion brands 
like Olay and Plenitude don’t 
even take a therapeutic mar- 
keting position. Their adver- 
tising and packing promise 
to enhance the natural beau- 
ty of the skin rather than 
just treat the skin. 

Olay, as the first mass 
market moisturizer, has 
been in the public’s eye the 
longest, and its advertising 
has been so successful in po- 
sitioning the products as 
beauty enhancers that more 
than nine out of every 10 
women recognize the Olay 
name. 

So it’s not surprising that 
Olay was mentioned most of- 
ten as a preferred brand; 19 
percent of the women who 
used a moisturizer did so. 

American women are also 
still more comfortable using 
a single product on their 
face rather than a regimen 
of products. Almost three- 
fourths (74 percent) of all 
skin moisturizer users told 


Gallup that they use just one 
product. However, 24 per- 
cent of all moisturizer uses 
do adopt a regimen ap- 
proach, and these users say 
they have at least two or 
three products they use reg- 
ularly to treat the skin. 

Price is something of a 
factor when it comes to buy- 
ing moisturizers, as 25 per- 
cent of all women who buy 
moisturizers said they usual- 
ly spend $4.99 or less for the 
brands they prefer. 

However, a large number 
of users, 43 percent, said 
they normally spend be- 
tween $5 and $11.99 for a 
moisturizer, and 19 percent 
said they spend between $12 
and $20 plus for facial mois- 
turizers. 


Mean expenditure: $9.04 


Although the rest of the 
respondents said they didn’t 
know how much they spent, 
the mean expenditure for a 
moisturizer was $9.04, which 
suggests that women expect 
to pay more for a high quali- 


ty skin care product. 

It also explains why dollar 
sales for skin care products 
were up an average 15 per- 
cent in drug stores last year, 
according to Nielsen Market- 
ing Research, and why food 
and mass merchandise 
chains are also getting dou- 
ble-digit increases in this 
category, up 14 percent and 
18 percent, respectively, last 
year in dollars. 

Even though food chains 
and mass merchandisers are 
obviously going after the 
skin care shopper with ex- 
panded space, discounted 
prices, and expanded prod- 
uct assortments, many buy- 
ers for chain drug stores 
think that skin care products 
give drug stores a unique 
opportunity for courting 
quality-minded department 
store shoppers. 

Many also feel that a 
strong skin care program 
can also help discourage the 
defection of shoppers into 
food and mass merchandise 
stores, primarily because 
these stores may not be as 
able as drug stores are to 
provide service in this im- 
portant category. They may 
also find it harder to carry a 
broad range of the higher 
quality lines. 

One buyer said that when 
drug stores aggressively a. 
vertise skin care and proper- 
ly merchandise and display a 
broad assortment of brands, 
including trusted brands, 
they have a better chance to 
attract the higher-income 
shopper.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 18, 1990 


Gallup: Hair care 


Gel, mousse use on upswing as women seek manageability 


0 help achieve and main- 


tain flattering hair 


styles, American wom- 
en buy shampoos and condi- 
tioners that promise to add 
sheen or height to hair, or 
make hair more manageable 
or softer. 

They also buy sprays, gels, 
spritzes, mousses and other 
styling aids with eagerness to 
look their best. 

So it’s understandable that 


Gallup has discovered that 
most American women, 60 
percent, do use some kind of 
styling product on their hair, 
and that both gel and mousse 
usage are increasing. 

Almost half (49 percent) of 
all women who use mousse 
told Gallup interviewers that 
they were using it more fre- 
quently today than they were 
several years ago; 61 percent 
of all gel users said they were 


using gels more frequently. 

Also, 38 percent of all wom- 
en who use a mousse or a gel 
use these products at least dai- 
ly. Another 33 percent use 
them at least two three 
times a week. 

Hair spray is used even 
more often: 72 percent of the 
women who use a spray said 
they use it at least once a day; 


and 17 percent use it two or 


three times a week. 


The heaviest styling aid us- 
ers are 18 to 34 years old. 

Black women were less like- 
ly to use sprays, mousse and 
spritzes than white women, 
but they were heavier users of 
gels, curl energizers, and 
sheens. More so than whites, 
they have problems with pro- 
cessed or overly dry _ hair; 
these are all products de- 
signed to help women cope 
with these difficult areas.

ately, many chain drug

asa “growth category” in their 
stores, up 12 percent to 20 per-

more attention from manufac- 
turers like Neutrogena, Jean 
Nate, Vitabath, Yardley, Le 
Spa, La Loren, Vaseline In- 
tensive Care, and a host of 
smaller, regional brands.

new category for drug store 
retailers—boutique bath 
products.

All color 


Fragrance, cosmetic sales each top $1B mark 


C olor cosmetic sales in drug 
stores increased 3 percent in 
1989 to $1.08 billion, accord- 
“~s Nielsen Marketing Research. 
rug store fragrance sales were 
also up, showing an increase of 5 
percent to $1.06 billion for the year. 

However, buyers for some of the 
industry’s most progressive drug 
chains say their cosmetic and fra- 
grance sales increases were a lot 
better than the norm—up 8 percent 
to 10 ger over the previous 
year. The reasons: merchandising 
and operational changes implement- 
ed in recent years and hot new prod- 
uct launches like Plenitude, New 
Definition Make-up, Ex Cla Ma 
Tion, Navy, California, Aspen, Grow 
Strong and Mattique. 

Some chains, though, report in- 
creases that were not as strong. 
Some buyers say sales were flat or 
up only marginally, and most attri- 
bute the lack of growth to sluggish 
economic conditions in their mar- 
kets. 

In most areas of the country, buy- 
ers also say they are continuing to 
feel pressure from low-price competi- 
tors, particularly discount chains such 
as K mart and Wal-Mart and dee 
discount drug operators such as 
Emporium, Phar Mor and F&M. 


Drug chain strategies 


Most of the drug chains inter- 
viewed for this report were among 
the top 15 companies in dollar vol- 
ume. Generally, the chains experi- 
encing above-average growth in cos- 
metics attribute their success to a 
variety of changes they have been 
making over the years in both mer- 
chandising and operations. 

Many of these chains report that 
they have been able to drive sales 
because they are putting more 
trained service personnel into cos- 
metics, a move that one source de- 
scribed as a “catalyst” for growth. 

In addition to service, many 
chains have latched onto merchan- 
dising strategies employed for years 
by department stores to build their 
cosmetic franchise. 

By emulating successful depart- 
ment store techniques, buyers be- 
lieve they are strengthening ties 
with their current shoppers, while 
also making their stores attractive 
to the potentially rich market repre- 
sented by department stores. 


rug 


Department store woes 


Yet buyers today are trying to 
take advantage of the fact that many 
department stores are in dire 


Merchandising and operational 
changes, along with hot new 
product launches, spark sales 
from 8 to 10 percent at some 

drug chains. 


straits, apparently unable to gener- 
ate enough traffic to sustain their 
fashion departments, including cos- 
metics. 

So, in addition to trying to rein- 
state service in their stores, many of 
today’s modern drug stores are try- 
ing to upgrade their mix to include a 
broader range of designer cosmetics 
and fragrances. 

Many chains are trying to create 
what buyers call “skin treatment 
centers” that put more emphasis on - 
the Gascioed brands and regimens 
of treatment products while at the 
same time making them easier to 
find and easier to understand. 

Most of the major chains like Wal- 


greens, Eckerd, Osco, Perry, Peo- 
les, Reveo, Arbor, Genovese, 

ongs, and SupeRx, as well as many 
smaller chains like Snyders, Crown 
and Bill’s, now sponsor training 
schools to teach cosmeticians selling 
skills. 

Chains are also testing different 
ways to improve the presentation of 
high anvwith or high profit “image” 
departments, such as skin care, bath 
products, cosmetic accessories, 
makeup brushes, jewelry, hosiery, 
ethnic products, and premium or 
semi-professional hair care brands. 


Eckerd tests department 
Eckerd Drug, for example, is cur- 


Sav-on in California uses an airy cosmetics presentation so women can browse com- 
fortably. The chain’s merchandising approach transforms just another department 


into an attractive cosmetic center. 


rently doing a 40-store test of a skin 
care department which houses mass 
and some prestige lines together in 
one convenient location. 

SupeRx has created a skin care 
planogram that features a 4-foot set 
of franchised brands like Almay, 
Max Factor, Clarion and Revlon 
treatments, leading into the mass 
brands in SupeRx’s toiletries aisle. 

It’s the same strategy many drug 
chains now use in their mass hair 
care planogram, leading off with a 
four-foot or larger presentation of 
premium priced professional or semi- 
professional lines, then branching 
out into mid-priced lines and finally 
ending with the value lines. 

More space in the mass planogram 
is also being given to hicktioed 

remium lines. In skin, that means 
ines like Plenitude, Neutrogena, Ni- 
vea and Olay as well as the top 
brands in the dry skin segment like 
Lubriderm and Keri. 

In hair, it means the professional 
lines such as Redmond, Aussie, In- 
fusium, All Set, TRESemmé, La 
Coupe, Vidal Sassoon, Pantene, and 
Jheri Redding, as well as some of 
the more cosmetic or conditioning 
brands that originated on the West 
Coast, such as Freeman’s hair and 
skin care, Amitee hair and skin care, 
Biotene 24-H, and Sleepy Hollow. 

Chains are also trying to “liven 
up” their stores, as one buyer put it, 
by periodically staging exciting 
events like fragrance samplings or 
nail care demonstrations or, in the 
case of deep discount chains like 
Drug Emporium, mini-fashion shows 
at holidays such as Mother’s Day. 


Chains use videos 


More chains are also using manu- 
facturer-supplied videos as part of 
their endcap displays. Usually these 
videos supplement the store’s at- 
tempts at providing service by ex- 
plaining how certain products 
work—like Plenitude’s serum lotion, 
for example—or telling customers 
what to buy if they have a specific 
problem with their nails or hair. 

Models supplied by major mass 
manufacturers such as Max “actor 
are also showing up in drug <tores, 
demonstrating how to layer fra- 
grances, and encouraging customers 
to buy a “wardrobe” of fragrances, 
not just a cologne, but also body 
tales, skin lotions and deodorants. 

And many drug chain buyers say 
they are experimenting with gift- 
with-purchase promotions, a promi- 
nent sales tool in “class” outlets.

New product development sparking film sales 


Once upon a time, the film 
market for drug chains and 
other mass merchants could 
pretty much be described in 
one word: Kodak. Since the 
mid-1970s however, Fuji 
Photo Film has used rapid- 
fire marketing and product 
innovation to challenge East- 
man Kodak’s continuing 
dominance of the market. 

More recently, Polaroid has 
attempted with apparently 
growing success to carve out a 
new niche with its all-occasion 


OneFilm for amateur point- 
and-shoot photo buffs, and 
small suppliers like Konica are 
making forays into the mass 
market. 

Those developments have 
forced chain drug merchan- 
disers to review and often to 
revamp their approach to the 
category, adding space for 
more brands and monitoring 
the performance of newer en- 
trants vs. Kodak. Neverthe- 
less, the increasing manufac- 
turer competition has also 
sparked more aggressive 
stag innovation and mar- 

eting efforts from the sup- 
liers as they battle for the 
oyalties of a new generation

ing.

Sticking with generics 
By Harold Cohen, R.Ph. 

EW YORK — Despite heavy flak taken by the generic in- 

dustry over the past year, generic drugs continue to be a 

strong contender for prescription business at chain drug 

stores. 

While some generic companies recorded a measurable drop in 
their sales volume last year in the wake of the FDA scandal, on a 
nationwide basis, Drug Store News/Inside Pharmacy’s 1990 Gener- 
ic Substitution Survey shows the scandal did not appreciably sway 
many physicians from prescribing, consumers from taking, cr phar- 
macists from dispensing generic drugs. 

The nationwide DrSNIP generic survey was answered by direc- 
tors of pharmacy representing more than 3,000 traditional chain 


drug stores, supermarket pharmacies and discount store pharma-

Reaction to scandal 


A Gallup survey done shortly af- 
ter the FDA scandal revealed that 
negative consumer reaction to the 
FDA/generic controversy was slight. 

Only 9 percent of the consumers 
polled who were taking generics 
asked a pharmacist or doctor to 
change their medication to a brand- 
ed product. More than three-quar- 
ters said they continued to believe 
that generic drugs were safe and ef- 
fective. Much of the same attitude 
was shared by a majority of store- 
level pharmacists. 

According to DrSN/IP’s generic 
survey, only 9 percent of the phar- 
macy directors surveyed said their 
pharmacists’ reaction to the generic 
controversy was negative. 

“The pharmacists anticipated more 
negative patient reaction to generic 
dispensing,” said one pharmacy di- 
rector. 

Others said their pharmacists re- 
acted positively to the generic issue 
or thought that everything was sta- 
tus quo at the retail level when it 
came to generic substitution.

line had few or no recalls,” com-

Personal opinion 


When asked if they would 
personally take a generic over 
a branded drug, 84 percent of 
the pharmacy directors an- 
swering the survey said 
“Yes.” Another 16 percent 
said “Sometimes.” None said 
they would not take a generic 
over a branded drug. 

The argument long used by 
branded drug companies is 
that loss of business to gener 
ics has greatly reduced the 
needed capital to carry on nec 
essary research and develop 
ment of new drugs. 

When the directors were 
asked if they thought that this 
was So, 96 percent said “No.” 
Only 4 percent agreed with 
the branded drug companies’ 
philosphy.

The purchase of Peoples by CVS 
caught many by surprise, but the deal 
makes sense for both sides. It signifi- 
cantly extends CVS’s regional pres- 
ence, where it will build on notable oper- 
ational strengths. For Imasco, which 
helped Peoples to foster a turnaround, 
the cash infusion gives a shot to the bot-

increase Melville’s drug store empire

erates 811 stores in 14 states, mainly in 
the Northeast, and Peoples’ 490 stores

Virginia, West Virginia, Pennsylva- 
nia, North Carolina and New York. 

“CVS and Peoples make an ideal 
geographic and strategic fit,” Stanley 
P. Goldstein, Melville’s chairman and 
ceo, said in Melville’s announcement.

Walgreen Rx’ers in Chicago settle strike 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Walgreen Co. pharmacists in the Chi- 
cago area ratified an extended, four-year contract and returned 
to work just a week after going out on strike. At issue was pay 
raises and working conditions. 

More than 600 striking union pharmacists from 223 Pa 
area stores were affected, and were temporarily pw by Wal- 

n pharmacists and pharmacy managers from other states on a 
shorter-hour basis. State regulators investigating union charges 
that some of the temporary pharmacists were dispensing without 
an Illinois license found no such viclations, the company reported. 

Under terms of the settlement, the Rx’ers are guaranteed an 
18 percent pay hike worth a total of $6 an hour in added pay by 
the fourth year of the contract. The raise will bring base pay up 9 
percent in the first year, to $49,920. 

The contract also provides for more frequent meetings be- 
tween pharmacists and managers to discuss work-related stress 
or other problems. 

“We’re happy it was able to be mediated so quickly,” said Wal- 
aha spokesperson Laurie Meyer. “Our pharmacists work 

ard, and we need them.” 


Phar-Mor, Osco to enlist satellites 


YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — Phar-Mor has decided to use a sat- 
ellite network system by Hughes Network Systems, Inc. to link 
all its stores for data, voice and video communication, Phar-Mor 
and Hughes announced. 

American Stores also will shortly announce that it will use 
Hughes equipment for a satellite network that links its Osco 
Drug stores, according to a source at Hughes. 

The Hughes Integrated Satellite Business Network, which 
employs VSAT or very small aperature terminal dishes at each 
store communicating with a central hub, is the same system 
Walgreens adopted several years ago. 

Pha -Mor said the $6 million project will be completed at 
year’s end when it expects to have 250 stores. Satellite was cho- 
sen as a less expensive alternative to terrestrial communica- 
tions and one which provides the best communications options, 
Phar-Mor said.

Allbright to Drug Emporium board 


COLUMBUS, Ohio — Bruce Allbright, 61, was elected to the 
board of directors of Drug Emporium, and will serve the remain- 
ing two years of an py term of Jane Trahey, who resigned. 

Allbright retired in February from Dayton Hudson Corp., 
where he last served as president and a director. He has had 
wide experience in top retail management posts. It includes a 
period as ceo of Dayton Hudson’s Target stores, and jobs as 
president and ceo of the B. Dalton book chain, executive vp and 
a director at F.W. Woolworth, and chairman and ceo of the 
Woolworth-Woolco division.

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 9, 1990 


Aggressive expansion costs and combo competition have 
caught up with Genovese in the short term. Chairman Leonard 
Genovese vows that vigorous expense slashing, continued strong 
pharmacy results, better employee productivity and customer ser- 
vice will quickly steer the chain ahead. 


By David Vaczek 


enovese curbs store growth 
nd focuses on cost cutting 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — Gen- 
ovese Drug Stores will de-em- 
phasize new store growth and 
renovations this year, as it 
slashes expenses following a 
period of rapid expansion and 
dampened profits. 

The 91-store chain hasn’t yet 
opened a store in 1990, and will 
open only two or three by fiscal 
year next January; that might 
include the chain’s first Bronx 
site. Genovese has recently 
sold two stores in Ridgewood 
and Franklin, N.J. to Thrift 
Drug, and has closed one 
Brooklyn store, company offi- 
cials told shareholders in June. 


Productivity check 


As Genovese downscales its 
historic plans of 10 percent an- 
nual new store growth, chair- 
man Leonard Genovese called 
for aggressive pursuit of pro- 
ductivity and customer service. 
“We are attacking productivity 


issues viciously,” he told stock- 
holders at the annual meeting. 

That includes increasing em- 
ployee productivity per hour 
and boosting sales per square 
inch of shelving. Employee pro- 
ductivity has already improved 
with average sales per man 
hour at $91, compared with $84 
last year, as the number of cus- 
tomers served increased 6 per- 
cent, Genovese said. 

While its Long Island, New 
York City, New Jersey, and 
Connecticut markets have the 
advantages of being densely 
populated and fairly affluent, 
they are also costly to operate. 
Also, Genovese was stung last 
year by higher interest costs 
and depreciation charges on 
high capital expenditures relat- 
ed to new stores, computers 
and an upgraded warehouse. 
Employee medical costs also 
rose by $1 million in 1990. 

The chain’s net profit-to- 


sales ratio has ranged in re- 
cent years from 1 percent to 
1.5 percent. In fiscal 1990, it 
stayed under 1 percent, com- 
pared with a two percent to 
three percent industry aver- 
age. On the bright side, sales 
growth, led by pharmacy, has 
been double-digit, and that 
trend continued in the first 
quarter ended May 25. 


A good trend 


“T believe this is an excep- 
tionally good trend we’re on,” 
Genovese said, noting that first 
quarter comp store sales were 
up 9 percent, with pharmacy 
sales up 19 percent on a five 
percent increase in scripts. 

Total sales in the first quar- 
ter increased 13.4 percent to 
$128.6 million, with net income 
of $1.05 million, compared with 
$1.12 million in last year’s com- 
parable quarter. This quarter’s 
net includes a $238,000 gain 
from the May 25 sale of the two 
New Jersey stores. 

With costs from opening 13 
stores in 18 months ended late 
1989, the expense-to-sales ratio 
increased to 26.7 percent from 
25.7 percent in the prior year.

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 9, 1990 


OPINION 1 


After a year of relatively slow takeover activity, the 
pace has picked up smartly. And that’s putting it mild- 
ly. The selloff of most of Revco’s more than 700-plus 
available stores to a variety of buyers was big news, 
but not all that surprising. The sale of Peoples was. 

Revco’s trip to the “retail spa” to slim 


down was a logical move that’s been 
made by other overweight and out-of- 
shape retailers. Peoples, on the other 
hand, seemed to have already emerged 
successfully from its total remake. Prof- 
its have been steadily rising. Six-month 
performance figures promise to be very 
strong. 

So why did Imasco, the Canadian 
company that agonized through Peo- 
ples’ lowest periods, decide to sell just 


IN THE MARKET 


as the repositioning efforts undertaken 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


by David Bloom and David Eisenberg 
really began to click? 


The answer involves a combination of 
factors. First, as successful as Peoples might become, 
its scale did not seem to Imasco to promise the long- 
term return that the Canadian holding company seeks 
in its properties. Second, the $390 million (Canadian) 
sale price will help reduce debt and interest expense 
and thus provide an immediate shot to Imasco’s bot- 
tom line. 

Third, like a father looking for a prospective hus- 
band for his daughter, Imasco was committed to find- 
ing a strong suitor for Peoples. It could not have cho- 
sen a better one than CVS. Geographically, the match 
seems to have been made in heaven. CVS is also wide- 
ly acknowledged as one of the best operators in the 
business. Like Peoples, it has a strong focus on phar- 
macy and core front-end categories. Peoples can only 
benefit from CVS’s operational strengths. As David 


CVS & Peoples: A solid pairing 


Bloom put it: “It’s a case of a successful company join- 
ing an even more successful company.” As important 
as Peoples’ locational strengths are, Bloom felt the 
chain’s “people strengths” — the management team 
headed by Eisenberg—was even more important. 

Harvey Rosenthal, CVS’ ceo, was characteristical- 
ly cautious in answering questions about Peoples’ fu- 
ture. His caution reflected, he said, his company’s 
“conservative, analytical and very thoughtful” ap- 
proach to decision-making. Rosenthal said he had 
made no prejudgments. He said CVS needed time to 
get to know Peoples and its management. 

However, he did say that CVS intended to retain the 
Peoples name because the chain’s more than 80 years in 
the D.C. market was reflected in “high consumer aware- 
ness and favorable reaction.” And he said the acquisition 
would provide more opportunities for future growth 
along the eastern seaboard as far south as Virginia. “As 
you know, CVS likes to grow,” he said.

At last, Rx cost containment on right track 


After years of bickering, back-biting and skirmish- 
ing, Congressional critics of the pharmaceutical indus- 
try finally appear to have the nation’s brand-name drug 
manufacturers in a hammerlock. 

Finally, Congress has stumbled across a way to focus 
Medicaid drug program cost-containment 


efforts where they belong: on the manu- 
facturers who have been raising prices to 
pharmacists, consumers and taxpayers at 
triple the nation’s general inflation rate. 

This new approach marks a radical de- 
parture from the way Medicaid has dealt 
with cost pressures in the past. For the 
last 25 years, when state or Federal drug 
program officials have felt the budget 
squeeze they have tightened the noose on 
pharmacy reimbursement. 


it ofa hy If enacted, Sen. David Pryor’s (D- 
Ark.) “Pharmaceutical Access and Pru- 
KEN RANKIN dent Purchasing Act” (PAPPA) would in- 


ject a healthy dose of competition into the 
Medicaid drug market by requiring brand-name phar- 
maceutical manufacturers to bid for Medicaid business. 

Specifically, it would encourage state Medicaid agen- 
cies to begin price negotiations with pharmaceutical 
manufacturers by the beginning of 1993. Among other 
things, state officials would have the flexibility to estab- 
lish restrictive formularies and to demand that manufac- 
turers charge Medicaid no more than the lowest price 
paid by hospitals or other institutions. 

State drug programs would realize their savings via 
periodic rebates from manufacturers, reflecting the dif- 
ference between the supplier’s normal selling price and 
the negotiated price. 

To safeguard the medication rights of the indigent, 
PAPPA would allow prescribers to demand that any 


“medically necessary” drug be dispensed to a patient, 
even if the prescribe: product is not on the state’s for- 
mulary. 

To protect pharmacists from unjustified reimburse- 
ment cuts by state Medicaid programs, the legislation 
would require that participating pharmacies be paid a 
“market-based pr.ze” (capped at the 90th percentile of 
all providers). 

Drug store industry groups regard such reimburse- 
ment reforms to be a major step forward for patients as 
well as for pharmacists. Indeed, NACDS contends that 
the reimbursement scheme envisioned by PAPPA 
would enable “today’s highly trained pharmacists to 
spend time with customers, so they can use their skills to 
identify costly and life-threatening adverse drug reac- 
tions, and to seek the advice of a physician familiar with 
the patient’s total care needs.” 

Not surprisingly, Sen. Pryor’s bill is less popular 
across town at the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Asso- 
ciation. PMA, which represents the brand name drug 
industry, has pulled out all the stops in an effort to scut- 
tle PAPPA. Part of PMA’s anti-PAPPA campaign in- 
cludes an industry-financed “study” of the legislation 
suggesting that Pryor’s scheme to trim Medicaid drug 
spending could cost more than it saves. 

Among other things, researchers for PMA contend 
that provisions of the legislation relaxing reimburse- 
ment restraints on pharmacists may at least partially 
offset any savings resulting from lower priced drugs. 

To my way of thinking, that’s hardly a flaw in the leg- 
islation! For decades pharmacists have been on the 
short end of the Medicaid reimbursement stick, while 
manufacturers have been free to raise product prices at 
will. It seems altogether fitting for PAPPA to earmark 
part of the cost savings from manufacturer price compe- 
tition for improved pharmacy reimbursement.

accounted for $785 million, or 
9.3 percent of sales in the 
H&BA categories tracked by 
Arbitron/SAML

just about double the levels in 
food stores. Private label pene-

of unit volume in miscellaneous 
proprietary remedies, to home 
testing kits and hair care, 
where there is little activity.

more than four out of 10 units in 
clinical thermometers, antisep- 
tics and natural vitamins, min- 
erals and supplements. 

Private label unit sales do not 
always peak and wane with cat- 
egories as a whole because im- 
portant new product introduc- 
tions can siphon away 
consumer interest in store

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 9, 1990 


y upgrading selections and dis- 
plays, drug stores clearly now 

ave a leg up on department 
stores in hosiery sales. Mainstream, 
conservative styles and color variety 
are attracting today’s practical and 
fashion-spun hosiery consumers, re- 
tailers and manufacturers told Drug 
Store News. 

Women in the workplace who val- 
ue their shopping convenience are a 
big part of the shift towards drug 
stores. “Pantyhose are part of the 
uniform,” said Bill Murray, director 
of sales and marketing for Rice Ho- 
siery. “Most women now work and 
wear pantyhose that are more of a 
mainstream style for the work- 
place.” 

Women are also viewing hosiery 
purchases differently. “Overall, 
women are looking at hosiery as a 
fashion accessory to help coordinate 
their outfits,” said Mary Gilbert, a 
L’eggs spokesperson. “That’s a very 


New products 
geared toward 
older customers 


As the population ages, new 
products are arriving on the 
scene to accommodate these 
older consumers. Sid Brodkin, 
president of Bubby Hosiery 
(Bubby meaning grandmother 
in Yiddish) has created a stock- 
ing marketed to the older wom- 
an, who is concerned about 
keeping her legs warm. 

“Pharmacists will tell you 
about the demographics; they’re 
getting more older consumers in 
their stores,” Brodkin said. “I 
started doing research and 
found that the industry wasn’t 
doing anything for the older ma- 
ture woman. The drug store 
market was a natural adjunct 
for our product.” 

The stocking is a natural cot- 
ton fiber in soft beige with a 
one-size-fits-all merchandising 
technique. 


fashion-conscious consumer out 
there, and it’s relatively inexpensive 
and appropriate to update the ward- 
robe with different colors and tex- 
tures.” 

Prices tend to be stable, ranging 
from $1.99 for private labels to $4.79 
for higher-grade lines, yet drug 
store consumers no longer hesitate 
to buy more expensive hosiery. 

Drug stores have an opportunity to 
trade-up consumers in this category 
of frequent replenishment. 

“Drug stores today are catering to 
the higher-priced range of hosiery,” 
said a buyer at a Northeastern 
chain. “Women are interested in 
quality, and so they will buy them 
even if they’re more expensive.” 


Colors attract sales 


Colors are hot in the current 
market, as retailers scurry to pro- 
mote their summer color lines. 
“Color really does well, especially 
during the spring, early summer 
and fall times,” Kathy Johannes, a 
buyer for Kerr Drug Stores, told 
Drug Store News. “We really do a 
lot of promotions and advertising 
during this time. We’re starting to 
really get aggressive with market- 
ing ae advertising (by adding ho- 
siery in more circulars) because 
chains such as Drug Emporium and 
Phar-Mor are wah rye agai and 
we’re trying to meet the competi- 
tion.” 

Color trends are changing, how- 
ever, said Jean Anne Hamm of 
Town & Country Drug Stores in 
Texas. “Customers are looking for 
something other than the nude or 
suntan lines,” she said. Toni Mark- 
ham, of Crown Drugs, agrees: 
“We’re seeing a lot more promo- 
tional displays for pink and violets 
during the summer months. These 
colors are a good sale even in the 
winter months.” 

This shift toward the “non- 
browns” has only occurred during 
the last two years, said Brad Worth- 
ley, executive vp of Volt, USA. 
“Brown or suntan used to be the ba- 
sic color,” he said. “Now, the first 
thing people are out of are the black

Murray uses U.S. Census data to

and off-black shades. Black now tends 
to outsell brown six-to-one. It’s no 
longer an accessory item—it’s a neces-

Upscale approach 


Volt, though fairly new to chain re- 
tailing, has adopted a unique approach 
for the now upscale drug store market. 
A year and a half ago, the company 
started merchandising to drug stores, 
marketing its same department store 
approach it had been using for six years. 
“We’ve tried to carve out a department 
store niche right in the drug store mar- 
ket,” he explained. Worthley contends 
that the uniqueness comes with the 
packaging, which features a fabric 
swatch on the outside of each package. 
“You see these in dep: artment stores ev- 
ery day. We feel it’s important that the 
consumer touch and feel the garment 
before they buy it,” he said. 

The company also markets 14 colors 
in its line. “Sure, they buy their 
L’eggs, No Nonsense, or whatever 
brand they use, but we also want them 
to pick up a pink, peach or yellow when 
they pick up their other brands,” 
Worthley said. 

Drug stores are looking to take ad- 
vantage of their fashion and conve- 


nience strengths by better organizing 
their hosiery displays. Historically, 
said Kerr’s Johannes, summing up the 
views of many retailers, “it’s just been 
hard to get this section to look good.” 


Hosiery displays 


Kerr, like many others, is installing 
L’eggs hosiery center in its stores—a 
full, eight-to-12-foot modular unit with 
headers. The display, free to retailers, 
lets them group hosiery primarily by 
brand (competing brands get space as 
well); after that, it can be organized in 
any desired fashion: by size, color, or 
fabric. 

The L’eggs Pantyhose Advisor—an 
interactive computer in the shape of a 
giant L’eggs egg—is another signifi- 
cant merchandising aid. Consumers 
punch in their height, weight and 
wearing occasion, said L’eggs’ Gilbert. 
Other questions, such as closed vs. 
open-toed shoes, standing vs. sitting 
occasions and any leg problems, are 
also addressed. In approximately 30 
seconds, the computer recommends a 
size and two different styles appropri- 
ate for the occasion. It also describes 
what the package looks like. She 

claims that the device has “increased 
sales by as much as 40 percent since 
last winter’s rollout.”

By Susan Ball 

SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — Now 
that a judge in Cleveland has thrown out 
the bribery case against Rite Aid and its 
president, Martin Grass, Rite Aid is con- 
sidering expanding the defamation suit 
filed last year against Ohio Board of Phar- 
macy member Melvin Wilczynski to in- 
clude others involved in the case. 

The civil suit against Wilczynski, who 
had been a consultant to Peoples Drug’s 
Lane division, was originally filed in May 
1989 and had been stayed pending the 
outcome of the bribery trial. The stay has 
now been lifted by Judge Alvin I. 
Krenzler of U.S. District Court for the 
Northern District of Ohio, in Cleveland. 


‘This [bribery] case was rotten 
from its inception and had no 
merit whatsoever. We don’t 
want to proceed like that; we 
will proceed with deliberation.’ 

—Moscarino 


One of the attorneys representing Rite 
Aid and Grass, George J. Moscarino of 
the Cleveland law firm of Jones, Day, 
Reavis & Pogue, said, “We have a lot of 
discovery to do, which we were prohibit- 
ed from doing” for the approximate year 


Rite Aid weighs leyal counterpunch 


“We will now have to determine wheth- 
er to add people to the suit, initiate other 
suits, or both, or neither,” Moscarino told 
~— Store News. 

“This [bribery] case was rotten from its 
inception and had no merit whatsoever,” 
he said. “We don’t want to proceed like 
that; we will proceed with deliberation.” 

The bribery trial, which began July 2, 
ended July 16, after the prosecution rest- 
ed its case and before defense testimony 
was to begin, when Judge Lillian J. 
Greene of Cuyahoga County Common 
Pleas Court granted a defense motion for 
a judgment of acquittal. Judge Greene

Eckerd places $123M in senior notes 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — Eckerd’s recent placement of $123 
million in senior secured notes (due 1997) with Merrill Lynch 
Capital Markets will be used in part to refinance senior bank 
debt and won’t increase Eckerd’s total debt, said Dorothy Lee, 
an analyst with Moody’s Investors Service. 

The placement was done along with a refinancing of Eckerd’s 
bank credit agreement with Morgan Guaranty Trust Co., an 
agent for the bank lending group. 

The new notes’ security will be subordinate to the remaining 
bank debt, and there will be no less security for holders of Eckerd’s 
nig ield bonds, said Lee. 

ckerd said that the move will provide added working capi- 
tal, and reduce the required principal amortization “over the 
next several years.” 


Nichols files for Chapter 11 protection 


NEW YORK — Despite a 15-month-long ot effort 
that included closing unprofitable stores and converting 16 of its 
discount Paha ane stores to deep discount drug stores under 
the name Pharmhouse, S.E. Nichols filed for Chapter 11 protec- 
tion Aug. 2 in the United States Bankruptcy Court, Southern 
District of New York. 

The company, which failed to pay the interest due June 1 on 
its 14%-percent debentures, had been pursuing financing alter- 
natives. In addition, Kenneth A. Davis, Nichols president and 
ceo, said the company “has encountered increasing problems in 
obtaining adequate vendor support.” 


Davis stated that seeking relief under Chapter 11 would enable 
the company to continue converting its stores to Pharmhouse out- 
lets and operating the stores converted, which the compa- 


ny said have shown encouraging results to date. The company 
announced it has received a commitment from Sterling National 
Bank for a revolving credit facility of up to $10 million.

SupeRx: No plans to divest Ariz. units 


PHOENIX — SupeRx Corp. chairman and 
chief executive Gerald Wolken firmly denied a 
published report that the bankrupt company had 
retained the former head of Wickes Cos. and was 
planning to divest its stores in Arizona. 

According to the report which surfaced last 
month in another newspaper, SupeRx had 
hired former Wickes Cos. chairman and ceo 
Sandy Sigoloff to help with its financial reorga- 
nization. Quoting “industry sources,” the re- 
+e stated that one of Sigoloff’s duties would 

e to divest the SupeRx stores in the compa- 
ny’s home state, leaving the firm with 89 Medi- 
care-Glaser stores in Missouri, Illinois and 
Connecticut. 

“There’s absolutely no truth to it,” Wolken 
told Drug Store News. “We haven’t hired Sigo- 
loff, and we will not do so.” 

Wolken also denied that the chain had any 

lans to sell the Arizona division or any other 
arge blocks of stores. “Our plan is to negotiate 
a Py an of financial reorganization and come out 
of Chapter 11 intact, as an ongoing concern,” he

eyes Fairlane deal

said. “That hasn’t changed.” 

Meanwhile, Wolken said, SupeRx is still “in 
the process of interviewing candidates” to select 
an investment banker to help in its reorganiza- 
tion efforts. The chain is also interviewing to fill 
the post of chief operations officer, which was va- 
cated with the departure of former president and 
chief operations officer Jim Mastrian in May, at 
the time of SupeRx’s bankruptcy filing. 

“We’re still pretty early in the process,” said 
Wolken. 

SupeRx filed for Chapter 11 protection May 
11 after failing to negotiate a new financial 
package oe the collapse of its chief lend- 
ing institution, the notorious Lincoln Savings 
& Loan, once headed by Charles Keating. Su- 
peRx moved quickly to close 11 underperform- 
ing drug stores and rebuild supply pipelines 
with vendors after the filing. 

Those efforts have paid off, Wolken said. 
“Our in-stock situation has seen dramatic im- 
provement,” he said. “For the most part our 
vendors have been very supportive.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, August 20, 1990 


chandising question this 

year is still whether to 
planogram by family or by cat- 
egory. 

Even though more chains 
are moving toward a family 
presentation, there is still vig- 
orous debate as to whether 
this is the smartest course. 

Some feel that a family ap- 
proach, although logical, is not 
appropriate for the average 
drug chain with less than 
12,000 square feet per store. 

“In categories like hair 
care, skin care and bath,” said 
a toiletries manager for a Top 
Five drug chain, “there isn’t 
enough room on many gondo- 
las to merchandise everything 
by family. You can’t get all the 
segments on one gondola, es- 
pecially if you have stores with 
gondolas averaging eighteen 
to twenty-four feet. 

“And then you have single 
items, and lines with just five 
SKUs, and these can be very 

ood sellers, but they will get 
ost if you try to do a family 
presentation. It isn’t fair to 
these vendors to go with a 
family set, plus it deprives me 
of their full sales potential.” 

The person in charge of toi- 
letries for another major drug 
chain also felt that a family set 
for hair care is not a produc- 
tive step to take. 

“If we put everything to- 

ether by families, it’s too con- 

using for customers,” the di- 
rector of toiletries said. “The 
items lose their identity. Peo- 
ple want to buy deodorants in 
deodorants. Shampoos in 
shampoo. 

Many chains are currently 
in what buyer described as a 
“transitional mode” in plano- 
graming hair care, meaning 
some categories have been 
given a family presentation 
(usually shampoos and condi- 
tioners), while some catego- 


: n hair care, the big mer- 


ries are still generic (hair 
sprays and styling aids). 

In this bridge state, some 
buyers find themselves facing 
an additional complication. 
Some hair sprays, such as 
Aqua Net, may have been tak- 
en from the generic set and 
mixed in with the rest of their 
family of shampoo, condition- 
ing and styling aid products. 
But other brands are not mer- 
chandised with a family. They 
are merchandised in the ge- 
neric set. 

Some buyers report cus- 
tomers are confused by this 
type of presentation, assum- 
ing that when can’t find a 
brand in the generic set, the 
store’s out of it, or vice versa if 
they can’t find it in the family 
presentation. 

Buyers know this approach 
isn’t working, but they haven’t 
found the answer for it. 

“Tt’s like realizing you can’t 
be half pregnant,” says Perry 
Drug’s Scott Gorley. “You 
have to go one way or the oth- 
er, but in a chain such as ours, 
where some stores are too 
small to do a family set, it’s not 
clear yet what to do. 


Perry space moves help some 
products grow 30%-plus 


“In our 5,000-square-foot 
stores, we have sixty-four-inch 
high gondolas that average 
eighteen to twenty feet. Space 
is too tight to do a family set. 

“In our 15,000-square-foot 
stores, we have the space and 
we can do it. But we also want 
all our stores to look the same, 
so what should we do?”

for their largest stores, the 
mass hair care department

with the therapeutic sham-

Chains read books, mag 
for turns, margins, loya 


oone disputes the fact 
that the magazine 
and paperback book 


business has undergone fun- 
damental changes. In the 
magazine industry, once- 
dominant titles have suffered 
big drops in ad revenues and 
newsstand sales, and some 
have folded or been merged. 
Niche marketing and the de- 
cline of general-interest mag- 
azines has unleashed a flood 
of new titles—all vying for pre- 
clous display space in the 
mass retail setting. 

Book publishers, mean- 
while, have been hit with a 
wave of mergers and take- 
overs. Distribution channels 
have proliferated as drug 
stores, supermarkets and dis- 
counters have pushed more 
aggressively into the book 
business. Unit sales in paper- 
backs are actually down, 
though revenues are up. The 
level of retail returns has 
climbed as high as 50 to 60 per- 
cent, according to reports. 

All the turmoil masks the 
fact that books and magazines 
remain a predictable source of 
revenue for drug chains, gener- 
ating quick turns, respectable 
gross margins and a x st of 
customer loyalty. In addition, 
the retail display allowances 
for magazine titles and guar- 
anteed return policy for paper- 
backs and magazines takes 
much of the risk out of the busi- 
ness for retailers. 


Magazines: niches and 
declining ad revenues 


Turmoil in the magazine in- 
dustry has gotten plenty of 
media attention in recent 
months. The market has be- 
come more and more segment- 
ed, with publishers aiming 
hundreds of new titles at very 
specific audiences with very 
specific interests. Last year, a 
record 584 new magazine ti- 
tles entered the market, ac- 
cording to the Periodicals In- 
stitute, swelling the 
newsstand total to more than 
2,800 magazines. 

“The distribution channel is 
going to have to develop much 
more sophisticated informa- 
tion systems in how they re- 
view the performance of ti- 
tles, and they’re going to have 
to stock more efficiently,” said 
Robert Cohn, vp-circulation 
for the Magazine Publishers of 
America, an industry group. 

“Sell-through efficiencies 
are going down, and costs are 
going up,” he continued. 

“We've had a record num- 
ber of new titles introduced in 
the last two years, and desk- 
top publishing had something 
to do with it,” added John

Meanwhile, general-interest 
and top-selling titles audited by 
ABC, the Audit Bureau of Cir- 
culation, have been hit with de- 
clining single-copy sales and a 
tougher fight for ad dollars as 
new titles oa exploded. 

According to the Publishers 
Information Bureau, ABC 
magazine ad revenues fell 
more than 3 percent for the 
first half of the year. And the 
Magazine Publishers of Amer- 
ica es reported dramatic de- 
clines in single-copy sales of 
some of the nation’s top maga- 
zine titles. 

Nevertheless, industry rep- 
resentatives see good news 
behind the bad. “The top 30 or 
40 titles are suffering, but the 
balance are not,” said Fitz- 
morris. “Overall, both unit 
sales and ad revenues are up.” 

“Dollars and unit sales are 
still significantly higher than 
five years ago,” added Cohn. 

Industry advocates argue 
that only a small percentage of 
titles, about 400, are audited 
by the ABC. “The fact is that 
while sales of ABC titles have 
declined from 91 million copies 
in 1980 to 80 million in 1989, 


overall newsstand sales and 
dollars, audited and unaudit- 
ed, have reported record 
gains,” noted the Periodicals 
Institute in a report. 

Indeed, total magazine rev- 
enues advanced 7.5 percent 
last year, to $3.67 billion, on 
relatively flat unit growth. 
The business will be built on 
“new products targeted to the 
special interest of consum- 


ers,” the Periodicals Institute 
argues, and retailers should 
allocate enough display space 
for at least 800 titles “demo- 
graphically targeted to store 
and shopper type.” 

One 1 al chain giving 
greater attention to maga- 
zines is Rite Aid, which is re- 
portedly adding 40 to 50 titles 
in some stores. The extra 
space is coming from the area 
formerly reserved for video 
rentals, a business Rite Aid 
exited earlier this year.

Tailoring to market 


In addition, Jim Schulz, 
Gemmel’s general merchan- 
dise manager, pointed out 
that the socioeconomic make- 
up of the neighborhoods Gem- 
mel serves affects how check- 
outs are merchandised. For 
example, a store in a less afflu- 
ent neighborhood may offer 
candy multipacks (five or 10 
for $1), while units in more up- 
scale areas might feature fra- 
grance specials or the 10 pa- 
perback best-sellers at 
checkout. Always near check- 
out are film, audiotapes (“a 
good niche for the smaller re- 


tailer,” Schulz said) and pho- 
tofinishing. A few stores are 
trying magazines, with the 
publisher supplying racks and 
retail display allowances 
(RDAs) for placement near 
checkout. “With the RDA, 
that becomes profitable,” 
Schulz commented. 

Schulz cited one store man- 
ager particularly successful 
with checkstand merchandise 
as using a run of merchandise 
as the divider between two 
parallel checkout areas. The 
items, including things like 
candy, beer and soda, change 
constantly, Schulz said. 

Jeffers of Price Less also al-

assistants to make checkstand 
decisions. “If they make mis- 
takes, they’re correctable,” he 
observed. “All you have to do 
is move the stuff out. I’d rath-

_ something that doesn’t 
sell.”

earnings: Robinson 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry 
Drug Stores is looking for a 
big boost in sales and earnings 
as it consolidates 40 former 
Revco drug stores in Michigan 
and continues its store reno- 
vation program. 

Perry chairman and ceo 
Jack Robinson told financial 
analysts the company was 
looking for sales of $720 mil- 
lion to $730 million next year, 
following the incorporation of 
30 of the Revco units pur- 
chased earlier this year and 
the closing of the remaining 
five. 

Speaking to about 75 ana- 
lysts, stock brokers and port- 
folio managers in Detroit in 
July, Robinson also predicted 
that Perry’s profits would rise 
more quickly than sales in fis- 
eal 1991. In addition, he said, 
“we are hopeful that we will be 
able to reinstate dividends in 
about a year.” 

Perry earned $7.1 million on 


sales of $670 million in fiscal . 


1989, and earnings momen- 
tum is still showing evidence 
of a successful turnaround af- 
ter two years of losses in fiscal 
1987 and 1988. Since the end of 
its last fiscal year in October, 
1989, it has added four new 
stores and closed or sold 10 
drug stores in Wisconsin, Chi- 
cago, Michigan and Indiana. 
In May, the company also sold 
its A. L. Price deep-discount 
drug store division to former 
F&M and Revco D.S. presi- 
dent Bill Edwards. 

Perry plans to open another 
four to six units this year, and 
accelerate its expansion plans 
to 20 stores a year. The chain 
opened its 14th store within 
the Detroit city limits July 25 
to considerable fanfare, bring- 
ing total store count to 206 
units in Michigan and 23 in the 
greater Chicago area. 

With its improving earnings 
picture, Perry is attractin 
more attention from Wal 
Street. Merrill Lynch analyst 
Fran Blechman Bernstein in 


July raised her investment 
rating for Perry from “neu- 
tral” to “above average.” 

“The earnings growth out- 
look for Perry has been accel- 
erated by the recent acquisi- 
tion of 40 stores from Revco, 
and by the disposition of its 
deep discount drug store divi- 
sion and the closing of unprof- 
itable stores,” Bernstein 
wrote in aJuly 19 report. “Al- 
though the turnaround of Per- 
ry Drug Stores has taken long- 
er than expected... 
accelerated growth is now [a] 
prospect.” 

Bernstein estimates that 
Perry’s earnings could in- 
crease 20 percent or more an- 
nually over the next three to 
five years.

MONTREAL — Improved 
sacar at the Shoppers 

rug Mart division helped 
Imasco increase net earnings 
and revenues for the second 
uarter and six months ended 
une 30.

ations increased $400,000 to 
$89.9 million. Net earnings for 
the six months increased 10 
percent to $158.6 million; con- 
tinuing operations earnings for 
the period climbed 8 percent, to 
$155.1 million. 

Second-quarter sales were 
4 16 percent to $3.8 billion; 
the six-month sales figure was 
up 15 percent to $7.8 billion. 
Peoples Drug Stores revenues 
were excluded for both peri- 
ods in Imasco’s report. 

At Shoppers Drug Mart, 
strong sales boosted quarterly 
earnings 22 percent to $34.2 
million, with six-month fig- 
ures climbing 25 percent to 
$17.4 million.

Revco gets further extensions 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — U. S. Bankruptcy Court in Akron, 
Ohio has again extended the deadlines under which Revco D.S. 
has exclusive rights to file and obtain approval for a plan of reor- 
ganization. The court gave Revco until Oct. 26 to file such a plan, 
and until Jan. 24, 1991 to gain acceptance for the plan from its 
creditors. 

In other news, Revco has signed Olympic gold medal gymnast 
Mary Lou Retton to an exclusive contract as corporate spokes- 
person. Retton, who —_— her 1984 Olympic triumph into a 
series of lucrative endorsement packages in the mid-1980s, will 
appear in print and television advertising and make promotional 
appearances on behalf of Revco. 

etton is not new to the company. In the spring, she made ap- 
pearances at Revco Health and Beauty Expos in Cleveland and 
Charlotte, N.C., and will be featured at future expos.

INDIANAPOLIS — Reliable Drug Stores, Inc.’s recent 
acquisition of over 200 former Revco units has led it to move to

The 25,000-square-foot facility is located at 10401 N. Merid- 
ian St., Suite 400, Indianapolis, Ind. 46290; (317) 580-0800 is the 
telephone number.

additional space for growth,” said Tony Montini, senior vp-pur- 
chasing and merchandising.

By David Vaczek 

CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
Eckerd Drug has named Lew- 
is Shealy, former loss preven- 
tion chief at the Marshall Field 
company, as vp-loss preven- 
tion. Shealy is reputed in the 
security industry for his ag- 
gressive programs at the Chi- 
cago-based department store 
chain. 

Shealy is likely to develop at 
Eckerd a more centralized se- 
curity department, which 
would play down the regional 
security managers’ account- 
ability to regional operating 
vps, security industry sources 
predicted. “My guess is, he’ll 
want the [regional] people re- 
porting to him,” said one. 

Security directors some- 
times have dotted line respon- 
sibility for setting policies and 
standards for security manag- 
ers to follow in the field. On a 
day-to-day basis, though, 
they report to the regional 
vice presidents, several loss 
prevention officers said. Eck- 
erd declined to specify its 
plans for the department. 

Shealy will join Mickey Car- 
ter, who has built a strong loss 
prevention program at Eck- 
erd over the past five years. 
Carter will be director of tech- 
nical operations. 

“It’s going to be an awesome

combination,” said one securi- 
ty industry source. 

Shealy named Operation 
Alert as an initial project in a 
prepared statement. It is a pilot 
program to promote education 
and awareness of store asso- 
ciates, plus merchandising, op- 
erations and audit staff, involv- 
ing 200 “opportunity stores.” 


Go out and catch ’em 


Shealy was described at 
Marshall Field as a “go-out- 
and-catch-’em type o is 
He emphasized internal theft 
prevention, and used closed 
circuit television systems and 
radio-guided store patrols, 
said one security professional. 

A recent “20/20” television 
rogram showed Marshall 
‘ield’s “Trojan Horse,” 
wherein a security officer is 
concealed in a one-way-mir- 
rored column through which 
he can observe shoppers. The 
column can be moved to criti- 
cal store areas. 

While some techniques used 
in the department stores 
might not be suitable for the 
drug store environment, oth- 
ers would be. 

One Eckerd program it 
seems likely Shealy will retain 
is civil recovery. Carter has 
built an in-house program oper- 
ating in five states, that has re-

IS loss prevention maven 


portedly been successful. In 
states with civil recovery laws, 
the retailer can often ass 
the court system and send let-

persons caught shoplifting. 
Marshall Field has histori- 
cally enjoyed a 90 percent re- 
covery rate on letters sent to 
offenders in its civil recovery 
program, Shealy was quoted 
as Saying in a security indus- 
try newsletter in 1988. 
Carter, an Eckerd pharma- 
cist, was enlisted to build the 
loss prevention program after 
Eckerd did its leveraged 
buyout. Security profession- 
als praise his efforts, which 
besides civil recovery, have 
included an emphasis on elec- 
tronic article surveillance.

innovative, though he’s had no

has looked for experience and 
in which Shealy will contrib-

as another member of the loss

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 24, 1990 


For the participants the weather couldn’t have been 
better: overcast and chilly, with a threat of rain in the 
air. For the spectators, it was something else, but no- 
body seemed to mind, not the thousands who lined the 
streets nor the enthusiastic crowd in Varsity Stadium. 

The event: the 12th running of the To- 


ronto Marathon, this year renamed the 
Shoppers Drug Mart Toronto Marathon. 
A year ago, Canada’s leading drug chain 
took on the challenge of breathing new life 
into the race. Under its previous sponsor, 
Wang Computers, the marathon had de- 
veloped a serious stitch in the side and, in 
fact, was cancelled in 1989. 

With his highly sensitive promotional 
antenna, David Bloom, SDM’s chairman 


IN THE MARKET 
BRUCE BUCKLEY 


and ceo, offered to take on the race. It 
seemed like an ideal tie-in to the health 
and fitness image Shoppers strives to 


maintain. Indeed, SDM stores sponsor 
some 1,500 youth teams across the coun- 
try in sports as diverse as baseball and hockey, soccer 
and ringette (a hockey-like game for girls). 

The team sponsorships represent one side of what 
Shoppers Drug Mart is about: a decentralized chain of 
stores with strong roots in their communities. The To- 
ronto Marathon represents the other side: A highly dis- 
ciplined, promotional powerhouse with electricity radi- 
ating coast to coast from its source in Toronto. SDM 
name recognition in Canada rivals that of even the best 
known U.S drug chains in their own country. Sponsor- 
ing the Marathon in Canada’s leading city (and commit- 
ting $450,000 of the $800,000 the event cost) is an invest- 
ment in keeping SDM a household name. 

Shoppers’ stamp on the event showed in other 
ways. A big chunk of the money raised went to Toron- 
to’s world-famous Sick Children’s Hospital. SDM hap- 
pens to be one of the foremost proponents of the idea 
that being a “good corporate citizen” is good business. 
Murray Koffler, the chain’s founder, brought the con- 
cept of reinvesting in the community to a high art, and 
David Bloom and his team remain strongly commit- 
ted. 


President Herb Binder and ceo David Bloom cheer 
runners. 


Like the sports teams sponsored by individual 
stores across the country, this giving back to the com- 
munity mainly takes place at local level. One store, for 
example, helped to raise money for a specialized piece 
of fire protection equipment in the wake of a child’s 
tragic death in a blaze. 

This year’s marathon had some bugs. Newspapers 
the next day criticized television coverage, which 
failed to keep up with the progress of the race. But 
considering that this was essentially an inaugural 
event, the marathon came off remarkably well. About 
4,000 athletes from around the world competed in 
events ranging from the marathon itself, to a 10K 
race, to a corporate team relay race sponsored by Ko- 
dak Copier. Millions watched the race on television. 

Next year’s race should be even better, as SDM 
builds on this year’s experience. Shoppers has com- 
mitted itself to a five-year sponsorship, and given the 
energy level of its corporate team, the marathon 
should become, by the time of the 1996 Olympics in To- 
ronto, one of the world’s premier races. 

The winners of this year’s events? All Canadians. 
The top man and woman marathoners both broke re- 
cords for the Toronto race. The other big winner of 
course was Shoppers Drug Mart itself. 


Service never goes out of style. But in delivering 
service, even well-meaning pharmacists, store man- 
agers and clerks can run afoul of proper etiquette 
when curiosity drives them beyond politeness. 

Consider the nun from the next town who came to a 

drug store for her birth control pills. 


The pharmacist unknowingly asked if 


THE HUMAN SIDE 


she was taking them back to the Catho- 
lic school a few miles away, for which he 
had never before filled a script. She said 
“no, they are for me.” 

He then had to ask, under the pre- 
tense of counseling, “are you taking 
them to keep you regular?” She said 
“yes,” paid for her pills and left. 


At another drug store some time ago, 
condoms and cigarettes were behind the 


AL HELLER 


counter and had to be requested by con- 
sumers. A man discreetly asked for a 


certain brand of condom, and the teen- 
age female clerk didn’t recognize the name. 

To the amusement of other clerks within earshot, 
she grabbed a book of matches and eyeballed the car- 
ton display. After searching half a minute, she yelled 
out to her co-workers: “Trojans. Are they filter tip or 
regular?” 

The customer mumbled something unintelligible 
and left the store. 


Then there was the 30-year-old man who bought 


Sometimes it pays to shut your mouth 


Fleet Enemas six at a time during his weekly visits to 
the drug store. 

After noticing this pattern for at least a month, the 
pharmacist piped up when the customer plunked his 
six on the counter. “Are these for you,” he asked, “be- 
cause if you have a problem, this frequency isn’t rec- 
ommended.” 

The man explained he was administering these to 
his dog, who did indeed have a problem. 


Another pharmacist met up with another dog lover, 
when he refused to fill the birth control prescription 
for a woman who had already gone through the six re- 
fills allowed by the doctor. 

The woman, who appeared past the age of use, had 
to endure the pharmacist telling her she had to speak 
to the doctor before he could dispense any more medi- 
cation. 

“T can’t,” she replied. “He’s a veterinarian. I’m giv- 
ing these to my dog.” 


Kudos to the store manager who handled this situa- 
tion: 

On Halloween night, a customer in a Donald Duck 
costume hopped into the drug store to buy Chap- 
Stick. He had inadvertently left his wallet in his car 
and had no money to pay. 

“That’s OK,” said the store manager. “I’ll put it on 
your bill.” 

-The six-foot-tall duck happened to be a local police 
officer and a regular shopper in the store.

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 24, 1990 


PRODUCT 
TRACKING 


ALAN MILLER 


Package size is an impor- 
tant line extension variable in 
lanning shelf displays, and 
ailure to include items which 
are in high demand or are in- 
creasing in their share of the 
product mix can result in lost 
sales. In some of the 14 catego- 
ries we measured, a high pro- 
ortion of retail sales volume 
is concentrated in just one or 
two sizes; in others, many dif- 
ferent size alternatives must 
be considered when deciding 
on an optimum product mix. 

In the hair spray category, 
for example, there are only 
three broad size groups, and 
more than half of the category 
volume is contributed by items 
in the size range of 7.1 ounces to 
10.0 ounces. Among shampoos, 
on the other hand, there are 10 
different ranges of product 
size, although nearly half of the 
sales are in packages ranging in 
content from 14.0 ounces to 
16.9 ounces. This size group is 
also exhibiting important 
growth, and dollar sales during 
the year ended June 15, 1990 
were 15.6 percent higher than 
during the corresponding year 
ago period. The high volume 
hair spray size group has 
shrunk 4.9 percent over the 
year, and the second most pop- 
ular size group, 7 ounces and 
under, has gained in share from 
37.8 percent to 40.6 percent, 
representing a volume increase 
of 4.9 percent. 

Trial sizes had important dol- 
lar gains among both shampoos 
and hair conditioning rinses, 
with increases measuring 29.4 
percent and 74.8 percent re- 
spectively. However, their 
share was only 1.7 percent 
among shampoos and 0.4 per- 
cent in the case of hair condi- 
tioning rinses. Of the three size 
groups in the hair spray catego- 
ry, the only gain was for items 7 
c'inces and under, where an in- 
crease of 4.9 percent was re- 
corded and the share of catego- 
ry volume rose from 37.8 
percent a year ago to the cur- 
rent level of 40.6 percent. 

Drug store sales of mouth- 
washes fell 3.0 percent and 
there were both volume and 
share losses in the two most 
important size groups: 15.1 
ounces to 21.0 ounces, where 
the share declined from 23.1 
percent to 20.2 percent and 


dollar volume fell 15.5 per- 
cent. Among those packages 
ranging from 4.1 ounces to 9.0 
ounces, there was a dollar vol-

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 24, 1990 


Drug chains profit from 


Ky kin care sales have been very good for most chain drug 
stores this year, and most buyers see this category—as 
well as the related segments of sun and bath—as offering 
above-average growth opportunities in the year tocome. 

“We’re expecting increases of 25 percent to 30 percent,” said 
one person in charge of toiletries for a major drug chain, “and 
that will be primarily due to Plenitude and Olay, and everything 
they’ve got going.” 

Although space is tight for this chain—as it is with most tradi- 
tional drug K eee, ae management wants to expand skin 
and bath because the categories’ growth potential. 

Right now the chain is testing a separate skin care set in select 
stores and is trying to find a way to bring bath, face, and hand 
and body together in one organized set. 

The chain feels that at least 30 feet is required to do justice to 
the set as well as to make a dramatic presentation. The pre- 
ferred location for the department is in cosmetics. 

The chain hopes it will have enough information from its cur- 
rent test to expand skin care in its 1991 planogram. 

The skin care center now being tested has light boxes and 
glass shelves. The effect, said our source, is so unusually glam- 
orous for a chain drug store that there is some fear it might in- 
timidate certain customers. 

This chain is also trying to organize the skin care categories 
more by type of product to make it easier for customers to shop 
for skin care and bath items. 

Although this chain wants their skin care department to have 
an upscale look, they want to achieve this in a compact, space- 
efficient manner, with a concept that gets as much product on 
display as possible. 

For this reason, this source particularly appreciates the new 
Olay fixtures from P&G. Shaped like kiosks, she says they hold 
a lot of product and they look good. a

advertising the category. Walgreens uses shelf talkers to create a positive low everyday price image.
