Arbor reaps benefits 


from expanded space 


At Arbor Drug in Detroit, 
the growth in skin care is “par- 
alleling” the chain’s overall 
sales growth, which this year 
is in double-digits, according 
to vp-purchasing Dennis Woz- 
niak. 

Arbor expanded space for 
skin by two or three feet last 
year when L’Oréal launched 
Plenitude, and depending on 
space, skin care now gets be- 
tween 16 and 24 feet in an av- 
erage store. 

The planogram also in- 
cludes space for the bath cate- 
gory, including cosmetic lines 
like Jean Naté and Vitabath, 
as well as toiletry lines like 
VIC and Jergens, bubble 
baths, and an assortment of 
year-round sun care items. 

Arbor reviews each depart- 
ment at least quarterly to de- 


cide if a category is worth ex- 


panding or needs to be cut 
back. 


Douglas Drug deais 


with space crunch 

Douglas Drug in Rhode Is- 
land merchandises all skin 
care, off-season sun and bath 
care products together in one 
28-foot set. Buyer Steve Du- 
bin says he would like to give 
the category more space be- 
cause it deserves it, but at this 
point there’s no room to ex- 
pand. And because there is no 
room to cross-merchandise, 
Dubin isn’t planning to devel- 
op a skin care center. 

He just revised his plano- 
gram to work Plenitude into 
the set, and he’s also brought 
in Olay’s new cleansers. 

Dubin says he would like to 
see more vendors develop dis-

Rx to OTC switches: 
A double-edged sword? 


By Elizabeth Richardson 
EW YORK — Over the next decade, dozens of medicines 
could be switched from prescription to over-the-counter 
status. While the switching process almost always spells in- 
stant sales successes for the products involved, many pharmacists 
believe it to be a double-edged sword. 

“The biggest advantage [of Rx to OTC switches], of course, is the 
counseling associated with them,” said Mike Salquist, director of 
pharmacy operations at K mart. “It’s great at building the confi- 
dence factor with the public and is a basic point to opening up lines of 
communication.”

Rx’ers juggle professionalism, business 


For as long as my career in pharmacy spans, some 25 
years, retail pharmacists have tried to answer the same 
question over and over: Is it possible to mix the business of 
running a drug store with the professionalism expected of 
a registered pharmacist? The answer I always give is a de- 
finitive “maybe.” 

It is a complicated question, and one that has been given 
considerable thought by pharmacists, academicians and 
consumers over the years. I think if you polled most retail 
pharmacists today, the answer would be “yes.” But when 
push comes to shove, do they really mean it? I’m not sure. 

The question of professionalism has been handled easily 
by scores of gg ye of pharmacy offering a Pharm.D.- 
only curriculum. It always seems to me their inference is 
that without the Pharm.D. degree in your hands upon 
graduation, professionalism in any pharmacy 


ny’s drug for schizophrenia, Clozaril. The requires 
close monitoring, the kind of monitoring that Sandoz be- 
lieves cannot be done at your average retail drug store. In- 
stead, Sandoz chose to go to a closed distribution system 
when it hired Caremark, a division of Baxter Labs, to do 
the necessary screening. Several national associations and 
dozens of state associations immediately came to the aid of 
hurt retail a by condemning Sandoz’s action. 
While I understand retai] pharmacy’s point of view, I also 
understand Sandoz’s. 


A juggling act 


You see, Sandoz is also doing a juggling act. There is no 
doubt that the company knew a pant distribution system 
would get the hairs of every retail pharmacist in the coun- 

try standing on end. But it also knew that not 


setting pore right out of the window. Does a 
Pharm.D. degree prepare a retail pharmacist 
to be oe more professional in a drug store 
setting than a B.S.? I’m not sure. 

But, there is apparently no question about 
rofessionalism in the minds of consumers. 
ust look at the latest Gallup study. Pharma- 

cists once again ranked as the most trusted 
health Det geen But does being the most

in every geographical area of the country. It 
would have been a nightmare to survey ever 
pharmacy to see if they could handle the prod- |

ly tract blood levels, etc. From a business and

“professionalism” on the table. Does it mean CAPSULES for pharmacists. I did not.

intelligible answers? Does it mean accepting prescriptions 
that have to be compounded, even if it does take extra time? 
Or does it mean doing blood screenings? To me, I think it 
means all of them and more. 


Maintaining a balance 


While I believe that most pharmacists would like to 
practice pharmacy with the highest degree of profession- 
alism, the reality is that they are still working in a business 
setting and the balance between professionalism and busi- 
ness must be maintained. To put it simply, the prescrip- 
tions still have to be filled while the questions keep com- 
ing. It is a difficult juggling act and probably the single 
most disturbing factor in practicing retail pharmacy to- 


day. 

The question of professionalism is once — under the 
spotlight when Sandoz Pharmaceuticals told retail phar- 
macists that they would not be able to handle the compa- 


One just has to look at Florida for a perfect op- 
portunity thrown away. Several years ago, when a law 
was passed in Florida that allowed pharmacists to dis- 
pense a very selective group of prescription drugs without 
a prescription, I took a trip down to the Sunshine State to 
see how things were progressing. I was dismayed to learn 
that with very few exceptions, most pharmacists were 
staying away from prescribing. I pene then that it was a 
golden professional opportunity being thrown away. My 
sources in Florida tell me that little has changed. The law 
is still on the books but not terribly effective. The reasons 
cited over and over again for not prescribing are the same: 
liability, lack of time to properly counsel patients, and ex- 
tra paperwork. 

I am sure there are many stores that can easily handle 
the requirements set forth in the Clozaril screening pro- 
cess. But if we really have the patients’ interests at heart, 
this is one time I think professionalism must win over busi- 
ness.

Vol. 5, No. 10 September 24, 1990 


Some two decades ago, I, along with 
my fellow graduating pharmacists, 
took the Hippocratic Oath. Although 
the specific words have since faded 
from my memory, I do remember the 
promise not to do anything to harm a 
fellow human being. 

As a pharmacist or a physician, 
where do we draw the line of what is or 
is not harm? I question this because I 
have just returned from the funeral of 
a longtime customer and friend whom 
I'll call Sam. 

Sam had the misfortune of being 
cursed with a bad back and had en- 
dured several episodes of surgery over 
the years to help eliminate his persis- 
tent pain. Unfortunately, he was nev- 
er able to attain long-term relief from 
his affliction. 

Equally unfortunate is the fact that 
Sam found a certain amount of relief 
from Darvocet N 100. But time passed, 
tolerance to the drug set in as did the 
persistent pain. Sam found that relief 
could only be achieved with daily doses 
that exceeded the recommended maxi- 
mum dose. 

Knowing that further surgery would 
probably be of little help, and perhaps in 
desperation, he turned to the only 
means that would help stop his pain and 
maintain a productive and meaningful 
life. He found new physicians who would 
prescribe Darvocet N 100 and was hav- 


ing them filled at several different phar- 
macies. How long this had been going 
on, no one knows for sure. But for him, 
the system was working. 

Where and how did Sam meet his 
downfall? His insurance company 
signed up with a national third-party 
provider. He had two prescriptions 
filled within two days. When the sec- 
ond prescription for Darvocet N 100 
was charged through’ the provider’s 
online adjudication terminal, the sys- 


tem flagged it and notified the crug ~ 


store submitting the claim. 

As a conscientious pharmacist, I no- 
tified the two physicians and the other 
pharmacy of the problem that existed. 
None of us considered the possibility of 
Sam’s physical or psychological addic- 
tion to the drug. Nor did any of us con- 
sider Sam’s need for some sort of pain 
management or his need for psycholog- 
ical help. All we saw was that Sam was 
a drug abuser and reacted as such. . . 
by cutting him off. 

Recently Sam’s wife, his two young 
children and a large number of friends 
said good-bye to this very kind and lik- 
able 37-year-old man. For you see, 
Sam discharged a hand gun into the 
side of his head, taking his life. Maybe 
Sam killed himself because he become 
depressed after his doctor “had cut off 
his pain medication” and was running 
out of medication and had no place to 


My way of thinking .. . 


turn, or maybe he knew that he would 
not be able to tolerate the pain that 
would inevitably return without his 
pain killers. Only Sam could answer 
these questions. 

Would more empathy and compas- 
sion by those involved have prevented 
this tragedy? One can only speculate. 

Sure Sam would have eventually de- 
stroyed his liver or kidneys on the path 
he was taking. But we must all under- 
stand that everyone who has a drug 
problem has an underlying psychologi- 
cal or physical problem or some combi- 
nation thereof. As health care profes- 
sionals, bound by the Hippocratic 
Oath, are we acting responsibly by 
“cutting off” these people without 
making every effort possible to see 
that they get some therapy? 

The next time you have to deal with a 
patient with a substance abuse aay 
and everyone is ready to “cut them off,” 
please think of Sam, his wife, and their 
two children. I know I will. 

Signed, 

A More Compassionate Pharmacist 
Editors note: We will not print any 
correspondence in this space without 
knowledge of who the author is. The 
above letter was received with a cover 
letter identifying its author. Because 
of the sensitivity of the material, he 
asked that we not publish his name. We 
respected that wish.

NEW YORK — Consumer 
advertising may or may not 
make an over-the-counter 
sage an instant sales hit, 

ut one thing is certain: it is 
very important in influencing 
buying decisions of OTC buy- 
ers at drug chains, discount 
stores and supermarkets. 

According to the 1990 Drug 
Store News/Inside Pharmacy 
Buyer Feedback Study, a sur- 
vey of OTC buyers at 35 major 
drug chains, discounters and 
supermarkets, consumer ad- 
vertising headed the list of in- 
fluences when buyers decide 
to stock one OTC product over 
another. 

Buyers were asked to rate a 
list of services offered by most 
manufacturers of over-the- 
counter products. Nearly ev- 
ery buyer who answered the 
survey told DrSN/IP that con- 
sumer advertising was “very 
important” in their buying de- 
cisions. 

Forty-one percent of those 
answering the question also 
picked consumer advertising 
as the single most important 
service in making their buying 
decision. A summary of ser- 
vices checked off by 50 percent 
or more of the respondents can 


On average, the buyers said 
that OTC products accounted 
for 21.42 percent of their total 
dollar annual sales. 


New product intros 


When it comes to making 
buying decisions on new prod- 
uct introductions, the survey 
uncovered that consumer ad- 
vertising was edged out by the 
product’s quality as being a 
“very important” factor. 
Ninety-one percent of the re- 
spondent aggregate picked 
product quality compared to 
the 82 percent that chose dol- 
lars budgeted for consumer 
advertising. 

But when the buyers were 
asked to choose the single 
most important factor in 
choosing whether or not to 
take on a new product, nearly 
a third chose dollars budgeted 
for consumer advertising.

the aggregate), uniqueness of 
the product and number of 
sku’s (each receiving 62 per- 
cent), display allowances (56

Buyers’ visits 


According to the survey, 
OTC buyers are quite satis- 
fied with the level of service 
they are currently getting 
from their OTC product reps. 
Nearly three-quarters of the 
respondents said they see 
their OTC product reps once 
a month, and that is just fine 
with them. Only three per- 
cent said they wanted to see 
them more frequently while 
15 percent said they wanted 
to see them less frequently. 
Of those buyers who an- 
swered they wanted to see 
their reps more or less fre- 

uently, the majority said 
that once every two to six 
months was fine with them. 


Nearly all the respondents 
(94 percent) indicated that 
the reps were allowed to 
make store visits. 


Average time 


The buyers reported spend- 
ing anywhere from 10 minutes 
to one hour with representa- 
tives from OTC product man- 
ufacturers. Most of the buyers 
said they spend, on average, 
from 20 to 30 minutes with 
reps. None of the buyers said 
they spend less than 10 min- 
utes or over an hour with any 
individual rep. 

But regardless of how much 
time the buyers spend with 
the reps, the majority said 
that visits from manufactur- 
ers’ reps was still the best 
method of receiving informa- 
tion about new and existing 
products. Nearly one-quarter 
of the buyers said that direct 
marketing was another impor- 
tant method of getting impor- 
tant information concerning 
their product lines. 


High marks 


The buyers gave the manu- 
facturers’ reps pretty high 
grades in when it comes to 
helping them identify the 
best products to stock. More 
than half (68 percent) the 
buyers said the reps do an 
“above average” or “ aver- 
age” job while just under a 
quarter of them (21 percent) 
said they do an “outstanding” 
job. Only 12 percent said they 
do a “below average” job and 
none said they do a “poor” 
job. 


Merchandising mix

end” OTC business continues 
to heat up in the marketplace, 
retailers are taking a careful 
look at their merchandising 
mix and how they promote 
these products.

most three-quarters of the 
buyers said they carry most 
major brands and sizes avail- 
able to give shoppers a broad 
variety of selection. Eighteen 

ercent said they carry at

number one or number two 
brands in a particular product 
category. 

More than half of the re- 
spondents said their pricing 
strategy is to rely on sales and 
low promotional prices rather 
than low every day prices (See 
Table 3).

created the need for heavy

OTC products. More than

Ziegler speaks out 


WASHINGTON — NACDS president Ron Ziegler was one of sev- 
eral industry executives who recently testified before the House 
Health Subcommittee urging Congress to reform the Medicaid 
program. Among their suggestions: having manufacturers negoti- 
ate prices with the program and pass some of the savings on to 
pharmacists in their reimbursement levels. (See story on p. 65)

NEWS IN Bixler 


CVS parent completes Peoples buy 


RYE, N.Y. — Melville Corp., which operates 820-store CVS, 
completed the acquisition of 490-store Peoples Drug Stores 
from Imasco Ltd. of Montreal Sept. 17. The purchase price was 
$325 million in cash. 

CVS sales in 1989 totaled $1.02 billion. Peoples had $1.02 bil- 
lion in sales for 1989. The acquisition significantly expands Mel- 
ville’s drug store business into new markets, notably the Wash- 
ington, D.C. metropolitan area. 

CVS has said the Peoples stores will keep their name, which 
has wide recognition in its markets. 

Imasco’s chairman, president and ceo, Purdy Crawford, said 
Imasco will use the proceeds of the Peoples sale to reduce Imas- 
co’s debt, which willresult in a stronger balance sheet and low- 
er interest expense. 


K mart unveils new logo 


TROY, Mich. — K mart unveiled 
a redesigned logo as part of a new 
identity program that will tie in 
with a planned refurbishment of all 
its stores. 

The new bright red logo replaces 
the company’s old sign—a red “K” 
followed by the word “mart” in tur- 
quoise. 

All ei built and expanded stores will have the new logo 
in external and internal signs and in details. Others will re- 
wees it as they are refurbished and by 1995 it will be chain- 
wide. 

The discounter is one of the most aggressive pharmacy retail- 
ers in the country, with prescription departments in over 1,250 
of its 2,331 stores. It plans to put departments in all new stores 
and in remodels where space allows.

Arbor signs Pistons star 


TROY, Mich. — All-star guard Joe Dumars of the Detroit 
Pistons will star in a series of TV spots for Arbor Drugs’ “Pic- 
ture! Picture!” photofinishing service. Dumars will be featured 
in four 30-second spots promoting the two-for-one print pro- 
gram, which generated 2.4 million orders last year. 

“Photofinishing and film sales are an important traffic builder 
in our stores,” said Arbor chairman and ceo Eugene 4. orton 
in making the announcement. “As a result of Picture! Picture!, 
Arbor photo and film sales, which have doubled in the last five 
years, now account for 7.4 percent of total sales, almost twice 
the national average for chain drug stores.” 

The Dumars spots will mene airing in mid-October, and 
eventually account for more than $1 million of commercial air 
time. 


Perry signs three more Mich. leases 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores has inked three 
leases for new stores in the Detroit metro and Grand Rapids ar- 
eas. 

Perry has opened six new drug stores, signed lease agree- 
ments for three additional sites and acquired and kept open 35 
former Revco drug stores in its current fiscal year, which ends 
Oct. 31. In fiseal 1991, the 207-store chain is planning to open an- 
other 20 units.

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 8, 1990 


or the first time in years, 
ethnic product buyers 
are reporting some 
growth in ethnic hair care 
product sales. 

The growth is not as dra- 
matic as it was in the boom 
years of the late "70s when the 
curl look was hot and hair 
maintenance products were 
flying out the door. 

But many buyers report 
sales increases of between 4 
percent and 10 percent. Some 
sources think that the growth 
could be even stronger in the 
next two to three years as new 
styling trends emerge. 

“Most of our customers are 
reporting sales increases of 
between seven and ten per- 
cent,” says Dave Pearlman, 

resident of North American 

eauty Supply. North Ameri- 
can services chain drugs, vari- 
ety stores and food stores in 
several major markets, in- 
cluding the South. 

Pearlman says the growth 
is the result of “hard work, ad- 
vertising, promotions, and 
keeping the merchandise on 
the shelf.” 

‘““We’re having nice in- 
creases, both from existing 
and new customers,” reports 
Tom Hood, vp of sales for Sa- 
vannah, Ga.-based Ben Shef- 
tall Distributors. 

“In drug stores, promotion- 
al activity is driving the busi- 
ness. Bonus packs, advertis- 
ing and in-store programs are 
what’s making it happen.” 

But, as is always the case in 
this category, growth is also 
fueled by fashion trends emerg- 
ing from professional salons. 

Geri Duncan Jones, presi- 
dent of the American Health 
and Beauty Aids Institute 
(AHBAT), reports there’s 
“quite a lot happening in the 
ethnic market right now,” and 
she says “much of it is driven by 
professional trends carrying 
over into the retail market.” 


Versatility is key 


According to sources we 
talked to, the fashion buzz- 
word in hair styles this year is 
“versatility.” 

“In fashion, it’s anything 
goes right now. It’s great,” 
says Lou Orenstein, president 
of Judith Lynn Beauty Sup- 
ply. “Some are wearing the 
curl. Some are going for the 
flattop look. Some are relax- 
ing their hair. It means you’re 
able to sell a lot of different 
kinds of maintenance products 
now, not just a trailer load of 
one thing needed for one par- 
ticular style.” 

“There isn’t any one style 


Ethnic hair care story: 
It’s fueled by fashion 


that’s everyone wants and 
that’s good,” says David 
Pearlman of North America 
Beauty Supply. “Men and 
women are changing their 


styles frequently, and that 
means they need a variety of 
products to maintain these dif- 
ferent styles.” 

“Today, it’s do whatever 
you want to do,” says Jones. 
“At the Bronner Brothers 
fashion show in Las Vegas, I 
was seeing a lot of asymmetri- 
cal cuts. Hair may be cut long 
on one side and short on the 
other. One part may be curled, 
the other may be straight.” 

This year, men seem to be 
wearing their hair slightly 
longer and many are opting for 
the High Top cut, which re- 
quires more maintenance than 
the short cuts that many men 
were favoring until recently. 

“Hair on guys is coming 
back,” says Mike O’Neil, who 
buys ethnic products for Harris 
Beauty Supply, headquartered 
in Alexandria, Va. “And what 
you're seeing are men using 
two or three products instead 
of one to maintain their styles.” 

‘Some men are wearing 
their hair back with a little po- 
nytail,” says Jones. For men 
to achieve this style, she adds, 
they have to let their hair 
grow out and then use a chemi- 
cal wave in their hair so they 
can bring it back and tie it. 

“And whether men are wear- 
ing their hair natural or

Along with relaxers, the

In salons, where styling

has caused a boom in the retail

Sheen Finishing Mist and Lo- 
tion and the new Right On Dry 
Curl Mist and Lotion. 

Retail sales of curl kits, 
which in the past few years 
have been declining, are now 
regaining ground. 

The salons now seem to be 
doing more hair weaving, a 
technique that can make hair 
look fuller as well as conceal 
imperfections like thinning 
hair or bald spots. 

Geri Duncan Jones, inter- 
viewed as she attended the 
Bronner Brothers Beauty 
show in Las Vegas this past 


Growth is fueled

August, reported that hair 
weaving was being demon- 
strated “all over.” 

She also saw a tremendous 
onslaught of styling products 
at the show, especially 
spritzes and gels, and prod- 
ucts that temporarily add col- 
or to the hair. 

As far as most buyers are 
concerned, all this new fashion 
activity should mean good 
news for retailers. 

Looking down the line, 
most of our sources felt that 
ethnic products are poised for 
even greater growth. Fashion 
seems to be on the category’s 
side, finally, and even a de- 
pressed economy could be a 
boon in disguise. 

“As the economy goes 
down, strangely enough, busi- 
ness picks up,” says Judith 
Lynn’s Lou Orenstein. “When 
times are tough, ethnic con- 
sumers seem to buy even more 
beauty care products. They 
want to look better because it 
helps them feel better.” 

Geri Duncan Jones sums it 
up this way: 

“If the stylists are wearing 


it, you just know their custom- 
ers are going to be wearing it.”

K mart, in particular, is mak-

thnic program to strengthen 


“They’re becoming very ag- 
gressive in the category. They 
want to be the leader in terms

went direct with the category, 
a move that facilitated the ex-

&B stores are also continu- 
ing to proliferate, although in 
some areas of the country, such 
as the East Coast and Middle- 
Atlantic regions, they have be- 
come so saturated that buyers 
are reporting the start of a 
shakeout. 


Product key to giving drug chains an edge 


ethnic category, drug chains should look 

very carefully at their product mix. 
That’s what knowledgeable distributors rec- 
ommend. 

They believe that chains have to stay on top 
of this category, weeding out slow movers and 
adding hot new items as they come out. 

“The successful retailers of the 90s,” says 
Kent Humphreys, president of Jack’s Service 
Company in Oklahoma City, “have to say to 
customers that they really are in the ethnic 
products category.” 

Humphreys says that making a statement in 
the category may even mean getting into acces- 
sories like shower caps, hosiery, cosmetics and 
even synthetic hair. 

“These types of items are all hot in beauty 
and barber shops right now, and what you see 
happening is that the beauty and barber shops 
are taking share away from the chain drug 
stores,” he adds. 

“B&B stores carry everything,” says Lou 
Orenstein, president of Judith ae Beauty 
Supply in hicago. “They don’t try to judge 
from yesterday what black consumers will 
want today. In this category, you can’t wait for 
Towne-Oller to make a report. They are not go- 
ing to have the latest hot new products, and 
that’s what drives sales.” 


: i " o enhance their competitive edge in the 


Orenstein also recommends that chain drug 
stores stock lastic shower ca s. “They’re our 
number-one item,” he says. Black consumers 
have to have them to process their hair. We sell 
millions of caps to the B&B shops.” 

The caps ad sell well in some drug chains, 
but not everyone stocks them. Thrift has done 
a good j jo ob in this category, our sources tell us, 
and so have some Oscos, but many other major 
chains are missing the boat. Distributors em- 
phasize that this is a high-use, high-tonnage 
category. 

Picks and combs are a similar type of oppor- 
tunity. Chuck Lewman of Paul’s Sundries calls 
them the “bread and butter of the category.” 
They’re not high priced. The use-up rate is 
high, and they’ve very popular with black con- 
sumers. Many distributors say drug chains as a 
whole neglect this category. “It’s almost like an 
afterthought,” says Lewman, “but you have to 
make a conscious decision to be in this category 
because you do need an assortment. It has to be 
more than just a Goody section, because a 
Goody section is not where most ethnic con- 
sumers shop. They shop the ethnic depart- 
ment.” 

Lewman thinks that the brand doesn’t mat- 
ter as much in this category as long as the prod- 
uct is good quality. He says , bow bristle 
brushes sell best because they are strong.

Fragrance merchandising audit 


Chains gearing up to maximize 
Christmas fragrance sales 


ow that the buying 
for Christmas 1990 is 
over, chain drug 


stores are getting ready for 
their next hardest task: imple- 
menting the merchandising 
programs developed to maxi- 
mize Christmas sellthroughs. 

The implementation process 
is especially critical for fra- 
grances. In many chains, buy- 
ers say this category literally 
lives and dies depending on 
how well it sells at Christmas. 

For the third consecutive 
year Drug Store News and 
SPAR/ Burgoyne Marketing 
and Information Services 
have done a Christmas fra- 
grance audit of chain drug 
stores.The audit’s purpose is 
to examine how effectively 
fragrances were merchan- 
dised at the store level. For 
the Christmas 1989 audit, 
SPAR/Burgoyne researchers 
visited 364 chain drug stores 
in 20 major markets. 

To help analyze the audit, 
Drug Store News, earlier this 


year, shared the SPAR/Bur- 
goyne findings with close toa 
dozen cosmetic merchandis- 
ers, buyers and fragrance 
venders. 

Basically the retailers were 
all with companies in the Top 
15 highest volume drug 
chains, and each reported 
some growth in their fra- 
grance sales last Christmas. 
Most attributed their gains to 
a variety of factors including: 
giving fragrances more dis- 
play space, trying to stay in 
stock on the most in demand 
brands, and trying to give cus- 
tomers a broader selection of 
the most popular department 
and designer brands. 

In analyzing where they gen- 
erated the strongest growth, 
most buyers said it came from 
new launches like Ex Cla Ma 
Tion!, Dare, California and As- 
pen as well as from department 
store brands like Red, Obses- 
sion, and Passion. 

But many buyers also said 
they were somewhat disap-

The Drug Store News 
Christmas fragrance audit 
was implemented by 
SPAR/ Burgoyne, a nation- 
al research firm that spe- 
cializes in marketing infor- 
mation and merchandising 
services for consumer prod- 
uct manufacturers. 

Through its national field 
organization of over 1,000 
people, SPAR/Burgoyne 
monitors brand and catego- 
ry activity among food, 
drug and mass merchandise 
and other retail outlets on 
an ongoing basis. 

The firm also provides an 
in-store merchandising 
force to support client ef- 
forts at point-of-sale. 

SPAR/Burgoyne’s re- 


Study methodology 


search capabilities also in- 
clude retail sales measure- 
ment and analysis of new 
product and advertising ac- 
tivities in hundreds of test 
markets across the coun- 
try. 

The firms Consumer- 
Views group provides cus- 
tom survey research and 
analysis among both con- 
sumers and trade audi- 
ences. 

For the 1989 Christmas 
fragrance audit, SPAR- 
/Burgoyne monitored fra- 
grance merchandising in 
364 chain drug stores in 20 
major markets. The audit 
was performed on Nov. 9, 
1989. All measurements 
were taken in linear inches.

Fragrance display space 


Overall, buyers who saw 
our survey were satisfied with 
the amount of total display 
space that fragrances were 
given for Christmas, 1989 and 
how fast the stores got their 
displays up. 

ee to the SPAR/ 
Burgoyne audit, 74 percent of 
the 364 stores in the survey 
had their holiday displays up 
by the week of Nov. 5. As one 
buyer said, that means most 
stores were capturing impulse 
gift purchases immediately af- 
ter Halloween clean-ups. 

Between regular shelf 
space and additional promo- 
tional display space, the fra- 
grance category was as visible 
in 1989 as it was in 1988. Men’s 
fragrances were given a a lit- 
tle more display space last 
Christmas than they were in 
1988, up 2 percent, while 
women’s were given a little 
less, down 1 percent in 1989 
versus the prior year. 

Distribution worries 


Since mass market fra- 
grance brands are the heart of 
most chain drug store fra- 
grance programs, buyers said 
they were surprised and 
somewhat worried about gaps 


in distribution. 

In the 364 stores: in the 
study there were cases of seri- 
ous out-of-stock problems on 
major brands like Jovan Musk 
for Women, Ex Cla Ma Tion!, 
Le Jardin de Max Factor, 
Hero, Engiish Leather, 
Chaps and Old Spice Cologne. 

In some cases, it was clear 
that some chains were moving 
slowly in getting new launches 
like Ex Cla Ma Tion!, Almay, 
Dare and California into their 
stores in time for Christmas . 

There were, for example, 
138 stores, 38 percent of the 
survey, that were not in stock 
on California, which is gener- 
ally considered the best mass 
women’s fragrance launch of 
1989. 

In other cases, it looked like 
some stores simply hadn't re- 
ceived deliveries on major es- 
tablished brands like Charlie, 
Jovan Musk for Women, Lady 
Stetson, Le Jardin, Chantilly, 
Old Spice Cologne, Stetson, 
and English Leather.

the stores we surveyed were 
not in stock with Lady Stetson 
the day of our Christmas au-

were out of Xia Xiang, and 27 
percent were not carrying Jo- 
van Musk for Women.

icture looked similar. Old

Inventory turns 


“Today, the financial people 
worry about nothing as much 
as turn of inventory,” said a

strengthen its cosmetic fran-

ment of profitability. But at 
some point if you cut back on 
presentations to reduce inven-

to reduce shrink, you wind up 
just about going out of busi- 
ness. 

“Many financial guys can 
even see the down the road 
consequences of cutting space 
themselves just as merchan- 
disers can. But in their posi- 
tion, they don’t see any way 
around the dilemma,” he add- 
ed.

scents.”

Mother’s Day. 


Shrink a problem 


At Christmas 1989, the 
SPAR/Burgoyne findings re- 
vealed that more chains felt 
compelled to merchandising 
fragrances under glass, even 
the mass brands whose selling 
prices are moderate compared 
to the $50 and $60 discounted 
prices for designer scents. 

“It’s unfortunate, but true,” 
said one buyer, “that if a fra- 
grance retails for anything 
over $10 these days, it has to 
be locked up. When something 
comes out for over $20, you 
can expect to find it in a safe.”

Fragrances competing for display space 


Continued from page 62 
“The fragrance category,” 
says another buyer, “yields 


the highest dollar returns for 


shoplifters. It’s the most de- 
sirable category to steal.” 
This year, chains like Rev- 
co, Thrifty, Genovese, Supe- 
Rx, Eckerd, and Austin are 
trying to work harder with 
venders like Cosmair, Revlon 
and Coty to find better ways 
to reduce shrink, and if possi- 


ble get fragrances back out in 
a self service environment. 

Some chains with bullpens in 
their cosmetic departments are 
experimenting with a modified 
enclosure that would leave one 
side of the bullpen open for self 
serve merchandising. 

Chains like Peoples, Fay’s, 
and Genovese are trying to 
adopt a department store fix- 
ture, a step platform, into one 
side of their bullpen. Three 


sides of the bullpen may be 
glass, but one side is left open 
and steps are installed where 
previously there would be a 
glass wall. Open stock can be 
displayed on these steps just 
as it is displayed in depart- 
ment stores.

ing the products made by the 
company they represent. 

To help keep inventories lean 
but sufficiently full to prevent 
out-of-stocks this Christmas, 
many chains are improving 
their reordering systems. DMs 
and cosmetic supervisors are 
teaching their store cosmeti- 
cians why reordering correctly 
is so important, and how it 
should be done so stores are 
neither out-of-stock nor over- 
stocked. 

Many chains cleaned out 
their fragrance inventory in 
June so they would be pre- 
pared for a leaner Christmas. 

This year too, chains are 
watching the number of gift 
sets they buy. Some buyers 
are going to try to maintain a 
65 percent or 75 percent ratio 
of basic stock to gift sets. 

Gift sets have to be re- 
turned if they don’t sell 
through or they have to be 
marked down, and some buy- 
ers can’t afford the expense of 
doing either. 

Also some buyers complain 
that venders don’t give enough 
of an allowance to cover the cost 
of mark-downs, meaning that 
for some chains, “marking 
down a gift set isn’t worth the 
bother. If we mark it down 50 
percent to sell it through and 
venders only give us 25 percent 
or less to cover the mark down, 
we wind up losing money. It’s 
better just to send it back and 
get the credit.” 

“T think a lot of people buying 
gifts prefer to put their money 
into the larger sizes of the per- 
fumes and cologne that they 
know a woman likes rather 
than to get her a tale or a 
cream that she might not use, 
said one buyer. 


Single-stock orders 


Some chains are trying to 
find the right conservative 
balance of stock by shifting 
single stock orders from head- 
quarters down to the store. 

One buyer said this Christ- 
mas, his company is letting 
each of its stores place their 
own orders for single stock. 
“Instead of us sending in a cer- 
tain pre-set number of items 
out in September like we did 
last year, we’re going to let the 
stores order what they think 
they'll need six weeks in ad- 
vance of an ad taking place. 
This way each store can buy 
into its needs and they can buy 
in closer to the event, so we 
may be able to prevent over- 
stocking.” 

This chain is also prohibit- 
ing any distribution of basic 
stock pre-packs into its stores 
to prevent over-inventorying 
any one item, and they’re also 
being very cautious with their 
color shade promotions.

Deep discounters lock horns in D.C. 


WASHINGTON, D.C. — 
Drug Emporium Corp. has 
signed leases for six former 
Fantle’s Drug stores, while 
F&M, Rite Aid and Peoples 
reportedly show keen interest 
in some of the other leases on 
the auction block as the Fan- 
tle’s liquidation proceeds. 

Drug Emporium president 
Bob Lyons sonal that the 
deep-discount drug chain has 
secured six leases for 20,000- 
to 25,000-square-foot stores in 
Virginia and Maryland sub- 
urbs, which will bring Drug 
Emporium’s total store count 
here to 14. 

The deep discounter is 
shooting for 20-25 stores in 
this market by February 
1992. That will pit it against 
F&M, which currently oper- 
ates 12 stores here, and is seri- 
ously considering picking up 
some Fantle’s leases. 

The six-lease Drug Empori- 
um deal, with an undisclosed 
pricetag, was negotiated with 


Combined Properties, after 
U.S. Bankruptcy Court in 
Rockville, Md., approved the 
$9.4 million sale of 12 leases to 
Combined Properties Aug. 
31. Thus, the deal with Drug 
Emporium does not require 
court approval. 

Combined Properties is 
controlled by the Haft family. 
Dart Drug was founded by 
Herbert Haft in the 1950s, 
was sold to a management 
group in 1984, and was bought 
in 1987 by a group led by Shel- 
don “Bud” Fantle, who oper- 
ated the stores as Fantle’s.

NEWS IN BIRIEF 


Publix branches out of Florida 


LAKELAND, Fla. — After catering exclusively to Florid- 
ians for 60 years, supermarket dynamo Publix will expand out of 
the state, with the planned opening of two stores in Georgia. 

The first will be a 48,000-square-foot Publix Food and Phar- 
macy in Kingsland, Ga.; the second, a 65,000-square-foot store, 
which Publix terms a “new prototype” to include pharmacy, in 
Savannah. Construction hasn’t yet begun on either store. Of its 
370 supermarkets, 28 have pharmacies. Of 20 more stores now 
under construction, 13 will have pharmacies, a spokesman said. 

Publix said both stores will employ Presto! automatic teller ma- 
chines, and Presto! electronic payment systems at the checkout. 


Harris lands $70M Yankee account 


SOLON, Ohio — Harris Wholesale Co. has struck an agree- 
ment worth $70 million with Yankee Alliance, a hospital buying 
group in the Northeast. The 36-month contract will bring ar- 
ris “a significant amount of business in New England and west- 
ern New York,” said Yankee Alliance spokesman James Oliver. 


Karp adds Moore ceo duties 


NEW BRITAIN, Conn. — Mark E. Karp, president of 
Moore Medical Corp., will become ceo on Jan. 1, 1991, and con- 
tinue as chief operating officer. Jerald K. Rome will continue as 
chairman and ceo through Dec. 31. 


Court okays Nichols financing 


NEW YORK — A federal bankruptcy court has approved a 
$10 miilion financing package from Sterling National Bank & 
Trust Co. that will enable S.E. Nichols Inc. to continue operat- 
ing during its reorganization. 

ichols, which filed for bankruptcy protection Aug. 2, runs a re- 
ional chain of deep discount super drug stores, called Pharm- 
ouse, which were converted from discount department stores. 

The loan was approved Sept. 25 by Judge Howard B. Buschman 
of U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York. 


Krelitz breaks off Eagle talks 


MINNEAPOLIS — Krelitz Industries announced it has broken 
off talks with Eagle Drugs about the possible acquisition of Eagle 
by Krelitz. Krelitz is an independent drug wholesaler serving the 
upper Midwest. It also distributes genral merchandise and devel- 
ops and markets computerized management systems. 


Weliby’s 39th store bows 


SCARBOROUGH, Maine — Wellby Super Drug Stores re- 
cently opened its 39th store—the 32nd in Maine—in Kennebunk 
on Route 1. 

“This location will expand our service in the south coastal re- 
gion of Maine, closing the gap between the Wells and Biddeford 
stores,” said Wellby vp Margaret Urquhart.

expensive—for the shoplifters.

collect from pilferers caught in 
the act penalties many times 
the value of damages and sto-

managers, under these stat- 
utes, don’t have to spend 
hours in court. |

part of loss prevention pro-

SPECIAL SAMI REPORT 


Leading H&BA brands are dominant in drug stores 


PRODUCT 
TRACKING 


ALAN MILLER 


In 15 of the 57 health and 
beauty aids categories 
tracked by Arbitron/SAMI, 
the dollar share of the top 
three brands in food stores 
topped 80%, during the 52 
weeks ended July 13. 1990. In 
drug stores, the leading brand 
share level surpassed 80% in 
just five categories. 

This special report on domi- 
nance also shows higher pri- 
vate label share penetration in 
H&BA categories in drug 
stores than in food stores. For 
all H&BAs combined, private 
labels account for just under 
5% of total dollar volume in 
food stores, but 9.3% in drug 
stores. There are 19 H&BA 
categories in which the drug 
store dollar share exceeds 
10%, but only seven in food 
stores. Obviously, private la- 
bel strength in drug stores ad- 
versely affects te perfor- 
mance of the top three brands 
in many H&BA categories. 

The top three brands ac- 
counted for all sales move- 
ment in food and drug outlets 
in the low-volume proprietary 
tranquilizer category. The 
dominant brand share among 
chest rubs exceeded 90% in 
both food and drug stores. But 
in the case of deodorant and 
taleum powders, the three 
leading brands accounted for 
95.8% of food store volume— 
but was far lower in drug 
stores at 71.1%. 

In three other categories, 
the top three brand share in 
food stores is 20 or more points 
higher than their achievement 
in drug stores: sleeping aids 
(+ 29.9%), nursing supplies 
(+ 22. 2%) and pre-shave lo- 
tions (+ 21.3%). Two primary 
reasons: in general, leading 
brand dominance is higher in 
food stores, and | space 
constraints in food stores. 
Drug stores often sell a great- 
er variety of H&BAs. 

Among baby needs, the top 
three brands’ share was high- 
er in food stores than drug 
stores in three out of four cate- 
gories. Infant clothes was the 
sole category where leading 
brands had higher strength in 
food versus drug stores. This 
was also the category with a 
higher, albeit small, share 
penetration level for food 
stores vis-a-vis drug stores. 
In food stores, the highest 
share level for private labels 
among food stores was the 
15.38% share for baby oils,

90 Triple A products | 
: earn tneir laurels 


riple A products are the thoroughbreds of drug store merchandise. They 

have earned their place on Drug Store News’ 1990 Triple A product 

charts because of their track records in dollar sales and unit movement 

over the past year. 

| But whether it’s the Triple Crown or Triple A, it takes a lot more than 

quality raw material to beat the competition. Top performances in both worlds result 
from the melding of several factors, including handling and grooming, the break 
from the starting gate and the ride down the track. 

Manufacturers dominate the first two stages, developing and making the products 
and ushering them to market. Once new products leave the starting gate, however, 
retailers take the reins, jockeying for position and exploiting any openings they find 
as they race for the winner’s circle. 

Drug store retailers generally don’t see themselves as playing a major role in cre-

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 22, 1990 


Motor Oil, Antifreeze 


With profit opportunities in motor oil hard 
to come by, chains are hoping that a Massa- 
chusetts law requiring retailers to accept the 
motor oil they sell for recycling does not be- 
come a fact of life elsewhere. 

The 1974 statute mandates that retailers 
keep on site state-approved barrels for re- 
turned oil, which they can then sell to re-refin- 
ers. Discount and auto accessory outlets typi- 
cally pay hundreds of dollars per store for a 
single barrel, and anywhere from $20 to $75 a 
shot for haulers to cart it away. 

Enforcement of the law has only taken 
Ss in the last year, according to Miles 

rown, a regional planner with Massachu- 
setts Dept. of Environmental Protection. 
“The enforcement effort corresponds with in- 
creased public education activity,” Brown 
told Drug Store News. “We don’t see the law 
affecting drug, food or discount stores too 
heavily—the person recycling oil will tend to 
be an auto center customer—and other retail- 
ers will only be seeing a very small amount of 
oil returned to their stores.” 

The enforcement agenda is currently tar- 
geting larger retailers. “Unless we receive a 
complaint, we’re not going to look at small 
stores for awhile,” Brown stated. 


Recycling law gives Mass. retailers the slip 


When the enforcement plan was first an- 
nounced, CVS was the only drug chain that in- 
formed the state it was planning to get out of 
the motor oil business, Brown said. “We’ve 
not heard from any of the others, and presume 
they’re still carrying motor oil,” he added. 

At press time, CVS executives had not re- 
turned this newspaper’s calls, but according 
to Gerald Weiner, president and CEO for 41- 
store Rix Dunnington, based in Auburndale, 
Mass., “I don’t know of any drug retailer who 
carried the product in the wake of the enforce- 
ment announcement.” 

Rix Dunnington had carried motor oil as a 
convenience but since “we sold 85 percent on 
promotion” wasn’t “making any money on it 
anyway,” and decided to drop the segment in 
the wake of the state’s enforcement an- 
nouncement. 

“It wouldn’t have been very much,” in 
terms of volumes of oil to be recycled, Weiner 
admits, “but the cost of compliance was too 
great, and too difficult to implement, 
throughout the chain.” 

New York also requires retailers to accept 
motor oil they sell for recycling, although en- 
forcement of the statute is not taking place. 
Other states are considering passing such laws.

A salute to 


As the probably noticed, this issue of Inside Phar- 
macy features our annual drug wholesaler report. As I was 
reading over the , Lcouldn’t help but think back to m 
retail pe store days. Once the owner of two stores, 
have great respect for drug wholesalers. This is an indus- 
try that very quietly, but efficiently, allows our excellent 
system of dru distribution in this country to flow without 
interruption. Even the mega-chains, with their mammoth 
distribution centers, rel vily on drug wholesalers to 
get them product that either their warehouse is out of or 
just doesn’t carry. 


‘ee jee ee ee ae 5 


wholesaler’s driver. He looked at me straight in the eye 
and said: “I’m sorry, but the roads hb. , 


Most of the pharmacists I’ve met, both 
chain and independents, hold a special fond- 
ness for the drug wholesaler. And well they 
should. What other industry gives their blend 
of services, and often at bargain-basement 
prices. Unfortunatel , like anything that op- 
erates with super efficiency, they are some- 
times taken for ted, until they are gone. 

Yes, while reading over the pages in this is- 
sue on wholesalers my mind wandered. . . 


which he had a delivery was still open. While 
he was on the phone, I opened the boxes to 
check my order to make sure the medicine I 
was waiting for was there. It was. I called my 
customer and told her I would get someone to 
take it over to her. I called my other customer 
with the four-wheel drive and asked him if he 
would make a delivery. He said he would be 
right down. I wished my driver good luck on 
the trip home and he said “See you tomor- 


It was a dark and stormy night... C — ga : 
I thought back to a stormy night one Febru- C pth GA Going the extra mile 
ary. The snow started to come down early in Yes, ay thoughts continued to wander. . . 
the day. Since the storm had been forecast, HAROLD COHEN back to the early days of my retail career. I 


business was brisk in the morning. By after- 
noon, roads became treacherous, and by nighttime, they 
were nearly impassable. A customer offered us his four- 
wheel drive vehicle to make deliveries. I iously ac- 
cepted. I guess I should have closed, but earlier in the day 
I promised a customer with a very sick child at home her 
medicine. Unfortunately, it was not a common item and 
we did not stock it. None of the surrounding stores had it. 
As I usually did in tight situations like this, I called my 
wholesaler. They had it! “Could you add it to my order?” 
“Sure” came the answer back. 

That was before the snow began. I called my customer 
to let her know that my order would be delayed. She ob- 
served that it was so nasty outside, and that, for the time 
being, her child was resting comfortably. She would wait. 
If things got worse, and the medicine still didn’t arrive, she 
would have to go to the hospital. As nightfall arrived, the 
streets were deserted. The only sounds were snowplows. I 
sent my clerks home early. Since I lived close to the store, I 


vividly remember my salesman, Bernie, who 
was more like a surrogate partner. Bernie, who worked 
for Bergen Drug Co. for what seemed like a lifetime, is re- 
tired now. It was no effort for Bernie to walk into my store 
at 8:00 p.m. or 9:00 p.m. for his weekly visit to do returns 
and show me what was new. But his visit was always more 
than business. It was a friend visiting. Bernie was also al- 
ways available for a phone call at home. For that matter, 
he still is. 

There are dozens of stories I can relate to you about my 
drug wholesalers. Suffice it to say, they were always there 
when I needed them. While I don’t profess to know every 
wholesaler intimately, I have met quite a few since my re- 
tailing days. All I can say is, the two stories I’ve told exem- 
pee the - working, efficient, and sometimes taken- 
sll i wholesaling industry. Anyone who has ever 
dealt with a drug wholesaler must agree with me that 
without them, an important part of our fine drug distribu- 
tion system would cease to exist.

Pay Less breaking down pharmacy walls 


By James Frederick 

WILSONVILLE, Ore. — Ask 
Dave Widen who Pay Less Drug 
Stores competes against, and he has a 
ready answer: everyone. 

“All the lines between different re- 
tailers are getting blurred,” said Wid- 
en, a veteran pharmacist who serves 
as vp-pharmacy operations at the 307- 
store drug chain. “Look at the mem- 
bership of NACDS, for instance. It’s 
not just a drug store organization any- 
more.” 

The blurring of those lines between 
drug, food and general merchandise 
retailers—with all of them now fight- 
ing for much of the same business—has 
been a big factor behind Pay Less’ re- 
cent efforts to renew its emphasis on 
pharmacy as the basis of its business. 
Another spur to those efforts has been 
the enormous growth anticipated for 
sales of pharmaceuticals as the popula- 
tion ages and health care plans turn 
more and more to expensive new drug 
therapies. 

“There are more older people, and 
more drugs being developed,” Widen 
noted. 

Both to distinguish itself from its 
mass-market competitors, and to posi- 
tion itself for the growth of the pre- 
scription drug component of the health 
care dollar, Pay Less is pushing hard 
to strengthen its pharmacy practice. 
“We’ve come back to pharmacy as a 
core department in our stores,” said 
Widen. “We’re a drug store first, with 
pharmacy at the forefront of our busi- 
ness.” 


Along those lines, the chain is mar- 
keting its pharmacy and core drug 
store departments more aggressively 
than it has for at least a decade. Among 
its newer marketing strategies are a 
gradual buildup in advertising for the 
pharmacy and H&BA side of the busi- 
ness, a new store prototype that gives 
the pharmacy prominent positioning 
as an anchor department at a front cor- 
ner of the store, and an enlarged phar- 
macy management team with the addi- 
tion of Gordon Barker as vp-pharmacy 
sales, a new position. 

Barker’s appointment reflects “the 
greater amines were placing on 
pharmacy and the core departments,” 
said Tim McAlear, executive vp and 
chief operations officer. “The volume 
was such that we needed someone to 
assist Dave by working with the store 
people and concentrating on sales and 
operations.” 

Barker, a Pay Less veteran who last 
served as general manager of store op- 
erations, will report directly to Widen. 
One of his biggest challenges, said 
Widen, will be to help integrate the 

harmacy with Pay Less’ traditionally 
road mix of store departments. 

“We’re trying to break down the 
walls between pharmacy and the rest 
of the store, to make the pharmacy a 
key part of the overall store,” said 
Widen. “The challenge is to emphasize 
pharmacies without eroding appeal of 
mass merchandise in our stores.” 

For Pay Less, that is no small task. 
Its stores range to well over 30,000 
square feet—the biggest in chain drug 


retailing on average—and they bristle 
with a huge array of general merchan- 
dise categories, from fishing gear to 
hardware. Most stores also include 
outdoor garden centers, large-scale 
domestics and notions departments, 
and even a sizeable sportswear and lei- 
surewear department. 

Successfully meshing this kind of as- 
sortment with a rejuvenated, reposi- 
tioned pharmacy has required a new 
store design, a new approach to the 
company’s image advertising, and a 
more comprehensive, strategic ap- 
proach to marketing and merchandis- 
ing at headquarters. The chain must 
strike a fine balance between the 
health and beauty care side of the busi- 
ness and the broad-based, one-stop ap- 
peal of its huge stores. 


Clarification 


Please note that the Par Phar- 
maceutical spread that appeared 
in the Sept. 24 issue of Drug 
Store News/Inside Pharmacy 
was in fact a paid advertise- 
ment. Its contents reflected the 
views of its sponsor and not 
those of Store News. We 

t that the usual “advertis-

have appeared on the top right

GIYBURIDERHOECHST: ROUSSEL 
FOR EFFECTIVE CONTROL OF TYPE Ii DIABETES 


Brief Summary 

DIABETA® (glyburide) Tablets 

CONTRAINDICATIONS: DIABETA® is contraindicated in patients with: 1. Known hypersensitivity to the 
drug. 2. Diabetic ketoacidosis, with or without coma. This condition should be treated with insulin 
SPECIAL WARNING ON INCREASED RISK OF CARDIOVASCULAR MORTALITY: The administration of 
oral hypoglycemic drugs has been reported to be associated with increased cardiovascular morta!- 
ity as compared to treatment with diet alone or diet plus insulin. This warning is based on the study 
conducted by the University Group Diabetes Program (UGDP), a long-term prospective clinical trial 
designed to evaluate the effectiveness of glucose-iowering drugs in preventing or delaying vascular 
complications in patients with noninsulin-dependent diabetes. The study involved 823 patients who 
were randomly assigned to one of four treatment groups (Diabetes 19(Suppi 2):747-830, 1970). 


UGDP reported that patients treated ior five to eight years with diet plus a fixed dose of tolbutamide 
(1.5 grams per day) had a rate of cardiovascular mortality approximately 2/2 times that of patients 
treated with diet alone. A significant increase in total mortality was not observed, but the use of 
tolbutamide was discontinued based on the increase in cardiovascular mortality, thus limiting the 
opportunity for the study to show an increase in overall mortality. Despite controversy regarding the 
interpretation of these results, the findings of the UGDP study provide an adequate basis for this 
warning. The patient should be informed of the potential risks and advantages of DIABETA™ and of 
alternative modes of therapy. 


Although only one drug in the sulfonylurea class (tolbutamide) was included in this study, it is 
prudent from a safety standpoint to consider that this warning may apply to other oral hypoglycemic 
drugs in this class, in view of their close similarities in mode of action and chemical structure 


PRECAUTIONS: General — Hypoglycemia: All sulfonylureas are capable of producing severe hypogly- 
cemia. Proper patient selection and dosage and instructions are important to avoid hypoglycemic 
episodes. Renal or hepatic insufficiency may increase the risk of serious hypoglycemic reactions 

Elderly, debilitated, or malnourished patients, and those with adrenal or pituitary insufficiency. are 
particularly susceptible to the hypoglycemic action of giucose-lowering drugs. Hypoglycemia may be 
difficult to recognize in the elderly and in people who are taking beta-adrenergic blocking drugs 

Hypoglycemia is more likely to occur when caloric intake is deficient, after severe or prolonged exercise 

when alcohol is ingested, or when more than one glucose-lowering drug 's used. Loss of Contro/ of 
Blood Glucose: \n diabetic patients exposed to stress such as fever, trauma, infection, or surgery, aloss 
of control may occur. It may then be necessary to discontinue DIABETA* and administer insulin 

Information for Patients: Patients should be informed of the potential risks and advantages of 
DIABETA® and of alternative modes of therapy. They also should be informed about the importance of 
adherence to dietary instructions, of a regular exercise program, and of reguiar testing of urine and or 
blood glucose. The risks of hypoglycemia, its symptoms and treatment, and conditions that predispose 
to its development should be explained to patients and responsible family members. Primary and 
secondary failure should also be explained. Laboratory Tests: Response to DIABETA® Tablets shoulJ 
be monitored by frequent urine glucose tests and periodic blood glucose tests. Measurement of 
glycosylated hemoglobin levels may be helpful in some patients. Drug Interactions: The hypoglycemic 
action of sulfonylureas may be potentiated by certain drugs including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory 
agents and other drugs that are highly protein bound — salicylates, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol, 
probenecid, coumarins, monoamine oxidase inhibitors, and beta-adrenergic blocking agents. Certain 
drugs tend to produce hyperglycemia and may lead to loss of control. These drugs include the thiazides 
and other diuretics, corticosteroids, phenothiazines, thyroid products, estrogens, ora! contraceptives, 
phenytoin, nicotinic acid, sympathomimetics, calcium channel blocking drugs, and isoniazid. A 
potential interaction between oral miconazole and oral hypoglycemic agents leading to severe hypogly- 
cemia has been reported. Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, and impairment of Fertility: Studies in rats 
at doses up to 300 mg/kg/d for 18 months showed no carcinogenic effects. Glyburide is nonmutagenic 
when studied in Salmonelia microsome test (Ames test) and in the DNA damage/alkaline elution assay 

Pregnancy: Jeratogenic Effects: Pregnancy Category B. Reproduction studies in rats and rabbits have 
revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus due to glyburide. There are no adequate 
and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. This drug should be used during pregnancy only if 
clearly needed. Insulin should be used during pregnancy to maintain blood glucose as close to normal 
as possible. Nonteratogenic Effects: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia (4 to 10 days) has been reported 
in neonates born to mothers who were receiving a sulfonylurea drug at the time of delivery. DIABETA" 
should be discontinued at least two weeks before the expected delivery date. Nursing Mothers: Some 
sulfonylurea drugs are known to be excreted in human milk. If DIABETA® is discontinued and if diet 
alone is inadequate for controlling blood glucose, insulin therapy should be considered. Pediatric Use: 
Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established 


ADVERSE REACTIONS: Hypoglycemia: See Precautions and Overdosage sections. Gastrointestinal 
Reactions: Cholestatic jaundice and hepatitis may occur rarely; DIABETA® Tablets should be discontin- 
ued if this occurs. Gastrointestinal disturbances, eg, nausea, epigastric fullness, and heartburn, are the 
most common reactions, having occurred in 1.8% of treated patients during clinical trials. They tend to 
be dose-related and may disappear when dosage is reduced. Liver function abnormalities, including 
isolated transaminase elevations, have been reported. Dermatologic Reactions: Allergic skin reac- 
tins, eg, pruritis, erythema, urticaria, and morbilliform or maculopapular eruptions, occur in 1 5% of 
treated patients. These may be transient and may disappear despite continued use of DIABETA®: if skin 
reactions persist, the drug should be discontinued. Porphyria cutanea tarda and photosensitivity 
reactions have been reported with sulfonylureas. Hematologic Reactions: Leukopenia, agranulocy- 
tosis, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, and pancytopenia have been reported 
with sulfonylureas. Metabolic Reactions: Hepatic porphyria and disulfiram-like reactions have been 
reported with sulfonylureas: however, hepatic porphyria has not been reported with DIABETA® and 
disulfiram-like reactions have been reported very rarely. Cases of hyponatremia have been reported 
with glyburide and all other sulfonylureas, most often in patients who are on other medications or have 
medical conditions known to cause hyponatremia or increase release of antidiuretic hormone. The 
syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion has been reported with certain other 
sulfonylureas, and it has been suggested that these sulfonylureas may augment the peripheral (anti- 
diuretic) action of ADH and/or increase release of ADH 


OVERDOSAGE: Overdosage of su!fonylureas, including DIABETA® Tablets, can produce hypoglycemia 

if hypoglycemic coma is diagnosed or suspected, the patient should be given a rapid intravenous 
injection of concentrated (50%) glucose solution. This should be followed by a continuous infusion of 
a more dilute (10%) glucose solution at a rate which will maintain the blood glucose at a level above 
100 mg/dL. Patients should be closely monitored for a minimum cf 24 to 48 hours, since hypoglycemia 
may recur after apparent clinical recovery Q69235-1288

DREF grants make a difference 


Diabetics in Kentucky have Condit Steil to thank for making the pharmacy a more understanding and 
informative place. In 1987, he put together an extensive educational program designed to teach pharma 
cists about diabetes, the needs of diabetic patients, and most important, how to improve patient adherence 


to a diabetes care regimen. 


Funds for Condit Steil’s work, as well as for other creative research 
and education initiatives in diabetes, are provided by the Diabetes 
Research and Education Foundation. Since its creation in 1984, the 
Foundation has disbursed over $4.3 million to fund 255 projects 
Foundation funds are derived solely from a percentage of revenues

BRIEF SUMMARY 


INDICATIONS AND USAGE 


Endometriosis. Danazo! is indicated for the treatment of 
endometriosis amenable to hormonal managemgnt 


Fibrocystic Breast Disease Most cases of symptomatic 
fibrocystic breast disease may be treated by simple measures 
(eg padced brassieres and anaigesics) 

In infrequent patients, symptoms of pain and tenderness may be 
severe enough to warrant treatment by suppression of ovarian 
function. Danazol is usually effective in decreasing nodularity 
pain, and tenderness. It should be stressed to the patient that 
this treatment is not innocuous in that it involves considerable 
alterations of hormone levels and that recurrence of symptoms 
iS very common after cessation of therapy 

Hereditary Angioedema. Danazo! !s indicated for the prevention 
of attacks of angioedema of all types (cutaneous, abdominal 
laryngeal) in males and females 


CONTRAINDICATIONS 
Danazo! should not be administered to patients with 
1. Undiagnosed abnormal genita! bleeding 
2. Markedly impaired hepatic, renal, or cardiac function 
3. Pregnancy 
4 Breast feeding 
WARNINGS 


Safe use of the drug in pregnancy has not be established 
Clinically. Therefore, a nonhormonal method of contraception 
should be recommended. If a patient becomes pregnant 
during treatment, administration of the drug should be 
discontinued. Continuing treatment may result in an 
androgenic efiect on the fetus, which to date has been limited 
to clitoral hypertrophy and lJabial fusion of the external 
genitalia in the female fetus. !f the patient becomes pregnant 
while taking danazol, she should be apprised of the petential 
risk to the fetus 

Before initiating therapy of fibrocystic breast disease with 
danazoi, carcinoma of the breast should be excluded However MEAN SERUM DANAZOL CONCENTRATIONS 

nodularity, pain, tenderness due to fibrocystic breast disease BY FORMULATION 

May prevent recognition of underlying carcinoma before AMERICAN THERAPEUTICS 
treatment is begun Therefore, if any nodule persists or 

enlarges during treatment, carcinoma should be considered ) vnvirener 

and ruled out 

Long-term experience with danazol is limited. Long-term therap, 
with other steroids alkylated at the 17 position has beer 
associated with serious toxicity (cholestatic jaundice, peliosis 
hepatis). The physician therefore should be alert to the 
possibility that similar toxicity may develop after long-tern 
therapy with danazol. Attempts should be made to determine the 
lowest dose that will orovide ade. protection. if the drug 
was begun at a time of exacerbation of angioneurotic edema due 
to trauma, stress or other cause, periodic attempts to decrease 
or withdraw therapy should be considered 

Patients should be watched closely for signs of virilization 

Some androgenic effects may not be reversible even when drug 
administration is stopped 

PRECAUTIONS 

Because danazol may cause some degree of fluid retention 
conditions that might be iifluenced by this factor, such as 
epilepsy, migraine, or cardiac or renal dysfunction, require 
Careful observation 

Since hepatic dysfunction has been reported in patients treated 
with danazoi, periodic liver function tests should be performed
